

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Asafoetida
======================================================================

{{Short description|Indian spice derived from Ferula roots}}
{{Use British English|date=July 2019}}
'''Asafoetida''' ([[Help:IPA/English|/æsəˈfɛtɪdə/]]; also spelled '''asafetida''') is the dried [[latex]] ([[Natural gum|gum]] [[oleoresin]]) exuded from the [[rhizome]] or [[tap root]] of several species of ''[[Ferula]]'', [[perennial]] [[herb]]s of the [[carrot family]]. It is produced in [[Iran]], [[Afghanistan]], [[India]], [[Central Asia]] and [[Northwest China|north-western China]] ([[Xinjiang]]). Different regions have different botanical sources.

Like other related resins, including [[galbanum]] and [[sagapenum]], asafoetida was known in [[Classical antiquity|Greco-Roman antiquity]]. Its historical use partly overlaps with that of the now-extinct [[Silphium (antiquity)|silphium]], a plant highly valued in the ancient Mediterranean world for its reputed [[medicinal plant|medicinal]] and [[gastronomy|culinary]] properties. Asafoetida is frequently mentioned in [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic]] texts, later in [[Arabic medicine|Arabo-Persian medical treatises]], in {{Interlanguage link|medieval herbals|fr|Herbier médiéval}}, in the literature of [[traditional Chinese medicine]], and in the [[pharmacopoeia]]s of the [[early modern period]].

The [[taxonomy]] of plants producing asafoetida is complex and has been subject to differing interpretations. The resin is most commonly associated with ''[[Ferula assa-foetida]]'' and ''[[Ferula foetida]]'', which were long treated as [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]]. ''[[Ferula narthex]]'' is also frequently cited as a source. Additional ''Ferula'' species are mentioned in the specialised literature, although they appear to be of lesser economic importance and may differ substantially in their [[phytochemistry|phytochemical]] composition. In many languages, the same term is used to refer both to the resin and to the plants from which it is derived.

In traditional medical systems, including Ayurveda, [[Unani medicine|Unani]] medicine, and Western [[phytotherapy]], asafoetida has been used for a variety of purposes, particularly in relation to the [[gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal]] and [[respiratory system|respiratory]] systems. The resin has been investigated in [[pharmacology|pharmacological]] research, and a range of biological activities has been reported. Its chemical composition includes compounds such as [[ferulic acid]], [[coumarin|sesquiterpene coumarins]], and [[organosulfur compound]]s, which are known to exhibit biological activity.

As a culinary ingredient, asafoetida is primarily used in Indian and Middle Eastern cuisines, where it is employed to complement or substitute for [[Allium|alliaceous]] ingredients such as [[garlic]] and [[onion]]. Its use in the [[Western world|West]] has historically been limited, largely because of its odour, although it is included in certain products such as [[Worcestershire sauce]]. Beyond food, asafoetida has also been used in [[perfumery]], mainly as a [[fixative (perfumery)|fixative]], and in some agricultural contexts as a {{Interlanguage link|plant protection product|fr|Produit phytosanitaire}}, including applications as a natural [[pesticide]].

Historically, [[Afghanistan]] and [[Iran]] have been the principal producers of asafoetida, exporting most of their production to [[India]] in raw form. In India, the resin is processed and packaged and is partly re-exported, sometimes in blended forms, to other markets. Since 2020, efforts have been undertaken in India to establish domestic cultivation, notably in [[Himachal Pradesh]], in response to increasing internal demand.

== Characteristics ==
=== Description ===
[[File:Asafoetida culture in South Khorasan 18.jpg|thumb|upright|Piece of gum-resin of Iranian origin, drying.|alt=Very irregularly shaped piece, amber-colored, with whitish areas on the upper surface that are still moist and glossy.]]
Asafoetida is an oleo-gum-resin obtained primarily from the [[taproot]], and occasionally from the [[rhizome]] and the [[Plant stem|stem]], of several species of the genus ''Ferula'', notably ''[[Ferula assa-foetida]]'', ''[[Ferula foetida]]'', and ''[[Ferula narthex]]''.<ref name="ISO676">{{cite book |author=International Organization for Standardization (ISO) |url=https://www.iso.org/fr/standard/4844.html |title=Norme internationale 676: Épices — Nomenclature botanique |date=December 15, 1995 |edition=2nd |pages=21 |language=French |trans-title=International Standard 676: Spices — Botanical nomenclature |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> It is found in irregularly shaped pieces of varying size. Externally, the resin is yellowish to brownish pink. The fractured surface is [[conchoidal fracture|conchoidal]], whitish or milky white, translucent, and [[nacreous]], with a [[wax]]y lustre. When exposed to light and air, a freshly fractured surface may develop a violet-red or peach-blossom red colouration within a few hours; this colouration gradually fades over days or weeks, turning yellowish brown or pinkish. Asafoetida is fusible and flammable, burning in air with a white flame and producing abundant smoke. It has an acrid, bitter taste and a strong, [[alliaceous]] odour.<ref name="Pereira1840">{{cite book |last=Pereira |first=Jonathan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DOtN2FjdRP0C |title=The Elements of Materia Medica |date=1840 |publisher=Longman, Orme, Brown, Green, and Longmans |volume=2 |location=London |pages=1043–1044 |language=English |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> The odour is primarily attributed to the presence of [[organosulfur compound]]s.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=217}}

Asafoetida is commercially available in three main forms. The form known as "tears" is considered the purest and consists of round or flattened grains measuring approximately 5 to 30&nbsp;mm in diameter, typically grey or dull yellow in colour. The mass form is more common and consists of agglomerated tears, often mixed with fragments of root and soil.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=217}} The paste form is soft and sticky and likewise contains varying amounts of foreign material.{{sfn|George|2012|p=158}}

=== Commercial varieties ===
[[File:Heing.JPG|thumb|upright|left|Mass asafoetida in Pakistan.|alt=Ball of resin with a waxy appearance and dark reddish-brown color.]]
In the Indian market, asafoetida is sold in several forms that are subject to distinct classifications, with prices generally reflecting differences in purity and [[organoleptic]] characteristics.

A primary distinction is made between ''Hing'' and ''Hingra''. ''Hing'' is generally regarded as the higher-grade product and is more aromatic. It is typically pale in colour and soluble in water. ''Hingra'' is darker in appearance and dissolves in oil.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}} ''Hing'' is commonly associated with ''F. assa-foetida'' and ''F. alliacea'', while ''Hingra'' is mainly derived from ''[[Ferula foetida|F. foetida]]'', and to a lesser extent from ''F. assa-foetida'' and ''F. narthex''.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=701}}

''Hing'' is further divided into categories based on geographic origin and physical characteristics. Resins originating from Iran are known as ''Irani Hing'' (formerly ''Abushaharee Hing''), reflecting their historical shipment through the port of [[Bushehr]] on the [[Persian Gulf]].<ref name="Dymock1876">{{cite journal |last=Dymock |first=M. W. |date=1876 |title=L'asa-fœtida sur le marché de Bombay |trans-title=Asafoetida on the Bombay market |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UCgFAAAAQAAJ |journal=Journal de pharmacie et de chimie |language=French |pages=149–151 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> These resins are typically dry and may contain woody residues. A milder variety, brown in colour, is obtained from a horizontal incision in the stem and may include stem fragments. A more bitter and often translucent variety is produced by incising the root.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}} Resins from Afghanistan are referred to as ''Pathani Hing'' or, less commonly, ''Kandaharee Hing'', after the province of [[Kandahar Province|Kandahar]]. These products are generally agglomerated and moist, with a stronger and more bitter taste and odour. Several commercial types are recognised, including ''Naya Chal'', ''Naya Zamin'', ''Charas'', ''Galmin'', ''Khawlal'', ''Kabuli'', ''Shabandi'', and ''Hadda'',<ref name="Sood-2020">{{cite journal |last=Sood |first=Ruchi |date=2020-12-09 |title=Asafoetida (''Ferula asafoetida''): A high-value crop suitable for the cold desert of Himachal Pradesh, India |url=https://journals.ansfoundation.org/index.php/jans/article/view/2418 |journal=Journal of Applied and Natural Science |language=en |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=607–617 |doi=10.31018/jans.v12i4.2418 |issn=2231-5209}}</ref> of which ''Hadda'' is described as particularly pungent and is typically sold at a higher price.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}} The product known as ''Bandhani Hing'' is not a distinct variety but a [[#Processing and derived products|composite product]] prepared to facilitate culinary use.{{sfn|Small|2011}}

''Hingra'', which is less commonly used in India, has historically been associated with lower-cost markets and export trade.<ref name="Dymock1876" /> It may originate from Iran or Afghanistan and is generally the form most often encountered in [[Europe]]. In commercial terminology, distinctions are sometimes made between '''asa foetida electa in granis''' (or ''in lacrimis'', in tears), ''in massis'' (or ''amygdaloides'', in mass), and ''asa foetida petraea'' (in stones).{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=701}} The last category, which is uncommon, consists of irregular, angular pieces resembling [[Dolomite (mineral)|dolomite]] and may represent an [[adulteration|adulterated]] product with a high [[gypsum]] content.<ref name="Pereira1840" />

=== Related products ===
[[File:Galbanum2.JPG|thumb|upright|Galbanum extracted from ''Ferula gummosa''.|alt=A bottle labeled "Galbanum – Ferula galbaniflua" containing a dark brown sticky mass.]]
The gum-resins produced by species of the genus ''Ferula'' have been known since [[Ancient history|antiquity]] and were frequently confused with one another in historical sources. Despite similarities in appearance and traditional use, these substances are obtained through different extraction methods and show notable differences in their [[phytochemistry|phytochemical]] composition. Some of these gum-resins have occasionally been marketed under the name '''asafoetida'''.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}}

Galbanum typically occurs as irregular, almost translucent "tears", which may agglutinate into a yellow-brown mass that becomes soft and sticky at body temperature.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}} ''[[Ferula gummosa]]'' (syn. ''Ferula galbaniflua'') is generally regarded as its principal source, although the resin is also obtained from ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula rubricaulis|fr}}'', ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula kokanica|fr}}'', and ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula varia|fr}}''. The resin exudes naturally at the base of the stem and from the [[leaf sheath]]s, and incisions are often unnecessary. Galbanum has a strong, distinctive odour, sometimes described as heavy or cloying.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=705}} Although it was recommended for medicinal use by authors such as [[Hippocrates]] and [[Pliny the Elder]], galbanum is now used mainly in perfumery.{{sfn|Gayet|2010}}

[[Sagapenum]] is a gum-resin with an odour similar to that of asafoetida. It is red or yellow externally and white internally. Also known as "seraphic gum", it is obtained by making grooves in the stem near the leaves.{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}} Sagapenum is produced primarily from ''[[Ferula persica]]'' and ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula szowitziana|fr}}''.{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=64}}

[[Ammoniacum|Ammoniacum gum]] continues to be used in traditional medicine, although its properties are not well documented,{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=532}} as well as in perfumery and in [[Illuminated manuscript|illumination]], where it serves as an adhesive for [[gold leaf]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Niederhauser |first=Marc |title=Alchimie de l'enluminure |date=2011 |publisher=Eyrolles |isbn=978-2212414080 |pages=56 |language=French |trans-title=Alchemy of Illumination}}</ref> It is most commonly associated with ''[[Dorema ammoniacum]]'', a species reassigned in 2015 to the genus ''Ferula'' on the basis of phylogenetic evidence.<ref name="Kraichak-2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Kraichak |first1=Ekaphan |last2=Huang |first2=Jen-Pan |last3=Nelsen |first3=Matthew |last4=Leavitt |first4=Steven D |last5=Lumbsch |first5=H Thorsten |date=2018-09-06 |title=A revised classification of orders and families in the two major subclasses of Lecanoromycetes (Ascomycota) based on a temporal approach |url=https://academic.oup.com/botlinnean/advance-article/doi/10.1093/botlinnean/boy060/5091569 |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |language=en |doi=10.1093/botlinnean/boy060 |issn=0024-4074}}</ref> The term ammoniacum gum is also applied to resins obtained from ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula orientalis|fr|Ferula orientalis}}'', ''[[Ferula tingitana]]'' (Moroccan ammoniacum gum), and ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula marmarica|fr}}'' (Cyrenaican ammoniacum gum).{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=64}}

[[Muskroot|Sumbul]], or "musk root", refers to the root of ''[[Ferula moschata]]'' (syn. ''Ferula sumbul'') or ''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula diversivittata|fr}}'' (syn. ''Ferula suaveolens'').{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=64}} It is marketed as spongy slices that appear marbled white and brownish grey in cross-section.{{sfn|Gayet|2010}} The associated resin, known as "sumbul resin", exudes from stems and roots through natural fissures caused by temperature variation or by damage from animals or insects.{{sfn|George|2012|p=155}}

== Names ==
In most languages, the names given to the resin also apply to the plants that produce it.

=== Spelling and etymology ===
[[File:Description of a plant yielding asa fœtida (1).jpg|thumb|left|alt=Drawing of a central umbel and two lateral umbels, with details of flowers and fruits|''Description of a plant yielding asa fœtida'', letter from [[John Hope (botanist)|John Hope]] to [[Joseph Banks]] in 1784.<ref name="Hope1785">{{cite journal |last=Hope |first=John |date=December 31, 1785 |title=Description of a plant yielding asa fœtida: In a letter from John Hope, M.D. F.R.S. to Sir Joseph Banks, Bart. P.R.S |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstl.1785.0005 |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |language=English |volume=75 |pages=36–39 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1785.0005 |issn=0261-0523 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>]]

The term "asafoetida" (French: ''ase fétide'', very rarely ''asse fétide'') entered English, [[French language|French]], and [[Occitan language|Occitan]] through borrowing from [[Medieval Latin]] ''{{lang|la|asa fœtida}}''. This designation remains in use in scholarly contexts in several European languages.<ref name="FEW">{{cite book |last=Wartburg |first=Walther von |url=https://apps.atilf.fr/lecteurFEW/index.php/page/lire/e/18775 |title=Französisches Etymologisches Wörterbuch |year=1928 |volume=XXV |pages=402–403 |language=German |trans-title=Etymological Dictionary of French |chapter=asa |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> The word has given rise to numerous orthographic and typographic variants, including "''asa-fœtida''",<ref name="ISO676" /> "''asa fétida''",<ref>{{cite book |last=Bouant |first=Émile |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qrntTBZqyAAC |title=Nouveau dictionnaire de chimie |date=1889 |publisher=J.-B. Baillière et fils |location=Paris |pages=114 |language=French |trans-title=New Dictionary of Chemistry |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> "''assa fœtida''",<ref>{{cite book |last=Stokvis |first=Barend Josef |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R9xs63ejx-kC |title=Lecons de pharmacotherapie |date=1905 |publisher=Octave Doin |volume=3 |pages=536 |language=French |trans-title=Lessons in Pharmacotherapy |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> "''assa fetida''",<ref>{{cite book |last=Teyssou |first=Roger |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uAxvuSV8ylwC |title=Quatre siècles de thérapeutique médicale : du XVIe au XIXe siècle en Europe |date=2007 |publisher=L'Harmattan |isbn=978-2-296-03827-1 |pages=20 |language=French |trans-title=Four Centuries of Medical Therapeutics: 16th to 19th centuries in Europe |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> and "''asafœtida''",<ref>{{cite book |last=Toussaint |first=Murielle |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MBiGDwAAQBAJ |title=D'ici ou d'ailleurs, les épices qui guérissent |date=2019 |publisher=Leduc.s |isbn=9791028514013 |language=French |trans-title=From Here or Elsewhere, the Spices That Heal |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> among others. The origin of the term has long been debated, and no single etymology has been universally accepted.<ref name="Miller1875">{{cite journal |last=Miller |first=Adolph W. |date=February 1875 |title=Orthography of Asafœtida |trans-title=Orthography of Asafœtida |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n4tLAAAAMAAJ |journal=American Journal of Pharmacy |language=English |volume=47 |pages=49–53 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

The element "fetid" (from {{lang|la|foetidus}}) refers to the resin’s odour and served to distinguish it from the "sweet asa" described by [[Arabic medicine|medieval Arab physicians]]. The epithet has been attested since the 14th century. In Old and Middle French, it was later replaced in common usage by the synonym "puant" ("stinking"). The terms "asafoetida" and "fetid asa" have consistently retained a learned or technical connotation, whereas popular usage favoured more colloquial names such as "devil's dung".<ref name="FEW" />

The earliest known occurrence in Latin of ''{{lang|la|asa}}'' is generally traced to the translations of [[Dioscorides]] produced by [[Constantine the African]] in the 11th century. The most widely cited hypothesis connects this term, along with its variants ''{{lang|la|assa}}'' and ''{{lang|la|asca}}'', to the [[silphium]] of antiquity.<ref name="MLW">{{cite book |author=Bayerische Akademie der Wissenschaften |url=https://www.mlw.badw.de/mlw-digital/mlw-open-access.html |title=Mittellateinisches Wörterbuch bis zum ausgehenden 13. Jahrhundert |publisher=Beck |year=1967 |isbn=978-3-406-68394-7 |volume=1 |location=Munich |pages=1012 |language=German |trans-title=Medieval Latin Dictionary up to the End of the 13th Century |chapter=asa |oclc=4005657 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> This plant was known to the [[Ancient Greece|Greeks]] as {{lang|grc|σίλφιον}} (''silphion''), a word whose own etymology is uncertain. It entered Latin as ''{{lang|la|sirpe}}'', and its sap was referred to as ''{{lang|la|lac sirpicium}}'' ("milk of silphium"), later shortened to ''{{lang|la|laserpicium}}'' or ''{{lang|la|laserpitium}}''.<ref name="Déniau-1868">{{cite book |last=Déniau |first=P. C. Félix |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WuJZAAAAcAAJ |title=Le Silphium (Asa fœtida) |year=1868 |language=fr |trans-title=Silphium (Asa foetida)}}</ref> These forms subsequently developed into ''{{lang|la|laser-picium}}'' through reinterpretation involving ''{{lang|la|pix}}'' (pitch). Once established as an independent term, ''{{lang|la|laser}}'' or ''{{lang|la|lasar}}'' is thought to have evolved into ''{{lang|la|asar}}'' by deglutination, and finally into ''{{lang|la|asa}}'' through regular morphological adaptation.<ref name="FEW" />

An alternative explanation derives ''{{lang|la|asa}}'' from the [[Persian language|Persian]] term ''{{lang|fa|azā}}'', meaning [[mastic (resin)|mastic]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Kurath |first=Hans |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q99NkQ1WitgC |title=Middle English Dictionary |date=1957 |publisher=University of Michigan Press |volume=3 |location=Ann Arbor |pages=415 |language=English |trans-title=Middle English Dictionary |chapter=asa-fetida |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> In Persian, however, this word refers specifically to the resin of the [[Pistacia lentiscus|mastic tree]], and the names used for asafoetida and its source plants differ.{{refn|name=FEW}} Another proposal links the term to Persian ''{{lang|fa|asā}}'', meaning "stick" or "club", a meaning that parallels the Latin ''ferula'' and may allude to the tall stature of the plant or the use of its dried stem as a staff or cudgel.<ref name="Miller1875" /> Other authors have suggested a [[Semitic languages|Semitic]] origin, deriving the word from roots meaning "to heal". In this interpretation, the Arabic ''{{lang|ar|asâ}}'' and Hebrew ''{{lang|he|asah}}'' would render asafoetida as a "fetid remedy".{{sfn|Vigier|1869|p=28}} An [[Ancient Greek]] derivation from {{lang|grc|ἄση}} (''asē''), meaning "disgust" or "nausea", has also been proposed, in reference to the substance’s [[emetic]] properties.<ref name="FEW" /> Finally, a [[Sumerian language|Sumerian]] origin has been suggested by [[Reginald Campbell Thompson]], who, in ''The Assyrian Herbal'', identified the term ''{{lang|sux|aš}}'' in texts dating to the 7th century BCE as a possible early designation of asafoetida.<ref name="Thompson">{{cite book |last=Thompson |first=Reginald Campbell |url=https://wellcomecollection.org/works/bprusxfh |title=The Assyrian herbal |date=1924 |publisher=Luzac and Co. |location=London |pages=17 |language=English |trans-title=The Assyrian Herbal |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> In this view, the term would have been transmitted into later languages through Greek and Arabic, as occurred with the names of several other plants.

=== Other languages ===
[[File:Description of a plant yielding asa fœtida (2).jpg|thumb|alt=Drawing of a finely divided leaf|Letter of John Hope: plant native to [[Gilan Province|Gilan]] in Persia, and successfully cultivated in [[Edinburgh]].<ref name="Hope1785"/>]]

In the [[Languages of Europe|European languages]], the resin is designated either by forms derived from its Latin name or by direct translations of it. In [[English language|English]], these include ''asafœtida'', ''stinking gum''{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}} and ''stinking assa'';<ref name="Déniau-1868" /> in [[German language|German]], ''Asafötida'', ''Asant'', or ''Stinkasant'';{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}} and in [[Italian language|Italian]], [[Spanish language|Spanish]], and [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]], ''assafétida'' and related orthographic variants.{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}}{{sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} In [[Russian language|Russian]], the term is {{Lang|ru|аса́фети́да}} (''asafetida'').{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}} In several [[Germanic languages]], names equivalent to the French expression "devil's dung" (''merde du diable'') are also used, such as English ''devil's dung'',{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}} German ''Teufelsdreck'',{{sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} Dutch ''duivelsdrek'', Swedish ''dyvelsträck'', Danish ''dyvelsdræk'', and Norwegian ''dyvelsdrekk''.

In [[Persian language|Persian]], the resin is designated by terms derived from Middle Persian (Pahlavi) ''{{Lang|pal|*anguzad}}'', with classical forms including {{Lang|fa|انگوزه}} [angūza], {{Lang|fa|انگژد}} [angužad], {{Lang|fa|انگیان}} [anguyān], and {{Lang|fa|انگدان}} [angudān].{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=361}} These forms are derived from the Proto-Indo-Iranian root ''*anga-'' ("bent, curved"), extended by semantic development to "branch", combined with the Proto-Iranian element ''*ǰátu'' ("gum, resin"). In Modern Persian, the substance is commonly known as {{Lang|fa|آنقوزه}} [ānqūzeh] or {{Lang|fa|آنغوزه}} [ânğuze], and is also referred to as {{Lang|fa|کما}} [koma] or {{Lang|fa|خوراکما}} [khorakma].

These Iranian terms were subsequently borrowed into several other languages, including Classical [[Arabic language|Arabic]] {{Lang|ar|أنجدان}} [ʾanjudān],{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=361}} Classical [[Armenian language|Armenian]] {{Lang|xcl|անգուժատ}} [angužat],{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=361}} and [[Middle Chinese]] {{Lang|lzh|阿魏}} [āwèi].

The [[Sanskrit]] term {{Lang|sa|हिङ्गु}} [hiṅgú] may share this Iranian origin, although the direction of borrowing has also been debated.{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=361}} It is the source of the terms used in most of the [[languages of India]], including [[Hindi]] {{Lang|hi|हींग}} [hīṅg] and [[Urdu]] {{Lang|ur|ہینگ}} [hīng]. The term was also borrowed into Chinese as {{Lang|lzh|形虞}} [xíngyú].{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=361}}

In the [[Semitic languages]], a distinct set of terms was used to designate both the plant and its resin. These include Mishnaic [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]] {{Lang|hbo|חלתית}} [ḥiltīt] or {{Lang|hbo|חילתית}} [ḥīltīt], [[Aramaic language|Aramaic]] {{Lang|arc|חלתיתא}} [ḥiltīṯā], and [[Syriac language|Syriac]] {{Lang|syc|ܚܠܬܝܬܐ}} [ḥeltīṯā], which was later borrowed into Arabic as {{Lang|ar|حلتيت}} [ḥiltīt]. These principal terms were cited and transcribed in altered forms by early European authors. [[Garcia de Orta]] refers to ''altiht'' or ''anjuden'' among Arab-Persian speakers and to ''imgu'' in India, while [[Engelbert Kaempfer]] describes in Persia a plant known as {{Lang|fa|هِينكِسَه}} [hingiseh].

== Historical aspects ==
Some authors have proposed that asafoetida was already included in ancient pharmacopoeias and may be identifiable in some of the earliest medical texts. It has been suggested, for example, that it is mentioned in the [[Ebers Papyrus]], an [[Ancient Egypt|Egyptian]] medical treatise dating to the 16th century BCE, where it appears in treatments for severe [[burn]]s and in ophthalmic [[collyrium]]s administered with a [[vulture]] feather.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Oliver-Bever |first=Bep |date=January 1966 |title=Pharmacognosie de l'époque pharaonique |trans-title=Pharmacognosy in the Pharaonic Period |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.3109/13880206609078054 |journal=Quarterly Journal of Crude Drug Research |language=fr |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=853–876 |doi=10.3109/13880206609078054 |issn=0033-5525 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref> The resin may also have been among the medicinal plants known and cultivated in [[Mesopotamia]].<ref name="Thompson"/> Its inclusion in the foundational texts of Ayurveda indicates that knowledge of the substance was well established in Asia prior to the [[Common Era]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Mahindru |first=Som Nath |title=Spices in Indian Life, 6500 B.C.-1950 A.D.: A Comprehensive and Critical Narration about the Role of Spices in Indian Life |publisher=Sultan Chand |year=1982 |pages=86 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Substitute for silphium ===
[[File:Coin minted in Achaemenid Barce (Barca).jpg|thumb|alt=Coin showing on one side a plant with sheathing leaves and on the other a profile portrait|Silphium ''(left)'' depicted on a coin minted in [[Barca (ancient city)|Barca]] in Cyrenaica in the 5th century BCE]]

The history of asafoetida is often discussed in relation to that of ancient [[silphium]], an unidentified plant whose [[sap]] was a major source of wealth for [[Cyrenaica]] (in present-day Libya). Valued both as a luxury spice and for its reputed medicinal properties, silphium held a prominent place in the ancient Mediterranean world. Although its precise botanical identity remains uncertain, it is generally considered that asafoetida was assimilated to silphium and entered the Mediterranean sphere following the conquests of [[Alexander the Great]] in the 4th century BCE.{{sfn|Dalby|2013}}

Asafoetida was brought to Europe by an expedition of Alexander the Great, who, after returning from a trip to northeastern [[ancient Persia]], thought that he had found a plant almost identical to the famed silphium of [[Cyrene, Libya|Cyrene]] in North Africa—though less tasty. [[Pedanius Dioscorides|Dioscorides]], in the first century, wrote, "the Cyrenaic kind, even if one just tastes it, at once arouses a humour throughout the body and has a very healthy aroma, so that it is not noticed on the breath, or only a little; but the Median [Iranian] is weaker in power and has a nastier smell." Nevertheless, it could be substituted for silphium in cooking, which was fortunate, because a few decades after Dioscorides' time, the true silphium of Cyrene became extinct, and asafoetida became more popular amongst physicians, as well as cooks.<ref name="Dalby">''Dangerous Tastes: The Story of Spices''. Andrew Dalby. 2000. University of California Press. Spices/ History. 184 pages. {{ISBN|0-520-23674-2}}</ref>

In his ''[[Anabasis (Arrian)|Anabasis]]'', [[Arrian]] quotes [[Aristobulus of Cassandreia]], who accompanied the [[Ancient Macedonian army|Macedonian army]] in Asia and reported that beyond the Caucasus—here referring to the [[Hindu Kush]], crossed by Alexander in the spring of 329 BCE—nothing grew except "the [[terebinth]] and the silphium".<ref>{{Cite book |url=http://hodoi.fltr.ucl.ac.be/concordances/arrien_anabase_03/lecture/9.htm |title=Anabasis |language=grc |trans-title=Anabasis |chapter=Book III, chapter 28, sections 6–7 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref> [[Strabo]] similarly relates in his ''[[Geographica|Geography]]'' that soldiers suffering from hunger were forced to eat raw meat for lack of fuel, but that their digestion was aided by silphium, "which grew in abundance in the country".<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://mediterranees.net/geographie/strabon/XV-2.html |title=Geography |language=grc |trans-title=Geography |chapter=Book XV, chapter 2, section 10 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref>

According to the account of [[Pliny the Elder]], the Cyrenaican silphium had become rare and may even have disappeared entirely: "For several years it has not been found in Cyrenaica, because the farmers of the pastures, finding greater profit in it, allow their flocks to graze in the places where this plant grows".<ref name="Pline">{{Cite book |last=Pliny the Elder |url=http://remacle.org/bloodwolf/erudits/plineancien/livre19.htm |title=Historia naturalis |language=la |trans-title=Natural History |chapter=Book XIX, chapter 15, section 1 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref> Asafoetida is commonly identified with the "silphium of [[Media (region)|Media]]", which appears to have gradually replaced the Cyrenaican product in its various uses.<ref name="Parejko2003">{{Cite journal |last=Parejko |first=Ken |date=June 2003 |title=Pliny the Elder's Silphium: First Recorded Species Extinction |trans-title=Pliny the Elder's Silphium: First Recorded Species Extinction |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1046/j.1523-1739.2003.02067.x |journal=Conservation Biology |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=925–927 |doi=10.1046/j.1523-1739.2003.02067.x |bibcode=2003ConBi..17..925P |issn=0888-8892 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref> Strabo notes in this respect that "another plant that Media also produces is silphium, and the sap extracted from it, called Median sap, although usually far inferior to the Cyrenaican sap, sometimes nonetheless surpasses it".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Strabo |author-link=Strabo |url=https://mediterranees.net/geographie/strabon/XI-13.html |title=Geography |language=grc |trans-title=Geography |chapter=Book XI, chapter 13, section 7 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref>

[[Dioscorides]] describes the method of resin extraction and draws attention to differences in quality and odour between the Cyrenaican product and its eastern counterparts:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dioscorides Pedanius of Anazarbus |author-link=Dioscorides |title=De materia medica |publisher=Olms-Weidmann |year=2005 |isbn=978-3-487-12881-8 |pages=218–220 |language=en |translator=Lily Y. Beck |trans-title=On Medical Matters |chapter=Book III, chapter 80}}</ref> {{blockquote|The sap [of silphium] is extracted from the root and stem by incision. The best sap is reddish and translucent; it has the smell of [[myrrh]] and a strong fragrance, is neither greenish nor unpleasant in taste, and quickly turns white. One should know that the Cyrenaican sap, even when tasted in very small quantity, immediately induces perspiration of the whole body and has a very sweet fragrance, so that the taster's breath smells only briefly. The saps of Media and Syria are decidedly weaker and their odour is rather foetid.}}
Pliny likewise emphasises the inferior quality of these substitutes and mentions frequent [[adulteration]]: "For a long time now we have received no other laser than that which grows abundantly in Persia, or in Media, or in Armenia; but it is far inferior to that of Cyrenaica; and even then it is adulterated with gum, or with [[sagapenum]], or with crushed [[broad bean]]".<ref name="Pline"/>

Roman and [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] medical authors writing after Dioscorides continued to cite silphium in their works. [[Galen]] (2nd century), [[Oribasius]] (4th century), [[Caelius Aurelianus]] (5th century), [[Aëtius of Amida]], [[Alexander of Tralles]] (6th century), and [[Paul of Aegina]] (7th century)<ref name="Adams1847">{{Cite book |last=Adams |first=Francis |author-link=Francis Adams (translator) |url=https://archive.org/details/sevenbooksofpaul03pauluoft/page/336/mode/2up |title=The seven books of Paulus Ægineta translated from the Greek: with a commentary embracing a complete view of the knowledge possessed by the Greeks, Romans, and Arabians on all subjects connected with medicine and surgery |publisher=The Sydenham Society |year=1847 |volume=III |pages=337–339 |language=en |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref> describe the resin and its properties, but largely reproduce earlier accounts without substantial additions.<ref name="Déniau-1868" /> Despite its scarcity, Cyrenaican silphium appears to have retained a primarily therapeutic role, and the question of its replacement by Persian resin was not definitively resolved. Some authors mention alternative preparations depending on availability: [[Soranus of Ephesus]] (2nd century), for example, gives recipes for four [[emmenagogue]] remedies, only two of which include silphium.

The latest generally accepted evidence for the presence of silphium in Libya comes from two letters by [[Synesius of Cyrene]], bishop of Cyrenaica, dated to the early 5th century. He refers to a silphium plant grown in his brother's garden and later to sap sent among other "luxury gifts" to a correspondent in [[Constantinople]]. These references suggest that the plant may by then have been rare in the wild and maintained primarily through cultivation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amigues |first=Suzanne |date=2004 |title=Le silphium - État de la question |trans-title=Silphium: State of the Question |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/jds_0021-8103_2004_num_2_1_1685 |journal=Journal des savants |language=fr |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=191–226 |doi=10.3406/jds.2004.1685 |issn=0021-8103 |access-date=December 24, 2025}}</ref>

Asafoetida is also mentioned numerous times in [[Jewish literature]], such as the [[Mishnah]].<ref>m. ''[[Avodah Zarah]]'' ch. 2; m. Shabbat ch. 20; et al.</ref> [[Maimonides]] also writes in the ''[[Mishneh Torah]]'' "In the rainy season, one should eat warm food with much spice, but a limited amount of mustard and asafoetida [{{lang|he|{{Script|Hebrew|חִלְתִּית}}|rtl=yes}} {{lang|he-Latn|chiltit}}]."<ref>''Mishneh Torah'', Laws of Opinions (Hilchot Deot) 4:8.</ref>

During the Italian Renaissance, asafoetida was used as part of the exorcism ritual.<ref name="Britannica-2024"/>

While it is generally forgotten now in Europe, it is widely used in India. Asafoetida is mentioned in the [[Bhagavata Purana]] (7:5:23-24), which states that one must not have eaten hing before worshipping the deity. Asafoetida is eaten by [[Brahmins]] and [[Jains]].<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance|editor1-first=Ghillean|editor2-last=Nesbitt|editor2-first=Mark|last=Pickersgill|first=Barbara|author-link=Barbara Pickersgill|date=2005|title=The Cultural History of Plants|publisher=Routledge|page=157|isbn=0415927463}}</ref> Devotees of the [[ISKCON|Hare Krishna]] movement also use hing in their food, as they are not allowed to consume onions or garlic. Their food has to be presented to [[Lord Krishna]] for sanctification (to become [[Prasadam]]) before consumption and onions and garlic cannot be offered to Krishna.<ref>{{cite web |title=Why no onions or garlic?|url=http://food.krishna.com/article/why-no-garlic-or-onions|website=food.krishna.com|publisher=Bhaktivedanta Book Trust|access-date=1 March 2021}}</ref>

=== ''Sweet asa'' and ''asafoetida'' ===

Arab [[Medicine in the medieval Islamic world|physicians of the Islamic Golden Age]], drawing in part on [[Ancient Greek medicine|Greek medical literature]], attributed to asafoetida properties similar to those ascribed to silphium by Dioscorides. [[Yuhanna ibn Masawaih|Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (Johannitius)]], [[Rhazes]] (9th century), [[Avicenna]] (11th century), and later [[Averroes]] (12th century), [[Serapion the Younger]], and [[Ibn al-Baitar]] (13th century), distinguished between two types of medicinal resins: one described as sweet-smelling and pleasant, and the other as having a strong and unpleasant odour.<ref name="Adams1847" /> These authors also provided indications of the geographical origin of the plants producing them; all these named regions lie between the Caspian Sea and the Indus River, in modern Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan. According to [[Abu Hanifa Dinawari|Abū Ḥanīfa]], as cited by Ibn al-Baitar,<ref name="Leclerc1877">{{cite book |last=Leclerc |first=Lucien |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JFT0Ntb2FyYC |title=Notices et extraits des manuscrits de la Bibliothèque nationale et autres bibliothèques |publisher=Imprimerie nationale |year=1877 |volume=23 |location=Paris |pages=141–145 |language=fr |trans-title=Notices and extracts from the manuscripts of the National Library and other libraries |chapter=Traité des simples par Ibn El-Beïthar |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> the plant grows in the sandy plains between [[Lashkar Gah|Bost]] and [[Qalat|Kikan]]; for [[Abu Mansur al-Tha'alibi|Abū Manṣūr]], the highest-quality variety comes from [[Merv]]; for [[Istakhri]], asafoetida is produced in large quantities in the desert between [[Sistan]] and [[Makran]]; whereas, according to [[Al-Idrisi]], it originates in a region at the confluence of the [[Helmand River|Helmand]] and the [[Arghandab River|Arghandab]].{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=354}} Ibn al-Baitar and [[Fakhr al-Din al-Razi]] described some positive medicinal effects on the respiratory system.<ref name="Britannica-2024"/>

Arabo-Persian medical knowledge was transmitted to medieval Europe through the [[Schola Medica Salernitana|School of Salerno]], and the term {{lang|la|asa}} entered Latin in the 11th century through the writings of [[Constantine the African]]. The {{lang|la|Circa instans}}, attributed to [[Matthaeus Platearius|Platearius]], is generally regarded as the earliest attestation of the compound {{lang|la|assa fetida}},<ref name="MLW" /> under which name the resin is subsequently cited by [[Albertus Magnus|Albert the Great]] and [[Arnaldus de Villanova|Arnau de Vilanova]].<ref name="Déniau-1868" /> By the late 13th century, a substantial tradition of illustrated [[herbal]]s had developed under the title {{lang|la|[[Tractatus de Herbis]]}}, later translated into French in the 15th century as the ''{{Interlanguage link|Livre des simples médecines|fr}}''. Asafoetida is consistently included in these works, although its depiction is typically schematic and not based on direct observation.<ref>{{cite book |last=Collins |first=Minta |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=s7c2EaxDYjUC |title=Medieval Herbals: The Illustrative Traditions |publisher=University of Toronto Press |year=2000 |isbn=0-8020-8313-7 |pages=239–298 |language=en |chapter=The ''Tractatus de Herbis'' and the Fifteenth-century Herbals |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

[[File:Assa fetida -alfa.l.09.28.jpg|thumb|left|upright|"Assa fetida", in a 1458 copy of the {{lang|la|Tractatus de Herbis}}. [[Biblioteca Estense]] of [[Modena]].|alt=Text in a narrow left column with colored initials and a colored drawing of a plant with oval entire leaves bearing resin-like fruits on the right.]]

In the [[early modern period]], likely as a result of a misinterpretation of [[Ludovico di Varthema]]'s description of the [[Benzoin (resin)|benzoin]] of [[Sumatra]],<ref>{{cite book |last=Temple |first=Richard Carnac |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WTVFCZ-nGjQC |title=The itinerary of Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna from 1502 to 1508 as translated from the original Italian edition of 1510 |publisher=Asian Educational Services |year=1997 |isbn=81-206-1269-8 |pages=xxii |language=en |trans-title=The itinerary of Ludovico di Varthema of Bologna |chapter=A Discourse On Varthema And His Travels In Southern Asia |access-date=24 December 2025 |orig-year=1928}}</ref> several authors identified this resin with the "Cyrenaic juice" described by Dioscorides and with the Arab notion of a ''sweet asa''. Although this identification was disputed from an early stage and is not supported by botanical or biogeographical evidence,{{sfn|Orta|1913|pp=58–65}} it nonetheless gained wide acceptance and persisted for an extended period.<ref name="Déniau-1868" /> As a result, some dictionaries and pharmaceutical reference works continue to list {{lang|la|assa dulcis}} as a synonym for benzoin resin.<ref>{{cite web |title=assa |trans-title=assa |url=https://www.cnrtl.fr/definition/assa |access-date=24 December 2025 |website=CNRTL |language=fr}}</ref>

=== Travelers' accounts ===

The earliest detailed account by a European observer of asafoetida is generally attributed to the Portuguese physician [[Garcia de Orta]], who was residing in [[Goa]] in [[Portuguese India|India]] in the mid-16th century.{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=356}} In his ''[[Colloquies on the Simples and Drugs of India]]'', published in 1563, he discusses—through a dialogue with the fictional interlocutor Ruano—the uncertainty and confusion surrounding the names applied to the resin. Although he was unable to determine the method of extraction or to identify the plant from which the gum was obtained, Orta established that it was transported to India from [[Khorasan]] via the port of [[Hormuz, Iran|Hormuz]]. He also distinguished asafoetida from {{lang|la|laserpitium}}, which he argued had been conflated by ancient and Arabic authors, and rejected the then-recent proposal equating it with benzoin. In addition, he noted that asafoetida was widely available in India and commonly used both medicinally and as a culinary seasoning.{{sfn|Orta|1913|pp=40–52}}

{{blockquote
|text=To me, the most unpleasant odor in the world is that of asafoetida; yet greens seasoned with it do not smell bad. You should not be surprised by this, for onions have a very bad smell, and yet dishes seasoned with them are very good. The truth is that there are many habits when it comes to odors.
|author=Garcia de Orta
|source=''Coloquio setimo: Do Altiht''{{sfn|Orta|1913|pp=40–52}}
}}

About a century later, the German traveller [[Johan Albrecht de Mandelslo]] visited Persia and India and recorded observations on a variety of unfamiliar products encountered there.{{sfn|Laufer|1919|p=357}} In his travel account published in 1669, he reports that ''hing'', referred to by European [[druggist]]s and [[apothecary|apothecaries]] as "asafoetida", originated chiefly in Persia and was produced by two distinct plants:

{{blockquote
|text=One grows like a shrub and has small leaves like those of [[Ruta|rue]]; the other resembles a [[turnip]], and its greenness is like that of [[fig]] leaves. It grows preferably in stony and dry places, and its gum begins to exude toward the end of summer, so that it must be harvested in autumn.
|author=Johann Albrecht von Mandelslo
|source=''The Voyages and Travels of J. Albert de Mandelslo into the East-Indies''<ref>{{cite book
|author=Johann Albrecht von Mandelslo
|title=The Voyages and Travels of J. Albert de Mandelslo into the East-Indies
|location=London
|year=1669
|pages=67
|language=en
|trans-title=The Voyages and Travels of J. Albert de Mandelslo into the East-Indies
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UPS_NYFKTzwC
|access-date=24 December 2025
}}</ref>
}}

[[File:Asa foetida Kaempfer.jpg|thumb|upright|Plate depicting ''Hingiseh'' or asafoetida in Kaempfer's work.|alt=Pen-and-ink drawing of a plant with a tuberous root, a rosette of leaves, and several umbels, with details of leaves and fruits.]]

The first comprehensive botanical description of the plant is generally credited to the German naturalist [[Engelbert Kaempfer]]. After travelling to [[Isfahan]] in 1684 as part of a mission associated with King [[Charles XI of Sweden]], Kaempfer entered the service of the [[Dutch East India Company]] as a physician. During the four years he spent in [[Iran|Persia]], he gathered extensive observations on the region’s natural history.{{sfn|Carrubba|1979}} His work ''{{Interlanguage link|Amoenitatum exoticarum|fr}}'' ("Exotic pleasures"), published in 1712, includes a full chapter devoted to "Asa foetida".<ref name="Kaempfer-1712">{{cite book |last=Kaempfer |first=Engelbert |author-link=Engelbert Kaempfer |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/147012 |title=Amœnitatum exoticarum politico-physico-medicarum, fasciculi V |publisher=Henricus Wilhelmus Meyer |year=1712 |location=Lemgo |pages=535–551 |language=la |trans-title=Exotic political, physical and medical delights |chapter=Observatio V: Historia Asae foetidae Disgunensis |trans-chapter=Observation V: History of Asafoetida}}</ref> This chapter is illustrated with a detailed plate of the plant and provides a systematic description of the successive stages of [[#Harvesting|resin extraction]] as practised in the village of ''Disguun'',{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}} located in a mountainous area along the [[Persian Gulf]], based on observations made in 1687.{{sfn|Carrubba|1979}}

=== Botanical discoveries and debates ===

In the system of [[biological nomenclature]] established in the mid-18th century by [[Carl Linnaeus]], the plant identified as producing asafoetida was assigned the [[binomial name]] ''Ferula assa-foetida''. At that time, the circumscription of the [[species]] was based solely on the description provided by [[Engelbert Kaempfer]], and subsequent botanical illustrations largely reproduced the plate published in ''Amoenitatum exoticarum''. In the 1840s, however, several additional asafoetida-producing plants were discovered and described independently. ''Ferula foetida'' (initially described as ''Scorodosma foetidum'') was collected by {{Interlanguage link|Alexander Lehmann|fr|Alexandre Adolfovitch Lehmann}} in the desert plains near the [[Aral Sea]] and later formally described by [[Alexander von Bunge]], who also observed the species in the vicinity of [[Herat]]. ''Ferula narthex'' was identified by [[Hugh Falconer]] in the [[Astor River|Astor]] valley of [[Kashmir]]. In Persia, between [[Jandaq]] and [[Yazd]], [[Friedrich Alexander Buhse]] collected material later recognised as representing ''Ferula alliacea''.{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}}

During the 19th and 20th centuries, the botanical origin of asafoetida and its relationship to silphium and other resins mentioned by ancient authors, such as galbanum and sagapenum, were the subject of sustained scholarly discussion.{{sfn|Vigier|1869|pp=15–26}}{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}} Both general and specialised literature has often presented divergent or inconsistent interpretations. More recent political developments in major producing regions—including the [[Iranian Revolution]], the [[War in Afghanistan|conflicts in Afghanistan]], and the [[dissolution of the Soviet Union]]—have further limited fieldwork and delayed comprehensive [[flora|floristic]] revisions and taxonomic reassessments.<ref name="Kraichak-2018" /><ref name="Pimenov2020">{{cite journal |last=Pimenov |first=Mikhail Georgievich |date=December 28, 2020 |title=Updated checklist of the Umbelliferae of Middle Asia and Kazakhstan: nomenclature, synonymy, typification, distribution |url=http://turczaninowia.asu.ru/article/view/9087 |journal=Turczaninowia |language=en |volume=23 |issue=4 |pages=127–257 |doi=10.14258/turczaninowia.23.4.12 |bibcode=2020Turcz..23d.127P |issn=1560-7267 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

== Botanical sources ==
[[File:Ferula distribution map fr (with types).svg|thumb|upright=1.4|Distribution ranges of the three main species producing asafoetida, after Chamberlain (1977),{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}} with modifications proposed by later authors.

Locations of collection sites for [[type (biology)|type]] specimens:

# ''Ferula assa-foetida''

# ''Ferula foetida''

# ''Ferula narthex''

# ''Ferula alliacea''

# ''Ferula pseudalliacea''

|alt=Map of Asia Minor and Central Asia showing colored distribution areas.]]

Species of the genus ''[[Ferula]]'' are [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennials]], often robust in habit and exhibiting [[plant sexuality|polygamous]] reproductive systems. The leaves are typically [[compound leaf|compound]], divided into two to four pairs of [[pinna (botany)|pinnae]], with bases that are usually [[leaf sheath|sheathing]]. The [[inflorescence]] is borne on a large, strongly branched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] and consists of numerous [[umbel]]s, each bearing many [[flower]]s. The central umbel is [[sessility (botany)|sessile]] or shortly pedunculate and fertile, whereas the lateral umbels are male or polygamous. The [[petal]]s are generally yellow and only rarely white. The [[fruit]] is a dorsally strongly compressed [[schizocarp]], [[wikt:elliptical|elliptical]] to [[wikt:oblong|oblong]] in shape, with conspicuously winged lateral ribs.{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}}

=== Main species ===
''Ferula assa-foetida'' L. and ''Ferula foetida'' (Bunge) Regel are the two species most frequently cited as botanical sources of asafoetida. Their application has been affected by persistent nomenclatural and taxonomic uncertainty, and the two names have long been—and in some contexts continue to be—treated as [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonyms]].

''F. assa-foetida'' is endemic to [[Southern Iran]] and is the source of asafoetida there. It has sulphur-containing compounds in the essential oil.<ref name="Sahebkar2">{{Cite journal|last1=Sahebkar|first1=Amirhossein|last2=Iranshahi|first2=Mehrdad|date=2010-12-01|title=Biological activities of essential oils from the genus ''Ferula'' (Apiaceae)|journal=Asian Biomedicine|language=en|volume=4|issue=6|pages=835–847|doi=10.2478/abm-2010-0110|s2cid=86139520|issn=1875-855X|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Farhadi20204">{{Cite journal|last1=Farhadi|first1=Faegheh|last2=Iranshahi|first2=Mehrdad|last3=Taghizadeh|first3=Seyedeh Faezeh|last4=Asili|first4=Javad|date=2020-11-01|title=Volatile sulfur compounds: The possible metabolite pattern to identify the sources and types of asafoetida by headspace GC/MS analysis|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0926669020307445|journal=Industrial Crops and Products|volume=155|article-number=112827|doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2020.112827|s2cid=224886254|issn=0926-6690|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Although it is often considered the main source of asafoetida on the international market,<ref name="Britannica-2024"/> this notion is attributable to the fact that several ''Ferula'' species acting as the major sources are often misidentified as ''F. assa-foetida''.{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}}<ref name="Panahi2">{{Cite journal|last1=Panahi|first1=Mehrnoush|last2=Banasiak|first2=łukasz|last3=Piwczyński|first3=Marcin|last4=Puchałka|first4=Radosław|last5=Kanani|first5=Mohammad Reza|last6=Oskolski|first6=Alexei A|last7=Modnicki|first7=Daniel|last8=Miłobędzka|first8=Aleksandra|last9=Spalik|first9=Krzysztof|date=2018-09-28|title=Taxonomy of the traditional medicinal plant genus ''Ferula'' (Apiaceae) is confounded by incongruence between nuclear rDNA and plastid DNA|journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=188|issue=2|pages=173–189|doi=10.1093/botlinnean/boy055|issn=0024-4074|doi-access=free}}</ref> In fact, the production of asafoetida from ''F. assa-foetida'' is confined to its native range, namely Southern Iran, outside which the sources of asafoetida are other species.<ref name="Farhadi20204"/><ref name="Farhadi20193">{{Cite journal|last1=Farhadi|first1=Faegheh|last2=Asili|first2=Javad|last3=Iranshahy|first3=Milad|last4=Iranshahi|first4=Mehrdad|date=2019-11-01|title=NMR-based metabolomic study of asafoetida|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0367326X19315758|journal=Fitoterapia|volume=139|article-number=104361|doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2019.104361|pmid=31629871|s2cid=204814018|issn=0367-326X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}} It was described by Linnaeus on the basis of the description and engraved plate published in 1712 by [[Engelbert Kaempfer]]. Kaempfer’s observations, as well as the herbarium specimen regarded as the [[holotype]] of the species, originate from the village of ''Disguun'' in southern Iran. Although the name has historically been applied in a broader sense, most botanists now restrict the [[taxon]] to this area, where it is considered [[endemism|endemic]]. Its [[phylogeny]]<ref name="Kraichak-2018" /> and [[systematics]] remain poorly resolved, and ''F. assa-foetida'' has been proposed as a possible synonym of several later-described species, including ''[[Ferula gummosa|F. erubescens]]'' Boiss., ''F. rubricaulis'' Boiss., and ''F. pseudalliacea'' Rech.f.{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}}{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|pp=697–698}}

[[File:Ferula assa-foetida - Kyzylkum (1).jpg|thumb|left|''Ferula foetida'' in the [[Kyzylkum Desert]], [[Uzbekistan]].|alt=Tall plant with a rosette of green leaves, a very thick yellowish-green stem, and a panicle of umbels of the same colour as the stem, growing in sandy desert conditions.]]
''F. foetida'' has a substantially wider distribution, occurring in [[Eastern Iran]], western [[Afghanistan]], western [[Pakistan]] and [[Central Asia]] ([[Karakum Desert]], [[Kyzylkum Desert]]).{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}}<ref name="Farhadi20193"/> Asafoetida derived from this species is likely the most widely traded form and the one that has been studied most extensively, although a significant portion of the literature refers to it under the name ''F. assa-foetida''. It has sulphur-containing compounds in the essential oil, the same way as ''F. assa-foetida''.<ref name="Farhadi20204"/> In European pharmaceutical usage, ''F. foetida'' is generally regarded as the principal botanical source of asafoetida.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=700}} From an economic perspective, it is thought to account for most of the harvests in Afghanistan,{{sfn|Samimi|Unger|1979}} a country that continues to play a leading role in global production and export.{{sfn|George|2012|p=153}}

''[[Ferula narthex|F. narthex]]'' has traditionally been cited in the literature as a third source of asafoetida. The species occurs naturally in northern Pakistan, as well as in eastern Afghanistan and southern [[Tajikistan]]. However, a study of Afghan production published in 1979 reported that the resin obtained from ''F. narthex'' lacked the organosulphur compounds considered characteristic of asafoetida.{{sfn|Samimi|Unger|1979}} In India, it is nevertheless regarded by regulatory authorities as a substitute with a comparable odour.<ref name="Raghavan-1974">Raghavan, G. (1974). ''Spices''. Indian Council of Agricultural Research.</ref>

=== Other cited sources ===
In pharmacopoeias, the three principal species are commonly cited with the addition “and other species of ''Ferula''”, without further specification. The names applied in the literature are affected by substantial taxonomic uncertainty, and the identity, economic significance, and resin yield of these additional species remain insufficiently documented.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=700}}{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}}

Among the species concerned are several taxa endemic to Iran, of which ''Ferula alliacea'' Boiss. is generally regarded as the most important. It occurs mainly in the north-eastern parts of the country and is mentioned in Iranian folk medicine as a medicinal plant.{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}} It has also been considered to have economic relevance.<ref name="Raghavan-1974" />{{sfn|Coppen|1995|p=109}} In the treatment of Umbelliferae in ''Flora Iranica'', however, ''F. alliacea'' is annotated as a ''nomen confusum'', since the published [[diagnosis (taxonomy)|diagnoses]] can be referred to other species.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=697}} The composition of the [[essential oil]] obtained from the roots was first investigated in 2016, revealing the presence of organosulphur compounds.<ref name="Kasaian-2016">{{Cite journal |last1=Kasaian |first1=Jamal |last2=Asili |first2=Javad |last3=Iranshahi |first3=Mehrdad |date=2016-10-02 |title=Sulphur-containing compounds in the essential oil of Ferula alliacea roots and their mass spectral fragmentation patterns |url=https://doi.org/10.3109/13880209.2016.1152279 |journal=Pharmaceutical Biology |volume=54 |issue=10 |pages=2264–2268 |doi=10.3109/13880209.2016.1152279 |issn=1388-0209 |pmid=26963574}}</ref> Subsequent work has suggested that comparative analyses of the types and concentrations of these compounds may help clarify the botanical sources of asafoetida produced in Iran.<ref name="Farhadi-2020">{{Cite journal |last1=Farhadi |first1=Faegheh |last2=Iranshahi |first2=Mehrdad |last3=Taghizadeh |first3=Seyedeh Faezeh |last4=Asili |first4=Javad |date=2020-11-01 |title=Volatile sulfur compounds: The possible metabolite pattern to identify the sources and types of asafoetida by headspace GC/MS analysis |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0926669020307445 |journal=Industrial Crops and Products |volume=155 |article-number=112827 |doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2020.112827 |issn=0926-6690}}</ref> ''Ferula lutensis'', like ''Ferula alliacea,'' is a source of asafoetida in Eastern Iran; both species have sulphur-containing compounds in their essential oil.<ref name="Farhadi20204"/><ref name="Farhadi20193"/>

[[File:Ferula jaeschkeana kz03.jpg|thumb|''{{Interlanguage link|Ferula jaeschkeana|fr}}'' at the [[Berlin Botanical Garden and Botanical Museum|Berlin Botanical Garden]].|alt=Colour photograph of the apex of a stem with a developing inflorescence protected by leaf sheaths.]]
Other Iranian species cited as potential sources include ''F. rubricaulis'' Boiss. {{sfn|Coppen|1995|p=109}}<ref name="Panahi2020">{{cite journal |last1=Panahi |first1=Mehrnoush |last2=Rezaee |first2=Mohammad-Bagher |last3=Jaimand |first3=Kamkar |date=September 2020 |title=A Review of Phytochemistry and Phylogeny that Aid Bio-prospecting in the Traditional Medicinal Plant Genus Ferula L. (Apiaceae) in Iran |trans-title=A Review of Phytochemistry and Phylogeny that Aid Bio-prospecting in the Traditional Medicinal Plant Genus Ferula L. (Apiaceae) in Iran |url=https://doi.org/10.22092/jmpb.2020.123118 |journal=Journal of Medicinal Plants and By-Products |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=133–148 |doi=10.22092/jmpb.2020.123118 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> and ''F. pseudalliacea'' Rech.f., endemic to western and southwestern [[Iran]] and sometimes considered conspecific with ''F. assa-foetida'';{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}}<ref name="Panahi2"/> and ''F. gabrielii'' Rech.f.<ref name="Panahi2020" /> The first of these is also frequently mentioned as a possible source of galbanum,{{sfn|George|2012|p=152}} whereas the second has been proposed as corresponding to bitter asafoetida, which is often regarded as deriving from a variety of ''F. assa-foetida''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hossein Jafari |first1=Samira |last2=Sepehry |first2=Adel |last3=Soltanloo |first3=Hassan |last4=Karimian |first4=Ali Akbar |date=February 2019 |title=Genetic differentiation between bitter and sweet asafetida plants using ISSR markers |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11033-018-4565-1 |journal=Molecular Biology Reports |language=en |volume=46 |issue=1 |pages=1069–1078 |doi=10.1007/s11033-018-4565-1 |pmid=30556109 |issn=0301-4851 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> The phylogeny and taxonomy of these taxa remain unresolved, as they are often based on incomplete material; for example, the leaves and stem of ''F. rubricaulis'' have not been described,{{sfn|Chamberlain|1977}} and the [[type (biology)|type]] specimen of ''F. gabrielii'' lacks fruits.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Safina |first1=Lucia K. |last2=Ostroumova |first2=Tatiana A. |last3=Pimenov |first3=Michael G. |date=April 2015 |title=Carpology of the species of Ferula subgen. Merwia (Umbelliferae-Apioideae) and some taxonomic implications |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1111/j.1756-1051.2013.00315.x |journal=Nordic Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=140–150 |doi=10.1111/j.1756-1051.2013.00315.x |bibcode=2015NorJB..33..140S |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

Additional species are occasionally cited. ''F. rigidula'' Fisch. ex DC.<ref name="Panahi2020" /> has a more westerly distribution, occurring in [[Turkey]] ([[Anatolia]]), the [[Caucasus]] ([[Armenia]] and [[Azerbaijan]]), and western Iran ([[Iranian Azerbaijan]]). Its aerial parts are used in traditional medicine in Turkey and contain several bioactive constituents, but its status as a source of asafoetida is not supported by available evidence.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zengin |first1=Gokhan |last2=Sinan |first2=Kouadio Ibrahime |last3=Ak |first3=Gunes |last4=Mahomoodally |first4=Mohamad Fawzi |date=October 2020 |title=Chemical profile, antioxidant, antimicrobial, enzyme inhibitory, and cytotoxicity of seven Apiaceae species from Turkey: A comparative study |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S092666902030488X |journal=Industrial Crops and Products |language=en |volume=153 |article-number=112572 |doi=10.1016/j.indcrop.2020.112572 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> ''F. jaeschkeana'' Vatke{{sfn|Ravindran|2017|p=63}} is distributed from the [[Caspian Sea]] to the [[Himalayas]] ([[Tibet]] and [[Bhutan]]). It is the only one of these species that occurs in [[India]], which accounts for the attention it has received there, given the country’s high consumption of asafoetida. The species is found mainly around [[Gulmarg]] in [[Jammu and Kashmir (union territory)|Jammu and Kashmir]] at elevations between {{convert|2000|and|4000|m}}. In this region, its roots are locally used to obtain a gum resin applied to wounds and contusions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gulati |first1=B. C. |title=Essential Oil Ferula Jaeschkeana Vatke |last2=Shawl |first2=A. S. |last3=Channa |first3=O. N. |date=1976 |publisher=Perfumery and Flavour Association of India |location=Calcutta |language=en}}</ref> It is not considered comparable to what is generally termed “authentic” asafoetida, as its essential oil does not contain organosulphur compounds.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=706}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sahebkar |first1=Amirhossein |last2=Iranshahi |first2=Mehrdad |date=January 2011 |title=Volatile Constituents of the Genus Ferula (Apiaceae): A Review |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0972060X.2011.10643969 |journal=Journal of Essential Oil Bearing Plants |language=en |volume=14 |issue=5 |pages=504–531 |doi=10.1080/0972060X.2011.10643969 |bibcode=2011JEOBP..14..504S |issn=0972-060X |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

Furthermore, ''Ferula latisecta'' is the source of asafoetida in Eastern Iran and southern [[Turkmenistan]],<ref name="Farhadi20193" /> with sulphur-containing compounds in its essential oil.<ref name="Sahebkar2"/> Lastly, ''Ferula sinkiangensis'' and ''Ferula fukanensis'' are endemic to [[Xinjiang]], [[China]]. They are the sources of asafoetida in China<ref name="药典">{{Cite book|author=国家药典委员会|title=中华人民共和国药典：2015年版|publisher=中国医药科技出版社|year=2015|isbn=978-7-5067-7337-9|volume=一部|location=北京|pages=190|trans-title=[[Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China]]|oclc=953251657}}</ref> and also have sulphur-containing compounds in their essential oil.<ref name="Sahebkar2" />

== Cultivation, extraction, and processing ==
[[File:Ase fétide .png|thumb|upright|Gum resin exuding from the stem after incision.|alt=Color photograph of a green Ferula stem exuding a milky white liquid.]]
''Ferula assa-foetida'' is a [[monoecious]], [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]], [[perennial plant]] of the family [[Apiaceae]]. It grows to {{convert|2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} high, with a circular mass of {{convert|30|–|40|cm|abbr=on|in|0}} leaves. Stem leaves have wide sheathing [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]. Flowering stems are {{convert|2.5|–|3|m|abbr=on|ft|0}} high and {{convert|10|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} thick and hollow, with a number of [[wiktionary:schizogenous|schizogenous]] ducts in the [[Cortex (botany)|cortex]] containing the resinous gum. Flowers are pale greenish yellow produced in large compound [[umbel]]s. Fruits are oval, flat, thin, reddish brown and have a milky juice. Roots are thick, massive, and pulpy. They yield a resin similar to that of the stems. All parts of the plant have a distinctive smell.{{Sfn|Ross|2005|p=224}}

Most plant [[exudate]]s available on the global market are obtained from trees; by contrast, asafoetida—together with [[tragacanth gum]]—is among the relatively few products derived from incisions made in the roots of a [[herbaceous plant]].{{sfn|Coppen|1995|p=108}} Although gum exudes from all parts of the plant when cut, traditional production of asafoetida involves making incisions at the surface of the [[root crown]].

Demand for the gum resin is high, while supply relies largely on harvesting from [[natural habitat]]s. This harvesting pressure has reduced the [[biocapacity]] of affected [[ecosystem]]s and poses a risk to the persistence of the species. For this reason, efforts to develop large-scale [[agriculture|cultivation]] have been undertaken, motivated by both economic and [[environmentalism|environmental]] considerations.<ref name="Elyasirad2017">{{cite journal |last1=Elyasirad |first1=Somayeh |last2=Mousavi |first2=Sied Gholamreza |last3=Sanjari |first3=Gholamreza |date=April 2017 |title=Effects of priming and salt stress on seed germination and emergence characteristics of Asafetida (Ferula assa foetida) |url=http://www.arpnjournals.org/jabs/research_papers/rp_2017/jabs_0417_858.pdf |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Biological Science |language=en |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=150–160 |issn=1990-6145 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> A range of [[cultivar]]s is commercially available; these are generally differentiated by country of origin and perceived quality rather than by precise botanical source.<ref name="Sood-2020" />

=== Cultivation parameters ===
The plant grows best under [[temperate climate|temperate]] and [[aridity|dry]] climatic conditions. Optimal annual [[precipitation]] is reported to range between 250 and {{convert|350|mm}}. Although the plant tolerates temperatures of up to {{convert|35|°C}}, optimal temperatures are around {{convert|15|°C}} for [[germination]] and between {{convert|10|and|20|°C}} for [[plant morphogenesis|vegetative growth]], under conditions of high light availability. Cultivation is reported from elevations between 600 and {{convert|2400|m}}, often on slopes steeper than 25%. The species favours fertile, well-drained soils of sandy or clayey [[loam]] type and tolerates a wide range of soil [[pH]], from acidic to alkaline.<ref name="Sood-2020" />

Propagation is most commonly achieved by [[seed]]. [[Vegetative reproduction]] through root division is possible in September but is generally discouraged because it causes substantial disturbance to the plant.<ref name="Sood-2020" /> Seeds are typically collected at the end of summer.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|p=4}} Under [[greenhouse]] conditions, sowing may take place in autumn as soon as seeds reach maturity, whereas in open-field cultivation sowing is usually carried out in December–January or in April. [[Germination]] generally begins after approximately {{convert|20|days}}. Winter sowing is associated with higher emergence rates and improved tuber yield but requires the use of protective [[mulch]]. Seeds exhibit prolonged [[seed dormancy|dormancy]] and relatively low germination rates; these constraints may be alleviated by [[Stratification (seeds)|stratification]], washing, or treatment with [[plant hormone|growth hormones]].<ref name="Sood-2020" /> An Iranian study also reported that [[Priming (agriculture)|priming]] techniques improved germination and reduced the adverse effects of [[salinity]] stress.<ref name="Elyasirad2017" />

</gallery>

During the first year of cultivation, an application of approximately {{convert|15|to|20|tonnes}} of [[manure]] per hectare is generally recommended. In subsequent years, nutrient inputs are typically supplied through [[fertiliser]]s, with application rates progressively increased up to about the tenth year of growth. Commonly cited initial application rates are {{convert|20|g}} of [[ammonium nitrate|N]], {{convert|18|g}} of [[superphosphate|P]], and {{convert|18|g}} of [[potassium oxide|K]] per plant. In soils identified as deficient in [[zinc]], a basal application of zinc sulphate at approximately {{convert|20|kg}} per hectare is reported to improve yields. Two periods of [[weeding]] per year are usually required (June–July and October–November), along with [[digging]] or loosening of the soil around plants in August–September.

[[Water stress]] is considered one of the main limiting factors for growth and productivity. Moist conditions are primarily required during germination, whereas prolonged or excessive moisture at later stages may be detrimental. Weekly [[irrigation]] is generally regarded as adequate under cultivated conditions. In high-altitude cultivation areas, water requirements may be met in part or entirely by spring [[snowmelt]].<ref name="Sood-2020" />

=== Harvest ===

The specific sequence and timing of operations vary by region, but the overall harvesting technique is broadly similar throughout the plant’s range. [[Engelbert Kaempfer]] provided a detailed account of the method used in the region of [[Lar, Iran|Lar]] in southern Iran at the end of the 17th century.<ref name="Kaempfer-1712" /> In the 19th century, [[Henry Walter Bellew]], followed by [[James Edward Tierney Aitchison]], documented comparable practices in the area around [[Herat]] in Afghanistan.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aitchison |first1=James Edward Tierney |author-link1=James Edward Tierney Aitchison |date=January 1891 |title=Notes to assist in a further Knowledge of the Products of Western Afghanistan and of North-Eastern Persia |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/03746609109468059 |journal=Transactions of the Botanical Society of Edinburgh |language=en |volume=18 |issue=1–4 |pages=1–228 |doi=10.1080/03746609109468059 |issn=0374-6607 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> Ethnobotanical surveys indicate that the preparation and harvesting methods used in rural areas of both countries remain broadly consistent with these historical descriptions.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|p=4}}

The plant generally requires about five years to reach full development, attaining heights of up to {{Convert|2|m}}.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|p=2}} Older individuals tend to yield larger quantities of resin.<ref name="Sood-2020" /> Plants selected for harvesting are often identified and marked by local collectors in November of the preceding year.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|p=4}} Collection of the [[latex]] begins when the foliage changes from green to yellow, typically in March or April, shortly before [[flowering]].{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=217}} The initial step involves clearing soil and stones from around the plant and removing the foliage and stem. The upper part of the root, surmounted by a brush-like structure, is exposed, then covered with loose soil and gravel and left for approximately five days. The brush is subsequently removed, and the top of the root is scraped over an area of up to {{Convert|6.5|cm2}}, after which it is covered with a dome-shaped structure made of twigs and stones.

After two or three days, a first incision is made and the exuding latex is collected. Two to three days later, a second incision, slightly deeper (about {{Convert|0.5|cm}}), is made to allow further exudation. This sequence of cutting and collection is repeated for ten to fifteen cycles, until latex production ceases.<ref name="Sood-2020" /> In an alternative method, the exudate is allowed to dry on the root and is then scraped off after several days.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=217}} After each operation, the exposed surface of the root is protected to prevent contamination by soil or gravel and to maintain cool conditions conducive to resin maturation.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Pruthi |first1=J. S. |title=Minor spices and condiments |publisher=Indian Council of Agricultural Research |year=2001 |location=New Delhi |pages=782 |language=en |chapter=Asafoetida}}</ref> The collected exudate is stored in a pit dug into the ground, the dimensions of which depend on the expected yield but may reach {{Convert|1.8|m}} in length and {{Convert|2.4|m}} in depth. The sides of the pit are lined with mud, and the opening is covered with plant stems, leaving an aperture of about {{Convert|30|cm}} in diameter through which the daily harvest is added.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=157–158}} The entire harvesting period lasts approximately three months. Average yields have been estimated at around {{Convert|40|g}} of resin per root, although individual plants may produce up to {{Convert|900|g}}.<ref name="Sood-2020" />

In [[South Khorasan Province|South Khorasan]], in eastern Iran, harvesting is conducted later in the year and follows a somewhat modified procedure. Collection takes place in 12 to 16 cycles of four to five days between June and August. In this region, the base of the stem is retained, and a thin slice is removed at each stage. These slices, known in Persian as ''keshteh'', are collected together with the exuded resin and allowed to dry. The dried material is then sold to processing facilities, where the crude gum-resin is extracted. An experienced harvester may process up to 1,000 plants per cycle and obtain between {{Convert|2|and|3|kg}} of raw product in favourable years.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|p=4}}

<gallery mode="packed" caption="Asafoetida harvesting in the village of Sorond near [[Tabas]], South Khorasan">
