The resin may also be obtained through a series of incisions made at the junction between the rhizome stem and the taproot.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=217}} In parts of Afghanistan, some [[Pashtuns]] collect resin by cutting the stems of wild plants and boiling them together with the roots to evaporate the water. Resin produced using this method is generally regarded as being of lower quality than that obtained through standard tapping techniques.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=157–158}}

=== Processing and derived products ===

The resin stored in pits is typically thick and sticky. It is characterised by a strong odour and a bitter, acrid taste, and its colour ranges from white to grey or dark red. During storage, the material continues to mature and can subsequently be hand-moulded and processed into forms commonly referred to as “tears”, “mass”, or “paste”. White asafoetida was traditionally wrapped in cloth and then placed in [[jute]] sacks, whereas the dark red variety was packed in goat or sheep skin, a method associated with more pronounced maturation. In contemporary practice, packaging is generally carried out using plastic bags or sheets, which are then placed in wooden boxes.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=159–160}}

[[File:Asafoetida.jpg|thumb|Different presentations of compounded asafoetida, also known in India as "yellow powder".|alt=Colour photograph of four plastic containers; in the foreground, the open container holds a yellow powder.]]

The principal derived products of asafoetida are the essential oil, the tincture, and the compounded powder. The [[essential oil]] is obtained by [[steam distillation]]. It is stored in airtight containers and kept in a cool environment ({{Convert|15|to|-25|°C}}). Because of its high concentration, handling practices generally recommend avoiding contact with the eyes or skin and limiting [[inhalation]] of vapours. The essential oil is used primarily in medicinal preparations. The [[tincture]] is produced by extracting the resin with [[ethanol]] and may vary in concentration according to its application. A commonly cited preparation involves macerating {{Convert|200|g}} of asafoetida in {{Convert|750|mL}} of 70 per cent alcohol for one week, followed by filtration and dilution to volume. When water is added, the tincture becomes milky as a result of [[emulsion|emulsification]] of the essential oil (the [[Ouzo effect]]). Tinctures are used mainly in the [[pharmaceutical industry]], the [[food flavouring]] industry, and [[perfumery]].{{sfn|George|2012|pp=159–160}}

The compounded form of asafoetida, known in India as ''Bandhani Hing'', is produced by diluting resin from one or more sources with substances such as [[gum arabic]], [[rice flour]] or [[wheat flour]], and [[turmeric]].{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=701}} This [[food adulteration|adulteration]] reduces odour intensity, limits clumping, and imparts colour to the preparation.{{sfn|Small|2011}} Compounding allows direct use in cooking without prior dilution, as the pure resin is highly concentrated and difficult to grate. Formulations vary among manufacturers and are generally treated as [[trade secret]]s, but the final product typically contains about 30% asafoetida.

''Bandhani Hing'' is especially popular in southern India and is marketed in powdered form or as bricks of compacted powder.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=159–160}}

== Composition and phytochemistry ==
[[File:Asafoetida2.jpg|thumb|Asafoetida in pieces and as a tincture.|alt=Two glass containers, one holding pieces of resin with plant debris, the other an orange-yellow tincture.]]

Asafoetida is an oleo-gum-resin (or gum oleoresin), consisting of three main groups of constituents: resinous compounds (approximately 40–64%), [[endogeneous]] gum (about 25%), and a volatile fraction in the form of essential oil (10–17%).

The total [[ash (chemistry)|ash]] content typically ranges from 1.5 to 10%.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=218}} The resin fraction contains up to 60% ferulic acid and its [[ester]]s, along with [[coumarin]]s and various [[terpenoid]]s, [[asaresinotannol]]s A and B, [[umbelliferone]], and four unidentified compounds.<ref name="Singhal">''Handbook of Indices of Food Quality and Authenticity''. Rekha S. Singhal, Pushpa R. Kulkarni. 1997, Woodhead Publishing, Food industry and trade {{ISBN|1-85573-299-8}}. More information about the composition, p. 395.</ref> The gum fraction is composed of [[monosaccharide|simple sugars]] ([[glucose]], [[galactose]], [[arabinose|L-arabinose]], [[rhamnose]], and [[glucuronic acid]]), as well as [[polysaccharide]]s and [[glycoprotein]]s. The volatile oil component is rich in various [[organosulfide]] compounds, such as 2-butyl-propenyl-disulphide, diallyl sulphide, [[Diallyl disulfide|diallyl disulphide]] (also present in garlic)<ref name="pharmacognosy">{{Cite journal|last1=Mahendra|first1=Poonam|last2=Bisht|first2=Shradha|date=2012|title=Ferula asafoetida: Traditional uses and pharmacological activity|journal=Pharmacognosy Reviews|volume=6|issue=12|pages=141–146|doi=10.4103/0973-7847.99948|issn=0973-7847|pmc=3459456|pmid=23055640|doi-access=free}}</ref> and [[dimethyl trisulfide]], which is also responsible for the odour of cooked onions. The organosulfides are primarily responsible for the odour and flavour of asafoetida.{{sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}}<ref name="Farhadi20204"/>

=== Ferulic acid ===
Ferulic acid is a [[Naturally occurring phenols|phenolic]] derivative of [[cinnamic acid]] that is widespread and abundant in the [[plant cell wall]]. It was first isolated in 1866 by the Austrian chemists [[Heinrich Hlasiwetz]] and [[Ludwig Barth zu Barthenau]] from asafoetida and was named after its botanical source (''Ferula'' sp.).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hlasiwetz |first1=Heinrich |author-link1=Heinrich Hlasiwetz |last2=Barth |first2=Ludwig |author-link2=Ludwig Barth zu Barthenau |date=1866 |title=Mittheilungen aus dem chemischen Laboratorium in Innsbruck |trans-title=Communications from the Chemical Laboratory in Innsbruck |url=https://chemistry-europe.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jlac.18661380111 |journal=Justus Liebigs Annalen der Chemie |language=de |volume=138 |issue=1 |pages=61–76 |doi=10.1002/jlac.18661380111 |issn=1099-0690 |access-date=2025-12-24}}</ref> Ferulic acid has been reported in the literature to exhibit a range of biological activities, including [[antioxidant]], [[antiallergic]], hepatoprotective, [[anti-cancer]], [[anti-inflammatory]], [[antimicrobial]], [[antiviral]], [[vasodilator]], and antithrombotic effects. It has also been studied for its effects on [[spermatozoon|sperm]] viability and for its involvement in [[chelation]], [[enzyme kinetics|modulation of enzymatic activity]], activation of [[transcription factor]]s, [[gene expression]], and [[signal transduction]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kumar |first1=Naresh |last2=Pruthi |first2=Vikas |date=December 2014 |title=Potential applications of ferulic acid from natural sources |journal=Biotechnology Reports |language=en |volume=4 |pages=86–93 |doi=10.1016/j.btre.2014.09.002 |pmid=28626667 |pmc=5466124 }}</ref> In asafoetida, ferulic acid occurs either in free form or as an ester of asaresinotannol.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=701}} The free acid is converted into [[umbelliferone]] during [[dry distillation]].{{sfn|George|2012|p=156}}

=== Sesquiterpene coumarins ===
[[File:Umbelliprenin.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|left|{{Interlanguage link|Umbelliprenin|fr|Ombelliprénine}} consists of a coumarin ([[umbelliferone]], in blue) linked via its [[hydroxyl]] group to a sesquiterpene ([[farnesol]], in red).|alt=Topological formula of a bicyclic aromatic benzopyran compound linked by an ether bridge to a fifteen-carbon chain.]]

Sesquiterpene coumarins are naturally occurring compounds with documented [[pharmacology|pharmacological]] activity, produced by certain plant species in the families [[Asteraceae]] (genus ''[[Artemisia (plant)|Artemisia]]''), [[Rutaceae]] (genus ''[[Haplophyllum (plant)|Haplophyllum]]''), and [[Apiaceae]] (genera ''[[Angelica]]'', ''[[Heptaptera]]'', ''[[Heracleum (plant)|Heracleum]]'', ''[[Peucedanum]]'', and ''[[Ferula]]'', which is particularly rich in these constituents). Structurally, they consist of a [[sesquiterpene]] ([[terpene]] with 15 carbon atoms) linked by an [[ether]] bond to a [[coumarin]] derivative. In the case of asafoetida, the coumarin moiety is predominantly [[umbelliferone]] ({{nobr|7-hydroxycoumarin}}).<ref name="Gliszczyńska">{{Cite journal |last1=Gliszczyńska |first1=Anna |last2=Brodelius |first2=Peter E. |date=March 2012 |title=Sesquiterpene coumarins |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11101-011-9220-6 |journal=Phytochemistry Reviews |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=77–96 |doi=10.1007/s11101-011-9220-6 |bibcode=2012PChRv..11...77G |issn=1568-7767 |access-date=2025-12-24}}</ref>

[[File:Farnesiferol A.svg|thumb|Structure of farnesiferol A: umbelliferone (in blue) linked to a cyclic sesquiterpene (in red).|alt=Topological formula of a bicyclic benzopyran compound linked by an ether bridge to a hydroxylated bicyclic fifteen-carbon chain.]]

The simplest compound in this group is umbelliprenin, which was first isolated in 1938 from the seeds of [[Angelica archangelica]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Späth |first1=Ernst |last2=Vierhapper |first2=Friedrich |date=3 August 1938 |title=Über die Konstitution des Umbelliprenins |trans-title=On the constitution of umbelliprenin |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/cber.19380710823 |journal=Berichte der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft |language=de |volume=71 |issue=8 |pages=1667–1672 |doi=10.1002/cber.19380710823 |access-date=2025-12-24}}</ref> Its biological properties were investigated in detail only in the 21st century, when studies reported [[anti-inflammatory]], [[antioxidant]], and [[antileishmanial]] activities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shakeri |first1=Abolfazl |last2=Iranshahy |first2=Milad |last3=Iranshahi |first3=Mehrdad |date=3 August 2014 |title=Biological properties and molecular targets of umbelliprenin – a mini-review |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10286020.2014.917630 |journal=Journal of Asian Natural Products Research |language=en |volume=16 |issue=8 |pages=884–889 |doi=10.1080/10286020.2014.917630 |pmid=24852499 |bibcode=2014JANPR..16..884S |issn=1028-6020 |access-date=2025-12-24}}</ref> Several derivatives of umbelliprenin have also been identified in asafoetida, including {{nobr|5-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}, {{nobr|8-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}, {{nobr|9-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}, asacoumarin ({{nobr|5,8-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}), {{nobr|5-acetoxy-8-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}, {{nobr|8-acetoxy-5-hydroxyumbelliprenin}} (reported to exhibit [[anti-inflammatory]] and [[antiviral]] activity), {{nobr|10-''R''-karatavicinol}}, {{nobr|6,7-dihydroxykaratavicinol}}, and {{nobr|10-''R''-acetoxy-11-hydroxyumbelliprenin}}.<ref name="Gliszczyńska" />

The resin also contains other cyclic compounds that have been investigated for potential therapeutic effects. {{nobr|Farnesiferols A}}, B, C, and D have been reported to show antiviral, anti-tumour, and anti-angiogenic activity. Conferol has been studied for antiviral and [[cytotoxicity|cytotoxic]] effects, as well as for [[synergy|synergistic]] interactions with anti-cancer agents such as [[vincristine]]. Galbanic acid has been reported, among other properties, to influence [[antibiotic resistance]] in [[Staphylococcus aureus]].{{sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=7}} Additional cyclic derivatives of sesquiterpene coumarins—including gummosin, {{nobr|assafoetidnol A}} and B, polyanthine, badrakemin, samarcandin, feselol, microlobidene, and kellerin—have been identified in asafoetida and other ''Ferula'' species, and several of these compounds continue to be the subject of pharmacological research.<ref name="Gliszczyńska" />

=== Organosulfur compounds ===
[[File:Asafoetida disulfide compounds.svg|thumb|left|Three of the main disulfides of asafoetida (''from top to bottom''):
{{Plainlist|

* disulfide of {{nowrap|2-butyl}} and {{nowrap|1-propenyl}};
* disulfide of {{nowrap|1-(methylthio)propyl}} and {{nowrap|1-propenyl}};
* disulfide of {{nowrap|2-butyl}} and {{nowrap|3-(methylthio)}}-{{nowrap|2-propenyl}}.
  }}|alt=Topological structural formulas.]]

Volatile [[Organosulfur compound]]s are [[Secondary metabolite]]s produced by plants and [[Microorganism]]s and are often characterised by strong odours. These odours arise from various [[Sulfur|sulphur-containing]] molecules, including [[Hydrogen sulfide]] (commonly described as having a rotten egg odour), [[Sulfur dioxide]] (sharp and irritating), and a range of [[Thiol]]s. In plants, such compounds are found primarily in the families ''[[Brassicaceae]]'', ''[[Apiaceae]]'', ''[[Liliaceae]]'', ''[[Caricaceae]]'', ''[[Capparaceae]]'', ''[[Solanaceae]]'', and ''[[Rutaceae]]''. From a pharmacological perspective, organosulfur compounds have been reported to exhibit [[Anti-inflammatory]], [[Immunomodulation|immunomodulatory]], [[Antihypertensive drug|antihypertensive]], [[Antioxidant]], and [[Hypercholesterolemia|hypocholesterolaemic]] activities. They are also used as indicators of quality and authenticity in commercial plant materials and derived products.<ref name="Farhadi-2020" />

The attribution of the characteristic odour and taste of asafoetida to sulphur-containing compounds, by analogy with garlic or onion, has been proposed since the late 19th century.<ref name="Takeoka2001">{{cite book |last=Takeoka |first=Gary |title=Aroma Active Compounds in Foods: Chemistry and Sensory Properties |publisher=American Chemical Society |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-8412-3694-3 |editor1-last=Takeoka |editor1-first=Gary R. |series=ACS Symposium Series |volume=794 |pages=33–44 |language=en |chapter=Volatile Constituents of Asafoetida |doi=10.1021/bk-2001-0794.ch004 |editor2-last=Güntert |editor2-first=Matthias |editor3-last=Engel |editor3-first=Karl-Heinz}}</ref> In 1891, the German chemist [[Friedrich Wilhelm Semmler]] demonstrated the presence of a [[Disulfide]] in the essential oil of the resin, although its precise structure could not be determined at that time.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Semmler |first=Friedrich Wilhelm |date=January 1891 |title=Ueber das in der Asa foetida enthaltene ätherische Oel |trans-title=On the essential oil contained in asa foetida |journal=Berichte der Deutschen Chemischen Gesellschaft |language=de |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=78–81 |doi=10.1002/cber.18910240112}}</ref> The disulfide of {{nowrap|2-butyl}} and {{nowrap|1-propenyl}} was subsequently identified in 1936 as the principal component of the volatile fraction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mannich |first1=Carl |last2=Fresenius |first2=Ph. |year=1936 |title=Über den Hauptbestandteil des ätherischen Öles der Asa foetida |trans-title=On the main constituent of the essential oil of asa foetida |journal=Archiv der Pharmazie |language=de |volume=274 |issue=8 |pages=461–472 |doi=10.1002/ardp.19362740802}}</ref> The concentration of this compound and the relative proportions of its ''Z'' and ''E'' [[Diastereomer]]s vary considerably depending on the species<ref name="Kasaian-2016" /> and the timing of harvest.<ref name="Kavoosi2013">{{cite journal |last1=Kavoosi |first1=Gholamreza |last2=Rowshan |first2=Vahid |date=June 2013 |title=Chemical composition, antioxidant and antimicrobial activities of essential oil obtained from Ferula assa-foetida oleo-gum-resin: Effect of collection time |journal=Food Chemistry |language=en |volume=138 |issue=4 |pages=2180–2187 |doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2012.11.131 |pmid=23497874 }}</ref>

The essential oil of asafoetida contains more than {{nowrap|80 compounds}}, including at least approximately thirty additional organosulphur compounds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Noleau |first1=Isabelle |last2=Richard |first2=Hubert |last3=Peyroux |first3=Anne-Sophie |date=July 1991 |title=Volatile Compounds in Leek and Asafoetida |journal=Journal of Essential Oil Research |language=en |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=241–256 |doi=10.1080/10412905.1991.9697935}}</ref> Several of these molecules activate the TRPA1 channel, a member of the [[Ion channel]] family of [[Transient receptor potential channel|transient receptor potential]] (TRP) channels, in a manner comparable to mustard essential oil or the sulphur compounds present in onion and garlic. This receptor is strongly expressed in the [[Oral cavity]] and the [[Respiratory tract]]. Its activation has been implicated in the [[pungency]] of asafoetida and, through desensitisation mechanisms, may contribute to the symptomatic relief of respiratory conditions traditionally associated with the spice.<ref name="Shokoohinia2013">{{cite journal |last1=Shokoohinia |first1=Yalda |last2=Chianese |first2=Giuseppina |last3=Appendino |first3=Giovanni |last4=Di Marzo |first4=Vincenzo |date=October 2013 |title=Some like it pungent and vile. TRPA1 as a molecular target for the malodorous vinyl disulfides from asafoetida |journal=Fitoterapia |language=en |volume=90 |pages=247–251 |doi=10.1016/j.fitote.2013.08.001 |pmid=23954176 }}</ref>

Beyond their contribution to the sensory and medicinal properties of the resin, organosulphur compounds may serve as [[Chemotaxonomy|chemotaxonomic]] markers for determining its botanical origin. A 2020 study applied this approach by establishing sulphur compound profiles of asafoetida-producing species in Iran using [[Gas chromatography]] coupled with [[Mass spectrometry]]. Analysis of commercially available resin samples allowed correlations to be drawn with specific taxa and their geographic origin. The results indicated higher absolute concentrations of organosulphur compounds in eastern species such as ''F. foetida'' and ''F. alliacea'', whereas samples of ''F. assa-foetida'' collected in southern Iran showed a higher relative content of [[Monoterpene]] compounds, notably [[Alpha-pinene|α-pinene]] and [[Beta-pinene|β-pinene]].<ref name="Farhadi-2020" />

== Effects and toxicity ==
=== Functional properties ===
In the 1990s, pharmacopoeias noted that the medicinal use of asafoetida was not supported by [[Clinical trial|clinical]] evidence.{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=702}} During the first two decades of the 21st century, however, a substantial body of [[Pharmacology|pharmacological]] research, mainly conducted in Iran, examined the properties of the oleo-gum-resin. These studies, primarily based on laboratory and preclinical models, have reported a range of biological activities that suggest pharmacological potential. The specific active phytochemical constituents have not yet been fully identified, and further investigation is required to establish their safety and clinical relevance.{{sfn|Amalraj|Gopi|2017}}

=== Toxicity ===
In adults, the ingestion of asafoetida is generally considered to be associated with low or negligible [[toxicity]]. A study involving ten volunteers reported no adverse effects following the ingestion of {{convert|3|g}} of oleo-gum-resin consumed on buttered bread, and doses of up to {{convert|15|g}} have also been described as tolerated. Adverse effects have nevertheless been reported after the ingestion of higher amounts, including occasional lip swelling and [[indigestion]], with fetid belching, [[flatulence]], and [[diarrhoea]]. [[Headache]]s, [[dizziness]], and increased [[libido]] have also been described.

In individuals described as nervous or sensitive, doses of approximately 0.05 to {{convert|0.1|g}} have been reported to induce [[convulsion]]s. The external application of resin-based [[poultice]]s to the abdomen has been associated with inflammation and swelling of the [[reproductive system|genital organs]].{{sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=703}} A case of [[methaemoglobinaemia]] has been documented in a five-week-old infant following the ingestion of glycerinated asafoetida administered as a folk remedy for [[colic]]. The infant was hospitalised approximately six hours after ingestion, presenting with [[tachypnoea]] and [[cyanosis]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kelly |first1=K. J. |last2=Neu |first2=J. |last3=Camitta |first3=B. M. |last4=Honig |first4=G. R. |date=May 1984 |title=Methemoglobinemia in an infant treated with the folk remedy glycerited asafoetida |journal=Pediatrics |language=en |volume=73 |issue=5 |pages=717–719 |doi=10.1542/peds.73.5.717 |issn=0031-4005 |pmid=6609339}}</ref>

The [[genotoxicity]] of asafoetida has been investigated in the [[laboratory mouse]]. Oral administration was reported to have a weak inducing effect on [[sister chromatid exchange]]s in [[spermatogonia]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abraham |first1=Suresh K. |last2=Kesavan |first2=P. C. |date=April 1984 |title=Genotoxicity of garlic, turmeric and asafoetida in mice |journal=Mutation Research/Genetic Toxicology |language=en |volume=136 |issue=1 |pages=85–88 |doi=10.1016/0165-1218(84)90138-1 |pmid=6717474 }}</ref> In a separate study, the resin was found to induce [[chromosomal abnormality|chromosomal abnormalities]] in [[spermatocyte]]s, an effect attributed to [[umbelliferone]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Walia |first=Karvita |date=1973 |title=Effect of Asafoetida (7-Hydroxycoumarin) on Mouse Spermatocytes |journal=Cytologia |language=en |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=719–724 |doi=10.1508/cytologia.38.719 |pmid=4783359 |issn=0011-4545}}</ref> By contrast, no [[mutagenesis|mutagenic]] effects were observed in [[Drosophila]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abraham |first1=Suresh K. |last2=Kesavan |first2=P. C. |date=August 1985 |title=A preliminary analysis of the genotoxicity of a few spices in Drosophila |journal=Mutation Research Letters |language=en |volume=143 |issue=4 |pages=219–223 |doi=10.1016/0165-7992(85)90084-3 |pmid=4022024 }}</ref> Because of its reported [[abortifacient]] properties, the use of asafoetida is generally discouraged during [[pregnant women|pregnancy]].{{sfn|George|2012|pp=160–161}}

== Uses ==
=== Spice ===
When the resin is sold in solid chunks, it is typically first broken up and ground in a [[mortar and pestle]] with an absorbent material such as [[rice flour]].{{sfn|Gayet|2010}} The resulting powder is then fried in oil or soaked in water, a process that produces an aroma reminiscent of onion or garlic.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=160–161}} The use of compounded asafoetida reduces the risk of excessive dosing, as only very small amounts are required: approximately one sixteenth of a [[teaspoon]] is sufficient to season a dish for one person. In powdered form, the spice retains its aroma for several years, while the pure resin can preserve its aromatic properties for decades.{{sfn|Small|2011}} The odour of the pure resin is so strong that the pungent smell will contaminate other spices stored nearby if it is not stored in an airtight container.<ref name="Britannica-2024">{{Cite web |date=2024-11-06|title=Asafoetida|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/asafetida|access-date=2024-11-24|website=Britannica}}</ref>

Whether silphium truly disappeared in the 1st century or became prohibitively expensive, it appears to have been interchangeable with asafoetida in [[ancient Roman cuisine]]. Both substances were used to flavour a wide variety of dishes, and their culinary role has been compared to that of the onion in modern European cooking.{{sfn|Dalby|2013}} According to the recipe collection ''[[De re coquinaria|The Art of Cooking by Apicius]]'', compiled at the end of the 4th century, ''laser'' "from Cyrenaica or from the [[Parthians]]" was dissolved either alone in [[garum]] (fish sauce) and [[vinegar]], or combined with [[Black pepper|pepper]], [[parsley]], [[Mentha|mint]], and [[honey]]. It was also recommended to store it in a jar with [[pine nut]]s, using the nuts gradually while replacing them with fresh ones to conserve the costly spice.<ref>{{cite book |author=Apicius |url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/16439/16439-h/apicius.htm |title=De re coquinaria |at=Book I, chapters XIII and XXX |language=la |trans-title=On the Subject of Cooking |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> In the [[Near East]] during the [[Talmudic period]], asafoetida was commonly used both as a seasoning and as a remedy. Typical preparations involved dissolving it in cold or hot water,<ref>{{cite book |title=Talmud Bavli, Shabbat 140a |language=he |trans-title=Babylonian Talmud, Tractate Shabbat 140a}}</ref> or in vinegar.<ref>{{cite book |title=Mishnah Shabbat 20:3 |language=he |trans-title=Mishnah, Tractate Shabbat 20:3}}</ref>

Asafoetida and garum appear to have fallen out of common culinary use in the early [[Middle Ages]], possibly replaced by new ingredients such as [[almond milk]] or by evolving combinations of [[spice]]s and [[herb]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last=Adamson |first=Melitta Weiss |title=Regional Cuisines of Medieval Europe: A Book of Essays |date=2013 |publisher=Taylor and Francis |isbn=978-1-135-30868-1 |pages=xviii |language=en}}</ref> Border conflicts between [[Ancient Rome|Rome]] and the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian Persia]] may also have restricted resin imports or significantly increased their cost. Asafoetida later reappeared in European [[pharmacopoeia]]s under the influence of Arabic medicine, but it appears to have been less commonly used as a culinary ingredient.<ref>{{cite book |last=Dalby |first=Andrew |title=Siren Feasts: A History of Food and Gastronomy in Greece |date=1997 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-134-96985-2 |pages=141 |language=en}}</ref> Nevertheless, recipes incorporating the resin are found in the ''[[Kitāb al-ṭabīẖ]]'', a 13th-century collection from [[Al-Andalus|Muslim Iberia]], as well as in the dietary guidance of [[Maimonides]] in the ''[[Mishneh Torah]]'', indicating its continued presence in medieval Mediterranean cuisines.<ref>{{cite book |last=Laurent |first=Jean-Michel |title=Traité de cuisine arabo-andalouse dit "Anonyme andalou" |date=2016 |publisher=Les Éditions du Net |isbn=978-2-312-04291-6 |pages=223 |language=fr |trans-title=Arab-Andalusian Cookbook Known as the "Anonymous Andalusian"}}</ref> In the modern period, however, most culinary traditions involving asafoetida are associated with Asian cuisines.

[[File:Indian spices (garam masala components) (49684334741).jpg|thumb|Asafoetida (''below the centre, a very small pile of white powder''), among other spices for preparing an Indian [[curry]].|alt=Various spices of different colours, whole or ground, arranged in small piles on a white plate.]]

In [[Indian cuisine]], asafoetida is widely used to flavour curries, soups, sauces, and [[South Asian pickle|pickles]], most often in combination with other allium-like aromatics. In southern regions of the subcontinent, it is commonly used in vegetarian dishes such as ''[[sambar (dish)|sambar]]'', ''[[Rasam (dish)|rasam]]'', and certain [[lentil]]-based curries. It is also sometimes added to fish dishes and is used in the preparation of ''[[papadum]]s'', flatbreads made from [[urad bean]] flour.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=160–161}} Asafoetida is also a component of traditional [[spice mix]]es such as ''[[chaat masala]]''.{{sfn|Gayet|2010}} In addition, it is an essential seasoning in ''chivda'', a category of snack mixes originating in [[Mumbai|Bombay]]. The resin continues to be used as a substitute for garlic or onion by certain communities that avoid these foods, including [[Jain]]s, who refrain from eating roots, and some [[Brahmin]]s, who traditionally regard garlic as a prohibited [[aphrodisiac]].{{sfn|NIIR|2006|p=44}} Asafoetida is quickly heated in hot oil before it is sprinkled on the food, a practice known as [[Chaunk|tempering]].<ref name="Britannica-2024"/> It is sometimes used to harmonise sweet, sour, salty, and spicy components in food.

In Afghanistan and Pakistan, Pashtun communities traditionally use asafoetida in the preparation of ''lahndi''. Fresh meat is rubbed with a mixture of resin and salt, threaded onto tall racks, and left to air-dry. This [[dried meat]] is then consumed during the winter months.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=160–161}}

Among the peoples of the former [[Soviet Union]], the [[Turkmen people|Turkmen]] are reported to be the primary consumers of asafoetida, where it is known as {{lang|tk|чомуч}} [tchomutch]. The [[Yomut]] tribe prepares a specific condiment from it called {{lang|tk|алажа}} [alaja].<ref name="Pokhlyobkin">{{cite book |last=Pokhlyobkin |first=William Vasilyevich |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DgYoAAAAMAAJ |title=Национальные кухни наших народов |date=1996 |publisher=Tsentrpoligraf |isbn=9785218002374 |location=Moscow |pages=470–471 |language=ru |trans-title=The National Cuisines of Our Peoples |access-date=24 December 2025 |orig-date=1978}}</ref> Young plant parts and roots are also used to produce a sweet preparation known as {{lang|tk|тошоп}} [tochop]. These are boiled for several hours until the liquid thickens into a dense, dark brown to black mass resembling [[molasses]]. The mixture is strained to remove fibrous residues, which are used as animal feed. The ''tochop'' is then seasoned with butter or melted sheep fat and eaten with bread.<ref>{{cite web |last=Mamedov |first=Yusup |date=19 July 2020 |title=О полезных свойствах растительной пищи |trans-title=On the beneficial properties of plant-based foods |url=https://ashgabat.in/2020/07/19/o-poleznyh-svojstvah-rastitelnoj-pishhi/ |access-date=24 December 2025 |website=Ashgabat Innovative |language=ru}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Yagmurova |first=Myakhri |date=12 October 2020 |title=Волшебная сила «чаши джейрана» |trans-title=The magical power of the "gazelle bowl" |url=https://orient.tm/volshebnaya-sila-chashi-dzhejrana/ |access-date=24 December 2025 |website=Orient.tm |language=ru}}</ref> Asafoetida was also used by [[Kazakhs]] in [[Xinjiang]] (China), as well as by [[Dungans]] and [[Uyghurs]] living in Kazakhstan. Because of its strong odour, it was not added directly to dishes; instead, a piece of resin was used to draw one or two lines on the bottom of the cooking vessel before adding rice, vegetables, and meat. This technique was sufficient to impart an allium-like flavour to the dish.<ref name="Pokhlyobkin" />

Asafoetida was among the formerly undisclosed ingredients of [[Worcestershire sauce]], which is used in Anglo-Saxon culinary traditions in soups, boiled meats, [[steak tartare]], and pork pies from [[Wiltshire]].{{sfn|Tucker|DeBaggio|2009}} According to documented recipes, {{convert|1|impgal|L usgal|lk=in}} of the condiment contains 6.5 [[British imperial fluid drachm|imperial drachms]] (23 mL; 0.78 US fl oz) of resin dissolved in {{convert|1|imppt|mL uspt|lk=in}} of [[brandy]] at 20 percent alcohol by volume.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Shurtleff |first1=William |title=History of Worcestershire Sauce (1837–2012): Extensively Annotated Bibliography and Sourcebook |last2=Aoyagi |first2=Akiko |date=2012 |publisher=Soyinfo Center |isbn=9781928914433 |pages=213 |language=en}}</ref> Despite its very small proportion, this amount contributes to the characteristic flavour of the sauce.{{sfn|Tucker|DeBaggio|2009}}

=== Botanical drug ===
[[File:Usage vétérinaire de l'Ase Fétide.png|thumb|left|Reproduction of an [[Illuminated manuscript|illumination]] (''{{nobr|MS Pal. 586}}'', {{century|14}}, [[National Central Library of Florence|Florence]]).<br>The presence of a dog may allude to veterinary uses.|alt=Color drawing of a shrub with oval, entire leaves showing incisions on the trunk from which whitish resin droplets exude. Behind the plant, a running dog, and to the right, a woman's face, both holding a piece of resin.]]

The medicinal uses of asafoetida as a [[botanical drug]] are long-standing and widespread. Several [[Assyriology|Assyriologists]], including [[Reginald Campbell Thompson]]<ref name="Thompson"/> and [[Samuel Noah Kramer]],<ref>{{Cite book|language=fr|first=Samuel Noah|last=Kramer|author-link=Samuel Noah Kramer|title=L'Histoire commence à Sumer|trans-title=History Begins at Sumer|publisher=Flammarion|year=1994|orig-year=1956|page=87|isbn=978-2-08-081298-8}}</ref> have suggested that the resin was already known in {{Interlanguage link|Mesopotamian medicine|fr|Médecine en Mésopotamie}}. Its introduction into the Mediterranean world has been debated, but it is generally considered likely that the “Medican juice” described by [[Dioscorides]] gradually replaced Libyan ''silphium'', which had been praised by [[Hippocrates]], [[Aristotle]] and [[Theophrastus]] for similar therapeutic uses.{{Sfn|Vigier|1869|p=15}} In the [[Orient]], asafoetida is reported in foundational Ayurvedic texts such as the ''[[Charaka Samhita]]'' and the ''[[Sushruta Samhita]]'' from the early [[Common Era]].{{Sfn|George|2012|p=161}} Around the same period, the [[Talmud]] refers to the resin, notably as a treatment for “heaviness [pain] of the heart”,<ref>Talmud of Babylon, tractate Shabbat, 140a.</ref> while also noting potential risks associated with its use.<ref>Talmud of Babylon, tractate Hullin, 58b–59a.</ref> Persian medical writings by [[Rhazes]] and [[Avicenna]] describe it as a long-established medicinal substance, and these accounts continue to inform Iranian traditional practices and [[Unani medicine]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hamedi |first1=Azadeh |last2=Zarshenas |first2=Mohammad M. |last3=Sohrabpour |first3=Maryam |last4=Zargaran |first4=Arman |year=2013 |title=Herbal medicinal oils in traditional Persian medicine |journal=Pharmaceutical Biology |language=en |volume=51 |issue=9 |pages=1208–1218 |doi=10.3109/13880209.2013.777462 |pmid=23746335 }}</ref> [[Traditional Chinese medicine]] adopted the resin under Indian and Persian influence, and its properties were described by [[Li Shizhen]] in the ''[[Bencao Gangmu|Compendium of Materia Medica]]'' at the end of the {{century|16}}.{{Sfn|Laufer|1919|p=358}}

In Western medicine, asafoetida was transmitted from medieval herbals into early modern pharmacopoeias and formed part of standard medical practice until the development of [[pharmaceutical chemistry]].<ref group="note">The product thus benefited from a [[monograph]] in the following works: ''Deutsches Arzneibuch 6'' (Germany, 1926), ''Nederlandse Pharmacopee V'' (Netherlands, 1926), ''Pharmacopée belge IV'' (Belgium, 1930), ''Pharmacopoea Helvetica V'' (Switzerland, 1933), ''Pharmacopeia of the United States of America XI'' (United States, 1935), ''Farmacopea Ufficiale del Regno d'Italia VI'' (Italy, 1940), ''British Pharmaceutical Codex V'' (United Kingdom, 1949), ''Indian Pharmaceutical Codex'' (India, 1953), ''Farmacopea Oficial Española IX'' (Spain, 1954), ''National Formulary X'' (United States, 1955), ''British Herbal Pharmacopoeia'' (United Kingdom, 1983), ''Pharmacopée française X'' (France, 1988), ''Pharmacopoeia of the People's Republic of China'' (China, 1988).</ref>{{Sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=703}} It is now mainly regarded as a traditional remedy. In France, asafoetida is included in List A of medicinal plants, for which sale is restricted to pharmacists, and is indicated for use in traditional European and [[Overseas France|overseas]] medicine.<ref>{{Cite book |author=Agence nationale de sécurité du médicament et des produits de santé |author-link=Agence nationale de sécurité du médicament et des produits de santé |url=https://ansm.sante.fr/uploads/2021/03/25/liste-a-des-plantes-medicinales-utilisees-traditionnellement-4.pdf |title=Liste A des plantes médicinales utilisées traditionnellement |date=January 2021 |page=5 |language=fr |trans-title=List A of medicinal plants traditionally used |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

The principal traditional indications for the resin concern the [[digestive system|gastrointestinal tract]]. In European, Iranian and Indian traditions, it is described as a [[carminative]] and [[antispasmodic]]. An aqueous extract of the dried gum has also been administered orally as an [[anthelmintic]], while Chinese medicine employs it as an intestinal [[antiparasitic]].{{Sfn|Ross|2005|p=224}} In Ayurveda, it is recommended roasted in ''[[ghee]]'' (clarified butter) for flatulence and related gastrointestinal complaints, a preparation believed to reduce irritation.{{Sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} Asafoetida has likewise been used in [[veterinary medicine]] for similar purposes.{{Sfn|NIIR|2006|p=743}}<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dun |first1=Finlay |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3AgBU7WYp5IC |title=Veterinary Medicines: Their Actions and Uses |date=1889 |publisher=David Douglas |page=254 |language=en}}</ref> [[Garcia de Orta]] recounts the following anecdote:
{{Blockquote|A Portuguese from [[Vijayanagara|Besnagar]] had a very expensive horse, but it suffered from gas, and the King did not wish to buy it for this reason. The Portuguese cured it by feeding it ''imgu'' [asafoetida] with flour. The King bought it at a good price after its recovery, and asked the man with what he had treated it. He replied that he had given it ''imgu''. The King retorted: "Do not be surprised, for you gave it the food of the gods, the nectar, as the poets say." The man then replied, but softly and in Portuguese, that they would have done better to call it the food of demons.|author=Garcia de Orta|source=''Colóquio sétimo: Do Altiht''{{Sfn|Orta|1913|loc=ch. 7|pp=40–52}}}}

[[File:Assa foetida2.JPG|thumb|upright|Asafoetida in a vial.|alt=Pieces of resin of varying sizes and brownish-pink color in a vial labeled "Assa foetida – Ferula assa-foetida".]]

Asafoetida has also been traditionally associated with [[expectorant]] effects and uses related to the [[respiratory system]]. In Ayurvedic and Iranian traditions, it is described as beneficial in cases of [[asthma]]. It has been used in Afghanistan, India and Saudi Arabia in the treatment of [[whooping cough]] and [[bronchitis]].{{Sfn|Ross|2005|p=224}} In ancient Rome, it is reported to have replaced ''silphium'' in treatments for [[tuberculosis]] and chronic [[cough]]s.{{Sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} Sedative or calming properties have also been attributed to it: it has been consumed in India and Afghanistan for [[hysteria]], and regarded as a [[sedative]] in Nepal.{{Sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} Its use has also been reported in traditional Iranian{{Sfn|Iranshahy|Iranshahi|2011|p=2}} and Moroccan medicine for [[epilepsy]], the latter recommending chewing the gum.{{Sfn|Ross|2005|p=224}}

Asafoetida has further been employed in contexts related to [[sexual health]] and [[reproductive medicine]]. It has a long-standing reputation as an [[aphrodisiac]] and has been reported as such in Brazil and the United States. In India, a hot extract has been used as an [[emmenagogue]], while in Malaysia the gum has been chewed in cases of [[amenorrhea]].{{Sfn|Ross|2005|p=224}} A study of traditional [[birth control]] practices in [[Alexandria]] (Egypt) during the 1970s found that more than half of the women surveyed reported using asafoetida as a [[contraceptive]], applied to the vaginal walls shortly before or after sexual intercourse.<ref>{{Cite book |last=El-Dean Mahmoud |first=A. A. G. |title=Study of indigenous (folk ways) birth control methods in Alexandria |publisher=University of Alexandria – Higher Institute of Nursing |year=1972 |language=en |type=PhD thesis}}</ref> During the [[Spanish flu|influenza pandemic]] following [[World War I]], the resin also gained some popularity as an [[antiviral]] remedy, for reasons that remain unclear.<ref name="Shokoohinia2013"/>

Finally, asafoetida has been used externally in a variety of traditional applications. Iranian medical practice prescribes it mixed with [[honey]] for toothache, in [[olive oil]] for relief of [[otitis]] pain, as a [[cerate]] for [[corn (medicine)|corns]] and [[wart]]s, and as a [[poultice]] in the treatment of [[alopecia]].{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}}

== Perfume and incense ==
Extracts of the gum-resin and the essential oil are used in [[perfumery]], primarily as a [[Fixative (perfumery)|fixative]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Groom |first=Nigel |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=krX1CAAAQBAJ |title=The Perfume Handbook |publisher=Springer Netherlands |year=1992 |isbn=978-94-011-2296-2 |page=16 |language=en |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> The asafoetida [[absolute (perfumery)|absolute]] is obtained by alcoholic extraction. It forms a semi-solid reddish-brown mass with a pronounced alliaceous odour. Beneath this initial note, it is described as having a softer, balsamic character. Upon desiccation, a component with similarities to [[vanillin]] becomes apparent. [[Ferulic acid]], present in relatively large amounts, is chemically related to the aromatic compound [[ferulaldehyde]], associated with the characteristic aroma of [[maple syrup]], as well as to [[isoeugenol]] and vanillin. Steam distillation of the extract can reduce sulphurous notes, yielding a material valued for its fixative properties. At low concentrations, asafoetida may contribute distinctive nuances to rose accords and heavy oriental compositions.

The essential oil ranges from pale yellow to yellow–orange in colour and has a strong garlic-like odour that is often described as acrid. It does not exhibit the same fixative capacity or balsamic base notes as the absolute.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Arctander |first=Steffen |title=Perfume and flavor materials of natural origin |publisher=Lulu.com |year=2017 |isbn=0-244-32921-4 |page=61 |language=en |orig-year=1960}}</ref> Asafoetida notes have been reported in fragrances such as ''[[Tendre Poison]]'' by [[Dior]], ''[[Cabochard]]'' by [[Madame Grès]], and ''Molinard'' by [[Molinard]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Asafoetida Perfumes |url=https://www.fragrantica.com/notes/Asafoetida-278.html |access-date=24 December 2025 |website=fragrantica.com |language=en}}</ref>

Asafoetida has also been burnt as [[incense]] for ritual, therapeutic, or symbolic purposes. This practice remains relatively limited in comparison with its culinary and medicinal uses and has not achieved the prominence of [[galbanum]], which is cited as a component of sacred incense in the [[Bible]]. Both gum-resins are nevertheless rich in sesquiterpene coumarins, which may act as precursors of odouriferous compounds formed through [[pyrolysis]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Niebler |first=Johannes |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-26932-0_4 |title=Springer Handbook of Odor |publisher=Springer International Publishing |year=2017 |isbn=978-3-319-26932-0 |editor=Andrea Buettner |series=Springer Handbooks |pages=13–14 |language=en |chapter=Incense Materials |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-26932-0_4 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

In Iran, in continuity with the Arabic pharmacological tradition,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Levey |first=Martin |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LtYUAAAAIAAJ |title=Early Arabic pharmacology: An introduction based on ancient and medieval sources |publisher=Brill |year=1973 |isbn=90-04-03796-9 |page=159 |language=en |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> asafoetida has sometimes been used in fumigations for abortive purposes.{{sfn|Barzegar|Salim|Badr|Khosravi|2020}} It has also been reported in [[Eastern esotericism|esotericism]], where it has been attributed various symbolic or ritual properties, including [[exorcism|exorcistic]] functions. The {{century|18}} [[occultism|occultist]] [[Karl von Eckartshausen]], for example, listed it among the substances used in fumigations intended to “provoke apparitions” or to “banish spectres”.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dannaway |first=Frederick R. |date=December 1, 2010 |title=Strange Fires, Weird Smokes and Psychoactive Combustibles: Entheogens and Incense in Ancient Traditions |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/02791072.2010.10400711 |journal=Journal of Psychoactive Drugs |language=en |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=485–497 |doi=10.1080/02791072.2010.10400711 |issn=0279-1072 |pmid=21305913 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

=== Pesticide and other uses ===
Asafoetida has also been reported to have [[agriculture|agricultural]] applications, including use as a natural [[pesticide]] or plant protection product. Medieval sources describe its recommendation for controlling [[caterpillar]]s on vegetables, its use as an [[infusion]] applied to [[squash (plant)|squash]] affected by worms, and its combination with [[vinegar]] to treat stored [[lentil]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zadoks |first=Jan C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4ddfAQAAQBAJ |title=Crop protection in medieval agriculture: studies in pre-modern organic agriculture |publisher=Sidestone Press |year=2013 |isbn=978-90-8890-232-1 |page=173 |language=en |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> In Afghanistan, it has been used against [[nematode]]s, and in India against [[termite]]s. Its [[Animal repellent|repellent]] properties have also been employed to deter animals such as cats, dogs, rabbits, or game.{{Sfn|Kubeczka|Bohn|1998|p=703}}

The [[insecticide]] properties of asafoetida essential oil have been investigated for the control of the [[black bean aphid]] in Iran.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bezerra |first1=L. L. A. |last2=Azevedo |first2=F. R. |last3=Evangelista-Júnior |first3=W. S. |last4=Paula-Filho |first4=F. J. |last5=Navarro |first5=D. M. a. F. |last6=Santos |first6=E. F. |date=2023 |title=Efficiency of essential oils in the control of the black bean aphid Aphis craccivora Koch (Hemiptera: Aphididae) |url=https://www.scielo.br/j/bjb/a/whdfbFKrLhSzcNQM4PmSbjv/?lang=en |journal=Brazilian Journal of Biology |language=en |volume=83 |article-number=e275069 |doi=10.1590/1519-6984.275069 |pmid=37792748 |issn=1519-6984}}</ref>

In southern India, an experimental application of the resin has been reported as a plant protection treatment in crops of [[squash (plant)|squash]], [[eggplant]], [[tomato]]es, [[sesame]], and [[peanut]]s. In this context, asafoetida is diluted in irrigation water at a rate of one kilogram per [[acre]], with reports of reduced reliance on synthetic pesticides and increased yields.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/success_stories/pdf/2010/farm%20innovation/An%20experiment%20with%20asafoetida.pdf |title=An experiment with asafoetida leads to a crop protection technique |language=en |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

In [[Pakistan]], treatment of eggplant and [[watermelon]] crops with a suspension of asafoetida combined with powdered species of [[algae]] has been reported to suppress the [[plant pathogen]]ic fungi ''[[Fusarium solani]]'' and ''[[Macrophomina phaseolina]]'', as well as the root-knot nematode ''[[Meloidogyne incognita]]''. Treated plants were described as having greater shoot length and mass and earlier [[fruiting]] than those in the [[control group]] or those treated with a synthetic [[fungicide]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baloch |first1=Ghulam Nabi |last2=Tariq |first2=Samrah |last3=Ehteshamul-Haque |first3=Syed |last4=Athar |first4=Mohammad |last5=Sultana |first5=Viqar |last6=Ara |first6=Jehan |year=2013 |title=Management of root diseases of eggplant and watermelon with the application of asafoetida and seaweeds |url=https://ojs.openagrar.de/index.php/JABFQ/article/view/2263 |journal=Journal of Applied Botany and Food Quality |language=en |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=138–142 |doi=10.5073/JABFQ.2013.086.019 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

The use of asafoetida as a natural [[fertiliser]] has produced mixed results. An experiment conducted in India on [[melon]] crops reported no significant effects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Randhawa |first1=K. S. |last2=Singh |first2=K. |year=1970 |title=Influence of foliar applications of certain chemicals on sex-behaviour, fruit-set and quality of muskmelon (Cucumis melo L.) |url=https://eurekamag.com/research/000/117/000117006.php |journal=Plant Science |volume=2 |language=en |issue=2 |pages=118–122 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref> By contrast, a study conducted in China reported that the addition of asafoetida extract to the [[growing medium]] of ''[[Pleurotus eryngii]]'' accelerated [[mycelium]] and [[sporophore]] development and was associated with changes in the [[organoleptic]] and nutritional characteristics of the mushrooms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Feng |first1=Zuoshan |last2=Bai |first2=Yujia |last3=Lu |first3=Fanglin |last4=Huang |first4=Wenshu |date=December 29, 2009 |title=Effect of Asafoetida Extract on Growth and Quality of Pleurotus ferulic |journal=International Journal of Molecular Sciences |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=41–51 |doi=10.3390/ijms11010041 |doi-access=free |issn=1422-0067 |pmc=2820988 |pmid=20162000 }}</ref>

In industrial contexts, asafoetida diluted in an aqueous salt solution has been investigated as a potential corrosion inhibitor for steel.<ref>{{Cite journal |year=2019 |title=Green corrosion inhibition of mild steel by Asafoetida extract in 3.5% NaCl |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214785319307783 |journal=Materials Today: Proceedings |language=en |volume=14 |pages=590–601 |doi=10.1016/j.matpr.2019.04.183 |issn=2214-7853 |access-date=24 December 2025}}</ref>

== Economic aspects ==
=== Production and trade ===
Information on the global production and trade of asafoetida is limited, as systematic data collection by producing or importing countries is lacking. The resin remains a wild-harvested product, and large-scale cultivation has not yet been developed using standardised scientific methods. [[Productivity]] could potentially be improved through the selection of high-[[Agricultural productivity|yield]] varieties and the refinement of [[Agronomy|agronomic]] practices. Harvesting and processing methods remain largely traditional and could be further developed to increase output and improve resin quality. Contamination of the raw product with foreign matter is reported to be relatively high.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=160–161}}

Afghanistan is the principal exporting country of asafoetida. Most production is collected in [[Herat Province]], near the Iranian border. Reliable information on cultivated areas or harvested volumes is unavailable, as production and trade are not centrally organised. Estimates suggest that annual production amounted to {{convert|500|to|600|tonnes}} in the 1990s, before declining as a result of prolonged political instability.{{sfn|George|2012|pp=153–154}} During the 2010s, production was reported to have increased again, reaching more than {{convert|335|tonnes}} in 2017.<ref>{{cite web |date=December 12, 2018 |title=آنقوزه 'بیشتر از تریاک' برای افغانستان دلار می‌آورد؟ |trans-title=Does asafoetida bring more dollars to Afghanistan than opium? |url=https://www.bbc.com/persian/afghanistan-46518911 |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=BBC News Persian |language=fa}}</ref>

[[File:Asafoetida packed for export - Iran.jpg|thumb|left|Crate of raw asafoetida intended for export in an Iranian warehouse.|alt=Close-up of a wooden crate lined with white fabric and filled with resin pieces of varying sizes, light yellow to dark brown in colour.]]
Iran ranks second among producing countries, with output reaching approximately {{convert|110|tonnes}} in favourable years. Asafoetida is mainly harvested in the regions around [[Mashhad]] and [[Kerman]].{{sfn|George|2012|pp=153–154}} Harvesting often constitutes a supplementary activity for rural populations, alongside [[agriculture]] and [[animal husbandry]]. In [[South Khorasan Province]], one of the country’s driest and least developed regions, asafoetida represents the most economically significant [[medicinal plant]]. Annual production in the province ranges from 15 to {{convert|60|tonnes}}, over an area exceeding {{convert|100000|ha}}. Approximately 99% of the resin is exported. In 2016, traditional harvesters reportedly received between 25 and 70 USD per kilogram of dried resin, while the same quantity sold for between 130 and 170 USD on international markets.{{sfn|Golmohammadi|2016|pp=12–13}} Wild harvesting of asafoetida in protected areas is prohibited but has been reported to occur, for example in the [[Bakhtegan Lake]] region.<ref>{{cite web |author=Rasool Haji Bagheri |title=برداشت غیرقانونی آنغوزه در پناهگاه حیات وحش بختگان برگرفته از |trans-title=Illegal harvesting of asafoetida in the Bakhtegan wildlife sanctuary |url=http://didebanstahban.blog.ir/1394/07/24/%D8%A8%D8%B1%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%B4%D8%AA-%D8%BA%DB%8C%D8%B1%D9%82%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%88%D9%86%DB%8C-%D8%A2%D9%86%D8%BA%D9%88%D8%B2%D9%87-%D8%AF%D8%B1-%D9%BE%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%87%DA%AF%D8%A7%D9%87-%D8%AD%DB%8C%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%88%D8%AD%D8%B4-%D8%A8%D8%AE%D8%AA%DA%AF%D8%A7%D9%86 |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=didebanstahban.blog.ir |language=fa}}</ref>

Countries of [[Central Asia]] were not traditionally producers of asafoetida. This has changed following declines in Afghan output, and Uzbekistan, [[Tajikistan]] and [[Kyrgyzstan]] are now among the suppliers to Indian importers.<ref name="TDB2017">{{cite web |author=Anishaa Kumar |date=July 2017 |title=From Afghanistan with love |url=https://www.thedollarbusiness.com/magazine/from-afghanistan-with-love/46065 |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=The Dollar Business |language=en}}</ref> One of the main wholesalers on the Indian subcontinent, ''Laljee Godhoo & Co.'', reported in 2018 that more than half of its asafoetida imports originated from [[Kazakhstan]].<ref name="ET2018">{{cite web |author=Shailesh Menon |date=March 27, 2018 |title=Meet the hing kings, who brought the spice to India over a century ago |url=https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/industry/cons-products/food/meet-the-hing-kings-who-brought-the-spice-to-india-over-a-century-ago/articleshow/63471891.cms |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=The Economic Times |language=en}}</ref> In Uzbekistan, an association of asafoetida producers and exporters was established in 2018, with plans to expand cultivation in areas with suitable climatic conditions and to develop technologies for the domestic production of medicines and plant protection products derived from the resin.<ref>{{cite web |date=March 31, 2018 |title=В Узбекистане появится Ассоциация производителей и экспортеров ферулы |trans-title=Uzbekistan to create an association of ferula producers and exporters |url=https://podrobno.uz/cat/economic/v-uzbekistane-poyavitsya-assotsiatsiya-proizvoditeley-i-eksporterov-feruly/ |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=podrobno.uz |language=ru}}</ref>

[[India]] is the largest importer of asafoetida. In 2007, it imported {{convert|686|tonnes}} of resin, valued at 16.5 million USD.{{sfn|George|2012|p=153}} Import values continued to increase, reaching 89 million USD in 2017,<ref name="TDB2017"/> corresponding to an estimated 6–8% of the Indian spice market.<ref name="ET2018"/> In that year, one kilogram of Afghan white asafoetida cost approximately 62 USD, while transport and insurance from [[Kabul]] to [[Mumbai]] amounted to 131 USD. The resin, acquired at a total cost of 193 USD per kilogram, was resold domestically for about 242 USD.<ref name="TDB2017"/> Most imported asafoetida is processed in India, with a portion re-exported after processing. The price of the processed composite product is considerably lower than that of the raw resin; for example, in 2010 it averaged 9.54 USD per kilogram at export, compared with 42.18 USD per kilogram at import. Export volumes vary substantially and peaked at {{convert|723|tonnes}} in 2005–2006. India’s principal export destinations include the [[United Arab Emirates]], followed by the [[United States]], the [[United Kingdom]], [[Singapore]], [[Thailand]] and [[Malaysia]].{{sfn|George|2012|pp=153–154}} Since 2020, experimental efforts have been underway to introduce the cultivation of asafoetida in the [[Himalayas]] of northern India.<ref name="IE2020">{{cite web |author=Anjali Marar |date=October 28, 2020 |title=Explained: Why scientists are trying to cultivate asafoetida or heeng in the Indian Himalayas |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/why-scientists-are-trying-to-cultivate-heeng-in-the-indian-himalayas-6792923/ |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=The Indian Express |language=en}}</ref> ''The domestic market for this processed asafoetida is highly regionalized; for example, in Central India, FMCG manufacturers like Pushp Masale hold up to 58% of the packaged asafoetida market share''<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 May 2026 |title=Pushp Brand files IPO papers with SEBI for OFS-only issue |url=https://upstox.com/news/market-news/ipo/pushp-brand-files-ipo-papers-with-sebi-for-ofs-only-issue/article-194369/ |url-status=live |work=Upstox}}</ref>''.''

=== Adulteration and quality standards ===
Asafoetida is frequently mixed with foreign substances and is widely regarded as one of the most commonly [[Adulteration|adulterated]] spices.<ref name="regencyspices2014">{{cite web |date=July 8, 2014 |title=Asafoetida, the most adulterated spice in existence |url=https://regencyspices.hk/blogs/spicetrade/asafoetida-the-most-adulterated-spice-in-existence |access-date=December 24, 2025 |website=regencyspices.hk |language=en}}</ref> Materials such as [[clay]], [[sand]] or stone are sometimes found mixed with the product. Because resin extraction methods are largely rudimentary, the exudate often contains soil, dust or fragments of plant material.{{sfn|George|2012|p=160}} Historical sources frequently note problems of product falsification. [[Pliny the Elder|Pliny]] reported the adulteration of Persian ''laser'' with gum, [[sagapenum]] or crushed [[fava bean]]. [[Engelbert Kaempfer|Kaempfer]] mentioned the fraudulent addition of [[silt]].<ref name="Kaempfer-1712" /> Accounts from the {{Century name from decade or year|1800s}} describe products sold on European markets that were manufactured entirely from [[pitch (resin)|pitch]] and the juice of [[garlic]].<ref name="Déniau-1868" /> In the {{Century name from decade or year|2000s}}, the weight of the resin has been reported to be artificially increased through the addition of substances such as [[gypsum]], [[rosin]], [[gum arabic]], [[chalk]], [[wheat flour]] or [[barley]], as well as slices of [[potato]] and other materials.{{sfn|Panda|2010|p=220}} Exudates from other plant species, not necessarily belonging to the genus ''Ferula'', are also reported to be incorporated and sold to less informed buyers.{{sfn|George|2012|p=160}}

As the principal importer of asafoetida, [[India]] has established regulations intended to limit resin adulteration. Under the 1954 ''Prevention of Food Adulteration Act'', the following quality standards apply to asafoetida products:{{sfn|George|2012|p=160}}

* ''Hing'' must not contain more than 15% total ash; ash insoluble in dilute [[hydrochloric acid]] must not exceed 2.5%; the alcoholic extract must not be less than 12%; and the [[starch]] content must not exceed 1% of the total mass;
* ''Hingra'' must not contain more than 20% total ash; ash insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid must not exceed 8%; the alcoholic extract must not be less than 50%; and the starch content must not exceed 1% of the total mass;
* composite products must not contain more than 10% total ash; ash insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid must not exceed 1.5%; and the alcoholic extract must not be less than 5%. The addition of [[rosin]], [[galbanum]], [[ammoniacum|ammoniac gum]] or any other foreign resin, [[dye]]s derived from [[coal tar]] or mineral [[pigment]]s is prohibited.

For consumers, several approximate methods are sometimes described for assessing product purity. When placed in the flame of an alcohol lamp, asafoetida ignites and burns rapidly, in a manner comparable to [[camphor]], with any non-combustible residue indicating impurities. In addition, asafoetida dissolved in water typically produces a milky white colour; the appearance of other colours may indicate the presence of adulterants or added colourants.<ref name="regencyspices2014"/>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Cabbage roll
======================================================================

{{short description|Dish of cabbage leaves with a filling}}
{{Unreliable sources|date=January 2021}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2025}}
[[File:Töltött káposzta, 2.jpg|thumb|Hungarian cabbage rolls]]

A '''cabbage roll''' is a dish consisting of cooked [[cabbage]] leaves wrapped around a variety of [[stuffing|fillings]]. It is common to the cuisines of [[Central Europe|Central]], [[Eastern Europe|Eastern]], and [[Southeastern Europe]] and much of [[Western Asia]], [[Northern China]], and parts of [[North Africa]].
Meat fillings are traditional in Europe, and include [[beef]], [[lamb (food)|lamb]], or [[pork]] seasoned with [[garlic]], [[onion]], and spices. [[Cereal|Grains]] such as [[rice]] and [[barley]], [[edible mushroom|mushrooms]], and vegetables are often included as well. Fermented cabbage leaves are used for wrapping, particularly in southeastern Europe. In Asia, seafood, tofu, and [[shiitake mushroom]]s may also be used. [[Chinese cabbage]] is often used as a wrapping.

Cabbage leaves are stuffed with the filling and then [[baking|baked]], [[simmering|simmered]], or [[steaming|steamed]] in a covered pot and generally eaten warm, often accompanied with a [[sauce]]. The sauce varies widely by cuisine. In Sweden and Finland, stuffed cabbage is served with [[lingonberry jam]], which is both sweet and tart. In Central and Eastern Europe, [[tomato]]-based sauces and sour cream are typical. In Lebanon, the cabbage is stuffed with rice and minced meat and only rolled to the size of a cigar. It is usually served with a side dish of [[yogurt]] and a type of lemon and olive oil [[vinaigrette]] seasoned with garlic and dried mint.

The cabbage roll is a staple in [[Romanian cuisine]], with variations of the recipe and sizing depending on the region, but typically taking up to six hours to cook. Traditionally made with pork, beef, bacon, rice, spices and aromatics, the cabbage rolls are broiled in a tomato sauce and served with [[polenta]], sour cream and spicy pickled peppers.

Cooking textbook author Nancy Krcek stated that the origins of the dish are unclear and that it is possible multiple groups of people invented it at the same time.<ref>{{cite web|author=Allen, Nancy Krcek|url=https://www.pearsoned.com/stuffed-cabbage-recipes-history-food/|title=Stuffed cabbage: From humble beginnings to staple comfort food|publisher=[[Pearson Education]]|date=27 December 2016|quote=Many cultures claim to have [...] her boiled cabbage leaves.|access-date=16 May 2020|archive-date=1 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801034418/https://www.pearsoned.com/stuffed-cabbage-recipes-history-food/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Another cooking book author, Malgorzata Caprari, stated it is believed that credit is owed to the poorer inhabitants of Central and Eastern European countries. Due to the widespread cultivation of cabbage in these regions, it is likely the cultures who inhabited them were the original inventors of this dish.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Caprari |first=Malgorzata |url=https://www.polana.com/collections/bookstore/products/book-domowa-kuchnia-polska-malgorzata-caprari |title=Domowa kuchnia polska |date=2 June 2021 |publisher=Wydawnictwo RM |publication-date=2 June 2021 |access-date=15 March 2024 |archive-date=15 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240315083628/https://www.polana.com/collections/bookstore/products/book-domowa-kuchnia-polska-malgorzata-caprari |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Cabbage rolls have found their way into popular culture, becoming one of the most recognizable dishes in Central and Eastern European cuisine. They often appear in literature and films as a symbol of homey comfort and tradition.

A version called [[holishkes]] is traditionally eaten by Jews on [[Simchat Torah]].<ref name="Lavine">{{cite news|author=Eileen M. Lavine|url=http://momentmag.com/moment/issues/2011/10/talkofthetable.html|title=Stuffed Cabbage: A Comfort Food for All Ages|work=Moment Magazine|date=September–October 2011|access-date=3 October 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111011080758/http://momentmag.com/moment/issues/2011/10/talkofthetable.html|archive-date=11 October 2011}}</ref> Recipes vary depending on region; for example, northern Poles prefer a savory sauce, while Galicia, Hungary and Ukraine favor sweet-and-sour.<ref name="Lavine" />

In Asia, cabbage rolls have been adapted into various regional cuisines. In China, they are sometimes prepared with a filling of minced pork, shrimp, and vegetables, seasoned with soy sauce, ginger, and sesame oil, then steamed or simmered in a light broth. A similar dish exists in Japan, known as {{lang|ja|ロールキャベツ}} ({{translit|ja|rōru kyabetsu}}), often stuffed with ground meat and simmered in a tomato-based or dashi broth.

* ''Kələm dolması'' – Azerbaijan<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://azcookbook.com/azeri/k%C9%99l%C9%99m-dolmasi/ |title=Kələm Dolması |date=6 February 2010 |access-date=12 December 2020 |work=AZCookbook|language=az }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://resept.az/kelem-dolmasi/ |title=Kələm dolması |date=8 December 2012 |access-date=12 December 2020 |work=Resept.az |language=az }}</ref>
* ''Kaghambi tolma'' (կաղամբի տոլմա) – Armenia
* ''Tolma'' (ტოლმა) – Georgia
* ''Dolmeye kalam'' (cabbage dolma) – Iran
* ''Malfoof mahshi'' (ملفوف محشي) – the Levant
* ''Mahashi malfoof'' (محاشي ملفوف) - The Arab states of the Gulf
* ''Mahshi kromb'' (محشى كرمب) – Egypt and Sudan
* ''{{interlanguage link|Kohlroulade|de}}'' and ''Krautwickel'' – Germany and Austria

===Europe===

====Armenia====
{{main|Dolma (food)}}
[[File:Hnaberd dolma festival (1).jpg|thumb|Armenian cabbage rolls]]
In [[Armenian cuisine]], cabbage rolls are stuffed with [[Bean|beans]] and tart fruits. It is wrapped with cabbage leaves, and stuffed with [[Red bean|red beans]], [[Chickpea|chickpeas]], [[Lentil|lentils]], [[cracked wheat]], [[tomato paste]], [[onion]] and multiple spices, mostly the spice mix of ''[[wiktionary:չաման|chaimen]]'', which is also used to coat [[Pastirma|basturma]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Armenian Spice Recipe - "Chaimen" |url=https://www.thegutsygourmet.net/chaimen.html |website=The Gutsy Gourmet}}</ref> Cabbage rolls are called ''Pasuts tolma'' (պասուց տոլմա; Lenten dolma) in [[Armenian language|Armenian]] where they are made of seven different grains – chickpea, bean, lentil, cracked wheat, pea, rice and maize.<ref name="Recipe Corner: Basoots Dolma (Lenten Tolma)">{{cite web |last1=Vartanian Datian |first1=Christine |title=Armenian Pasuts Dolma Recipe |url=https://mirrorspectator.com/2020/06/04/recipe-corner-basoots-dolma-lenten-tolma/ |website=The Armenian Mirror Spectator |date=4 June 2020 |access-date=25 December 2023}}</ref> Armenian cooks sometimes use [[rose hip]] syrup or [[grape syrup]] to flavor stuffed cabbage rolls.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Duguid |first1=Naomi |title=Taste of Persia: A Cook's Travels Through Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Iran, and Kurdistan |date=6 September 2016 |publisher=Artisan Books |isbn=978-1-57965-727-7 |pages=400 }}</ref>

====Azerbaijan and Turkey====
[[File:Kalam dolmasi Azerbaijan.jpg|thumb|right|Azerbaijani cabbage roll ({{langx|az|kələm dolması }})]]
{{main|Sarma (food)}}
Stuffed cabbage leaves ({{langx|az|kələm dolması}}; {{langx|tr|lahana dolması}}) are popular all year in Azerbaijan and Turkey, but especially in winter when other vegetables are less plentiful. The stuffing usually consists of rice and herbs such as coriander, mint and dill, onions and meat, although there is a variation, ''yalançı dolma'' (Azerbaijani), ''yalancı dolma'' (Turkish) ("fake" ''dolma''), which is meat-free.<ref>Azerbaijani Cuisine—National Tourism Promotion Bureau, 2017.</ref>

==== Balkans ====
{{main|Sarma (food)}}
Cabbage rolls are a culinary standard in [[Turkey]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Greece]], [[North Macedonia]], [[Albania]], [[Serbia]], [[Montenegro]], [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]], [[Croatia]], [[Slovenia]], [[Romania]], [[Moldova]] and [[Hungary]]. They are traditionally made with leaves of brined cabbage stuffed with ground beef, pork and rice, while meat can also be omitted or substituted with crushed walnuts, pine nuts and raisins. In [[Bulgaria]], [[Romania]], [[Hungary]], and parts of [[Greece]], cabbage rolls are a favorite dish during Christmas time and other non-fasting holidays. In some countries, such as [[Serbia]], cabbage rolls are traditionally simmered at length in a paprika-based sauce with chunks of smoked bacon.

==== Romania and Moldova ====
{{main|Sarma (food)}}
In Romania, there are different variations and sizing depending on the region.
Sarmale are Romanian stuffed cabbage rolls traditionally served on [[Christmas]] and [[New Year's Eve]] but also served throughout the year at weddings, baptism parties, and other large celebrations. It is considered a winter dish and starts with the orthodox celebration of St. Ignatie day – Preparing the Pig, when Romanians traditionally slaughter the pigs for Christmas. 
Ground pork or beef is mixed with sauteed caramelized onions and rice, stuffed in a cabbage leaf, pickled sauerkraut leaf or grape leaf. For flavor, they usually consist of layers with bacon, smoked ribs, or smoked sausage. 
Seasoned with spices and aromatics, it is traditionally served with [[polenta]], sour cream and pickled spicy peppers.

==== Hungary ====
{{main|Sarma (food)}}
''Töltött káposzta'', ''szárma'' or ''sarma'', the traditional Hungarian cabbage roll, can be made from sweet or sauerkraut cabbage leaves filled with a mixture of minced pork meat (or sometimes [[Turkey (bird)|turkey]]), eggs, onions, and rice seasoned with caraway, salt, and pepper. In [[Transylvania]] and [[Great Hungarian Plain|Alföld]] regions, it is called ''takart''. The Hungarian version often contains minced [[paprika]] and is served with [[sour cream]] on top. It used to be seasoned with saffron. Many Hungarians serve this food during Christmas and New Year's Eve, although it is a common dish throughout the year (a sweet version during summer and fall, and a sour version during winter and spring). The sour stuffed cabbage is part of the traditional Hungarian pig slaughter menu and it is said that eating this during the holiday season will bring wealth and health for the new year.

There are many regional variations: in [[Zakarpattia Oblast|Kárpátalja]] and Nyírség, for example, they make small töltött káposzta for weddings.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Márta |first=Mondik |date=22 May 2023 |title=Öt érdekesség a kárpátaljai töltött káposztáról |url=https://karpatalja.ma/karpatalja/szines/ot-erdekesseg-a-karpataljai-toltott-kaposztarol/ |access-date=8 May 2024 |website=Kárpátalja.ma |language=hu}}</ref>

Although the rolling up of cabbages was first mentioned in the 1695 book of [[Miklós Tótfalusi Kis]], a similar dish, ''káposztás hús'' (not to be confused with ''[[székelykáposzta]]''), was known long before it. 

Káposztás hús was very popular. This traditional cabbage stew had a special significance to [[Hungarians|Hungarian]] people. The 17th-century manuscript cookbook of the [[Csáktornya]] court, written sometime before 1662, begins its list of dishes with the phrase, "The cabbage meat is the coat of arms of Hungary". "In the old days, there was no dish more suitable for Hungarians than cabbage", said [[Péter Apor]], praising it as the meal of the lords. Around 1730, [[Matthias Bel|Mátyás Bél]] also called "Cabbage with bacon, the coat of arms of Hungary". Lippay also calls it the "coat of arms of Hungary" and states that [[Hungarians|Hungarian]] people cannot live without it. [[Kelemen Mikes]], when traveling to [[Turkey]], also writes back, "The beautifully written letter pleases the mind, as do these cabbages with dill and sour cream". Mikes also finds it fitting for a coat of arms: "Even if I had no other praise to say about it, is it not enough to say that it is the Transylvanian coat of arms?"

The cabbage roll itself also appears as a motif in the culture. In [[Zsigmond Móricz]]'s short story "Tragedy", the protagonist János Kis dies while eating stuffed cabbage, of which he had vowed to eat fifty.

==== Poland ====
{{main|Gołąbki}}
Stuffed cabbage rolls are a popular Polish dish. Pork and beef mixed with rice or barley are nestled in a cabbage leaf and cooked in the oven or on the stove until tender.

[[File:00101 Rindfleisch - Kohlroulade, Podkarpackie.JPG|thumb|Gołąbki in tomato sauce]]

The cabbage rolls are called ''gołąbki'' in Polish, ''holubky'' by Czechs and Slovaks, or ''sarma'' / ''сарма'' by Serbs, Croatians and Bulgarians. The sauce is often the main difference in regional variations.
In a less popular version called ''leniwe gołąbki'' (lazy cabbage rolls) the ingredients are chopped, combined and baked or fried.

==== Ukraine ====
In Ukraine, the filling of ''holubtsi'' varies throughout the country. In the [[Carpathian]] region corn grits are used, whereas in the [[Poltava]] area [[buckwheat]] groats are preferred. The cereal is lightly cooked, mixed with fried [[onions]], [[shkvarky]] ([[Pork rind|pork cracklings]]) or raw minced meat. The mixture is combined with spices and seasonings, and is then used as the filling for steamed fresh or pickled cabbage leaves. In spring cabbage leaves are often replaced with fresh [[beetroot]] leaves, and in the southwest – with fresh young grape leaves. The ''holubtsi'' are lightly fried and then stewed with sour cream, or tomato, mushroom or some other sauce. During [[Lent|Lenten periods]] this might be water mixed with [[kvass|kvas]], while at other times it might be a meat broth.

In [[Left Bank Ukraine]] and in the south, ''holubtsi'' are usually big, made from the entire cabbage leaf, while in the [[Dniester]] region and the Carpathians the cabbage leaf is divided into several pieces. In the latter regions, cooks who made large holubtsi were considered lazy. In Poltava cooks preferred the large holubtsi because they were juicier. In most of Ukraine holubtsi were an everyday dish, but in most of [[Right Bank Ukraine]], with the exception of [[Polissia]], they were also included in holiday meals. Beginning in the 1920s, holubtsi began to be stuffed with a rice-meat mixture, and, instead of kvas, they began to be cooked in tomato juice, sauce or paste. This is the most common way they are prepared nowadays.

Holubtsi are a popular dish for both everyday meals and as special occasion treats. For [[Twelve-dish Christmas Eve supper|Sviata Vecheria]] (Christmas Eve supper) in many regions of Ukraine, holubtsi constitute one of the twelve traditional dishes served on the night. Only Lenten ingredients are used in this case.<ref>Yakovenko, Svitlana 2016, [http://sovabooks.com.au/tradition-on-a-plate-ukrainian-christmas-eve-supper/ ''Ukrainian Christmas Eve Supper: Traditional village recipes for Sviata Vecheria''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103204019/http://sovabooks.com.au/tradition-on-a-plate-ukrainian-christmas-eve-supper/ |date=3 January 2017 }}, Sova Books, Sydney</ref><ref>Faryna, Natalka (Ed.) 1976, ''Ukrainian Canadiana'', Ukrainian Women's Association of Canada, Edmonton</ref> On occasion of Sviata Vecheria, Boykos and Transcarpathians make holubtsi from "kryzhavky" (pickled whole heads of cabbage). Into these "pickled" holubtsi they put a stuffing of rice and mushrooms. Carpathian-style holubtsi are usually made from fresh cabbage and stuffed with corn grits, or with grated raw potato (vorokhta, verkhovyna, kvasy). These are best served with mushroom gravy. To differentiate the different types of holubtsi, they are wrapped into different shapes: corn-filled ones are made into the shape of envelopes, with the edges folded in, potato-filled are simply rolled up. A classic Halychian (Galician) Sviata Vecheria dish is holubtsi stuffed with grated potato and served with a mushroom machanka (dipping sauce).

On 4 May 2023, the cooking of holubtsi, a Ukrainian traditional dish, was inscribed in the National Inventory of Elements of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Ukraine.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 May 2023 |title=Голубці внесли до переліку нематеріальної культурної спадщини України |url=https://www.unn.com.ua/uk/news/2026864-golubtsi-vnesli-do-pereliku-nematerialnoyi-kulturnoyi-spadschini-ukrayini |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=УНН |language=uk}}</ref>

==== Russia ====

The Russian version of cabbage rolls usually consists of [[Ground meat|minced meat]] mixed with cooked rice (or buckwheat) wrapped in cabbage leaves and stewed in a mixture of either sour cream or tomato sauce or both.

There is an easier-to-make variation of that dish called ''lenivye golubtsy'' ("lazy" cabbage rolls): the cabbage is chopped and mixed with minced meat and rice so there is no need to wrap every meatball in a cabbage leaf.<ref>[http://rbth.ru/articles/2009/10/28/281009_golubtsy.html The ultimate Russian comfort food] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130823001117/https://rbth.ru/articles/2009/10/28/281009_golubtsy.html |date=23 August 2013 }}, 28 October 2009, [[Russia Beyond the Headlines]]e</ref>

Russians refer to the [[bell pepper]] variant of the dish as "perchiki" ("little peppers" - consistent with the pattern of forming food names using diminutives, despite the large size of bell peppers relative to other peppers).{{citation needed|date=May 2023}}
