[[Kapampangan cuisine]] originates from the provinces of [[Pampanga]] and parts of [[Tarlac]] in [[Central Luzon]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Castro|first=Alex D. r|date=June 7, 2007|title=VIEWS FROM THE PAMPANG: 34. KUSINANG KAPAMPANGAN*|url=https://viewsfromthepampang.blogspot.com/2007/06/34-kusinang-kapampangan.html|access-date=2021-02-06|website=VIEWS FROM THE PAMPANG}}</ref><ref>Larkin, John A. 1972. The Pampangans: Colonial Society in a Philippine Province. University of California Press</ref> It is characterized by its bold and rich flavors and its use of locally available ingredients, including a wide range of meat cuts and offal.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Martinez|first=Angelito|date=February 7–8, 2018|title=Pamanese The Art of Cooking, The Virtue of Caring|url=https://www.dlsu.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/pdf/conferences/arts-congress-proceedings/2018/acp-01.pdf|access-date=|website=}}</ref> Among its most well-known dishes are ''[[sisig]]'', made from chopped pork parts with [[calamansi]], onions, and chili; ''[[kare-kare]]'', a peanut-based stew with oxtail and vegetables; and ''[[tocino]]'', locally known as ''pindang'', a sweet-[[Curing (food preservation)|cured]] pork dish.<ref>Gonzales, Gene R. 1993. Cocina Sulipeña: Culinary Gems from Old Pampanga. University of California</ref>

Other [[Kapampangan people|Kapampangan]] traditional dishes include ''[[Burong isda|buro]]'', a fermented rice dish with shrimp or fish often paired with blanched vegetables; ''asadung matua'', a marinated stewed pork with sweet and savory flavors; and ''[[bringhe]]'', a Kapampangan version of [[paella]] made with glutinous rice and coconut milk.<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 2, 2020|title=How to cook like a Kapampangan|url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/369965/how-to-cook-like-a-kapampangan/|access-date=2021-02-06|website=Inquirer Lifestyle|language=en-US}}</ref> Additional dishes such as ''[[tid-tad]]'' a pork with curdled blood and innards; ''sipo egg,'' a creamy dish with quail eggs, ham, and vegetables; ''kilayin'' a pork and organ meats cooked in vinegar, and ''pulutok'' ''a'' minced pork lungs and heart.<ref>{{Cite web|date=July 21, 2014|title=Top 10 Foods|url=https://pampangaprovince.wordpress.com/foods/|access-date=2021-02-06|website=Kapampangans|language=en}}</ref>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Tibok-tibok, Queen of Kapampangan dessert.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Tibok-tibok]]'', a pudding made with [[carabao]] and coconut milk, topped with caramel or latik.
| image2            = 07212jfPulilan Market foods kakanin landmarksfvf 25.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Moche (food)|Moche]]'', a glutinous rice balls filled with sweet bean paste.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

Traditional desserts include ''[[tibok-tibok]]'', a carabao milk pudding; ''plantanillas'', carabao milk [[pastillas]] wrapped in soft egg-yolk crepes; ''[[Moche (food)|moche]]'', glutinous rice balls with bean paste filling; ''[[Lelut balatung|lelut balatong]]'', toasted mung beans with glutinous rice cooked in coconut milk; ''kalame ube'', a rice cake made with ube; and ''saniculas'', crumbly arrowroot-based cookies traditionally stamped with the image of [[Nicholas of Tolentino|San Nicolas de Tolentino]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Severo |first=Jan Milo |title=Pan de San Nicolas: Pampanga's famed cookies believed to have healing powers |url=https://www.philstar.com/lifestyle/food-and-leisure/2022/01/14/2153890/pan-de-san-nicolas-pampangas-famed-cookies-believed-have-healing-powers |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=Philstar.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Orejas |first=Tonette |date=2017-12-17 |title=A feast of Kapampangan food |url=https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/953070/a-feast-of-kapampangan-food |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=INQUIRER.net |language=en}}</ref>

The cuisine of the [[Tagalog people]] varies by province. [[Bulacan]] is popular for [[Chicharrón]] ([[pork rind]]s) and steamed rice and tuber cakes like ''puto''. It is a center for ''panghimagas'' or desserts, like brown [[rice cake]] or ''kutsinta'', ''sapin-sapin'', ''[[suman (food)|suman]]'', [[cassava]] cake, ''ube halaya'' and the king of sweets, in [[San Miguel, Bulacan]], the famous [[carabao]] milk [[candy]] ''pastillas de leche'', with its ''pabalat'' wrapper.<ref>[http://www.gmanews.tv/video/25212/-100-Pinoy--Pinoy-Panghimagas "100% Pinoy: Pinoy Panghimagas"]. (July 4, 2008). [Online video clip.] GMA News. Retrieved December 13, 2009.</ref> [[Cainta]], in [[Rizal (province)|Rizal]] province east of [[Manila]], is known for its Filipino [[rice cake]]s and puddings.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Lafamilia22jf.JPG
| caption1          = Filipino cuisine prepared in [[Baliuag, Bulacan]].
| image2            = Sinaing na Tulingan (braised fish).jpg
| caption2          = ''Sinaing na tulingan'', a [[Tagalog people]] dish of [[mackerel tuna]] slowly cooked with salt and sometimes wrapped in banana leaves.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = right
}}

These are usually topped with ''latik'', a mixture of coconut milk and brown sugar, reduced to a dry crumbly texture. A more modern, and time saving alternative to ''latik'' are coconut flakes toasted in a frying pan. [[Antipolo]], straddled mid-level in the mountainous regions of the Philippine [[Sierra Madre (Philippines)|Sierra Madre]], is a town known for its ''suman'' and cashew products.

[[Laguna (province)|Laguna]] is known for ''buko pie'' (coconut pie) and ''panutsa'' (peanut brittle). [[Batangas]] is home to [[Taal Lake]], a body of water that surrounds [[Taal Volcano]]. The lake is home to 75 species of freshwater fish, including landlocked marine species that have since adapted to the Taal lake environment. Eight of these species are of high commercial value. These include a population of [[giant trevally]] locally known as ''maliputo'' which is distinguished from their marine counterparts which are known as ''talakitok''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alaira |first1=Sofia A. |last2=Rebancos |first2=Carmelita M. |title=Maliputo (''Caranx ignobilis'' Foorskal) fish cage farming practices among selected operators in Taal Lake, Batangas, Philippines |journal=Journal of Nature Studies |date=2014 |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=25–40 |url=http://www.journalofnaturestudies.org/files/JNS13-2/13(2)%2025-40%20Alaira-fullpaper.pdf}}</ref>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Crispy Tawilis.jpg
| caption1          = Fried ''[[Sardinella tawilis|tawilis]]'', a popular dish in [[Batangas]] and [[Tagaytay]].
| image2            = Bibingkoy in Cavite City Public Market.jpg
| caption2          = ''Bibingkoy'', a glutinous rice dumpling delicacy originating from [[Cavite City]].
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

Another commercially important species is the ''[[tawilis]]'', the only known freshwater [[sardine]] and [[endemic]] to the lake. [[Batangas]] is also known for its special coffee, ''[[Kape Barako|kapeng barako]]''. [[Quezon]], especially the town of [[Lucban]], is also known for its culinary dishes, with [[Lucban longganisa]], pancit habhab, and hardinera being the most notable. The influence of coconut milk dishes, such as laing (called ''tinuto'' in some places in Quezon) and sinantol, is also felt in the province because of its proximity to [[Bicol Region|Bicol]].

''Suman'' is also a notable food in the province, especially in the town of [[Infanta, Quezon|Infanta]] and the city of [[Tayabas]], though having the same ingredients as the one in [[Antipolo]], the things that makes Infanta and Tayabas suman unique is its packaging and size; Infanta's suman is smaller in size and is usually grouped into 20 per pack, while Tayabas' suman is also unique in packaging, with a long tail that makes it look like a lit candle, in connection to its tradition of throwing ''suman'' during the feast of the city's patron, [[Isidore the Laborer]].

[[Bicol Region]] is noted for its gastronomic appetite for fiery or [[Chili pepper|chili]]-hot dishes, often combined with [[coconut milk]], with ''natong'' ([[taro]] leaves) as a common ingredient in dishes such as ''[[Laing (food)|laing]]'' and ''[[Pinangat (Bicolano cuisine)|pinangat]]''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bicol Native Cuisine|url=http://98.130.222.111/~camgov/cuisine.php|work=Camarines Sur Provincial Government|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130628035649/http://98.130.222.111/~camgov/cuisine.php|archive-date=June 28, 2013}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{cite news |last1= Aspiras|first1= Reggie|title='Laing,' 'kinunot na pagi' and 'ginutaang balaw'–Bicol specialties, by a Bicolano priest |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/59105/laing-kinunot-na-pagi-and-ginutaang-balaw-bicol-specialties-by-a-bicolano-priest/ |access-date=May 17, 2024 |publisher= [[Philippine Daily Inquirer]]|date=July 26, 2012}}</ref> One of the most well-known dishes is [[Bicol express]], a spicy stew made with pork, coconut milk, and chili peppers.<ref name="Pinas Sarap 2017">{{Cite web |date=Mar 24, 2017|title=Pinas Sarap: Pinagmulan ng Bicol express|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WQI7fJ6X3Lc|access-date=2024-07-30|website=[[GMA Public Affairs]]}}</ref> Other notable dishes include ''kinunot'', made with shredded fish (commonly [[stingray]] or shark) cooked in coconut milk with spices and chili;<ref>{{cite news |last1= |first1= |title=Kinunot|url= https://www.tasteatlas.com/kinunot|access-date=May 17, 2024 |publisher=[[TasteAtlas]] |date=May 1, 2019}}</ref> ''[[sinanglay]]'', a dish of fish simmered in coconut milk with vegetables; and ''kandingga'', consisting of chopped pork offal sautéed with garlic, onions, vinegar, and chilies.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Salcedo |first=Margaux |date=2014-08-02 |title=A tour of Bicol, by way of food |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/167460/a-tour-of-bicol-by-way-of-food/ |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":14">{{Cite web |title=Bicolano Cuisine in the Philippines |url=https://www.whetstonemagazine.com/journal/bicolano-cuisine-in-the-philippines |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=Whetstone Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

Bicolano noodle dishes include ''[[kinalas]]'' from [[Naga, Camarines Sur|Naga City]], a noodle soup made from meat scraped from pork or beef head and offal,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Palma|first1=Renzelle Ann|title=Naga's Pride: Kinalas|url=https://www.choosephilippines.com/go/local-flavors/143/nagas-pride-kinalas|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170723012212/http://www.choosephilippines.com/go/local-flavors/143/nagas-pride-kinalas|url-status=usurped|archive-date=July 23, 2017|website=ChoosePhilippines|access-date=April 9, 2019}}</ref> and ''pancit Bato'' from [[Bato, Camarines Sur]], a stir-fried dish using sun-dried wheat noodles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lim |first=Ron |title=Check out the delicious pancit bato with dinuguan |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/lifestyle/food/100556/check-out-the-delicious-pancit-bato-with-dinuguan/story |access-date=2026-03-23 |website=www.gmanetwork.com |language=en}}</ref>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Pili nuts candies in Naga City.jpg
| caption1          = Pili nut candies, sweet confections made from roasted pili nuts from [[Camarines Sur]].
| image2            = 1st Collonial Grill's Sili Ice Cream (Level1).jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Sili ice cream]]'', an ice cream flavored with chili peppers for a spicy-sweet taste.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

The region is also known for desserts and delicacies made with ''[[pili nuts]]'', such as ''pili tarts,'' ''pili nuts candies, caramelized pili nuts'', and ''pili [[Marzipan|marzipa]]''[[Marzipan|n]], as well as ''biniribid'' a twisted rice dough fritters;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Serafica |first=Gladys |date=2023 |title=Bicol's 'pasalubong' list |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1216072 |access-date=March 23, 2026 |website=Philippines News Agency}}</ref> ''binutong'' a glutinous rice with coconut cream wrapped in leaves; ''carmadelo,'' a carabao milk candy similar to pastillas from the town of [[Milagros, Masbate]]; ''[[sili ice cream]]'' a chili-flavored ice cream, and ''[[pinakro]]'' a saba bananas cooked in coconut milk and sugar.<ref name=":14" />

=== Visayas ===
{{Multiple image

In [[Visayas]], another souring agent in dishes in the form of ''batuan'' (''Garcinia binucao'') is used. It is a fruit that is greenish, yellowish, somewhat rounded, and four centimeters or more in diameter. They have a firm outer covering and contain a very acid pulp and several seeds.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.philstar.com/region/2012/11/18/868159/resource-id-ilonggo%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cbatuan%E2%80%9D-fruit-undergoes-dna-barcoding|title=For resource id Ilonggo's "batuan" fruit undergoes DNA barcoding|work=philstar.com|access-date=April 7, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925022344/http://www.philstar.com/region/2012/11/18/868159/resource-id-ilonggo%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cbatuan%E2%80%9D-fruit-undergoes-dna-barcoding|archive-date=September 25, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Tultul, a type of rock salt, is another ingredient made only in [[Guimaras]], where it is sprinkled on cooked rice to serve as a side dish. The salt is an assortment of reeds, twigs and small pieces of bamboo carried to the shore by the sea tide where they have been soaked in seawater for some time and is then burned in large quantities while continually being doused with salt water on a daily basis. The ashes then is strained continuously by {{transliteration|tl|kaings}} and are then cooked in pans.

[[Bacolod]] is the capital of Negros Occidental. There are a plethora of restaurants in Bacolod that serve delicious local dishes which are popular with visitors.<ref>{{cite web|title=Foods You Shouldn't Miss When Visiting Bacolod|url=http://www.islandsofthephilippines.com/foods-you-shouldnt-miss-when-visiting-bacolod/|work=Islands of the Philippines|access-date=June 26, 2013}}</ref> It is known for ''[[inasal]]'' which literally translates to "cooked over fire". The "chicken ''inasal''" is a local version of chicken barbecue. It is cooked with red achuete or annatto seeds giving it a reddish color, and brushed with oil and cooked over the fire. The city is also famous for various delicacies such as ''[[Piaya (food)|piaya]]'', ''[[mille foglie|napoleones]]'' and ''pinasugbo'' (deep-fried and caramelled banana sprinkled with sesame seeds).

[[Leyte (province)|Leyte]] is home to ''[[Binagol]]'', [[Pastillas|Carabao Milk ''Pastillas'']], ''Suman Latik'' and [[Moron (food)]]. [[Tacloban]]on cuisine is made unique by the wide use of {{transliteration|tl|kinagod}} (grated coconut) and ''hatok'' (coconut milk). It is common to find ''hinatokan'' (dishes integrated in coconut milk) dishes in the city. ''[[Humba]]'' is said to have originated from the province since the taste in the region's cuisine distinctly has a slightly sweeter taste than the rest of the country. Because Leyte borders the sea, it is common to find multiple seafood dishes in the province. ''Masag'' (crab), ''tilang'' (scallops) and ''pasayan'' (shrimp) are common sea food in the region. Waray taste varies, allowing each family/''angkan'' (clan) to create unique recipes. Other native delicacies from the province are ''[[Roscas (Filipino cuisine)|Roskas]]'' (hard cookies made from lard, anise, flour, sugar, butter and eggs) and [[Bukayo]] (coconut strip candies).

[[Aklan]] is synonymous with ''[[inubarang manok]]'', chicken cooked with ''ubad'' (banana [[pith]]), as well as ''[[Binakol|binakol na manok]]'', chicken cooked in [[coconut water]] with lemongrass. Of particular interest is ''[[tamilok]]'' ([[shipworm]]), which is either eaten raw or dipped in an acidic sauce such as vinegar or calamansi.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gmanetwork.com/news/story/373927/newstv/biyahenidrew/adventurous-in-aklan-a-biyahe-ni-drew-itinerary|title=Adventurous in Aklan: A 'Biyahe ni Drew' itinerary|work=GMA News Online|date=August 8, 2014 |access-date=April 7, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://balita.ph/2014/06/25/tamilok-shipworm-now-a-tourism-lure-in-aklan/|title="Tamilok" (shipworm) now a tourism lure in Aklan|work=balita.ph – Online Filipino News|access-date=April 7, 2016|archive-date=April 23, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160423120951/http://balita.ph/2014/06/25/tamilok-shipworm-now-a-tourism-lure-in-aklan/|url-status=dead}}</ref> There is a special prevalence of chicken and coconut milk (''gata'') in Akeanon cooking.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.admu.edu.ph/ls/soss/news/features/ateneo-students-go-food-tripping-kalibo|title=Ateneo Students Go Food Tripping in Kalibo|work=Ateneo de Manila University|access-date=April 7, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150627033152/http://admu.edu.ph/ls/soss/news/features/ateneo-students-go-food-tripping-kalibo|archive-date=June 27, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Batchoy of Iloilo.jpg

[[Iloilo]] is home of the ''[[batchoy]]'', derived from "ba-chui" meaning pieces of meat in Hokkien Chinese. The authentic ''batchoy'' contains fresh egg noodles called ''miki'', ''buto-buto'' broth slow-cooked for hours, and beef, pork and ''[[bulalo]]'' mixed with the local ''[[guinamos]]'' (shrimp paste). Toppings include generous amounts of fried garlic, crushed chicharon, scallions, slices of pork intestines and liver.<ref>{{cite web|last=Diaz|first=Anton|title=Ilo-ilo Food Trip|url=http://www.ourawesomeplanet.com/awesome/2013/01/iloilo-food-trip-where-are-the-best-places-to-eat-in-iloilo.html|work=Our Awesome Planet|date=January 25, 2013|access-date=June 27, 2013}}</ref> Another type of [[pancit]] which is found in the said province is ''[[pancit Molo]]'', an adaptation of wonton soup and is a specialty of the town of [[Molo, Iloilo City|Molo]], a well-known district in Iloilo. Unlike other pancit, ''pancit Molo'' is not dry but soupy and it does not make use of long, thin noodles but instead wonton wrappers made from rice flour.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.choosephilippines.com/eat/recipes/464/pancit-molo-soup/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130728024917/http://www.choosephilippines.com/eat/recipes/464/pancit-molo-soup/|url-status=usurped|archive-date=July 28, 2013|title=A Big Warm Bowl of Flavorful Molo|author=ABS-CBN Corp.|work=Choose Philippines|access-date=April 7, 2016}}</ref> Iloilo is also famous for its two ''[[Cajanus cajan|kadios]]'' or pigeon pea-based soups. The first is KBL or ''[[Kadyos, baboy, kag langka|kadios baboy langka]]''. 
[[File:KBL (Kadios, Baboy, Langka).jpg|left|thumb|224x224px|''KBL'' (''[[Kadyos, baboy, kag langka|Kadios, Baboy, Langka]]''), a stew made with pigeon peas, pork, and jackfruit.]]
As the name implies, the three main ingredients of this dish are ''kadyos'', ''baboy'' (pork), and ''langka'' (unripe jackfruit is used here).<ref name=":10">{{cite web|url=https://www.pinoyrecipe.net/kadyos-baboy-langka-recipe/|title=Kadyo Baboy Langka Recipe|access-date=April 7, 2016}}</ref> Another one is KMU or ''[[Kadyos, manok, kag ubad|kadios manok ubad]]''. This dish is composed mainly of ''kadyos'', ''manok'' (preferably free range chicken called ''Bisaya nga manok'' in Iloilo), and ''ubad'' (thinly cut white core of the banana stalk/trunk). Both of these dishes utilize another Ilonggo ingredient as a souring agent. This ingredient is ''batwan'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pinoyrecipe.net/top-6-health-benefits-of-batuan-batwan-fruit-and-filipino-recipes-you-can-cook-with/|title=Top 6 Health Benefits of Batwan Fruit|access-date=December 18, 2017}}</ref> or ''Garcinia binucao'',<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.experiencenegros.com/batuan-fruit-is-the-best/|title=Batuan Fruit is the Best|date=December 14, 2017 |access-date=December 16, 2017}}</ref> a fruit closely related to mangosteen, which is very popular in [[Western Visayas]] and neighbouring [[Negros Island]], but is generally unknown to other parts of the Philippines.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bar.gov.ph/index.php/test-archive/42-september-2012-issue/1354-binucao-the-underutilized-souring-agent|title=Bureau of Agricultural Research Chronicle}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

[[Roxas, Capiz|Roxas City]] is another food destination in Western Visayas aside from Iloilo City and Kalibo. This coastal city, about two to three hours by bus from Iloilo City, prides itself as the "Seafood Capital of the Philippines" due to its bountiful rivers, estuaries and seas. Numerous seafood dishes are served in the city's Baybay area such as mussels, oysters, scallops, prawns, seaweeds, clams, fishes and many more.[[File:Boholano delicacy Kalamay.png|thumb|201x201px|''[[Bohol]] kalamay'', made from glutinous rice, coconut milk, and brown sugar, traditionally packed in coconut shells.]]In [[Bohol]], ''[[kalamay]]'' is popular. In [[Palawan]], [[crocodile meat]] is boiled, cured, and turned into ''[[tocino]]s''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Yum yum… crocodile meat, anyone? |url=https://www.philstar.com/news-commentary/2013/07/31/1033871/yum-yum-crocodile-meat-anyone |access-date=2026-03-19 |website=Philstar.com}}</ref> In [[Romblon]], a specialty dish is pounded and flavored shrimp meat and rice cooked inside banana leaves.

[[Cebu]] is known for its [[lechon|lechón]] variant. Lechon prepared "Cebu style" is characterized by a crisp outer skin and a moist juicy meat with a unique taste given by a blend of spices. Cebu is also known for sweets like dried [[mango]]es and caramel tarts.

===Mindanao===
{{unref section|date=July 2026}}[[File:TIKTOK VIRAL FOOD - CHICKEN PASTIL.jpg|left|thumb|224x224px|Chicken ''Pastil'', packed rice dish originating from the [[Maguindanao people|Maguindanaon people]].]]In [[Mindanao]], the southern part of [[Palawan]] island, [[Sulu Province|Sulu]] and [[Tawi-Tawi]], dishes are richly flavored with the spices common to [[Southeast Asia]]: [[turmeric]], [[coriander]], [[lemon grass]], [[galangal]], [[cumin]], zest and/or leaves from varieties of native limes, [[cinnamon]], and chillies—ingredients not commonly used in the rest of Philippine cooking. The cuisine of the indigenous ethnolinguistic nations who are either [[Christians|Christian]], [[Muslim]] or [[Lumad]] peoples of [[Mindanao]] and the [[Sulu archipelago]] has much in common with the rich and spice-paste centric [[Malay cuisine]]s of [[Malaysian cuisine|Malaysia]] and [[Brunei]], as well as [[Indonesian cuisine|Indonesian]] and [[Thai cuisine|Thai]] cuisine, and other Southeast Asian cuisines.[[File:Ginanggang (Philippines) - grilled saba bananas - 01.jpg|thumb|''[[Ginanggang]]'', a snack food made of grilled [[saba banana]] with margarine and sugar|221x221px]]Mindanaoan cuisine represents the cultural achievements of prehispanic Philippine cuisine in other most parts of the country immediately prior to Spanish colonization between in the late 16th to early 17th centuries. Hints of similar dishes and flavors can also found in the Bicol region and the Cordilleras, which still prefer a coconut and spice-paste rich palate similar to Mindanao.[[File:SattiTamu.jpg|thumb|upright|220px|The [[Sulu province|Southern Philippine]] dish ''satti'', served with ''[[Pusô|ta'mu]]'' rice cakes|left]]Well-known Mindanao and Sulu dishes include ''[[Satay|satti]]'' (satay) and ''ginataang manok'' (chicken cooked in spiced coconut milk). Certain parts of Mindanao are predominantly [[Muslim]], where pork is rarely consumed, and lamb, mutton, goat and beef are the main red meats of choice.

''[[Rendang]]'' is an often-spicy beef curry whose origins derive from the [[Minangkabau people|Minangkabau]] people of [[Sumatra]]; ''[[biryani]]'', ''[[korma|kulma]]'', and {{transliteration|tl|[[pilaf|kiyoning]]}} (pilaf) are dishes originally from the [[Indian subcontinent]] <!-- These dishes are NOT from the Middle East - a simply check at their Wikipedia articles will confirm they are from India, Pakistan, Bangaladesh and Afghanistan. Islamization of the Philippines happened via the Indonesian archipelago, which was highly influenced by Indian subcontinent both before and after Islamization -->, that were given a Mindanaoan touch and served on special occasions.[[File:Piaparan a Manok.jpg|thumb|213x213px|''[[Piaparan]]'', a Maranao dish of chicken or fish cooked in coconut milk with turmeric and spices.]]''[[Piyanggang manok]]'' is a Tausug dish made from barbecued chicken marinated in spices, and served with coconut milk infused with toasted coconut meat.

''Chupá culo'' and ''curacha con gatâ'' are examples of Zamboangueño dishes made from shells cooked with coconut milk and crab with sauce blended in coconut milk with spices, respectively. There are other known Zamboangueño dishes like ''[[estofadong baboy]]'', ''sicalañg'', ''[[alfajor]]'', ''endulzao'', ''[[tamal]]'', ''[[paella]]'', ''arroz a la Valenciana'', ''rebosao'', ''toron'', and more.

Popular crops such as [[cassava root]], [[sweet potato]]es, and [[Yam (vegetable)|yams]] are grown.

''[[Sambal]]'', a spicy sauce made with [[belacan]], [[tamarind]], aromatic spices and chilies, is a popular base of many dishes in the region.

''[[Palapa (condiment)|Palapa]]'', is a popular condiment unique to, and widely used in, Maranao and Maguindanaon cuisines, and consists of a base of shredded old coconut, sakurab (a variant of [[green onion]]), ginger, galangal, chillies, salt, pepper, and turmeric.

Another popular dish from this region is ''[[tiyula itum]]'', a dark broth of beef or chicken lightly flavored with ginger, galangal, chili, turmeric, and toasted coconut flesh (which gives it its dark color).

''[[Lamaw]]'' (Buko salad), is a mixture of young coconut, its juice, milk or orange juice, with ice.

== Vegetables ==
[[Vegetable]]s are a prominent component of Filipino cuisine, reflecting the country's long-standing agricultural traditions and the variety of crops commonly grown in rural households, often associated with the ''[[bahay kubo]]'' (traditional nipa hut).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kirshenblatt-Gimblett |first=Barbara |last2=Fernandez |first2=Doreen G. |date=2003-02-01 |title=Culture Ingested: On the Indigenization of {{sic|Phil|lipine|nolink=y}} Food |url=https://online.ucpress.edu/gastronomica/article/3/1/58/46623/Culture-Ingested-On-the-Indigenization-of |journal=Gastronomica |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=58–71 |doi=10.1525/gfc.2003.3.1.58 |issn=1529-3262|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lema |first=Nona |title=Gulay |date=2005 |publisher=Penchant Publishing |volume=1 |location=Quezon City |pages=106 |language=en}}</ref> Vegetable dishes are usually cooked simply [[Steaming|steamed]], [[Boiling|boiled]], or [[Blanching (cooking)|blanched]] to keep their natural flavor.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bartell |first=Karen Hulene |title=Fine Filipino Food |publisher=[[Hippocrene Books]] |year=2003 |isbn=0-7818-0964-9 |location=New York |pages=197 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Editorial Committee |title=Filipino Cuisine : A concoction of different vegetables |publisher=Academic Publishing |year=2007 |location=[[Quezon City]]}}</ref> They can also be [[Grilling|grilled]], [[Sautéing|sautéed]], stewed, fried, or [[Pickling|pickled]], and are often seasoned with salt, [[coconut milk]], vinegar, soy sauce, and [[fermented fish]] products such as ''[[Patis (sauce)|patis]]'', ''[[bagoong alamang]]'', and ''[[bagoong isda]]''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dirige |first=Ofelia V. |title=Global Filipino Cuisine: Healthy Recipes. Revised Edition of 100 Modified Recipes |last2=Oades |first2=Riz A. |last3=Cudal |first3=Aurora |date=2009 |publisher=KCS Publishing |isbn=978-0-9758695-2-9 |location=[[California]] |publication-date=2009}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=[[Department of Agriculture (Philippines)]]-Information Service |title=Mga Katutubong gulay = Indigenous Vegetables |date=2012 |location=[[Quezon City]] |pages=53}}</ref>

{{Multiple image

''[[Sinabawang gulay]]'' is a traditional [[vegetable soup]] typically seasoned with salt or ''patis'' and made from leafy greens such as ''[[Moringa oleifera|malunggay]]'', ''[[Corchorus olitorius|saluyot]]'', ''[[Brassica juncea|mustasa]]'', ''[[Bok choy|pechay]]'', and [[Chili pepper|''chili leaves'']], along with [[eggplant]], [[okra]], squash (''[[Calabaza|kalabasa]]''), and [[Asparagus bean|long beans]] (''sitaw'').<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Best Sinabawang Gulay Recipes Ngayong Tag-ulan |url=https://www.maggi.ph/sdp/best-sinabawang-gulay-recipes-ngayong-tag-ulan/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=www.maggi.ph |language=en}}</ref> It is known by various regional names, including ''bulanglang'' in South-Central Luzon,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2012-01-14 |title=Bulanglang Recipe |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/bulanglang/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> ''gule magalang'' in [[Pampanga]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raymund |date=2021-03-19 |title=Gule Magalang |url=https://www.angsarap.net/2021/03/19/gule-magalang/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Ang Sarap (A Tagalog word for "It's Delicious") |language=en-NZ}}</ref> ''laswa'' in [[Western Visayas]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is Laswa? Why it's Erwan Heussaff's favorite food |url=https://www.pep.ph/lifestyle/food/183989/laswa-erwan-heussaff-favorite-food-a718-20241118 |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=PEP.ph |language=en}}</ref> and ''law-oy'' or ''utan'' in parts of the [[Visayas]] and [[Mindanao]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Saif |date=2022-04-28 |title=Law Uy Recipe (Utan Bisaya) |url=https://theodehlicious.com/law-uy-utan-bisaya-recipe/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=The Odehlicious |language=en-US}}</ref>

In [[Northern Luzon]], it is closely related to ''[[dinengdeng]]'' or ''inabraw'', which differ primarily in the use of ''bagoong isda'' as a seasoning, giving the dish a distinct savory and earthy flavor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NewsPublish |date=2024-03-15 |title=A 'dinengdeng' diary |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/485945/a-dinengdeng-diary/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref> A variation known as ''[[buridibod]]'' includes [[sweet potato]]es and moringa pods.<ref>{{cite web |title=Buridibud Ilocano Vegetable Recipe|url=https://www.overseaspinoycooking.net/2022/05/buridibud-ilocano-vegetable-recipe.html|access-date=7 October 2023|website=Overseas Pinoy Cooking|language=en}}</ref> These dishes are often accompanied by smoked or fried fish, seafood, or [[dried shrimp]].

''[[Pinakbet]]'' is a classic Filipino vegetable dish known for its savory and earthy flavors.<ref name=":112">{{Cite journal |last=Talbo|first=Wendelyn R.|date=December 6, 2022|title=Traditional Foods of Ilokanos|url=https://vector.unp.edu.ph/index.php/1/article/download/291/268/1424|journal=The Vector: International Journal of Emerging Science, Technology and Management|volume=31|issue=1|via=The Vector}}</ref> It typically consists of a variety of vegetables such as [[Momordica charantia|bitter melon]], eggplant, long beans, and okra.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tayag|first=Claude|title=Pakbet, love it or hate it|url=https://www.philstar.com/lifestyle/food-and-leisure/2009/03/12/447269/pakbet-love-it-or-hate-it|access-date=2026-01-14|website=Philstar.com}}</ref> The authentic [[Ilocano cuisine|Ilocano]] version includes sweet potatoes and [[legume]]s, seasoned with ''bagoong isda'', and is traditionally cooked by combining all ingredients without prior sautéing. In contrast, Tagalog versions often incorporate squash (''kalabasa'') and [[shrimp paste]] (''bagoong alamang''), with the ingredients sautéed before simmering.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last1=Belinda A. Ramos|last2=Ivy A. Bartido|date=2021|title=Ethnic Variants of 'Pinakbet': Versatility of a Filipino Exotic Food|url=https://ejournals.ph/article.php?id=18504|journal=Salettinian Open Academic Review|language=en-US|volume=3|issue=1|pages=1}}</ref> Regional variations may also include the addition of coconut milk, particularly in parts of [[Southern Luzon]], [[Bicol Region|Bicol]], and the Visayas, as well as the addition of seafood in Pampanga.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ginataang Pinakbet {{!}} Nestlé Goodnes |url=https://www.nestlegoodnes.com/ph/recipes/ginataang-pinakbet |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=www.nestlegoodnes.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":02"/>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Laing, Bicolano dish.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Laing (food)|Laing]]'', a [[Bicolano people|Bicolano]] dish made from dried [[taro]] leaves cooked in [[coconut milk]] and spices.
