''[[Ginataan]]'' is a general term for dishes cooked in [[coconut milk]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Corbyn |first=Mark |date=2023 |title=Knowing Filipino Food: Ginataan |url=https://theadobros.substack.com/p/knowing-filipino-food-ginataan |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=For the Love of Adobo}}</ref><ref name="comst">{{cite book|author=Myke Sarthou|editor=Angelo Comsti|title=The Filipino Family Cookbook: Recipes and Stories From Our Home Kitchen|publisher=Marshall Cavendish International Asia Pte Ltd|year=2014|page=92|isbn=9789814634946}}</ref> One of the most well-known examples is ''[[Laing (food)|laing]]'' or ''pinangat'', a [[Bicolano people|Bicolano]] dish made from dried [[Taro|taro leaves]], often combined with taro stems or tubers, and cooked in coconut milk with spices such as [[ginger]], [[Cymbopogon|lemongrass]], and chili peppers.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Pinangat & Laing - Another Famous Bicol Treats|url=http://touringbicol.blogspot.com/2010/01/laeng-2nd-famous-dish-in-bicol.html|website=Touring Bicol|access-date=January 10, 2019}}</ref> Numerous vegetable-based variations of ''ginataan'' exist, including ''[[ginataang kalabasa]]'' (squash and long beans), ''[[ginataang langka]]'' ([[jackfruit]]), ''[[ginataang ampalaya]]'' (bitter melon), ''[[ginataang labong]]'' ([[bamboo shoot]]s), and ''ginataang puso ng saging'' ([[banana blossom]]).<ref name="comst" /><ref name="polistico" /> ''Lawot-lawot'', a coconut milk dish from [[Cebu]] and [[Mindanao]], consists of mixed vegetables in a viscous broth, usually thickened by okra, [[Luffa|loofah]], and other slimy ingredients.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-02-19 |title=Forgotten Foods: Lawot-lawot (Philippines) |url=https://asianfarmers.org/philippines-forgotten-foods-lawot-lawot/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Asian Farmers Association for Sustainable Rural Development |language=en-US}}</ref>

In Pampanga and [[Nueva Ecija]], ''[[gising-gising]]'' is a related dish made from winged beans cooked in coconut milk and typically seasoned with shrimp paste and chili.<ref name="pascual">{{cite web |last1=Pascual|first1=Marie|title=#FoodMemories: Gising-gising|url=https://www.rappler.com/life-and-style/food-drinks/33627-marie-pascual-gising-gising/|website=Rappler|date=July 12, 2013|access-date=September 22, 2018}}</ref> In the provinces of [[Laguna (province)|Laguna]] and [[Quezon]], ''[[kulawo]]'' refers to vegetable dishes such as ''[[kulawong talong]]'' (roasted eggplant) or ''[[kulawong puso ng saging]]'' (banana blossom), seasoned with onion, salt, vinegar, black pepper, and coconut milk.<ref name=":7">{{cite news | author = Fenix, Mickey. | title = Ringside view of pinikpikan process | url = http://showbizandstyle.inquirer.net/lifestyle/lifestyle/view_article.php?article_id=4174 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120318151117/http://showbizandstyle.inquirer.net/lifestyle/lifestyle/view_article.php?article_id=4174 | url-status = dead | archive-date = March 18, 2012 | newspaper = The Philippine Daily Inquirer | date = June 7, 2006 | access-date = December 14, 2009 }}</ref><ref name="FEATR">{{cite AV media |people=FEATR|date=August 9, 2022|title=How Burnt Coconut is used in Laguna Philippines (Kulawo and Minanok)|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=syhH-NFZuJs|publisher=Youtube}}</ref>
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Adobong Sitaw and garlic 01.jpg
| caption1          = ''Adobong sitaw'', a long beans cooked in vinegar, soy sauce, and garlic.
| image2            = Adobong Kangkong (water spinach adobo, Philippines).jpg
| caption2          = ''Adobong kangkong'' a water spinach sautéed in garlic, vinegar, and soy sauce.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

[[Philippine adobo|''Adobo'']]-based vegetable dishes adapt the traditional adobo cooking method <ref>{{Cite web |last=Makalintal |first=Bettina |date=2023 |title=Adobo Every Vegetable |url=https://www.eater.com/23588138/filipino-adobo-use-for-vegetables |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Eater |language=en-US}}</ref> braising in [[soy sauce]], vinegar, garlic, and black pepper, to vegetables such as [[Ipomoea aquatica|water spinach]] (''[[adobong kangkong]]'')<ref>{{Cite web |last=Manalo |first=Lalaine |date=2023-03-20 |title=Adobong Kangkong |url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/adobong-kangkong/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Kawaling Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> and long beans (''adobong sitaw'').<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2010-06-10 |title=Adobong Sitaw Recipe |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/adobong-sitaw-string-bean-recipe/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Paksiw]]-based vegetable dishes, in contrast, are prepared by simmering vegetables like eggplant, okra, bitter melon (''ampalaya''), and green chili peppers in vinegar with spices, producing a distinctively sour flavor. In [[Pampanga]], a related dish known as ''paksing demonyu'' features mixed vegetables stewed in vinegar.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orejas |first=Tonette |date=2014-05-21 |title=Heirloom dishes shine in food tour |url=https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/603842/heirloom-dishes-shine-in-food-tour |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=INQUIRER.net |language=en}}</ref> In Northern Luzon, the Ilocano dish ''tinimtim'' similarly features leafy vegetables such as ''saluyot'' (jute mallow) cooked in vinegar.
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Ensaladang Pako with salted egg.jpg
| caption1          = ''Ensaladang pako'', a [[fern]] salad with tomatoes and salted egg.
| image2            = Katuray Flower Salad.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Kinilnat]]'', made from [[Sesbania grandiflora|katuray]] dressed with tomatoes, onions, and bagoong isda.
| direction         = vertical
| image3            = Ensaladang Lato (Seaweed Salad) - Philippines 2.jpg
| caption3          = ''Ensaladang lato'', a [[Caulerpa lentillifera|sea grapes]] salad with tomatoes, onions, and vinegar.
}}

''Ensalada'', derived from the Spanish word for “''[[salad]]'',” refers to a category of dishes that typically function as [[side dish]]es or palate cleansers.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |title=Ensalada: A Healthy Filipino Salad You Can Make Anywhere |url=https://www.campfirecrates.com/blog/ensalada-a-healthy-filipino-salad-you-can-make-anywhere |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Campfire Crates |language=en-US}}</ref> These dishes commonly consist of fresh, blanched, or grilled vegetables paired with ingredients such as [[tomato]]es, green [[mango]]es, onions, vinegar, or ''bagoong alamang''.<ref name=":8" /> Examples include ''ensaladang talong'', made from grilled or blanched eggplant with tomatoes and ''bagoong'';<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-04-11 |title=Ensaladang Talong (Filipino Eggplant Salad) |url=https://www.pepper.ph/recipes/ensaladang-talong-filipino-eggplant-salad |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=www.pepper.ph |language=en}}</ref> ''ensaladang itlog na maalat'', which combines tomatoes, onions, and [[Salted duck egg|salted eggs]];<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2014-10-30 |title=Salted Eggs and Tomato Salad |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/salted-eggs-tomato-salad/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> and ''ensaladang ampalaya'', prepared from blanched bitter melon.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Easy Ampalaya Salad Recipe |url=https://www.yummy.ph/recipe/easy-ampalaya-salad-recipe-a394-20220112 |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Yummy.ph |language=en-US}}</ref>

In [[Ilocos Region]], similar dishes are known as ''[[kinilnat]]'',<ref>{{cite web |title=Kinilnat {{!}} Traditional Salad From Ilocos {{!}} TasteAtlas|url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/kinilnat|website=www.tasteatlas.com|access-date=27 September 2023}}</ref> which typically feature blanched leafy vegetables, [[blossom]]s, and [[Plantar calcaneocuboid ligament|shoots]]—such as ''[[Sesbania grandiflora|katuray]]'', moringa flowers, ferns, ''[[Vallisneria spiralis|ballaiba]]'', okra, and sweet potato leaves—dressed with a mixture commonly referred to as KBL (''kamatis'', ''bugguong'', and ''[[Shallot|lasona]]'').<ref>{{Cite web |last=Marketman |date=2007-10-23 |title=KBL, Ilocos Style (Kamatis, Bagoong, Lasona) / Tomatoes, Fish Sauce & Onion Relish |url=https://www.marketmanila.com/archives/kbl-ilocos-style-kamatis-bagoong-lasona-tomatoes-fish-sauce-onion-relish |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Market Manila |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Seaweed]]-based salads are also common, such as ''ensaladang lato'' or ''arosep'' ([[Caulerpa lentillifera|sea grapes]]) mixed with tomatoes, onions, and vinegar.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2016-08-11 |title=Seaweed Salad Recipe (Ensaladang Lato) |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/seaweed-salad-recipe-ensaladang-lato/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> Other edible seaweeds include ''[[Eucheuma|guso]]'' in the Visayas and Mindanao, particularly in Tawi-Tawi, and ''[[Codium edule|pokpoklo]]'' or ''[[Gracilaria|guraman]]'' in [[Ilocos Region|Ilocos]].<ref name=":9" />
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Ginisang Munggo, Apr 2024.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Ginisang munggo]]'', a sautéed mung bean soup with leafy vegetables.
| image2            = 
| caption2          = 
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

[[Legume|''Legumes'']] and [[Bean|''beans'']] are commonly stewed, forming the basis of several popular dishes. ''[[Ginisang munggo]]'' is a [[mung bean]] stew typically sautéed or simmered with tomatoes, onions, garlic, ''patis'', and leafy vegetables such as moringa, bitter melon, and chili leaves, often garnished with ''[[tinapa]]'' or ''[[Chicharrón|chicharon]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lopez |first=Sarah |date=April 18, 2025 |title=Today I Learned: Why Friday is Ginisang Monggo Day in the Philippines |url=https://www.esquiremag.ph/culture/food-and-drink/today-i-learned-ginisang-monggo-a7994-20250418 |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Esquiremag.ph}}</ref> ''Habichuelas'', made from [[Navy bean|white beans]], are slowly cooked with tomatoes, pork knuckles, and ''[[Chorizo de Bilbao]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raymund |date=2021-02-15 |title=Habichuelas |url=https://www.angsarap.net/2021/02/15/habichuelas/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Ang Sarap (A Tagalog word for "It's Delicious") |language=en-NZ}}</ref> The Ilocano version, often called ''pusi'', ''bitsuelas'', or ''pinablad'', is seasoned with ''bagoong isda'' and includes bitter melon leaves.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Raymund |date=2025-08-18 |title=Pata Ken Pusi |url=https://www.angsarap.net/2025/08/18/pata-ken-pusi/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Ang Sarap (A Tagalog word for "It's Delicious") |language=en-NZ}}</ref>

In the [[Cordillera Administrative Region|Cordillera Region]], [[Black turtle bean|black beans]] are cooked with preserved meats such as ''etag'' or ''kiniing'', seasoned with salt, and often combined with highland vegetables like [[cabbage]] and ''[[Napa cabbage|wombok]]''.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |url= |title=Heirloom Recipes of the Cordillera |publisher=Philippine Task Force for Indigenous People’s Rights and Partners for Indigenous Knowledge Philippines |year=2019 |isbn=978-621-96088-0-0 |location=[[Baguio City]] |publication-date=2019 |pages=55–88 |language=en}}</ref> In Western Visayas, KBL (''[[kadyos, baboy, kag langka]]'') consists of stewed pork with [[pigeon pea]]s (''kadyos'') and [[jackfruit]] (''langka''), soured with ''[[Garcinia binucao|batuan]]'' and enriched with leafy vegetables.<ref name=":10" /> In Mindanao, ''papis'' is a bean stew prepared with canned pork or slow-cooked beef with tendons, flavored with local spices.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Manalo |first=Lalaine |date=2023 |title=Papis |url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/papis/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Kawaling Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{Multiple image
| image1            = 2013 Angeles Philippines Trip Day 5 - Lumpiang Ubod.jpg
| caption1          = ''Lumpiang ubod'' a fresh spring roll with [[heart of palm]], vegetables, and wrapped in a soft crepe.
| image2            = Lumpiang Toge.jpg
| caption2          = ''Lumpiang toge'', a spring roll made from [[mung bean sprouts]].
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

''[[Lumpia]]''-based dishes include a variety of vegetable-filled [[spring roll]]s that may be served fresh or fried.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":12">{{cite web |title=Filipino Lumpia: History and Variants|url=https://www.panlasangpinoy.com/lumpia/|website=Panlasang Pinoy|access-date=2025-12-07}}</ref> ''[[Lumpiang gulay]]'' refers to deep-fried spring rolls composed of mixed vegetables such as cabbage, carrots, sweet potato, and green beans (''[[Green bean|Baguio beans]]'' or ''sitaw'').<ref>{{cite web |title=Lumpiang Gulay (Mix Vegetables Spring Rolls) Recipe|url=http://www.filipinofoodrecipes.org/lumpiang-gulay-mix-vegetables-spring-rolls-recipe|website=FilipinoFoodRecipes.org|access-date=January 13, 2019}}</ref> Variants include ''[[lumpiang toge]]'' ([[Sprouting|bean sprouts]]), ''[[lumpiang labong]]'' (bamboo shoots), and ''[[lumpiang singkamas]]'' ([[Pachyrhizus erosus|jicama]]).<ref name=":12" /> ''[[Dinamita|Dynamite]]'' is a modern variation consisting of green chili peppers stuffed with cheese or ''[[giniling]]'', wrapped and deep-fried.<ref>{{cite web |title=Dynamite Lumpia (Vegan)|url=https://sweetsimplevegan.com/dynamite-lumpia/|website=Sweet Simple Vegan|access-date=2025-12-07}}</ref> ''[[Lumpiang sariwa]]'' (“fresh lumpia”) is made with a soft egg or flour [[crêpe]] filled with vegetables such as sweet potato, cabbage or [[lettuce]], [[tofu]], and jicama, and is typically served with a sweet garlic sauce and crushed [[peanut]]s;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2009 |title=Lumpiang Sariwa (Fresh Spring Rolls Recipe) |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/asian-vegetable-dish-fresh-spring-roll-lumpiang-sariwa-recipe/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> a related version, ''[[lumpiang hubad]]'', is served without the wrapper. In [[Silay|Silay City, Negros Occidental]], ''[[lumpiang ubod]]'' features [[heart of palm]] (''ubod'') as the primary filling.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016 |title=So good – Fresh Lumpiang Ubod |url=https://www.philstar.com/the-freeman/cebu-lifestyle/2016/07/15/1603008/so-good-fresh-lumpiang-ubod |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=PhilStar}}</ref>
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Rellenong talong.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Tortang talong]]'', a grilled eggplant [[omelette]].
| image2            = Mac MG 5988.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Okoy]]'', a crispy fritter made with calabasa, sweet potatoes, and mixed with shrimp.
| direction         = vertical
}}

''Torta'' refers to [[omelette]]-style dishes that often incorporate vegetables. ''[[Tortang talong]]'' is a grilled [[eggplant]] omelette typically combined with eggs and sometimes mixed with tomatoes, onions, or ''giniling''.<ref name="polistico" /> A related dish, ''[[Poqui poqui|poqui-poqui]]'', consists of grilled eggplant that is sautéed and [[Scrambled eggs|scrambled]] with eggs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Poqui poqui {{!}} Traditional Egg Dish From Ilocos {{!}} TasteAtlas|url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/poqui-poqui|access-date=2024-08-09|website=www.tasteatlas.com}}</ref> Other sautéed vegetable-and-egg dishes include ''ginisang ampalaya'' (bitter melon with egg),<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2021-12-22 |title=Ginisang Ampalaya (Sauteed Bitter Melon) |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/healthy-bitter-melon-ginisang-ampalaya-recipe/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> ''ginisang kamatis at itlog'' (tomatoes with egg), and ''[[Sarsiado|siarsiado]]'', as well as [[Kapampangan cuisine|Kapampangan]] variants such as ''kultyas'', ''tuchas'', or ''tutyas''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Manalo |first=Lalaine |date=2024 |title=Kultyas |url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/kultyas/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Kawaling Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> ''[[Okoy]]'' is a crisp, deep-fried fritter made with a batter and various vegetables such as squash (''kalabasa''), sweet potato, bean sprouts, or cassava, often combined with small shrimp.<ref name="polistico" /><ref name="cailan">{{cite web |last1=Cailan|first1=Alvin|title=Ukoy: A Filipino Fritter Side Dish|url=https://www.kcet.org/shows/the-migrant-kitchen/ukoy-a-filipino-fritter-side-dish|website=The Migrant Kitchen|publisher=KCET|access-date=December 14, 2018}}</ref>

''[[Atchara]]'' or ''burong gulay'', a pickled vegetables that are widely served as side dishes.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NewsPublish |date=2025-09-15 |title=The heart of pickling |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/549630/the-heart-of-pickling/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref> The most popular form is pickled [[Papaya|green papaya]], typically prepared with carrots, onions, ginger, and bell peppers, and preserved in a solution of vinegar and water with added spices; variations depend on the vegetables used.<ref>{{cite book |last=Zabilka|first=G.|title=Customs and Culture of the Philippines|publisher=Tuttle Publishing|year=2007|isbn=978-1-4629-1302-2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KqDTAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT111|access-date=November 3, 2017|page=pt111}}</ref> In the [[Ilocos Region]], ''inartem'' or ''artem'' refers to a traditional pickling method that uses ''[[Sukang iloko|sukang Iloko]]'' ([[sugarcane vinegar]]) to preserve unripe fruits, vegetables, and spices, including ''balayang'' (wild banana),<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inartem Balayang (Pickled Wild Banana) - Arca del Gusto |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/inartem-balayang-pickled-wild-banana/ |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Slow Food Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> tamarind, [[radish]], and [[Sandoricum koetjape|santol]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dy-Zulueta |first=Dolly |title=Make Ilocos' Inartem with Karamay or Iba Insik |url=https://www.philstar.com/lifestyle/food-and-leisure/2025/06/08/2445944/make-ilocos-inartem-karamay-or-iba-insik |access-date=2026-03-21 |website=Philstar.com}}</ref>

==Desserts==
{{Further|List of Philippine desserts}}{{Multiple image
| image1            = "Kakaning Pinoy" (The Filipino Rice Cakes).jpg
| caption1          = A variety of traditional Filipino [[rice cake]] (''[[kakanin]]'') desserts.
| image2            = Halu-halo.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Halo-halo]]'', a popular Filipino dessert made with mixed sweet ingredients, shaved ice, and milk.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

As the Philippines is a tropical country, many desserts are made from rice and coconuts. One often seen dessert is ''[[bibingka]]'', a hot [[rice cake]] optionally topped with a pat of butter, slices of ''[[kesong puti]]'' (white cheese), ''itlog na maalat'' (salted duck eggs), and sometimes grated coconut. There are also glutinous rice sweets called ''[[Kalamay|biko]]'' made with sugar, butter, and coconut milk.

In addition, there is a dessert known as ''bitsu-bitsu,'' also known as a Pinoy donut, made with fried rice flour which is then coated with [[muscovado]] sugar syrup. There is also ''karioka'', made from glutinous rice flour, coconut, and coconut milk, fried and skewered and slathered with a brown sugar glaze. Another brown [[rice cake]] is ''[[kutsinta]]''.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Rice cakes variety.jpg
| caption1          = An array of traditional Filipino desserts, including [[cassava cake]], [[Puto (food)|puto]], and [[tikoy]].
| image2            = Kakanin sa Bilao.jpg
| caption2          = Rice cakes in a bilao, featuring [[sapin-sapin]], [[palitaw]], and [[kutsinta]].
| direction         = vertical
| align             = right
| image3            = Ube Turon.jpg
| caption3          = Ube [[Turon (food)|Turon]]
}}

''[[Puto (food)|Puto]]'' is another well-known example of sweet steamed rice cakes prepared in many different sizes and colors. ''[[Sapin-sapin]]'' (sapin means layer) are three-layered, tri-colored sweets made with rice flour, purple yam, and coconut milk characterized by its gelatinous appearance. ''[[Palitaw]]'' are rice patties that are covered with sesame seeds, sugar, and coconut; and ''[[Pitsi-pitsî|pitsi-pitsi]]'' are [[cassava]] patties coated with cheese or coconut.

''Tibok-tibok'' is based on carabao milk, being similar to [[maja blanca]]. As a snack, ''[[binatog]]'' is made with corn kernels with shredded coconut. Packaged snacks may be wrapped in banana or palm leaves then steamed. ''[[Suman (food)|Suman]]'' is made from sticky rice and steamed. For chilled desserts there is ''[[halo-halo]]'', a dessert made with shaved ice, milk, and sugar, with additional ingredients like coconut, ''[[ube halaya]]'' (mashed purple yam) or [[ube ice cream]], ''leche flan'', [[Plantain (cooking)|plantains]], [[jackfruit]], red beans, [[tapioca]] and ''[[pinipig]]''.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Saging con Yelo.jpg
| caption1          = ''Saging con Yelo'', a shaved ice dessert with sweetened bananas.
| image2            = Leche flan Filipinas.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Leche flan]]'', a custard dessert made with eggs, milk, and caramelized sugar.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

Other similar treats made with shaved ice include ''saba con yelo'' which is shaved ice served with milk; ''[[minatamis na saging]]'', ripe plantains chopped and caramelized with brown sugar; ''mais con yelo'' shaved ice served with steamed corn kernels, sugar, and milk; and ''buko pandan'', sweetened grated strips of coconut with ''[[gulaman]]'', milk, and the juice or extract from pandan leaves.

''[[Sorbetes]]'' (ice cream) is popular, as well, with some local versions utilizing coconut milk instead of cow milk. [[Freezie|Ice candy]] is a popular frozen snack usually made from [[fruit juice]], [[chocolate]] or local ingredients such as [[mung beans]] and [[Dioscorea alata|ube]]. It can be various flavors depending on the producer, chocolate and ''buko'' (coconut) flavored are two of the most popular. 
[[File:09814jfFilipino foods fruits Bulacan landmarksfvf 26.jpg|thumb|210x210px|''[[Sorbetes]]'', traditional Filipino ice cream, often sold by street vendors.]]
Another dessert, often served during Christmas and New Year's Eve, is [[mango float]],<ref>{{cite news |author=Elizabeth Ann Quirino |title=Have Filipino food, will travel |url=http://globalnation.inquirer.net/115686/have-filipino-food-will-travel/ |newspaper=Philippine Daily Inquirer |date=December 16, 2014 |access-date=December 21, 2014 }}</ref> a dessert composed of [[graham crackers]], mangoes, cream and milk,  layered together in a dish and then refrigerated or blast chilled.

==Bread and pastries==
{{Multiple image
| image1            = 09929jfCuisine Breads Fruits Baliuag Landmarks Bulacanfvf 06.jpg
| caption1          = ''Panaderia'', a traditional Filipino neighborhood [[bakery]] offering affordable, freshly baked bread and pastries.
| image2            = Pinoy Pandesal.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Pandesal]]'', the most popular traditional Filipino bread.
| direction         = vertical
}}

In a typical Filipino bakery, ''[[pandesal]]'', ''[[Monay (bread)|monay]]'' and ''[[ensaymada]]'' are often sold. ''Pandesal'' comes from the Spanish ''pan de sal'' (literally, bread of salt), and is a ubiquitous breakfast fare, normally eaten with (and sometimes even dipped in) coffee.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.196flavors.com/philippines-pan-de-sal/|title=Philippines: Pan De Sal (Pandesal)|date=April 12, 2019|website=196 flavors|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> It typically takes the form of a bread roll, and is usually baked covered in bread crumbs. Contrary to what its name implies, ''pandesal'' is not particularly salty as very little salt is used in baking it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eater.com/2016/2/16/11007854/pandesal-philippines-bread-filipino-breakfast|title=How Pandesal Became a Filipino Breakfast Staple|last=Shah|first=Khushbu|date=February 16, 2016|website=Eater|language=en|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''Monay'' is a firmer slightly denser heavier bread.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kusinamasterrecipes.com/filipino-monay-bread/|title=Filipino Monay Bread Recipe!|date=November 25, 2014|website=Kusina Master Recipes|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''[[Ensaymada]]'', from the Spanish ''ensaimada'', is a pastry made using butter and often topped with sugar and shredded cheese that is especially popular during Christmas.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.spot.ph/i-think-therefore-i-ham/72231/ensaymada-panaderia-philippine-bread-a209-20171205-lfrm2|title=From Mallorca to Manila: How a Spanish Pastry Became a Filipino Favorite|date=December 5, 2017|first=Yvette|last=Tan|website=spot.ph|language=en|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tagaloglang.com/ensaymada/|title=Ensaymada {{!}} Filipino Snack|date=January 1, 2020|website=Tagalog Lang|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> It is sometimes made with fillings such as ''[[Purple yam|ube]]'' (purple yam) and ''[[macapuno]]'' (a variety of coconut, the meat of which is often cut into strings, sweetened, preserved, and served in desserts).

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Ensaymada from -ValeriosBakery (15379638761).jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Ensaymada]]'', with sugar-coated and cheese-filled.
| image2            = Spanish bread (Señorita bread) - Philippines 05.jpg
| caption2          = ''Spanish bread'', a popular Filipino sweet bread roll often enjoyed as a merienda (snack).
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

Also commonly sold in Filipino bakeries is ''[[pan de coco]]'', a [[sweet roll]] filled with shredded coconut mixed with molasses.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/pan-de-coco/|title=Pan de Coco|date=April 16, 2018|website=kawaling pinoy|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''Putok'' (also known in some localities as "star bread" or "pinagong"), which literally means "explode", refers to a small, hard bread roll whose cratered surface is glazed with sugar.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mamasguiderecipes.com/2019/01/15/star-bread-putok/|title=Star Bread (Putok)|last=Sison|first=Jainey|date=January 15, 2019|website=Mama's Guide Recipes|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''Kababayan'' (Filipino muffins) is a small, sweet gong-shaped muffin that has a moist consistency.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mamasguiderecipes.com/2017/06/30/kabayan-bread/|title=Kababayan Bread|last=Sison|first=Jainey|date=June 30, 2017|website=Mama's Guide Recipes|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''Spanish bread'' (nothing to do with the Spanish bread of Spain – ''Pan de Horno'') refers to a rolled pastry which looks like a croissant prior to being given a crescent shape, and has a filling consisting of sugar and butter.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.foxyfolksy.com/filipino-spanish-bread-recipe/|title=Filipino Spanish Bread Recipe|last=Bebs|date=February 3, 2017|website=Foxy Folksy|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://lutongfilipino.com/spanish-bread/|title=Spanish Bread Recipe – Filipino Recipes from Lutong Filipino|date=June 5, 2015|website=Lutong Filipino|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref>

There are also rolls like ''[[Pionono|pianono]]'', which is a chiffon roll flavored with different fillings.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/pianono/|title=Pianono (Filipino Sponge Cake Roll)|date=April 23, 2018|website=kawaling pinoy|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> ''[[Brazo de Mercedes|Brazo de mercedes]]'', a rolled cake or jelly roll, is made from a sheet of [[meringue]] rolled around a custard filling.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.foxyfolksy.com/brazo-de-mercedes/|title=Brazo de Mercedes|last=Bebs|date=May 1, 2016|website=Foxy Folksy|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> Similar to the previous dessert, it takes on a layered presentation instead of being rolled and typically features caramelized sugar and nuts for ''[[sans rival]]''. ''[[Silvana (food)|Silvañas]]'' are large, oval-shaped, cookie-sized desserts, with a thin meringue on either side of a buttercream filling and dusted with crumbed cookies.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kawalingpinoy.com/silvanas/|title=Silvanas|date=April 13, 2019|website=kawaling pinoy|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.pingdesserts.com/sylvana-recipe/|title=Sylvana Recipe|date=June 4, 2013|website=Filipino Dessert Recipes by PingDesserts.com|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref> Not overly sweet, they are rich, crisp, chewy, and buttery all at the same time. ''[[Barquillo]]s'' use sweet thin crunchy wafers rolled into tubes that can be sold hollow or filled with ''[[Polvorón|polvoron]]'' (sweetened and toasted flour mixed with ground nuts).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tagaloglang.com/barkilyos/|title=Filipino Snack: Barkilyos (Philippine Barquillos)|date=September 2, 2019|website=TAGALOG LANG|language=en-US|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.choosephilippines.com/eat/recipes/5606/barquillos-barquiron-ilonggo-snacks|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170805065927/http://www.choosephilippines.com/eat/recipes/5606/barquillos-barquiron-ilonggo-snacks|url-status=usurped|archive-date=August 5, 2017|title=Barquillos And Barquiron: Spanish-Inspired Ilonggo Snacks That Filipinos Love|website=Choose Philippines|language=en|access-date=February 27, 2020}}</ref>

[[Meringue]]s are also present in the Philippines, due to the Spanish influence, but they are called ''merengue'' – with all the vowels pronounced. ''[[Leche Flan|Leche flan]]'' is a type of caramel custard made with eggs and milk similar to the French [[creme caramel]]. ''Leche flan'' (the local term for the original Spanish ''flan de leche'', literally "milk flan") is a heavier version of the Spanish flan made with condensed milk and more egg yolks. ''Leche flan'' is usually steamed over an open flame or stove top, although on rare occasions it can also be seen baked. ''Leche flan'' is a staple in celebratory feasts. A heavier version of ''leche flan'', ''[[Crème caramel|tocino del cielo]]'', is similar, but has significantly more egg yolks and sugar.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Brazo de mercedes.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Brazo de Mercedes]]'', a traditional Filipino meringue roll filled with custard and dusted with powdered sugar.
| image2            = Buko pie (Philippines).jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Buko pie]]'', a traditional Filipino [[pie]] made with young [[coconut]] (malauhog).
| direction         = vertical
}}

The ''[[egg pie]]'' with a very rich egg custard filling is a mainstay in local bakeries. It is typically baked so that the exposed custard on top is browned. [[Buko pie|''Buko'' pie]] is made with a filling made from young coconut meat and dairy. Mini pastries like ''[[Turrones de casúy|turrones de casuy]]'' are made up of cashew [[marzipan]] wrapped with a wafer made to resemble a candy wrapper but take on a miniature look of a pie in a size of about a [[Quarter (United States coin)|quarter]]. There is also ''[[napoleones]]'' – again with all the vowels pronounced – a [[mille-feuille]] pastry stuffed with a sweet milk-based filling.

There are hard pastries like ''[[biskotso]]'' a crunchy, sweet, twice-baked bread. Another baked goody is ''sinipit'' which is a sweet pastry covered in a crunchy sugar glaze, made to resemble a length of rope. Similar to ''sinipit'' is a snack eaten on roadsides colloquially called ''shingaling''. It is hollow but crunchy with a salty flavor.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Tortang mamon (Philippines) 2.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Mamón|Mamon]]'', a light, airy Filipino [[sponge cake]].
| image2            = Mango float (Crema de Mangga) - Philippines.jpg
| caption2          = Mango float, an [[icebox cake]] version of [[crema de fruta]] made with cream, Graham crackers, condensed milk, and ripe mangoes.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

For a softer treat there is ''[[Mamón|mamon]]'' a chiffon-type cake sprinkled with sugar, its name derived from a slang Spanish term for breast. There is also ''[[crema de fruta]]'', which is an elaborate sponge cake topped in succeeding layers of cream, custard, candied fruit, and gelatin. Similar to a sponge cake is ''mamoncillo'' which generally refers to slices taken from a large ''mamon cake'', but it is unrelated to the [[Mamoncillo|fruit]] of the same name. Sandwich pastries like ''[[inipit]]'' are made with two thin layers of chiffon sandwiching a filling of custard that is topped with butter and sugar. Another ''mamon'' variant is ''mamon tostada'', basically ''mamoncillo'' toasted to a crunchy texture.

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Pinoy Empanada.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Empanada]]'', a Filipino-style pastry typically filled with [[picadillo]].
| caption2          = ''[[Siopao]]'', a popular Filipino steamed bun typically filled with [[asado]].
| direction         = vertical
| image2            = Roberto's Siopao Iloilo - 8768607976.jpg
}}

Stuffed pastries that reflect both Western and Eastern influence are common. One can find [[empanada]]s, a turnover-type pastry filled with a savory-sweet meat filling. Typically filled with ground meat and raisins, it can be deep fried or baked. ''[[Siopao]]'' is the local version of Chinese [[baozi]]. ''Buchi'' is another snack that is likely of Chinese origin. Bite-sized, ''buchi'' is made of deep-fried dough balls (often from rice flour) filled with a sweet mung bean paste, and coated on the outside with sesame seeds; some variants also have ''[[Purple yam|ube]]'' as the filling. There are also many varieties of the mooncake-like ''[[Bakpia|hopia]]'', which come in different shapes (from a flat, circular stuffed form, to cubes), and have different textures (predominantly using flaky pastry, but sometimes like the ones in [[mooncake]]s) and fillings.

==Beverages==

===Chilled drinks and shakes===
{{unref section|date=July 2026}}{{Multiple image
| image1            = Samalamig (2378832517).jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Samalamig]]'', a variety of sweet, chilled Filipino drinks.
| caption2          = Sago't [[gulaman]] in [[Ilonggo]] style.
| direction         = vertical
| image2            = Guinomis (Ilonggo Sago Gulaman) at Imay's.jpg
| total_width       = 200}}Chilled drinks are popular due to the tropical climate. Stands selling cold fruit drinks and fruit shakes are common in many of the city areas, where some are based on [[Mandarin orange|green mandarin orange]] (''dalandan'' or ''dalanghita''), [[pomelo]] (''suha''), [[pineapple]] (''pinya''), [[banana]] (''saging''), and [[soursop]] (''guyabano''). The shakes usually contain crushed ice, evaporated or condensed milk, and fruits like [[mango]], [[avocado]], [[cantaloupe]], [[durian]], [[papaya]], [[strawberry]] and [[watermelon]], to name a few.

Other chilled drinks include ''sago't gulaman,'' a flavored ice drink of pre-Hispanic [[Malay race|Malay]] origin (Malay: ''[[gula melaka]]'') with [[sago]] and [[agar]] [[gelatin]] with banana extract sometimes added to the accompanying syrup; fresh ''buko'' or [[coconut juice]], the water or juice straight out of a young [[coconut]] via an inserted straw, a less fresh variation of which is from bottled coconut juice, scraped coconut flesh, sugar, and water; and kalamansi juice, the juice of [[kalamansi]] or Philippine limes usually sweetened with honey, syrup or sugar.

===Brewed beverages===
{{Multiple image
| image1            = Kapeng Barako.jpg
| caption1          = ''Kapeng Barako'', a strong, bold coffee from [[Batangas]].
| image2            = Salabat tea with babana chips.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Salabat]]'', a ginger tea.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left
}}

The Philippines is a predominantly coffee-drinking nation. One of the most popular variants of coffee coming from the mountains of [[Batangas]] is known as ''[[Kape Barako|kapeng barako]]''. Another well-known variant of coffee is the ''[[kopi luwak|civet coffee]]''. It is called ''kape motit'' in the Cordilleras, ''kape alamid'' in Tagalog region, and ''kape musang'' in Mindanao. The [[Kalinga (province)|Kalinga]] coffee known for its organic production is also rapidly gaining popularity. Highlands coffee, or [[Benguet]] coffee, is a blend of Robusta and Excelsa beans.<ref>{{cite web|title=Garcia's Pure Coffee|url=http://www.garciacoffee.com/typesofcoffee.html|publisher=Garcia's Kape, Tinapay Atbp.|access-date=March 21, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502012525/http://www.garciacoffee.com/typesofcoffee.html|archive-date=May 2, 2013}}</ref>

Even before the establishment of coffeehouses in the Philippines, coffee has been part of the Filipino meal. Carinderias would often serve them along with meals. The opening of [[Starbucks]] in 1997 paved the way for other [[coffee shops]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.starbucks.ph/|title=Home|website=Starbucks Coffee Company}}</ref>

[[Tea]] consumption in the Philippines is driven primarily by growing health consciousness amongst middle- to high-income consumers.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tea in the Philippines|url=http://www.euromonitor.com/tea-in-the-philippines/report|publisher=euromonitor.com}}</ref> Tea is commonly prepared using [[Carmona retusa|Philippine wild tea]] or [[Thea sinensis|tea tree]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Philippine Medicinal Plants – Tsaang Gubat|url=http://www.stuartxchange.com/Tsaang.html|publisher=www.stuartexchange.com}}</ref> There are several known variations of tea using different additives. Pandan iced tea is one of these, made with [[Pandanus|pandan]] leaves and [[lemongrass]] (locally known as ''tanglad''). [[Ginger tea|''Salabat'']], sometimes called ginger tea, is brewed from [[ginger]] root and usually served during the cold months, and when illnesses such as flu or sore throat strikes.

The late 2010s saw the opening of teahouses in major cities, and with a glass of milk tea being more affordable than the usual cold designer coffee, it paved the way into making tea a well-known food trend. Notable teahouse chains in the Philippines are [[Chatime]] and [[Serenitea]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Consunji|first=Bianca|title=The Mad Tea Party|date=May 20, 2011|url=http://lifestyle.inquirer.net/1300/the-mad-tea-party|publisher=Inquirer}}</ref>
[[File:PutoMaya and Sikwate.jpg|thumb|267x267px|''[[Tsokolate|Sikwate]]'', a Filipino [[hot chocolate]] made from [[Theobroma cacao|cacao]].]]
''[[Tsokolate]]'' is the Filipino style of hot chocolate. It is traditionally made with ''tablea'', which are pure cacao beans that are dried, roasted, ground and then formed into tablets.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://tablea.com.ph/|title=dotPH domains available portal|website=tablea.com.ph|access-date=March 22, 2013|archive-date=June 12, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110612153325/http://tablea.com.ph/|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is also popular during [[Christmas in the Philippines|Christmas season]], particularly among children.

===Alcoholic beverages===
{{Further|Beer in the Philippines|Philippine wine}}

The Philippines has various locally manufactured alcoholic drinks. [[Red Horse Beer|Red Horse]] is one of the most popular beer.
; Traditional drinks
{{unref section|date=July 2026}}{{Multiple image
| image1            = Coconut Vodka Lambanog QuezonB.jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Lambanog]]'', a traditional Filipino distilled coconut liquor.
| image2            = Merienda with tapuy and biko.jpg
| caption2          = ''[[Tapuy]]'', a rice wine made from fermented glutinous rice from Cordillera.
| direction         = vertical
| align             = left}}''[[Palm wine|Tuba]]'' (toddy) is a type of hard liquor made from fresh drippings extracted from a cut young stem of palm. The cutting of the palm stem usually done early in the morning by a ''mananguete'', a person who climbs palm trees and extracts the ''tuba'' to supply to customers later in the day. The morning's accumulated palm juice or drippings are then harvested by noon, and brought to buyers then prepared for consumption. Sometimes this is done twice a day so that there are two harvests of ''tuba'' occurring first at noon-time and then in the late-afternoon.

Normally, ''tuba'' has to be consumed right after the ''mananguete'' brings it over, or it becomes too sour to be consumed as a drink. Any remaining unconsumed ''tuba'' is then often stored in jars to ferment for several days and become palm vinegar. ''Tuba'' can be distilled to produce ''[[lambanog]]'' (arrack), a neutral liquor often noted for its relatively high alcohol content.

''[[Lambanog]]'' is an alcoholic beverage commonly described as coconut wine or coconut vodka. The drink is distilled from the sap of the unopened coconut flower, and is known for its potency and high alcohol content (80 and 90 proof). Most of the Lambanog distilleries are in the Quezon province of Luzon, Philippines. Constant efforts at standardizing lambanog production has led to its better quality. Presently, lambanog is being exported to other countries and continues to win foreign customers over due to its natural ingredients as well as its potency.

''[[Tapuy]]'' is a traditional Philippine alcoholic drink made from fermented ''[[glutinous rice]]''. It is a clear wine of luxurious alcoholic taste, moderate sweetness and lingering finish. Its average alcohol content is 14% or 28 proof, and it does not contain any preservatives or sugar. To increase the awareness of ''tapuy'', the [[Philippine Rice Research Institute]] has created a cookbook containing recipes and cocktails from famous Filipino chefs and bartenders, featuring ''tapuy'' as one of the ingredients.
; Modern drinks
{{Multiple image
| image1            = San Miguel Pale Pilsen Beer (Philippines) 02.jpg
| caption1          = ''Cerveza'', specifically San Miguel Pale Pilsen, a popular Filipino beer.
| caption2          = 
| direction         = vertical
| image2            = 
| total_width       = 200}}[[Beer]] or ''serbesa'' (from the Spanish "cerveza") is the most widely available alcoholic drink in the Philippines. [[San Miguel Beer|San Miguel Pale Pilsen]] is the most popular and widely sold brand. Together with associated San Miguel beer brands such as San Mig Light and Gold Eagle Beer the company holds an aggregate market share of 92.7%.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ong |first1=Henry |title=Financial Advisor |url=https://www.entrepreneur.com.ph/news-and-events/financial-adviser-5-things-to-know-about-the-san-Miguel-food-and-beverage-s-follow-on-offering-and-how-to-profit-from-it-a23-20180911-1frm |access-date=October 6, 2018 |publisher=Entrepreneur Philippines |date=September 11, 2018 }}{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> [[File:Red Horse Beer (47993535798).jpg|left|thumb|253x253px|''[[Red Horse Beer|Red horse]],'' a stronger [[beer]].]]Beer na Beer produced by local conglomerate [[Asia Brewery]] is another widely sold pale Pilsner style beer. Asia Brewery also produces under license and distributes a number of other mass market beers such as Colt 45, Asahi Super Dry, Heineken and Tiger Beer. Other beer labels include [[Red Horse Beer]], Lone Star, Lone Star Light, Lone Star Ultra, Carlsberg, Coors Light, San Miguel Superdry, San Mig Strong Ice, and just recently, Manila Beer. Echoing trends in international markets, bars in urban areas have also begun to serve locally produced and imported craft beers in a variety of styles.

[[Rum]] is often associated with [[Tanduay]].

Several [[gin]]s, both local varieties like [[Ginebra San Miguel]] (as well as GSM Blue and GSM Premium Gin) and imported brands like [[Gilbey's]], are commonly found. Some people refer to gin by the shape of the bottle: ''bilog'' for a circular bottle and ''kwatro kantos'' (literally meaning four corners) for a square or rectangular bottle. Gin is sometimes combined with other ingredients to come up with variations.

==Street food==
[[File:Filipino-street-food-.jpg|thumb|240x240px|Filipino street vendor in [[Manila]] sells various street foods such as ''[[tokneneng]]'', ''kwek-kwek'', ''kikiam'', one-day-old, squid balls, and more.]]
[[File:Filipino Streetfood.jpg|thumb|240x240px|A bunch of Filipino street food skewers.]]
[[File:Dinagyang 2009 grilled meat on display.jpg|thumb|221x221px|Inihaw skewers street foods in [[Iloilo City]]]]
Aside from pastries and desserts, there are heartier snacks for ''merienda'' that can also serve as either an appetizer or side dish for a meal. ''Siomai'' is the local version'' of Chinese [[shaomai]].''
''[[Lumpia]]'' are spring rolls that can be either fresh or fried. Fresh ''lumpia'' (''lumpiang sariwa'') is usually made for fiestas or special occasions as it can be labor-intensive to prepare, while one version of fried ''lumpia'' (''lumpiang prito''), ''lumpiang shanghai'', is usually filled with ground pork and a combination of vegetables, and served with a sweet and sour dipping sauce.<ref>{{cite book |title=Memories of Philippine Kitchens |author1=Besa, Amy |author2=Dorotan, Romy |publisher=Stewart, Tabori & Chang |year=2006 |isbn=1-58479-451-8}}</ref> Other variations are filled with minced pork and shrimp and accompanied by a vinegar-based dipping sauce. ''Lumpia'' has been commercialized in [[frozen food]] form. [[Pares (food)|Beef pares]] is a common street food in Manila. Middle Eastern food such as the [[shawarma]] became popular in the Philippines in the late 1980s.
[[File:09300jfBarangays Caloocan Longos Malabon Avenues Landmarks Roadsfvf 32.jpg|left|thumb|228x228px|''[[Banana cue]],'' is a popular street food made from caramelized saba bananas.]]
There is a distinct range of [[street food]] available in the Philippines. Some of these are skewered on sticks in the manner of a [[kebab]]. One such example is ''banana-cue'', a whole [[banana]] or [[Plantain (cooking)|plantain]] skewered on a short thin bamboo stick, rolled in brown sugar, and pan-fried. ''Kamote-cue'' is a peeled [[sweet potato]] skewered on a stick, covered in brown sugar and then pan-fried. [[Fish ball]]s or [[squid ball]]s, including ''[[calamares]]'', are also pan-fried, then skewered on bamboo sticks and given to the customer, who then has a choice of dipping in a sweet or savory sauce. These are commonly sold frozen in markets and peddled by [[Hawker (trade)|street vendors]].

''[[Turon (food)|Turon]]'', a kind of ''[[lumpia]]'' consisting of an eggroll or [[phyllo]] wrapper commonly filled with sliced [[Plantain (cooking)|plantain]] and occasionally [[jackfruit]], is fried and sprinkled with sugar.

[[File:Taho.JPG|thumb|A ''magtataho'' ([[taho]] vendor) in [[Vigan|Vigan City.]] ]]
''[[Taho]]'' is a warm treat made of soft [[beancurd]] which is the ''taho'' itself, dark caramel syrup called ''arnibal'', and [[tapioca]] pearls. It is often sold in neighborhoods by street vendors who yell out "''taho!''" in a manner like that of vendors in the stands at sporting events yelling out "hotdogs" or "peanuts". Sometimes, ''taho'' is served chilled, and flavors have recently been added, such as chocolate or strawberry. ''Taho'' is derived from the original [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]] snack food known as ''[[douhua]]''.

There is also ''iskrambol'' (from the English "to scramble"), a kind of iced-based treat similar to a sorbet. The shaved ice is combined with various flavorings and usually topped with chocolate syrup. It is eaten by "scrambling" the contents or mixing them, then drinking with a large straw. It was later modified into ''ice scramble'', or simply ''scramble'', but with added skim milk, chocolate or strawberry syrup, and a choice of toppings such as [[marshmallows]], chocolate or candy sprinkles, rice crispies, or tapioca pearls.
[[File:Balot Penoy.jpg|left|thumb|230x230px|[[Balut (food)|Balut]] and penoy street vendor]]
[[File:Inihaw na Balut2.jpg|left|thumb|232x232px|Grilled balut]]
Street food featuring eggs include ''[[kwek-kwek]]'' which are hard-boiled quail eggs dipped in orange-dyed batter and then deep fried similar to [[tempura]]. ''Tokneneng'' is a larger version of ''kwek-kwek'' using chicken or duck eggs. Another Filipino egg snack is ''[[Balut (egg)|balut]]'', essentially a boiled pre-hatched poultry egg, usually duck or chicken. These fertilized eggs are allowed to develop until the embryo reaches a pre-determined size and are then boiled. They are consumed, usually along with vinegar and salt.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Magat|first=Margaret|date=2002|title= Balut: "Fertilized Duck Eggs and Their Role in Filipino Culture"|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1500289|journal= Western Folklore|volume=61|issue=1|pages=63–96|doi=10.2307/1500289|jstor=1500289|url-access=subscription}}</ref> There is also another egg item called ''penoy,'' which is basically hard-boiled unfertilized duck eggs that does not contain embryo. Like ''taho'', ''balut'' is advertised by street hawkers calling out their product.

''Okoy'', also spelled as ''ukoy'', is another batter-covered, deep-fried street food in the Philippines. Along with the batter, it normally includes bean sprouts, shredded pumpkin and very small shrimps, shells and all. It is commonly dipped in a combination of vinegar and chilli.
[[File:Laoag Dap-Ayan to Ilocos Norte - Empanada Stall.jpg|thumb|An empanada vendor selling Ilocos empanadas, a famous street food from the [[Ilocos Region]].]]
[[File:6142Street food (Tupig) vendors in the Philippines 02.jpg|thumb|[[Tupig]] cart street vendor with an improvised [[sheet metal]] grill selling the dessert as street food.]]
Among other street food are already mentioned [[#Pulutan|pulutan]] like ''[[isaw]]'', seasoned hog or chicken intestines skewered onto a stick and grilled; ''betamax'', roasted dried chicken blood cut into and served as small cubes, from which it received its name due to its crude resemblance to a [[Betamax]] tape; ''[[Adidas (food)|Adidas]]'', grilled chicken feet named after the popular [[Adidas|shoe brand]]; and ''[[Proven (food)|proven]]'', the [[proventriculus]] of a chicken coated in cornstarch and deep-fried. Fries made from [[sweet potatoes]] have also been dubbed "Pinoy fries". Most street foods are usually found near certain schools and universities, one example would be at Metro Manila's [[University Belt]].

Numerous 24/7 burger stands across the country include [[Burger Machine]] (nicknamed "the burger that never sleeps"), Angel's Burger, Franks N' Burgers, and Minute Burger.

''[[Pagpag]]'' is [[leftover]] food from restaurants (usually from [[fast-food]] restaurants) scavenged from [[garbage]] sites and [[Garbage dump|dumps]].<ref name="cnn">{{cite web|title='Garbage chicken' a grim staple for Manila's poor|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2012/04/30/world/asia/philippines-pagpag-slums/|publisher=[[CNN]]|date=May 30, 2012 |access-date=September 4, 2014}}</ref> ''Pagpag'' food can also be expired frozen meat, fish, or vegetables discarded by supermarkets and scavenged in garbage trucks where this expired food is collected<ref>{{cite web|url=http://library.pcw.gov.ph/sites/default/files/Sarbey%20hinggil%20sa%20Kahirapan_FINAL.pdf|title=Sarbey hinggil sa Sosyo-ekonomikong Kalagayan at Pamumuhay ng mga Kababaihan sa Ilang Piling Maralitang Komunidad sa Bansa|language=tl|website=[[Philippine Commission on Women]]|access-date=June 13, 2016|archive-date=February 20, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180220005522/http://library.pcw.gov.ph/sites/default/files/Sarbey%20hinggil%20sa%20Kahirapan_FINAL.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> and eaten by people suffering from the extreme [[poverty in the Philippines]]. Selling ''pagpag'' was a profitable business in areas where poor people live.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://cnnphilippines.com/metro/2015/06/17/Selling-pagpag-has-become-a-thriving-business.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150729055021/http://cnnphilippines.com/metro/2015/06/17/Selling-pagpag-has-become-a-thriving-business.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 29, 2015|title=Pagpag: A thriving business|last=Cruz|first=Gen|newspaper=[[CNN Philippines]]|date=June 22, 2015|access-date=June 13, 2016}}</ref> ''Pagpag'' is basically more often than not food collected by homeless individuals at the end of the day from various local fastfood restaurants in the Philippines.<ref name="rcam">{{cite web|url=http://www.rcam.org/news/157-archdiocese-of-manila-achieves-zero-waste-management-prevents-pagpag-eating-by-waste-pickers|title=Archdiocese of Manila achieves Zero Waste Management; prevents 'Pagpag' eating by waste pickers by Romulo S. Arsenio, Ph.D.|website=[[Archdiocese of Manila]]|access-date=June 13, 2016}}</ref>

==Exotic dishes==
Exotic dishes in ''Filipino cuisine r''efer to foods prepared from [[unconventional]] or less commonly consumed ingredients, often reflecting indigenous practices, rural resourcefulness, and historical necessity, particularly during periods such as [[World War II]].<ref name=":16">{{Cite web |last=Sunnexdesk |date=2013 |title=Pinoy exotic food |url=https://www.sunstar.com.ph/more-articles/pinoy-exotic-food |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=SunStar Publishing Inc. |language=en}}</ref>

{{Multiple image
| image1            = Balut (Still Lives).jpg
| caption1          = ''[[Balut (food)|Balut]]'', a boiled fertilized duck egg, typically eaten with salt and spiced vinegar.
| image2            = Adidas - Chicken Feet.jpg
| caption2          = ''Adidas'', a [[chicken feet]] skewers.
| direction         = vertical

}}

One of the most widely recognized Filipino exotic foods is ''[[Balut (food)|balut]]'', a boiled fertilized [[duck egg]] known for its savory broth and commonly sold as street food.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Balut: The National Bizzare Dish in the Philippines – Food in History |url=https://wordpress.kpu.ca/foodhistory/2023/04/02/balut-the-national-bizzare-dish-in-the-philippines/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |language=en-CA}}</ref> Other street foods include ''[[isaw]]'' (grilled chicken intestines), [[Adidas (food)|''adidas'']] (chicken feet), and ''betamax'' (coagulated chicken blood skewers).<ref name=":16" /> ''[[Soup No.5|Soup No. 5]]'', a broth made from [[bull]]'s genitals, ([[Testicles as food|testicles]] and [[Penis as food|penis]]), is served in some eateries, especially along Ongpin Street in [[Binondo]].<ref>{{cite web | title =Bizarre food with Andrew Zimmern – Philippines| url=http://www.travelchannel.com/TV_Shows/Bizarre_food/Episodes_Travel_Guides/Episode_Philippines | access-date = July 16, 2007}}</ref><ref>Sutherland, Matthew. (February 6, 2000). [http://www.tingog.com/culture/philippines-from-a-british-perspective.html "All a matter of taste"]. ''The Filipino Express''. Retrieved October 3, 2010, from www.tingog.com.</ref> It is also called ''“Remember Me”'' in [[Cagayan de Oro]] and ''[[lansiao]]'' in [[Cebu]]. In [[Davao City]], ''crocodile [[Suckling pig|lechon]]'', or whole roasted [[crocodile]], is a local specialty, with similar dishes also found in [[Palawan]] and [[Tanay, Rizal|Tanay]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Quiros |first=Judy |date=2011 |title=Davao trader pushes 'crocodile lechon' as new Pinoy exotic dish |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/17953/davao-trader-pushes-crocodile-lechon-as-new-pinoy-exotic-dish/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref>

In agricultural areas, especially rice fields, various species considered pests or invasive are utilized as food. [[Frog (food)|Frogs]] (''palakang bukid'' or ''betute'') are prepared in dishes such as ''[[adobo]]'', ''[[ginataan]]'' (with coconut milk), ''[[tinola]]'', or deep-fried.<ref>{{Cite web |last=lalos |date=2017-07-29 |title='Adobong puti,' 'Betute'—your latest guide to dining in Pampanga |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/269532/adobong-puti-betute-latest-guide-dining-pampanga/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref> [[Freshwater snail]]s (''kuhol'' or ''suso'') are commonly cooked as ''[[ginataang kuhol]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Merano |first=Vanjo |date=2015-10-09 |title=Apple Snails in Coconut Milk (Ginataang Kuhol) |url=https://panlasangpinoy.com/apple-snails-in-coconut-milk-ginataang-kuhol/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Panlasang Pinoy |language=en-US}}</ref> Insects such as [[mole cricket]]s or ''camaru'' ([[Kapampangan language|Kapampangan]])<ref>{{Cite web |title=Amazing Earth: Three ways to cook Kapampangan exotic food camaru |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/entertainment/tv/amazing_earth/107723/amazing-earth-three-ways-to-cook-kapampangan-exotic-food-camaru/evideo/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=www.gmanetwork.com |language=en-US}}</ref> or ''ararawan'' ([[Ilocano language|Ilocano]]),<ref name=":15" /> are [[Sautéing|sautéed]] or deep-fried, while in [[South Cotabato]] and [[Nueva Ecija]], ''tipaklong'' ([[Grasshopper as food|grasshoppers]]) are eaten fried for their crisp texture.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2023 |title=This grasshopper delicacy is a hit in South Cotabato |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/lifestyle/food/879572/this-grasshopper-delicacy-is-a-hit-in-south-cotabato/story/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=GMA News Online |language=en}}</ref> In coconut plantations, [[coconut worm]]s (''uok, batod, abaling''), are also consumed, it is typically prepared grilled, fried, or as ''[[kilawin]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lim |first=Ron |title=This exotic dish from Rizal is made from worms |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/lifestyle/food/122772/this-exotic-dish-from-rizal-is-made-from-worms/story |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=www.gmanetwork.com |language=en}}</ref> In [[Luzon|Northern Luzon]], ''abal-abal'' ([[june beetle]]s)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Baga-Reyes |first=Vangie |date=2011 |title=For a change, something exotic–'adobong salagubang' |url=https://lifestyle.inquirer.net/2394/for-a-change-something-exotic%E2%80%93%E2%80%98adobong-salagubang%E2%80%99/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Lifestyle.INQ |language=en-US}}</ref> are consumed seasonally and ''abuos'' ([[weaver ant]] larvae)<ref>{{Cite web |last=Adriano |first=Leilanie |date=2025 |title=Gameng Festival: A celebration of rich cultural heritage |url=https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1242576 |access-date=March 24, 2026 |website=Philippine News Agency}}</ref> are also traditionally eaten, typically toasted or sautéed. In the [[Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras|rice terraces]] of [[Ifugao]], [[swamp eel]]s (''kiwit'') are consumed since it is destroying the rice terraces, it is commonly grilled and stewed.<ref name=":13" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Roque |first=Anselmo |date=2019-02-22 |title=Swamp eels: From bane to boon for farmers |url=https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1088649/swamp-eels-from-bane-to-boon-for-farmers |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=INQUIRER.net |language=en}}</ref>

As an archipelagic country, the Philippines also features a range of exotic seafood. These include ''buriring'' ([[Pufferfish as food|pufferfish]]), a seasonal delicacy in parts of [[Luzon]] and the [[Visayas]], prepared as sour stews such as ''[[linarang]]'' or ''[[inun-unan]]'', or fried.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Singuay |first=Mae |date=2025 |title=Cadiz to stage 'buriring' cooking competition |url=https://www.panaynews.net/cadiz-to-stage-buriring-cooking-competition/ |access-date=March 24, 2026 |website=Panay News}}</ref> In [[Bohol]], [[jellyfish]] (''bubog lutaw'') are consumed as ''kinilaw'', and are also eaten in [[Palawan]] and [[Polillo Island]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bubog Lutaw, isang Jellyfish na inihahain sa Bohol, masarap nga ba?! {{!}} Pinas Sarap |url=https://www.gmanetwork.com/gtv/magazine/pinas_sarap/201479/bubog-lutaw-isang-jellyfish-na-inihahain-sa-bohol-masarap-nga-ba-pinas-sarap/video |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=www.gmanetwork.com |language=en}}</ref> [[Sea cucumber]] (''balat'' ''or balatan'') is similarly prepared as ''kinilaw'' in parts of the Visayas and Northern Luzon.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-07-04 |title=Homes for the Holothurians: Optimizing sea cucumber management strategies through biophysical modeling - UP Marine Science Institute |url=https://msi.upd.edu.ph/sea-cucumber-management/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> Other examples include ''saang'' ([[Conch|spider conch]]), typically grilled or cooked in soup;<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021-11-18 |title=Skewered Saang: Cebu's underrated street food favorite {{!}} Sugbo.ph |url=https://sugbo.ph/2021/skewered-saang-cebu/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |language=en-US}}</ref> ''[[tamilok]]'' (wood-boring [[Mollusca|mollusks]] or shipworms), harvested from [[Mangrove|mangrove trees]] in Palawan, [[Aklan]], and [[Capiz]] and eaten raw in vinegar;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tamilok - Arca del Gusto |url=https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/tamilok/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Slow Food Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> and ''puyoy'', a brackish-water worm eel delicacy from [[Capiz]], which is prepared grilled, fried, or dried.<ref>{{Cite web |title=PUYOY |url=https://cmpg.upv.edu.ph/heritage/puyoy/ |access-date=2026-03-24 |website=Cultural Mapping of Panay and Guimaras |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Cooking methods==
The [[Filipino language|Filipino]] words commonly used for cooking methods and terms are listed below:<ref name="polistico">{{cite book|author =Polistico, Edgie|title =Philippine Food, Cooking, & Dining Dictionary|publisher =Anvil Publishing, Incorporated|year =2017|isbn =9786214200870|url =https://books.google.com/books?id=iz8_DwAAQBAJ&q=Arroz+caldo}}{{Dead link|date=April 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

{{div col|colwidth=30em}}
* '''[[Adobo (Filipino cuisine)|Adobo]]''' (''inadobo'') − cooked in vinegar, oil, garlic and soy sauce.
* '''[[Afritada]]''' – braised in tomato sauce.
* '''Babad''' (''binabad'', ''ibinabad'') − to marinate.
* '''Banli''' (''binanlian'', ''pabanli'') − to blanch.
* '''Bagoong''' (''binagoongan'', ''sa bagoong'') − fermented or cooked with fermented fish/shrimp paste (''[[bagoong]]'')
* '''[[Bibingka]]''' – baked cakes, traditionally [[glutinous rice]].
* '''Binalot''' – literally "wrapped". This generally refers to dishes wrapped in banana leaves, pandan leaves, or even aluminum foil. The wrapper is generally inedible (in contrast to ''[[lumpia]]''—see below).
* '''Buro''' (''binuro'') − fermented, pickled, or preserved in salt or vinegar. Synonymous with ''[[tapai|tapay]]'' in other Philippine languages when referring to fermented rice.
* '''[[Daing]]''' ({{transliteration|tl|dinaing}}, {{transliteration|tl|padaing}}) − salted and dried, usually fish or seafood. Synonymous with ''tuyô'', ''bulad'' or ''buwad'' in other Philippine languages
* '''Giniling''' – ground meat. Sometimes used as a synonym for [[picadillo]], especially in ''[[arroz a la cubana]]''.
* '''[[Guinataan]]''' (''sa gata'') − cooked with coconut milk.
* '''Guisa''' (''guisado'', ''ginuisa'') − sautéed with garlic and onions. Also spelled ''gisa'', ''gisado'', ''ginisa''.
* '''[[Hamonado]]''' (''endulsado'') – marinated or cooked in a sweet pineapple sauce. Sometimes synonymous with ''pininyahan'' or ''minatamis''
* '''Halabos''' (''hinalabos'') – mostly for shellfish. Steamed in their own juices and sometimes carbonated soda.
* '''[[Halo-halo]]''' - made up of crushed ice, evaporated milk or condensed milk, and various ingredients including, ube, sweetened beans, coconut strips, sago (pearls), gulaman (gelatin), pinipig rice, boiled taro or soft yams in cubes, fruit slices, flan, and topped with a scoop of ube ice cream.
* '''Hilaw''' (''sariwa'') – unripe (for fruits and vegetables), raw (for meats). Also used for uncooked food in general (as in ''[[lumpia]]ng sariwa'').
* '''Hinurno''' – baked in an oven (''pugon'') or roasted.
* '''Ihaw''' (''inihaw'') − grilled over coal. In Visayas, it is also known as ''sinugba''; ''inasal'' refers to grilling meat on sticks.
* '''[[Kinilaw]]''' or '''[[Kilawin]]''' − fish or seafood marinated in [[vinegar]] or [[calamansi]] juice along with [[garlic]], [[onion]]s, [[ginger]], [[cucumber]], [[Capsicum|peppers]]. Also means to eat raw or fresh, cognate of ''Hilaw''.
* '''Lechon''' (''nilechon'') − roasted on a spit. Also spelled ''litson''.
* '''Lumpia''' – savory food wrapped with an edible wrapper.
* '''Minatamis''' (''minatamisan'') − sweetened. Similar to ''[[hamonado]]''.
* '''Nilaga''' (''laga'', ''palaga'') − boiled/braised.
* '''Nilasing''' − cooked with an alcoholic beverage like wine or beer. 
* '''Paksiw''' (''pinaksiw'') − cooked in vinegar.
* '''[[Pancit]]''' (''pansit'', ''fideo'') – noodle dishes, usually of [[Filipino Chinese cuisine|Chinese Filipino]] origin.
* '''Pangat''' (''pinangat'') − boiled in salted water/brine with fruit such as tomatoes or ripe mangoes.
* '''Palaman''' (''pinalaman'', ''pinalamanan'') − "filled" as in ''siopao'', though "palaman" also refers to the filling in a sandwich.
* '''[[Pinakbet]]''' (''pakbet'') − to cook with vegetables usually with ''sitaw'' ([[yardlong beans]]), [[calabaza]], ''talong'' (eggplant), and ''ampalaya'' ([[bitter melon]]) among others and ''[[bagoong]]''.
* '''Pinakuluan''' – boiled.
* '''Pininyahan''' – marinated or cooked with pineapples. Sometimes synonymous with ''hamonado''.
* '''Prito''' (''pinirito'') − fried or deep fried. From the Spanish ''frito''.
* '''[[Puto (food)|Puto]]''' – steamed cakes, traditionally glutinous rice.
* '''Relleno''' (''relyeno'') – stuffed.
* '''Sarza''' (''sarciado'') – cooked with a thick sauce.
* '''Sinangag''' – garlic fried rice.
* '''Sisig''' - is a traditional food of Filipino specially partnered with beer. It made by different parts of pig.
* '''[[Sinigang|Sigang]]''' (''sinigang'') − boiled in a sour broth usually with a [[tamarind]] base. Other common souring agents include [[guava]], raw [[mango]]es, calamansi also known as [[calamondin]].
* '''[[Tapa (Filipino cuisine)|Tapa]]''' or '''[[Tinapa]]''' – dried and smoked. ''Tapa'' refers to meat treated in this manner, mostly marinated and then dried and fried afterwards. ''Tinapa'' meanwhile is almost exclusively associated with [[smoked fish]].
* '''[[Tapai|Tapay]]''' – fermented with [[yeast]], usually rice, traditionally in [[tapayan]] jars. Synonymous with ''buro'' in early phases. Can also refer to various products of fermented rice, including [[rice wine]]s. A very briefly fermented glutinous rice version is known as ''[[galapong]]'', which is an essential ingredient in Filipino ''[[kakanin]]'' (rice cakes). Cognate of ''tinapay'' ([[leavened]] [[bread]]).
* '''Tosta''' (''tinosta'', ''tostado'') – toasted.
* '''[[Torta]]''' (''tinorta'', ''patorta'') – in the northern Philippines, to cook with eggs in the manner of an [[omelette]]. In the southern Philippines, a general term for a [[torta mamon|small cake]].
{{div col end}}
