======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Israeli cuisine
======================================================================

{{Short description|Culinary traditions of Israel}}
{{pp-extended|small=yes}}
[[File:The 7 Breakfasts - Café Café.jpg|thumb|300px|[[Israeli breakfast]], a distinctive style of breakfast that originates from the modern culture of the ''[[kibbutz]]im'']]
'''Israeli cuisine''' primarily comprises dishes brought from the [[Jewish diaspora]], and has more recently been defined by the development of a notable [[fusion cuisine]] characterized by the mixing of [[Jewish cuisine]] and [[Arab cuisine]].<ref name="region">Gold, Rozanne [https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/20/garden/a-region-s-tastes-commingle-in-israel.html?pagewanted=all ''A Region's Tastes Commingle in Israel''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110917205613/http://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/20/garden/a-region-s-tastes-commingle-in-israel.html?pagewanted=all|date=2011-09-17}} (July 20, 1994) in ''The New York Times'' Retrieved 2010–02–14</ref> It also blends together the culinary traditions of the various diaspora groups, namely those of [[Mizrahi Jewish cuisine|Middle Eastern Jews]] with roots in [[Jewish exodus from the Muslim world|Southwest Asia and North Africa]], [[Sephardic Jewish cuisine|Sephardi Jews]] from [[History of the Jews in Spain|Iberia]], and [[Ashkenazi Jewish cuisine|Ashkenazi Jews]] from [[History of the Jews in Europe|Central and Eastern Europe]].<ref name="region" /><ref name="Ashkenazi2020">{{cite book |author=Michael Ashkenazi |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oM4DEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA2 |title=Food Cultures of Israel: Recipes, Customs, and Issues |date=10 November 2020 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-1-4408-6686-9 |pages=2}}</ref>

The country's cuisine also incorporates food and drinks traditionally included in other [[Middle Eastern cuisine]]s (e.g., [[Iranian cuisine]] from [[Persian Jews]] and [[Turkish cuisine]] from [[Turkish Jews in Israel|Turkish Jews]]) as well as in [[Mediterranean cuisine]]s, such that spices like ''[[za'atar]]'' and foods such as ''[[falafel]]'', ''[[hummus]]'', ''[[msabbaha]]'', ''[[shakshouka]]'', and ''[[couscous]]'' are now widely popular in Israel.<ref>Sardas-Trotino, Sarit [http://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-3850942,00.html ''NY Times presents: Israeli cuisine course''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303193243/http://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-3850942,00.html |date=2016-03-03}} (February 19, 2010) in ''Ynet&nbsp;– LifeStyle'' Retrieved 2010–02–19</ref><ref name=Gur>Gur, ''The Book of New Israeli Food'', pg. 11</ref> However, the identification of Arab dishes as Israeli has led to accusations of [[cultural appropriation]] against Israel by [[Palestinians]] and other [[Arabs]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/food/heres-why-palestinians-object-to-the-term-israeli-food-it-erases-us-from-history/2020/02/14/96974a74-4d25-11ea-bf44-f5043eb3918a_story.html|title=Here's why Palestinians object to the term 'Israeli food': It erases us from history |first=Reem |last=Kassis|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=18 February 2020}}</ref><ref name="Pilcher">{{cite book|last=Pilcher|first=Jeffrey M.|title=Food in World History|publisher=Routledge|year=2006|page=115|isbn=978-0-415-31146-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lbEVK2DSu3AC&q=falafel}}</ref>

Other influences on the cuisine are the availability of foods common to the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]], especially certain kinds of fruits and vegetables, dairy products, and fish; the tradition of observing ''[[kashrut]]''; and food customs and traditions (''[[minhag]]'') specific to [[Shabbat]] and other [[Jewish holidays]]. Examples of these foods include ''[[challah]]'', ''[[jachnun]]'', ''[[malawach]]'', [[gefilte fish]], ''[[hamin]]'', [[Jerusalem mixed grill|''me'orav yerushalmi'']], and [[Sufganiyah|''sufganiyot'']].

New dishes based on agricultural products such as oranges, avocados, dairy products, and fish, and others based on world trends have been introduced over the years, and chefs trained abroad have brought in elements of other international cuisines.<ref name=Roden2>Roden, ''The Book of Jewish Food'', pp 202–207</ref>

==History==
===Origins===
{{See also|Ancient Israelite cuisine}}
[[File:JEWISH NATIONAL FUND POSTER FROM THE 1940'S PROMOTING LAND REDEMPTION IN PALESTINE. כרזה משנות ה 40 של הקרן הקימת לישראל (קק"ל).D247-006.jpg|thumb|Poster by the Jewish National Fund displaying the "[[Seven Species]]" of agricultural products that are documented in the [[Hebrew Bible]] as being special products of the [[Land of Israel]] (January 1945)]]
Israel's culinary traditions comprise foods and cooking methods that span 3,000 years of history. Over that time, these traditions have been shaped by influences from Asia, Africa and Europe, and religious and ethnic influences have resulted in a culinary melting pot. Biblical and archaeological records provide insight into the culinary life of the region as far back as 1000 BCE.<ref name="Ansky1">Ansky, ''The Food of Israel'', pp. 6–9</ref>

[[Ancient Israelite cuisine]] was based on several products that still play important roles in modern Israeli cuisine. These were known as the [[seven species]]: olives, figs, dates, pomegranates, wheat, barley and grapes.<ref>Zisling, Yael, [http://www.gemsinisrael.com/e_article000039885.htm ''The Biblical Seven Species''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303230339/http://www.gemsinisrael.com/e_article000039885.htm|date=2016-03-03}} in ''Gems in Israel'', Retrieved 2010-02-14</ref> The diet, based on locally grown produce, was enhanced by imported spices, readily available due to the country's position at the crossroads of east–west trade routes.<ref name="Ansky1" />

During the [[Second Temple period]] (516 BCE – 70 CE), [[Hellenistic]] and [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] culture heavily influenced cuisine, particularly of the [[Kohen|priests]] and aristocracy of [[Jerusalem]]. Elaborate meals were served that included piquant entrées and alcoholic drinks, fish, beef, meat, pickled and fresh vegetables, olives, and tart or sweet fruits.<ref name="Ansky1" />

After the [[destruction of the Second Temple]] and the [[galut|exile]] of the majority of Jews from the Land of Israel, Jewish cuisine continued to develop in the many countries where Jewish communities have existed since [[Late Antiquity]], influenced by the economics, agriculture, and culinary traditions of those countries.{{Citation needed|date=February 2023}}

===Old Yishuv===
{{Main|Old Yishuv#Food}}
The [[Old Yishuv]] was the Jewish community that lived in [[Ottoman Syria]] prior to the [[Zionism|Zionist]] [[Aliyah]] from the [[Jewish diaspora|diaspora]] that began in 1881. The cooking style of the community was [[Sephardi cuisine]], which developed among the [[History of the Jews in Spain|Jews of Spain]] before their [[Alhambra Decree|expulsion in 1492]], and in the areas to which they migrated thereafter, particularly the [[Balkans]] and [[Ottoman Empire]]. Sephardim and Ashkenazim also established communities in the Old Yishuv. Particularly in Jerusalem, they continued to develop their culinary style, influenced by [[Ottoman cuisine]], creating a style that became known as Jerusalem Sephardi cuisine.<ref name="gurhistory">Gur, pg. 10-16</ref> This cuisine included pies like [[Samosa|''sambousak'']], [[Pastel (food)|pastels]] and [[Börek|''burekas'']], vegetable [[gratin]]s and stuffed vegetables, and rice and [[bulgur]] [[pilaf]]s, which are now considered to be Jerusalem classics.<ref name="Roden2" />

Groups of [[Hasidic Judaism|Hasidic Jews]] from [[Eastern Europe]] also began establishing communities in the late 18th century, and brought with them their traditional [[Ashkenazi cuisine]], developing, however, distinct local variations, notably a peppery, caramelized noodle pudding known as ''[[Kugel Yerushalmi|kugel yerushalmi]]''.<ref name="Marks203">Marks, ''The World of Jewish Cooking'' pg. 203</ref>

===Jewish immigration===
[[File:PikiWiki Israel 5701 Cooking Lesson.jpg|thumb|Cooking class at a Jewish girls' school in [[Jerusalem]], {{Circa|1936}}]]

Beginning with the [[First Aliyah]] in 1881, Jews began immigrating to the area from [[Yemen]] and Eastern Europe in larger numbers, particularly from Poland and Russia. These [[Zionism|Zionist]] pioneers were motivated both ideologically and by the Mediterranean climate to reject the Ashkenazi cooking styles they grew up with, and adapt by using local produce, especially vegetables such as [[zucchini]], [[Bell pepper|pepper]]s, [[eggplant]], [[artichoke]] and [[chickpea]]s.<ref name="Roden2"/> The first Hebrew cookbook, ''[[How to Cook in Palestine]]'', written by [[Erna Meyer]] and published in the early 1930s by the Palestine Federation of the [[Women's International Zionist Organization]], exhorted cooks to use Mediterranean herbs and Middle-Eastern spices and local vegetables in their cooking.<ref name=gurhistory/> The bread, olives, cheese and raw vegetables they adopted became the basis for the ''[[kibbutz]]'' breakfast, which in more abundant forms is served in Israeli hotels, and in various forms in most Israeli homes today.<ref name="Roden2"/><ref name=gurhistory/>

===Early years of the State===
[[File:Israel Austerity.jpg|thumb|250px|Residents of [[Tel Aviv]] standing in line to buy food rations during the [[Austerity in Israel|austerity period]], 1954]]

The State of Israel faced enormous military and economic challenges in its early years, and the period from 1948 to 1958 was a time of food rationing and [[Austerity in Israel|austerity]], known as ''tzena''. In this decade, over one million Jewish immigrants, mainly from Arab countries, but also including European [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] survivors, inundated the new state. They arrived when only basic foods were available and ethnic dishes had to be modified with a range of mock or simulated foods, such as chopped "liver" from eggplant, and turkey as a substitute for veal ''[[schnitzel]]'' for Ashkenazim, ''[[kubbeh]]'' made from frozen fish instead of [[ground meat]] for [[Iraqi Jews]], and turkey in place of the lamb [[kebab]]s of the [[Mizrahi Jews]]. These adaptations remain a legacy of that time.<ref name="Roden2" /><ref name="gurhistory" />

Substitutes, such as the wheat-based rice substitute, ''[[ptitim]]'', were introduced, and versatile vegetables such as eggplant were used as alternatives to meat. Additional flavor and nutrition were provided from inexpensive canned tomato paste and puree, ''[[hummus]]'', [[tahini|''tahina'']], and mayonnaise in tubes. Meat was scarce, and it was not until the late 1950s that herds of beef cattle were introduced into the agricultural economy.<ref name="Nathan1">Nathan, ''The Foods of Israel Today''</ref>

''[[Malva nicaeensis#Plant uses and properties|Khubeza]]'', a local variety of the [[Malva|mallow]] plant, became an important food source during the War of Independence. During the [[Siege of Jerusalem (1948)|siege of Jerusalem]], when convoys of food could not reach the city, Jerusalemites went out to the fields to pick ''khubeza'' leaves, which are high in iron and vitamins.<ref>[https://www.jpost.com/ArtsAndCulture/FoodAndWine/Article.aspx?id=167135 Superfoods to the rescue] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121018094950/http://www.jpost.com/ArtsAndCulture/FoodAndWine/Article.aspx?id=167135 |date=2012-10-18 }}, [[Jerusalem Post]]</ref> Instructions for cooking it broadcast by Jerusalem-based radio station Kol Hamagen, were picked up in Jordan, which convinced the Arabs that the Jews were dying of starvation and victory was at hand.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://www.haaretz.com/1.4999570 | title=Don't Leave These Alone | author=Doram Gaunt | date=2008-05-07 | website=[[:en:haaretz]] | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190720175223/https://www.haaretz.com/1.4999570 | archive-date=2019-07-20 | access-date=2021-09-30 }}<!--[http://www.haaretz.co.il/hasen/spages/961709.html Haaretz]{{dead link|date=March 2016}}--></ref> In the past decade, food writers in Israel have encouraged the population to prepare ''khubeza'' on [[Israel Independence Day]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.encyclopedia.com/doc/1P1-2279989.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080607133148/http://www.encyclopedia.com/doc/1P1-2279989.html|url-status=dead|title=Independence Day: The feast that moved away from home|archive-date=7 June 2008|access-date=8 November 2021}}</ref> Local chefs have begun to serve ''khubeza'' and other wild plants gathered from the fields in upscale restaurants.<ref>[http://www.the-eucalyptus.com/phyllis.html Our man cooks slowly: Eucalyptus restaurant], [[Jerusalem Post]] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090630040746/http://www.the-eucalyptus.com/phyllis.html |date=June 30, 2009 }}</ref> The dish from the independence war is called [[Khubeza patties|''ktzitzot khubeza'']] and is still eaten by Israelis today.{{Citation needed|date=February 2023}}

===Impact of immigration===
[[File:Halva IMG 2412.JPG|thumb|250px| [[Halva]] for sale at [[Mahane Yehuda Market]] in [[Jerusalem]], 2010]]
Immigrants to Israel have introduced elements of the cuisines of the cultures and countries from whence they came.<ref name=region /> In the nearly 50 years before 1948, there were successive waves of [[Aliyah|Jewish immigration]], which brought a whole range of foods and cooking styles. Immigrants arriving from central Europe brought foods such as ''[[schnitzel]]'' and [[strudel]]s, while Russian Jews brought [[borsht|borscht]] and herring dishes, such as [[schmaltz herring]] and ''vorschmack'' (''gehakte herring'').<ref name="Roden2" />

Ashkenazi dishes include [[chicken soup]], ''schnitzel'', [[lox]], [[chopped liver]], [[gefilte fish]], [[knish]]es, [[kishka (food)|''kishka'']] and ''[[kugel]]''. The first Israeli [[Pâtisserie|''patisseries'']] were opened by [[Ashkenazi Jews]], who popularized cakes and pastries from central and Eastern Europe, such as yeast cakes (''[[babka (food)|babka]]''), nut spirals (''schnecken''), chocolate rolls and layered pastries. After 1948, the greatest impact came from the large migration of Jews from Turkey, Iraq, Kurdistan and Yemen, and [[Mizrahi Jews]] from North Africa, particularly Morocco. Typically, the staff of army kitchens, schools, hospitals, hotels and restaurant kitchens has consisted of Mizrahi, [[History of the Jews in Kurdistan|Kurdish]] and [[Yemenite Jews]], and this has had an influence on the cooking fashions and ingredients of the country.<ref name="Roden2" />

Mizrahi cuisine, the cuisine of Jews from North Africa, features grilled meats, sweet and savory puff pastries, rice dishes, stuffed vegetables, pita breads and salads, and shares many similarities with [[Arab cuisine]]. Other North African dishes popular in Israel include ''[[couscous]]'', ''[[shakshouka]]'', ''[[matbucha]]'', carrot salad and ''[[chraime]]'' (slices of fish cooked in a spicy tomato sauce).

[[Sephardic cuisine|Sephardic dishes]], with [[Balkan]] and Turkish influences incorporated in Israeli cuisine include [[Börek|''burekas'']], [[yogurt]] and ''[[taramosalata]]''. Yemenite Jewish foods include ''[[jachnun]]'', ''[[malawach]]'', ''[[skhug]]'' and [[Kubaneh|''kubane'']]. Iraqi dishes popular in Israel include [[amba (condiment)|''amba'']], various types of ''[[kubba]]'', stuffed vegetables ({{transliteration|ar|mhasha}}), [[kebab]], ''[[sambusac]]'', ''[[sabich]]'' and [[Tursu|pickled vegetables]] (''hamutzim'').

===Modern trends===
[[File:Beduin market, Beersheba - panoramio.jpg|thumb|Assortment of pickled vegetables at a predominantly [[Bedouin]] market in [[Beersheba]], 2007]]
As Israeli agriculture developed and new kinds of fruits and vegetables appeared on the market, cooks and chefs began to experiment and devise new dishes with them.<ref name="Nathan1" /> They also began using "biblical" ingredients such as honey, figs, and pomegranates, and indigenous foods such as [[Opuntia|prickly pears]] (''tzabar'') and [[chickpea]]s. Since the late 1970s, there has been an increased interest in international cuisine, cooking with wine and herbs, and [[vegetarianism]].<ref name="Roden2" />

A more sophisticated food culture in Israel began to develop when cookbooks, such as ''From the Kitchen with Love'' by Ruth Sirkis, published in 1974, introduced international cooking trends, and together with the opening of restaurants serving cuisines such as Chinese, Italian and French, encouraged more dining out.<ref name="gurhistory" /><ref>Ansky, pp. 24–26</ref>

The 1980s were a formative decade: the increased optimism after the signing of the [[Egyptian–Israeli Peace Treaty|peace treaty with Egypt]] in 1979, the economic recovery of the mid-1980s and the increasing travel abroad by average citizens were factors contributing to a greater interest in food and wine. In addition, high-quality, locally produced ingredients became increasingly available. For example, privately owned dairies began to produce handmade cheeses from goat, sheep and cow's milk, which quickly became very popular both among chefs and the general public. In 1983, the [[Golan Heights Winery]] was the first of many new Israeli winemakers to help transform tastes with their production of world-class, semi-dry and dry wines. New attention was paid to the making of handmade breads and the production of high quality olive oil. The successful development of [[aquaculture]] ensured a steady supply of fresh fish, and the agricultural revolution in Israel led to an overwhelming choice and quality of fresh fruit, vegetables and herbs.<ref name="gurhistory" />

Ethnic heritage cooking, both [[Sephardic]] and [[Ashkenazi]], has made a comeback with the growing acceptance of the heterogeneous society. Apart from home cooking, many ethnic foods are now available in street markets, supermarkets and restaurants, or are served at [[Jewish wedding|weddings]] and [[bar mitzvah]]s, and people increasingly eat foods from ethnic backgrounds other than their own. Overlap and combinations of foods from different ethnic groups is becoming standard as a multi-ethnic food culture develops.<ref name="Roden2" /><ref name="gurhistory" />

The 1990s saw an increasing interest in international cuisines. [[Sushi]], in particular, has taken hold as a popular style for eating out and as an entrée for events. In restaurants, [[fusion cuisine]], with the melding of classic cuisines such as French and Japanese with local ingredients has become widespread.{{citation needed|date=November 2021}}

In the 2000s, the trend of "eating healthy" with an emphasis on [[organic food|organic]] and [[whole grain|whole-grain]] foods has become prominent, and medical research has led many Israelis to re-embrace the [[Mediterranean diet]], with its touted health benefits.<ref>"Celebrating sixty years of Israeli cuisine" (May 2008), ''Derech HaOchel'', No. 82, pp. 36–38 ('''Hebrew''')</ref>

==Characteristics==
Geography has a large influence on Israeli cuisine, and foods common in the [[Mediterranean region]], such as olives, wheat, chickpeas, dairy products, fish, and vegetables such as tomatoes, eggplants, and zucchini are prominent in Israeli cuisine. Fresh fruits and vegetables are plentiful in Israel and are cooked and served in many ways.<ref name=mjl>[http://www.myjewishlearning.com/culture/2/Food/Ashkenazic_Cuisine/Israel.shtml?CLAA ''Overview: Israeli Food''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517121222/http://www.myjewishlearning.com/culture/2/Food/Ashkenazic_Cuisine/Israel.shtml?CLAA |date=2014-05-17 }} Retrieved 2009-09-10</ref>

[[File:Cucina israeliana.JPG|thumb|right|A typical Israeli [[Meze|''mezze'']] spread, with ''[[hummus]]'' and [[pita]], [[Israeli salad]], olives, and pickles]]

There are various climatic [[Geography of Israel|areas in Israel]] and areas it has settled that allow a variety of products to be grown. Citrus trees such as orange, lemon and grapefruit thrive on the coastal plain. Figs, pomegranates and olives also grow in the cooler hill areas.<ref name="Ansky1"/>

The subtropical climate near the Sea of Galilee and in the Jordan River Valley is suitable for mangoes, kiwis and bananas, while the temperate climate of the mountains of the Galilee and the Golan is suitable for grapes, apples and cherries.<ref>Homsky, Shaul, author of ''Fruits Grown in Israel'' quoted in Nathan, ''The Foods of Israel Today''</ref>

[[File:Israeli salad and cheese.jpg|thumb|Cucumber-and-tomato salad with ''[[Strained yogurt|labane]]'' and ''[[za'atar]]'']]
Israeli eating customs also conform to the wider Mediterranean region, with lunch, rather than dinner, being the focal meal of a regular workday.

"[[Kibbutz]] foods" have been adopted by many Israelis for their light evening meals as well as breakfasts, and may consist of various types of cheeses, both soft and hard, yogurt, ''[[labne]]'' and sour cream, vegetables and salads, olives, [[Boiled egg|hard-boiled eggs]] or omelets, pickled and [[Herring as food|smoked herring]], a variety of breads, and fresh orange juice and coffee.<ref name="Roden2" />

In addition, [[Jewish holidays]] influence the cuisine, with the preparation of traditional foods at holiday times, such as various types of ''[[challah]]'' (braided bread) for [[Shabbat]] and festivals, jelly doughnuts (''[[sufganiyot]]'') for [[Hanukkah|Hanukah]], the ''[[hamantaschen]]'' pastry (''oznei haman'') for Purim, ''[[charoset]]'', a type of fruit paste, for Passover, and dairy foods for [[Shavuot]].

The Shabbat dinner, eaten on Friday, and to a lesser extent the Shabbat lunch, is a significant meal in Israeli homes, together with holiday meals.<ref name="mjl" />

Although many, if not most, Jews in Israel do not keep [[kosher]], the tradition of ''[[kashrut]]'' strongly influences the availability of certain foods and their preparation in homes, public institutions and many restaurants, including the separation of milk and meat and avoiding the use of non-kosher foods, especially pork and shellfish.

During [[Passover]], bread and other leavened foods are prohibited to [[Shomer Shabbat|observant Jews]] and [[matza]] and leaven-free foods are substituted.<ref>Ansky, pp 15-20</ref>

==Foods==
Israel does not have a universally recognized national dish; in previous years this was considered to be ''[[falafel]]'', deep-fried balls of seasoned, ground chickpeas.<ref>Nathan, Joan, [http://www.myjewishlearning.com/culture/food/IsraeliFood/FalafelRecipe.htm ''Falafel: About Israel's signature food''] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081024212900/http://www.myjewishlearning.com/culture/food/IsraeliFood/FalafelRecipe.htm |date=October 24, 2008 }} in ''My Jewish Learning'', Retrieved 2010–02–14</ref><ref>Roden pg. 273</ref> Street vendors throughout Israel used to sell ''falafel''. It was a favorite "street food" for decades and is still popular as a ''mezze'' dish or as a top-up for ''hummus''-in-pita, though it is less common nowadays as a sole filling in pita because people are more aware of the health effects of deep-frying food in oil.<ref name="Nathan1"/>

The Israeli breakfast has always been largely healthy, by today's standards, and one book called the [[Israeli breakfast]] "the Jewish state's contribution to world cuisine".<ref name=Dubois>{{cite book
 | last1 =Dubois
 | first1 =Jill
 | last2 =Rosh
