According to Blassingame's research, some enslaved people received the bare minimum in food and had to supplement their diets by hunting, fishing, and foraging for food.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Blassingame |first1=John |title=The Slave Community: Plantation Life in the Antebellum South |year=1972 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780195025637 |pages=39, 155–158 |url=https://archive.org/details/slavecommunitypl0000blas/mode/2up?q=food}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Brown |first1=Shayla |title=Slavery, Soul Food and the Power of Black Women |url=https://www.northjersey.com/in-depth/life/2020/12/02/slavery-soul-food-black-women/5980490002/ |access-date=3 June 2024 |agency=North Jersey News |date=2020 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603145224/https://www.northjersey.com/in-depth/life/2020/12/02/slavery-soul-food-black-women/5980490002/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Louisiana slave records showed enslaved people ran away because of inadequate food and overwork. To survive, slaves stole food from their enslavers, killed cattle from nearby farms, and hunted and fished for food.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Midlo Hall |first1=Gwendolyn |title=Africans In Colonial Louisiana The Development of Afro-Creole Culture in the Eighteenth-Century |year=1995 |publisher=Louisiana State University Press |isbn=9780807141076 |pages=142–143, 179, 310 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7B5fDwAAQBAJ&q=theft%20of%20food}}</ref>

Research from the [[National Park Service]] and professor George Estabrook said that enslaved people supplemented their diets "By boiling black-eyed peas, turnip greens, and pork fat in a single kettle and serving the mixture with grits made from home-ground corn, slaves cooked up meals that satisfied their dietary requirements, as well as their appetites." The black-eyed peas were a source of protein and the greens provided fiber and vitamins C and A.<ref>{{cite web |title=Early diet of soul food proven to be "remarkably nutritious. |url=https://www.nps.gov/ethnography/aah/aaheritage/lowCountry_pop4.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160202083158/http://www.nps.gov/ethnography/aah/aaheritage/lowCountry_pop4.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=February 2, 2016 |website=African American NPS Ethnography Program |publisher=National Park Service |access-date=16 June 2024}}</ref> Boiling greens in a kettle produced a vitamin-packed beverage called [[pot liquor]] that was consumed by the enslaved during the Antebellum era to maintain their health. White plantation owners ate the greens prepared by their slaves and left the green liquid (broth) for the slaves to drink not realizing the nutrients was in the broth. Pot liquor (also called potlikker) has Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, and iron. The enslaved and their descendants created healing remedies using pot liquors.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Edge |first1=John |title=The Potlikker Papers: A Food History of the Modern South |url=https://egrove.olemiss.edu/libarts_book/9/#:~:text=During%20the%20antebellum%20era%2C%20slave,poor%2C%20both%20black%20and%20white. |journal=Liberal Arts Faculty Books |date=January 2017 |publisher=The University of Mississippi |access-date=17 June 2024 |archive-date=17 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240617193008/https://egrove.olemiss.edu/libarts_book/9/#:~:text=During%20the%20antebellum%20era%2C%20slave,poor%2C%20both%20black%20and%20white. |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Torrence |first1=Jackie |title=The Importance of Pot Liquor |date=1994 |publisher=August House |isbn=9780874833386 |pages=9–10, 49–50 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H0mbhpckTO4C&q=slaves%20pot%20liquor}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wright |first1=Tanya |title=Soul Food Reconsidered |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/10/07/magazine/soul-food-reconsidered.html |access-date=17 June 2024 |agency=The New York Times |date=1990 |archive-date=17 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240617193008/https://www.nytimes.com/1990/10/07/magazine/soul-food-reconsidered.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Corbin |first1=Melissa |title=Potlikker Is A Simple Soul Food Dish With A Deep History |url=https://www.tastingtable.com/1093323/potlikker-is-a-simple-soul-food-dish-with-a-deep-history/ |website=www.tastingtable.com |date=9 November 2022 |publisher=Tasting Table |access-date=17 June 2024 |archive-date=17 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240617195313/https://www.tastingtable.com/1093323/potlikker-is-a-simple-soul-food-dish-with-a-deep-history/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Slave gardens were important in the slave community; they supplemented slaves' nutrient-deprived diets because slaveholders did not provide enough food to feed them.<ref>{{cite web |title=Slave Gardens |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/applied-and-social-sciences-magazines/slave-gardens |website=www.encyclopedia.com |publisher=Encyclopedia.com |access-date=16 June 2024 |archive-date=16 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616135050/https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/applied-and-social-sciences-magazines/slave-gardens |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=How Enslaved Africans Influenced American Diet |url=https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/how-enslaved-africans-influenced-american-diet/4816356.html |website=VOA News Arts and Culture |date=15 March 2019 |publisher=VOA News |access-date=16 June 2024 |archive-date=30 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530154623/https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/how-enslaved-africans-influenced-american-diet/4816356.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kelley |first1=Susan |title=Seeds of survival: Botanic Gardens honors the Black experience |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2022/08/seeds-survival-botanic-gardens-honors-black-experience-0 |website=Cornell Chronicle |publisher=Cornell University |access-date=23 June 2024 |archive-date=23 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240623174052/https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2022/08/seeds-survival-botanic-gardens-honors-black-experience-0 |url-status=live }}</ref> Slaveholders allowed their slaves to grow food in gardens because it saved their enslavers money, giving them an excuse not to buy food for their slaves. Some slaveholders provided the enslaved seeds to grow their own food. Slaves also made money by selling some of the food they grew to their enslavers.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Harte |first1=Tiffany |title=Celebrate Juneteenth by Planting an 'Emancipation Garden' |url=https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/celebrate-juneteenth-by-planting-an-emancipation-garden/ |website=Atlanta History Center |date=10 June 2022 |access-date=12 July 2024 |archive-date=12 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712192958/https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/celebrate-juneteenth-by-planting-an-emancipation-garden/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Chitlins.jpg|thumb|left|Chitlins in chicken broth]]

[[Chitterlings]] (also known as chitlins) are cleaned pig intestines; they are cooked in a pot and seasoned. This food has been associated with enslaved Black people in the American South; however, eating animal innards (intestines) is practiced in other cultures such as Asia, Europe, and West Africa. The [[Hausa people]] in West Africa eat chicken intestines. Enslaved Africans in the American South continued their traditions of cooking, seasoning, and eating animal innards. Enslaved people added extremely hot peppers for additional flavor and spice to their chitlins. Cooking chitlins was time-consuming; field slaves slow-cooked their pig intestines while they were working in the field. White plantation owners gave the parts of the pig they did not eat to the enslaved, who used these to season food and prepare one-pot meals, soups, and chitlin dishes.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bower |first1=Anne |title=African American Foodways Explorations of History and Culture |date=2009 |publisher=University of Illinois Press |isbn=9780252076305 |page=51 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gF8NCxGHyMMC&q=chitlin%20recipe%20of%20slaves |archive-date=2024-07-07 |access-date=2024-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240707133909/https://books.google.com/books?id=gF8NCxGHyMMC&q=chitlin%20recipe%20of%20slaves |url-status=live }}</ref> The dish is also considered a delicacy in other cultures.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lowery |first1=Sharelle |title=Chitlin's From Slave Food to Delicacy The Black American Kitchen |url=https://baystatebanner.com/2014/01/08/chitlins-from-slave-food-to-delicacy-the-black-american-kitchen/ |access-date=9 June 2024 |agency=The Bay State Banner |date=2014 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609133640/https://baystatebanner.com/2014/01/08/chitlins-from-slave-food-to-delicacy-the-black-american-kitchen/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Due to the time it takes to clean pig intestines, chitterlings were preserved for special occasions and holidays. Some cooks season chitterlings with onions, celery, garlic, salt, pepper, and butter.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stewart |first1=Vernetta |title=In Defense of Chitterlings |url=https://ediblenortheastflorida.ediblecommunities.com/food-thought/chitterlings-soul-food-chitlins |website=Edible Northeast Florida |access-date=9 June 2024 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609134449/https://ediblenortheastflorida.ediblecommunities.com/food-thought/chitterlings-soul-food-chitlins |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Booker T. Washington]] wrote that enslaved people ate chitlins during the Christmas season. Christmas in Virginia was a time when slaves hired to work on other plantations came home to visit their families at their enslaver's plantations. Enslaved families were supplied with food that consisted of chitlins, sausage, and side meats. After the American Civil War, cornbread, pigs' feet, hogs' ears, peas, and chitlins were prepared for Booker T. Washington's daughter, [[Portia Washington Pittman]], 87th birthday.<ref>{{cite journal |title=African-American Food History |journal=26 |date=2010 |volume=Repast |issue=1 |page=9 |url=https://aadl.org/files/cooks/repast/2010_Winter.pdf |access-date=8 August 2024}}</ref>

===Foodways on the Underground Railroad===
[[File:Oyster shuckers at Apalachicola, Fla. This work is carried on by many young boys during the busy seasons. This is a... - NARA - 523162.jpg|thumb|Black men worked in the oyster industries to support their families. A few were able to start their own oyster business creating soul food meals from oysters.<ref>{{cite news |title=Black Foodways and Cuisine |url=https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/black-foodways-and-cuisine |website=National Museum of African American History and Culture |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |access-date=30 June 2024 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630133101/https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/black-foodways-and-cuisine |url-status=live }}</ref>]]

[[Fugitive slaves in the United States|Freedom seekers]] (runaway slaves) foraged, fished, and hunted for food on their journey to freedom on the [[Underground Railroad]]. With these ingredients, they prepared one-pot meals (stews), a West African cooking method. Enslaved and free Black people left food outside their front doors to provide nourishment to the freedom seekers. The meals created on the Underground Railroad became a part of the foodways of Black Americans called soul food. For example, [[Thomas Downing (restaurateur)|Thomas Downing]] was born enslaved in 1791 on [[Chincoteague, Virginia|Chincoteague Island]], on the Eastern Shore of Virginia. He learned how to harvest [[clam]]s, [[oyster]]s, and [[terrapin]] from the [[Chincoteague Bay]], a lagoon of the Atlantic Ocean between Chincoteague and Assateague islands, and prepared meals from this seafood. Downing left Virginia during the [[War of 1812]] and traveled to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, a city that had Black Americans working in the culinary industry. There, he settled in the free Black community and found work catching oysters. Gaining his freedom in 1819, Downing, his wife, and sons moved to New York City, where the [[Hudson River]] provided work for New York's African American men working on the water harvesting oysters.  By 1825 he had opened an oyster cellar, "Downing's Oyster House", on Broadway Street, in the city's business district. There he served raw, fried, and stewed oysters, oyster pie, fish with oyster sauce, and poached turkey stuffed with oysters. In the basement of his restaurant, Downing and his eldest son George hid people who were escaping slavery and seeking freedom. Downing became known as the "Oyster King of New York".<ref>{{cite web |title=Thomas George Downing (1791–1866) |url=https://encyclopediavirginia.org/entries/thomas-george-downing-1791-1866/ |website=Virginia Humanities |publisher=Encyclopedia of Virginia |access-date=20 June 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Soul Food Got Its Start From Freedom Seekers Surviving Off The Land |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/soul-food-freedom-seekers-surviving-off-the-land/ |access-date=20 June 2024 |agency=CBS News |date=2022 |archive-date=20 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240620154709/https://www.cbsnews.com/pittsburgh/news/soul-food-freedom-seekers-surviving-off-the-land/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Downing's Oyster House |url=https://maap.columbia.edu/place/1.html |website=Mapping the African American Past |publisher=Columbia University |access-date=20 June 2024 |archive-date=7 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240707120948/http://www.maap.columbia.edu/place/1.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Filippenko |first1=Alexandra |title=Original soul food wrapped in rich history |url=https://www.museeum.com/original-soul-food-wrapped-in-rich-history/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200428040343/https://www.museeum.com/original-soul-food-wrapped-in-rich-history/ |url-status=usurped |archive-date=April 28, 2020 |website=www.museeum.com |date=26 June 2017 |publisher=Museeum |access-date=20 June 2024}}</ref>

===Slave recipes===
[[File:Homelard.jpg|thumb|Enslaved people fried their foods in lard, which is rendered pork fat.]]

In the 1930s, the [[Works Progress Administration]] paid American writers to gather stories from the last generations of African Americans born into slavery that are called [[Slave Narrative Collection|slave narratives]]. Alongside the narratives are collections of recipes for sauces, desserts, and cooked meat and seafood dishes made by formerly enslaved African Americans. These records have been studied by [[John W. Blassingame|John Blassingame]], [[Michael W. Twitty|Michael Twitty]], [[Jessica B. Harris]], and other historians as they reveal the food culture and diets of enslaved people. The narratives show how enslaved people created new dishes that influenced Southern cuisine in the United States.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate: Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9798216164265 |pages=39–42, 89 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |archive-date=2024-07-08 |access-date=2024-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708183352/https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |url-status=live }}</ref> The foods enslaved people prepared in the kitchens for white plantation families influenced the diets and cooking methods of European Americans.<ref name="auto1">{{cite web |title=Seeds of Survival and Celebration: Plants of the Black Experience |url=https://cornellbotanicgardens.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/panels.pdf |website=Cornell Botanical Gardens |access-date=16 June 2024 |archive-date=16 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616141509/https://cornellbotanicgardens.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/panels.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

Research from slave narratives showed enslaved people cooked sweet potatoes by roasting or frying them in [[lard]]. Sweet potatoes were mashed and sweetened with [[molasses]]. A traditional soul food dessert in Black families for Thanksgiving and Christmas is sweet potato pie.<ref name="auto1"/> Enslaved people also  consumed [[pot liquor]], the liquid left behind after boiling greens. George Key, who was born enslaved in Arkansas, said: "We had stew made out of pork and potatoes, and sometimes greens and pot liquor, and we had ash cake mostly, but biscuits about once a month."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Yetman |first1=Norman |title=Voices from Slavery 100 Authentic Slave Narratives |date=2012 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=9780486131016 |page=202 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dLfCAgAAQBAJ&q=pot%20liquor}}</ref> Making pot liquor continued after emancipation. Jackie Torrence, an African American storyteller, remembers her grandmother making pot liquor from mustard greens, collard greens, pinto beans, peas, and white potatoes as gravy. Pot liquor was also used as a healing remedy to treat earache and ingrown toenails.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Torrence |first1=Jackie |title=The Importance of Pot Liquor |date=1994 |publisher=August House |isbn=9780874833386 |pages=49–50 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H0mbhpckTO4C&q=pot%20liquor}}</ref>

[[File:Dried spicy red peppers (4888546786).jpg|thumb|Slaves used red peppers and vinegar with other ingredients and made a homemade barbecue sauce.]]

A former slave named Wesley Jones from South Carolina gave a recipe to make a vinegar-based [[barbecue sauce]] using black and red peppers and [[vinegar]]. Wesley said slaves barbecued meats often, smoking and basting their meats with this homemade barbecue sauce; they would stay up all night slow cooking the meat. Other slave narratives described barbecuing as a preferred method of cooking because it added flavor and spice to food. Slaves barbecued their foods for special occasions and on their days off. Henry Bland, a former slave who lived in Georgia, said slaves had July 4 (Independence Day) off from work, allowing them to barbecue food, play ball games, wrestle, and make music.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate: Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9798216164265 |pages=89–90, 199–200 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |archive-date=2024-07-08 |access-date=2024-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708183352/https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Twitty2015">{{cite news |last1=Twitty |first1=Michael |title=Barbecue is an American Tradition – of Enslaved Africans and Native Americans |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2015/jul/04/barbecue-american-tradition-enslaved-africans-native-americans |access-date=4 June 2024 |agency=The Guardian |date=2015}}</ref>

A former slave named Callie Elder from Georgia said her grandfather cooked catfish with lard, salt, and pepper, and rolled the catfish in [[cornmeal]] before baking. Former slave Clara Davis from Alabama cooked catfish using tomatoes and potatoes or prepared baked catfish with a tomato gravy and sweet potatoes. Slaves in the South fried catfish in [[lard]] or other fats and seasoned their food with salt acquired from evaporated sea water.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9798216164265 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=salt%20sea%20water}}</ref> Enslaved people made use of fruits like apples and peaches that had been introduced to North America by European colonists. Some fruits, such as apples, were battered and deep fried in oil, fruit fritters were also fried, and peaches were stewed. Former slaves Mose King from Arkansas and Rose Williams from Texas described eating [[goat]]. Mary Minus Biddie was a former slave from Florida and said enslaved people cooked goat in a smokehouse. David Goodman Gullins was a former slave from Georgia and said they prepared barbecued goat. Goat is a traditional meat in West Africa and was commonly cooked and eaten in the American south by slaves.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9798216164265 |pages=104–105, 129, 171–172, 174 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways}}</ref>

[[File:A Southern Barbecue.jpg|thumb|Black Americans preparing a southern barbecue]]

Enslaved people also barbecued [[squirrel]]s. One recipe for barbecued squirrels that might have been similar to the way slaves cooked them was given in an 1879 cookbook: "Put them in the oven and let them cook until done. Lay them on a dish and set near the fire. Take out the bacon, sprinkle one spoonful of flour in the gravy and let it brown. Then pour in one teacup of water, one tablespoon of butter and some tomato or walnut catsup. Let it cool, and then pour it over the squirrel." Barbecuing and preparing barbecue sauce and hot sauce were done to season lower grades of meats.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate: Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9780313374982 |pages=89, 125 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-k7EEAAAQBAJ&q=barbecue&pg=PA59}}</ref> Enslaved people living near rivers and the Atlantic Ocean caught [[crab]] and made stews with the crab meat in a pot with okra, sometimes adding a sauce. Cooking seafood with okra is a traditional cooking method from West Africa that slaves continued on Southern plantations.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate: Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9780313374982 |page=42 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-k7EEAAAQBAJ&q=crabs&pg=PA59}}</ref> Some of these recipes made by former slaves were published in African-American cookbooks. The earliest such cookbook was self-published in 1866 by [[Malinda Russell]] as a pamphlet titled, ''A Domestic Cookbook: Containing a Careful Selection of Useful Receipts for the Kitchen''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Watson |first1=Robin |title=1866 African-American cookbook from Michigan woman offers voice from the past |url=https://www.detroitnews.com/story/life/food/2020/02/19/1866-african-american-cookbook-offers-voice-past/4785067002/ |access-date=4 June 2024 |agency=The Detroit News |date=2020 |archive-date=4 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604202222/https://www.detroitnews.com/story/life/food/2020/02/19/1866-african-american-cookbook-offers-voice-past/4785067002/ |url-status=live }}</ref> A cookbook published in 1900 in the city of [[Charleston, South Carolina]] had recipes used by formerly enslaved Gullah people. [[Sesame|Benne seeds]] from ''sesame'', a plant native to West Africa, were eaten raw with sugar or milk. Enslaved people also made cakes, wafers, and brittles from them for white plantation families whom they called "[[buckra]]"<ref>{{cite journal |last1=West |first1=Kai |title=Buckra: Whiteness and Porgy and Bess |journal=Journal of the American Musicological Society |date=2022 |volume=75 |issue=2 |pages=319–377 |doi=10.1525/jams.2022.75.2.319 |url=https://online.ucpress.edu/jams/article/75/2/319/185498/Buckra-Whiteness-and-Porgy-and-Bess |access-date=10 June 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (a [[Gullah language|Gullah word]] for white people).<ref>{{cite book |title=Confections delicacies sweets from the Old Slave Mart |date=1900 |publisher=Old Slave Mart |page=5 |url=https://digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/collection/sccookbook/id/4 |archive-date=2024-06-10 |access-date=2024-06-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240610172834/https://digital.tcl.sc.edu/digital/collection/sccookbook/id/4 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=History of Benne in the Lowcountry |url=https://www.charlestonspecialtyfoods.com/pages/history-of-the-benne-seed-and-the-benne-wafer-in-the-lowcountry |website=www.charlestonspecialtyfoods.com |publisher=Charleston Specialty Foods |access-date=10 June 2024 |archive-date=10 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240610172833/https://www.charlestonspecialtyfoods.com/pages/history-of-the-benne-seed-and-the-benne-wafer-in-the-lowcountry |url-status=live }}</ref>

Archeologist, historian, and former professional chef, Kelley Fanto Deetz, wrote a book, ''Bound to the Fire How Virginia's Enslaved Cooks Helped Invent American Cuisine'', that said recipes prepared by enslaved cooks in [[History of slavery in Virginia|Virginia]] contributed to some of the well-known fried and baked meat and vegetable dishes in American southern cuisine. The foods from West-Central Africa brought to the United States by way of the [[Atlantic slave trade|trans-Atlantic slave trade]] were used by enslaved cooks and combined with North American ingredients using West African, Native American, and European cooking methods to create meals that in the 17th century were necessary for survival that later influenced the foodways of southern Americans generally.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Deetz |first1=Kelley Fanto |title=Bound to the Fire How Virginia's Enslaved Cooks Helped Invent American Cuisine |year=2017 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |isbn=9780813174747 |pages=4–6, 50–57, 100, 122–124 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m4I2DwAAQBAJ&q=dishes}}</ref>

===Barbecue traditions===
[[File:Barbecueing meat at a Masonic picnic- Kissimmee, Florida (4876969466).jpg|thumb|People gather to barbecue meat at a Masonic picnic in Kissimmee, Florida in 1886]]

Enslaved Africans in the American south contributed their own influence to the [[Barbecue in the United States|American barbecue]] tradition.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kein |first1=Sybil |title=Creole: The History and Legacy of Louisiana's Free People of Color |date=2000 |publisher=Louisiana State University Press |isbn=9780807126011 |page=246 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HSKsSihlN7IC&pg=PA246}}</ref> The first people to barbecue food in North America were [[Native Americans in the United States|Indigenous people/Native Americans]]. West and Central Africans had their own method of barbecuing food that they brought to the Americas and the West Indies. The [[Hausa people]] in West Africa had a term for barbecue, ''babbake''. This term is used "...to describe a complex of words referring to grilling, toasting, building a large fire, singeing hair or feathers and cooking food over a long period of time over an extravagant fire".<ref name="Twitty2015"/> The blending of Native American and African styles of barbecuing meat contributed to the creation of the current barbecuing culture in the US.<ref name="Rao2021">{{cite news |last1=Rao |first1=Vidya |title=Barbecue: The Black and Indigenous roots of an American tradition |url=https://www.today.com/food/barbecue-black-indigenous-roots-american-tradition-t222467 |access-date=30 June 2024 |agency=USA Today |date=2021 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630151255/https://www.today.com/food/barbecue-black-indigenous-roots-american-tradition-t222467 |url-status=live }}</ref> During slavery times, white plantation owners left the labor-intensive work of preparing and barbecuing food to their slaves.<ref name="Regelski2016">{{cite web |last1=Regelski |first1=Christina |title=The Soul of Food Slavery's Influence on Southern Cuisine |url=https://ushistoryscene.com/article/slavery-southern-cuisine/ |website=U.S. History Scene |date=3 November 2016 |access-date=30 June 2024}}</ref> Food historian [[Adrian Miller]] said the history of Black people and barbecue during slavery: "Blackness and barbecue were wedded in the public imagination because old-school barbecue was so labour intensive. Someone had to clear the area where the barbecue was held, chop and burn the wood for cooking, dig the pit, butcher, process, cook and season the animals, serve the food, entertain the guests and clean up afterward. Given the racial dynamics of the antebellum South, enslaved African Americans were forced to do that work. The media, in turn, took note that a barbecue, as a social event, was a black experience from beginning to end."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=How the long history of black barbecue was erased |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/life-style/food-and-drink/media-barbecue-black-america-history-b1903832.html#comments-area |access-date=30 June 2024 |agency=Independent |date=2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=Black Smoke African Americans and the United States of Barbecue |date=2021 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |isbn=9781469662817 |pages=22–25, 39–49, 50–57 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Lc_9DwAAQBAJ&q=Black+Smoke:+African+Americans+and+the+United+States+of+Barbecue}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Béchard |first1=Deni |title=The Bard of Barbecue |url=https://stanfordmag.org/contents/the-bard-of-barbecue |website=Stanford Magazine |date=22 February 2021 |publisher=Stanford University |access-date=30 June 2024 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630151255/https://stanfordmag.org/contents/the-bard-of-barbecue |url-status=live }}</ref> On [[Independence Day (United States)|Fourth of July]] celebrations, the enslaved prepared barbecued food for white politicians and their enslavers.<ref name="Twitty2015"/>

[[File:Turning the Meat in a barbecue smoker chicago.jpg|thumb|Turning the meat in a barbecue smoker in [[Chicago]], Illinois]]

Enslaved people brought their own influences on the creation of [[barbecue sauce]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dehart |first1=Rob |title=Tasting the History of Barbecue |url=https://tnmuseum.org/Stories/posts/tasting-the-history-of-barbecue |website=Tennessee State Museum |access-date=30 June 2024 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630175350/https://tnmuseum.org/Stories/posts/tasting-the-history-of-barbecue |url-status=live }}</ref> Hot and sweet sauces are used in West and Central African cuisine to add flavor, heat, and moisture to food.<ref name="Regelski2016"/> In 1748, Peter Kalm, a Swedish-Finnish botanist, noted enslaved Africans in Philadelphia cultivated [[guinea pepper]]s and the pods were pounded and "mixed with salt preserved in a bottle" to make sauces poured over fish and meats.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Houck |first1=Brenna |title=Regional Barbecue Sauce Styles, Explained |url=https://www.eater.com/2016/6/18/11966056/barbecue-sauce-styles |website=Eater |date=18 June 2016 |access-date=30 June 2024 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630185913/https://www.eater.com/2016/6/18/11966056/barbecue-sauce-styles |url-status=live }}</ref> Frederick Douglass Opie, writing in his book ''Hog and Hominy'', describes the origins of soul food in Africa: "African women cooked most meats over an open pit and ate them with a sauce similar to what we now call a barbecue sauce, made from lime or lemon juice and hot peppers."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Vaughn |first1=Daniel |title=How Southern Barbecue Got to Texas |url=https://www.texasmonthly.com/bbq/how-southern-barbecue-got-to-texas/ |access-date=30 June 2024 |agency=Texas Monthly |date=2015 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630184738/https://www.texasmonthly.com/bbq/how-southern-barbecue-got-to-texas/ |url-status=live }}</ref> "Slaves made up a large percentage of the Texas population by 1860. During this time they brought with them the idea of cooking over an open fire and dousing meats with a sauce, that sounds an awful lot like the barbecue sauce we know today."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Donahue |first1=Emily |title=The Historic Connection Between Slave Recipes and Today's Barbecue |url=https://www.texasstandard.org/stories/how-old-slave-recipes-became-todays-texas-bbq/#:~:text=Slaves%20made%20up%20a%20large,barbecue%20sauce%20we%20have%20today. |access-date=30 June 2024 |agency=Texas Standard |date=2015}}</ref> After the American Civil War, a Black pitmaster named Arthur Watts, brought his family's barbecue sauce recipe and barbecuing methods to [[Kewanee, Illinois]] and became a well-known pitmaster.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Alexander |first1=Steve |title=A family legacy of barbecue sauce emerges from the darkness of slavery |url=https://wgnradio.com/the-business-of-food-with-steve-alexander/a-family-legacy-of-barbecue-sauce-emerges-from-the-darkness-of-slavery/ |access-date=30 June 2024 |agency=WGN Radio 720 |date=2022 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630175346/https://wgnradio.com/the-business-of-food-with-steve-alexander/a-family-legacy-of-barbecue-sauce-emerges-from-the-darkness-of-slavery/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In [[African-American neighborhood|African-American communities]], barbecuing food became a preferred method of cooking during [[Emancipation Day]] celebrations.<ref name="Twitty2015"/>

===Emancipation===
[[File:"Emancipation Day in South Carolina" - the Color-Sergeant of the 1st South Carolina (Colored) addressing the regiment, after having been presented with the Stars and Stripes, at Smith's LCCN99614128.jpg|thumb|Emancipation Day celebration in Beaufort]]

On January 1, 1863, Gullah people in the Sea Islands of South Carolina celebrated their freedom on New Year's Day at [[Camp Saxton Site|Camp Saxton]] in Beaufort with food and barbecues. Black people in the barrier islands of South Carolina became free early during the [[American Civil War]] after the [[Battle of Port Royal]] on November 7, 1861, when many of the plantation owners and white residents fled the area after the arrival of the Union Navy and Army. As a result, over 10,000 African Americans became free on that day.<ref>{{cite web |title=Beaufort's Reconstruction Era National Historical Park |url=https://southcarolinalowcountry.com/beauforts-reconstruction-era-national-historical-park/ |website=South Carolina Lowcountry Resorts and Lands |date=23 May 2022 |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> However, their freedom was not official in government writing until the passage of the [[Emancipation Proclamation]] on New Year's Day in 1863. Thousands of newly freed people celebrated their freedom with food, song, and dance.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brack |first1=Andy |title=Emancipation Day celebrations |url=https://www.statehousereport.com/2019/12/27/history-emancipation-day-celebrations-2/ |website=www.statehousereport.com |publisher=State House Report |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> [[Charlotte Forten Grimké|Charlotte Forten]], the first black teacher at the [[Penn Center (Saint Helena Island, South Carolina)|Penn School]] on [[Saint Helena Island (South Carolina)|St. Helena Island]] in Beaufort, attended the Emancipation Day celebration at Camp Saxton and recorded in her journal they ate roasted oxen and barbecue.<ref>{{cite web |title=This First Day of January |url=https://clements.umich.edu/exhibit/proclaiming-emancipation/this-first-day-of-january/ |website=William L. Clements Library |publisher=University of Michigan |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=5 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240605201822/https://clements.umich.edu/exhibit/proclaiming-emancipation/this-first-day-of-january/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Forten |first1=Charlotte |title=The Journals of Charlotte Forten Grimké |date=1988 |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=431 |isbn=978-0-19-505238-1 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3uHylBU24jMC&q=oxen}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Moss |first1=Robert |title=BBQ Evolution |url=https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2010/09/01/bbq-evolution/ |access-date=1 June 2024 |agency=Charleston City Paper |date=2010 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601203753/https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2010/09/01/bbq-evolution/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Susie King Taylor]], a Geechee woman born enslaved in [[Liberty County, Georgia]], wrote in her memoir that she had also attended the Emancipation Day celebration at Camp Saxton: "It was a glorious day for us all, and we enjoyed every minute of it, and as a fitting close and crowning event of this occasion we had a grand barbecue".<ref>{{cite book |last1=King Taylor |first1=Susie |title=Reminiscences of My Life in Camp with the 33d United States Colored Troops Late 1st S. C. Volunteers |date=1902 |publisher=Harvard University |page=18 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v3-cyYKvZr8C&q=barbecue}}</ref> Other Emancipation Day celebrations were celebrated with a barbecue feast, a tradition that originated in the [[The Slave Community|slave community]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Covey |first1=Herbert |last2=Eisnach |first2=Dwight |title=What the Slaves Ate Recollections of African American Foods and Foodways from the Slave Narratives |date=2009 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9798216164265 |pages=89–90, 199–200 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |archive-date=2024-07-08 |access-date=2024-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240708183352/https://books.google.com/books?id=cq72EAAAQBAJ&q=What+the+slaves+are+recollections+of+african+american+foods+and+foodways |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Twitty |first1=Michael |title=Barbecue is an American tradition – of enslaved Africans and Native Americans |url=https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2015/jul/04/barbecue-american-tradition-enslaved-africans-native-americans |access-date=4 June 2024 |agency=The Guardian |date=2015}}</ref>

[[File:2017 Juneteenth Celebration on the Square20170617 0009 (35406892355).jpg|thumb|A 2017 Juneteenth Celebration showing soul food vendors|left]]

After the [[American Civil War]], 4 million African Americans were freed from slavery. They celebrated their newly won freedom with barbecues and [[Emancipation Day#United States|Emancipation Day]] celebrations and prepared soul food meals. Two months after the Civil War ended in April 1865, slaveholders in Galveston, Texas refused to tell their slaves the Civil War had ended and they were free. On June 19, 1865, United States Brigadier [[Gordon Granger|General Gordon Granger]] and his troops arrived in Galveston and issued [[General Order No. 3|General order No. 3]]. This order enforced the Emancipation Proclamation which declared enslaved people in Texas were now free.<ref>{{cite web |title=Featured Document Display: The Emancipation Proclamation and Juneteenth |url=https://museum.archives.gov/featured-document-display-emancipation-proclamation-and-juneteenth |website=National Archives Museum |publisher=National Archives and Records Administration |access-date=20 June 2024 |archive-date=17 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210917214153/https://museum.archives.gov/featured-document-display-emancipation-proclamation-and-juneteenth |url-status=live }}</ref> To celebrate their freedom, African Americans in Galveston, and other Black communities in the United States, gathered at public parks and prepared red foods that represent the color of freedom. These celebrations are called [[Juneteenth]], which became a national holiday under the Biden Administration in the year 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Juneteenth: A Celebration of Freedom |url=https://www.nps.gov/articles/juneteenth-origins.htm |website=www.nps.gov |publisher=The National Park Service |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601140504/https://www.nps.gov/articles/juneteenth-origins.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>
[[File:Picayune Creole Cookbook (cropped).jpg|thumb|Picayune Creole Cookbook]]
According to food historian [[Michael W. Twitty|Michael Twitty]], the reason African Americans eat red food on Juneteenth is that it reminds them of the blood of their ancestors that was shed during slavery, and the cultural colors of the [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] and [[Kongo people|Bakongo people]], who were enslaved in the Southern United States and brought to North America under the slave trade. Among the Yoruba and Bakongo people, the color red represents power, sacrifice, and transformation.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Meaning and History of Juneteenth Foods |url=https://www.pbs.org/articles/the-meaning-and-history-of-juneteenth-foods |website=www.pbs.org |publisher=Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601134548/https://www.pbs.org/articles/the-meaning-and-history-of-juneteenth-foods |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Juneteenth |url=https://nmaahc.si.edu/juneteenth |website=National Museum of African American History and Culture |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601142535/https://nmaahc.si.edu/juneteenth |url-status=live }}</ref> The red foods eaten at Juneteenth are, watermelon, red lemonade, and [[red velvet cake]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Tastes of Resilience |url=https://nmaahc.si.edu/juneteenth#Tastes |website=National Museum of African American History and Culture |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |access-date=1 June 2024}}</ref> In addition to red foods, BBQ, fried foods, and other cooked meals are prepared to celebrate the day of freedom.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ayele Djossa |first1=Christina |title=The Story Behind Red-Hued Juneteenth Food and Drink |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/what-is-juneteenth |website=www.atlasobscura.com |date=19 June 2018 |publisher=The Atlanta Obscure |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601134556/https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/what-is-juneteenth |url-status=live }}</ref>

After [[Emancipation Proclamation|emancipation]], many Black Americans in the South became [[Sharecropping|sharecroppers]] and cooked what was available in their region. This created regional styles of cooking with similar dishes passed down orally in [[The Black Family in Slavery and Freedom|Black families]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wallach |title=Dethroning the Deceitful Pork Chop: Rethinking African American Foodways from Slavery to Obama |date=2015 |publisher=University of Arkansas Press |isbn=9781610755689 |pages=200–210, 211–220 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rWuJCgAAQBAJ&q=sharecropping}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Ferguson |first1=Sheila |title=Soul Food: Classic Cuisine from the Deep South |date=1993 |publisher=Grove Press |isbn=9780802132833 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-RoZrySwkxIC&q=sharecropper}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=2023 Black History Month: Family Traditions: Feeding the Spirit and Soul |url=https://dcps.libguides.com/c.php?g=1175843&p=8592802 |website=www.dcps.libguides.com |publisher=District of Columbia Public Schools |access-date=20 May 2024 |archive-date=20 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520204618/https://dcps.libguides.com/c.php?g=1175843&p=8592802 |url-status=live }}</ref> Due to slave laws, it was illegal in many states for slaves to learn to read or write. Soul food [[recipe]]s and cooking techniques were passed down orally until after emancipation.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Opie |first=F.D. |title=Hog and Hominy: Soul Food from Africa to America |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=2008 |isbn=9780231146395 |pages=35}}</ref>

The first soul food [[cookbook]] is attributed to [[Abby Fisher]], entitled ''[[What Mrs. Fisher Knows About Old Southern Cooking]]'' and published in 1881. ''Good Things to Eat'' was published in 1911; the author, Rufus Estes, was a former slave who worked for the [[Pullman Company|Pullman]] [[railway]] car service. Many other cookbooks were written by Black Americans during that time, but as they were not widely distributed, most are now lost.<ref>{{cite news|url= https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/food/1995/11/29/rediscovering-the-first-black-cookbook/c8dc66e9-a512-487f-807d-4bfb1bdd848d/|title=Rediscovering the First Black Cookbook|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Global spread of African-American cuisine===
[[File:"... troops in Burma stop work briefly to read President Truman's Proclamation of Victory in Europe." - NARA - 531341.jpg|thumb|250px|Black American soldiers in [[Burma Campaign|Burma]] reading President Truman's Proclamation of Victory in Europe, May 9, 1945.]]
The global spread of soul food came during [[World War I]] and [[World War II]]. Thousands of [[Military history of African Americans|Black Americans enlisted]] in the army as soldiers and nurses. Some Black soldiers chose to stay overseas than return to the United States where [[Jim Crow laws]], racism, and [[lynching]]s were widespread. African American service men and women opened soul food restaurants in Europe, Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, and Japan and introduced African-American cuisine to people in foreign countries. In the 1920s through the 1940s, [[African-American culture]] was popular in France. French people enjoyed [[jazz]], [[African-American dance]], and cuisine. Food historian [[Adrian Miller]] said the global spread of soul food: "The global spread of soul food really took off after the end of World War II. After the war, recently discharged black military veterans in the European theater stayed overseas to open and operate restaurants. At first, they cooked mainly for African Americans who were active-duty military and serving at nearby bases. In some of the countries where the United States had a military presence, like France, Germany, Japan, Vietnam, and Thailand, it was easy for these entrepreneurs to find the cheap ingredients they needed for their recipes, because the locals ate similar foods: chicken, fish, greens, okra, pork, sweet potatoes."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=How the U.S. Military Brought Soul Food to the World |url=https://www.zocalopublicsquare.org/2018/04/02/u-s-military-brought-soul-food-world/ideas/essay/ |website=Zocalo |date=2 April 2018 |access-date=14 July 2024}}</ref>

===Mid-20th century to present day===
[[File:Chitterling, fish and sugar cane on street in Negro Section,... (3110576314).jpg|thumb|left|Black-owned night-clubs during the Jim Crow era were called the Chitlin' Circuit—they were safe places for Black people to eat.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Jeffries |first1=Fran |title=Chitlin' Circuit: Black performers' soulful showcase during segregation |url=https://www.ajc.com/news/national/chitlin-circuit-black-performers-soulful-showcase-during-segregation/srbp9fswLEa3tsiOe5Z54M/ |access-date=9 June 2024 |agency=The Atlanta-Journal Constitution |date=2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Martin |first1=Roland |last2=Ostberg |first2=Rene |title=Chitlin Circuit |url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/chitlin-circuit |website=www.britannica.com |publisher=Encyclopedia Britannica |access-date=9 June 2024 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609165305/https://www.britannica.com/topic/chitlin-circuit |url-status=live }}</ref>]]

The introduction of soul food to cities such as [[Washington, D.C.]], [[Baltimore]], and [[Harlem]] came during the [[Great Migration (African American)|Great Migration]] as African Americans moved to the North looking for work. [[Sylvia Woods]] was born in [[Hemingway, South Carolina]] in 1926. When Woods was a teenager she moved to Harlem and worked in a [[Brooklyn]] factory. In 1954, Woods changed jobs and started working at Johnson's Luncheonette located in central Harlem. Seven years later, Woods and her husband purchased the luncheonette and opened it as a soul food restaurant in 1962, calling it [[Sylvia's Restaurant of Harlem|Sylvia's Restaurant]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Sylvia's Restaurant - A Harlem Institution Since 1962 |url=https://www.harlemamerica.com/harlemlove/sylvias-restaurant-a-harlem-institution-since-1962/ |website=www.harlemamerica.com |date=15 September 2020 |publisher=Harlem America |access-date=13 June 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Jones |first1=James |title=Sylvia Woods (1926-2012) |url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/woods-sylvia-1926-2012/ |website=www.blackpast.org |date=15 April 2014 |publisher=Black Past |access-date=13 June 2024 |archive-date=13 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240613202319/https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/woods-sylvia-1926-2012/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Sylvia Woods became known as the "queen of soul food."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kranz |first1=Rachel |title=African-American Business Leaders and Entrepreneurs |date=2004 |publisher=Facts On File, Incorporated |isbn=9781438107790 |page=298 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NCHX6P8ETI0C&q=soul%20food}}</ref>

Food historian [[Adrian Miller]] studied soul food's development in Maryland and in Northern American states. Soul food in Maryland's Black communities added local flavors from seafood from the [[Chesapeake Bay]]. People in Maryland fried chicken in shallow fat in a frying pan, covering it with  a lid, thus frying and steaming the chicken, which was served with waffles.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=Soul Food: The Surprising Story of an American Cuisine, One Plate at a Time |date=2013 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |isbn=9781469607634 |page=53 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Od8VAAAAQBAJ&q=Maryland}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Braga |first1=Brunno |title=Culinary Gems: 7 Must Try Black-Owned Restaurants in Baltimore |url=https://travelnoire.com/black-owned-restaurants-in-baltimore |access-date=9 June 2024 |agency=Travel Noire |date=2023 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609140324/https://travelnoire.com/black-owned-restaurants-in-baltimore |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Chicken and waffles]] became a common soul food item to eat in Black communities in Maryland and in [[Harlem|Harlem, New York]]. During the [[blues]] and [[jazz]] era, musicians and singers performed and practiced late into the night and stopped at black-owned restaurants for food where cooks prepared fried chicken and waffles for their customers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Opie |first1=Frederick |title=Hog and Hominy: Soul Food from Africa to America |date=2008 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=9780231146395 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FMGrAgAAQBAJ&q=chicken%20and%20waffles}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Thomas |first1=Amelia |title=A Harlem soul food fix |url=https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20110701-a-harlem-soul-food-fix |website=www.bbc.com |date=11 July 2011 |publisher=BBC |access-date=9 June 2024 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609150636/https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20110701-a-harlem-soul-food-fix |url-status=live }}</ref> Nightclubs in Black communities in the United States during the [[Jim Crow laws|Jim Crow era]] were called the [[Chitlin' Circuit]], named after the dish that was usually associated with Black southerners and soul food.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=Soul Food: The Surprising Story of an American Cuisine, One Plate at a Time |date=2013 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |isbn=9781469607634 |pages=104–105 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Od8VAAAAQBAJ&q=chitlin%20circuit}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=Inside the 'Chitlin Circuit', a Jim Crow-Era Safe Space for Black Performers |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/chitlin-circuit |website=www.atlasobscura.com |date=28 June 2022 |publisher=Atlas Abscura |access-date=9 June 2024 |archive-date=28 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240528180207/https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/chitlin-circuit |url-status=live }}</ref> The Chitlin' Circuit was given its name by entertainers because it included black-owned night clubs that served [[Chitterlings|chitlins (chitterlings)]] and soul food.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Brown |first1=Tanya |title=The Origin (And Hot Stank) Of The 'Chitlin' Circuit' |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2014/02/16/275313723/the-origin-and-hot-stank-of-the-chitlin-circuit |website=www.npr.org |date=16 February 2014 |publisher=NPR South Carolina public radio |access-date=16 June 2024 |archive-date=16 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616153434/https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2014/02/16/275313723/the-origin-and-hot-stank-of-the-chitlin-circuit |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:The Busy Bee Café.jpg|thumb|[[The Busy Bee Café]] is a soul food restaurant frequented by civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.]]

During the [[civil rights movement]], soul food restaurants were places where civil rights leaders and activists met to discuss and strategize civil rights protests and ideas for implementing social and political change.<ref>{{cite book |last1=J. Wallach |first1=Jennifer |title=Every Nation Has Its Dish: Black Bodies and Black Food in Twentieth-Century America |date=13 November 2018 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |isbn=9781469645223 |pages=145–155 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bWN5DwAAQBAJ}}</ref> Paschal's Restaurant in Atlanta, like Georgia Gilmore's eatery in Montgomery, had an important part in the civil rights movement. Upon returning to Atlanta from Montgomery, Martin Luther King got permission "to bring his team members and guests to Paschal's to eat, meet, rest, plan, and strategize."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Opie |first1=Frederick D. |title=Southern Food and Civil Rights Feeding the Revolution |year=2021 |publisher=Arcadia Publishing |isbn=9781439659212 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4sSNDQAAQBAJ&pg=PT102 |pages=102–106}}</ref> The [[Atlanta History Center]] said: "Throughout the civil rights movement in Atlanta, soul food restaurants were hubs of change where civil rights leaders could convene, converse, and strategize, and in times of terror and violence, these places were retreats where leaders could plan their next tactical moves, giving many of these spots a legacy beyond good cooking". Soul food restaurants in [[Atlanta|Atlanta, Georgia]] served as the primary meeting places for numerous civil rights leaders and supporters of the movement. Many politicians and civil rights leaders gathered to discuss plans about the movement at [[Paschal's|Paschal's Restaurant]] on West Hunter Street. In the 1950s and 1960s, civil rights icons such as [[Andrew Young]], [[John Lewis]], [[Martin Luther King Jr.]], [[Julian Bond]], [[Adam Clayton Powell Jr.]], and [[Jesse Jackson]] frequented the restaurant, staying late into the night talking about civil rights strategies and politics. Several soul food restaurants were located on West Hunter Street because [[Jim Crow laws]] restricted where African Americans were allowed to operate their businesses.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Singh |first1=Rachel |title=The Restaurants that Fueled the Civil Rights Movement |url=https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/the-restaurants-that-fueled-the-civil-rights-movement/#:~:text=Throughout%20the%20civil%20rights%20movement,these%20spots%20a%20legacy%20beyond |website=Atlanta History Center |date=10 January 2022 |access-date=26 May 2024 |archive-date=26 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526124330/https://www.atlantahistorycenter.com/blog/the-restaurants-that-fueled-the-civil-rights-movement/#:~:text=Throughout%20the%20civil%20rights%20movement,these%20spots%20a%20legacy%20beyond |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Goldmon |first1=Camille |title=Paschal's Restaurant |url=https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/paschals-restaurant/ |website=Georgia Encyclopedia |publisher=Emory University |access-date=26 May 2024 |archive-date=26 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526184018/https://www.georgiaencyclopedia.org/articles/arts-culture/paschals-restaurant/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Ben's Chili Bowl - facade.jpg|thumb|Ben's Chili Bowl is a black-owned restaurant in Washington, D.C.|left]]

In 1963, a few days before the [[March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom]] in Washington D.C., where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his ''[[I Have a Dream|I Have a Dream Speech]]'' on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, King ate at a soul food restaurant called the Florida Avenue Grill. During the years of the civil rights movement, other civil rights leaders and activists met at the restaurant, planning and strategizing for the movement. Before King was assassinated on April 4, 1968, at the [[National Civil Rights Museum|Lorraine Motel]] in Memphis, Tennessee, he ate at the Four Way restaurant and had fried catfish and lemon icebox pie. Throughout his civil rights career, King frequented several soul food restaurants where he ate and met with other local and national civil rights leaders.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Miller |first1=Adriane |title=Black Restaurants that Fed the Civil Rights Movement |url=https://www.southernliving.com/culture/black-restaurants-civil-rights-movement |website=www.southernliving.com |publisher=Southern Living |access-date=31 May 2024 |archive-date=31 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240531194702/https://www.southernliving.com/culture/black-restaurants-civil-rights-movement |url-status=live }}</ref> After King's assassination, riots broke out in [[1968 Washington, D.C., riots|Washington D.C.]], and the leader of the [[Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee]] (SNCC), [[Stokely Carmichael]], asked the owner of [[Ben's Chili Bowl]] restaurant to remain open to provide food for police officers, student activists, and firefighters as they worked together to stop the riot. Authors Hoekstra and Khan said in their book, ''The People's Place: Soul Food Restaurants and Reminiscences from the Civil Rights Era to Today'', that soul food restaurants served as places to bring communities and families together in times of trouble during the Jim Crow era and helped in the fight against segregation laws by allowing white and Black people to eat together.<ref>{{cite web |title=The People's Place: Soul Food Restaurants and Reminiscences from the Civil Rights Era to Today |url=https://ppld.overdrive.com/media/2397348 |website=Pikes Peak Library District |access-date=2 June 2024 |archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602185033/https://ppld.overdrive.com/media/2397348 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Staff of Sylvia's, a legendary soul-food restaurant in Harlem, New York LCCN2011632427.tif|thumb|Staff of Sylvia's, a legendary soul food restaurant in [[Harlem|Harlem, New York]]]]

In [[Montgomery, Alabama]], civil rights protestors convened and organized for the movement at soul food restaurants because they provided a safe haven and a place to eat and relax. Martha's Place and Chris' Hotdogs were visited by protestors. During this period of activism, Jereline and Larry James Bethune, the owners of the restaurant Brenda's BBQ, also in Montgomery, taught African Americans how to register to vote and how to read a ballot when Jim Crow laws and [[literacy test]]s prevented Black people from voting. Civil rights activists frequented the restaurant for moral and financial support. The owners also helped to print out fliers for the movement and allowed protestors to have secret meetings in the back of the restaurant.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Greene |first1=Lydia |title=Soul Food Was at the Heart of the Civil Rights Movement in Montgomery |url=https://www.wideopencountry.com/soul-food-montgomery/ |website=www.wideopencountry.com |date=15 November 2021 |publisher=Wide Open Country |access-date=26 May 2024 |archive-date=31 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240531200843/https://www.wideopencountry.com/soul-food-montgomery/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Atlanta's oldest black-owned restaurant, the Evelyn Jones Cafe, was founded in 1936 by Evelyn Jones and her sister. In the mid-1940s, Evelyn and her husband, Luther Frazier, enlarged the restaurant and renamed it Frazier's Cafe Society. It is located at 880 Martin Luther King Jr. Drive (then known as West Hunter Street). The Jones family challenged Jim Crow laws when they allowed whites and blacks to eat together. It was the first interracial restaurant on West Hunter Street. The cafe also served as a location for civil rights leaders to meet. The foods the restaurant served were Virginia baked ham, pork chop dinner, jumbo shrimp, roast beef, and other classic Southern dishes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Camerino |first1=Taria |title=A Seat at the Table with Evelyn J. Frazier |url=https://discoveratlanta.com/dining/culinary-scene/a-seat-at-the-table-with-evelyn-j-frazier/ |website=Atlanta Convention & Visitors Bureau |access-date=26 May 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Cintron |first1=Daniela |title=Atlanta's Culinary Evolution: Unveiling Michelin Guide's Love for the City |url=https://discoveratlanta.com/stories/eat/atlantas-culinary-evolution-unveiling-michelin-guides-love-for-the-city/ |website=Atlanta Convention & Visitors Bureau |date=9 November 2023 |access-date=26 May 2024 |archive-date=26 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240526191138/https://discoveratlanta.com/stories/eat/atlantas-culinary-evolution-unveiling-michelin-guides-love-for-the-city/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Club from Nowhere was a black-owned soul food restaurant that opened in 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, operated by civil rights activist [[Georgia Gilmore]]. Gilmore's [[fried chicken]], macaroni and cheese, stuffed pork chops, stuffed peppers, and coleslaw were popular among her black and white customers. These were dishes she learned how to make from the women in her family. Gilmore's restaurant provided food for civil rights leaders during the [[Montgomery bus boycott]], and her soul food was a favorite among Martin Luther King Jr.<ref name="Blalock2019">{{cite news |last1=Blalock |first1=Bob |title=African-Americans have shaped Alabama's and America's cuisine |url=https://alabamanewscenter.com/2019/02/06/african-americans-shaped-alabamas-americas-cuisine/ |access-date=6 July 2024 |agency=Alabama News Center |date=2019 |archive-date=6 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240706140821/https://alabamanewscenter.com/2019/02/06/african-americans-shaped-alabamas-americas-cuisine/ |url-status=live }}</ref>    Several soul food restaurants served black and white people before the passage of the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]], which made segregated facilities illegal.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ruane |first1=Laura |title=Black-owned restaurants nourished the activist soul |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/02/18/black-history-month-restaurants/5591989/ |access-date=3 June 2024 |agency=USA Today |date=2014 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603184727/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2014/02/18/black-history-month-restaurants/5591989/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Draughn |first1=Janay |title=(Southern) Black Women's Presence in Invisibility: Miss Georgia Gilmore & The Club from Nowhere |url=https://www.mdcinc.org/2022/08/23/southern-black-womens-presence-in-invisibility-miss-georgia-gilmore-the-club-from-nowhere/ |website=www.mdcinc.org |publisher=MDC |access-date=3 June 2024 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603184724/https://www.mdcinc.org/2022/08/23/southern-black-womens-presence-in-invisibility-miss-georgia-gilmore-the-club-from-nowhere/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

During the Jim Crow era in the 20th century, it was not safe for Black Americans to travel on the road as they faced possible violence from white supremacists. Black people needed to know what places were safe to stop for food, gas, and motels. In 1936, an African American postal worker from Harlem, New York, named [[Victor Hugo Green]] created ''[[The Negro Motorist Green Book|The Green Book]]'' for Black people to travel safely in the Southern United States, where Jim Crow laws were widespread. Several soul food restaurants were listed in the book because they were safe havens for African Americans to eat. One restaurant listed in the Green Book was Swett's, which opened in 1954.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Green Book Sites Were A Welcome Relief From The Ominous Presence of Jim Crow |url=https://negromotoristgreenbook.si.edu/virtual-exhibit/south/ |website=The Negro Motorist Green Book |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |access-date=2 June 2024 |archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602192757/https://negromotoristgreenbook.si.edu/virtual-exhibit/south/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Importance of "The Green Book: Guide to Freedom" |url=https://www.uwci.org/blog/the-importance-of-the-green-book-guide-to-freedom#:~:text=The%20annual%20guidebook%20was%20first,serve%20them%20along%20the%20road. |website=United Way of Central Indiana |access-date=2 June 2024 |archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602192756/https://www.uwci.org/blog/the-importance-of-the-green-book-guide-to-freedom#:~:text=The%20annual%20guidebook%20was%20first,serve%20them%20along%20the%20road. |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Ulmann, African-American Church.jpg|thumb|African-Americans in church during a church service. Black churches served soul food meals to feed the [[African-American neighborhood|African-American community]].|left]]

The [[Black church|Black Church]] (African-American churches) played a key role in Black communities as they provided food and a place of worship. Researchers from [[Public broadcasting|PBS]] said: "Religion played a key role in the proliferation of soul food, as well as the diversification of the cuisine. Black churches, crucial during slavery and in the Civil Rights movement, were also crucial as gathering places, where Black communities could eat and rejoice over plates of chicken and dumplings, black-eyed peas and rice, [[red drink]]s, and the classic Black American church dish, fried catfish and spaghetti".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stewart |first1=Kayla |title=The Spirit of Soul Food: More Than Just Shrimp and Grits |url=https://www.pbssocal.org/shows/the-migrant-kitchen/the-spirit-of-soul-food-more-than-just-shrimp-and-grits |website=Public Broadcasting SoCal |date=15 February 2022 |publisher=PBS SoCal |access-date=3 June 2024 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603132623/https://www.pbssocal.org/shows/the-migrant-kitchen/the-spirit-of-soul-food-more-than-just-shrimp-and-grits |url-status=live }}</ref> Chris Carter is an African American pastor and professor of history who published a book about the Black Church and soul food in 2021 titled, ''The Spirit of Soul Food: Race, Faith, and Food Justice''. According to Carter, soul food in the African-American community addresses food injustice tied to poverty; Black churches prepare meals throughout the week and on Sundays to feed their community.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Spirit of Soul Food: Race, Faith, and Food Justice |url=https://memphisseminary.edu/2022/02/08/the-spirit-of-soul-food-race-faith-and-food-justice-with-rev-dr-christopher-carter/ |website=Memphis Theological Seminary |date=8 February 2022 |access-date=3 June 2024}}</ref>

Since the mid-20th century, many cookbooks highlighting soul food and African-American foodways have been compiled and published. One notable soul food chef is celebrated traditional Southern chef and author [[Edna Lewis]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=The cooking gene : a journey through African American culinary history in the Old South|last=Twitty |first= Michael |author-link= Michael W. Twitty |isbn=9780062379290|edition= First|location=New York, NY|oclc=971130586|year= 2017}}</ref> who released a series of books between 1972 and 2003, including ''A Taste of Country Cooking'' in which she weaves stories of her childhood in [[Freetown, Virginia]] into her recipes for "real Southern food".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Biography: Edna Lewis |url=https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/edna-lewis |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=Biography: Edna Lewis |language=en}}</ref>

Another early and influential soul food cookbook is [[Vertamae Grosvenor]]'s ''[[Vibration Cooking|Vibration Cooking, or the Travel Notes of a Geechee Girl]]'', originally published in 1970, focused on [[South Carolina]] [[Lowcountry]]/[[Geechee]]/[[Gullah]] cooking. Its focus on spontaneity in the kitchen—cooking by "vibration" rather than precisely measuring ingredients, as well as "[[Improvise|making do]]" with ingredients on hand—captured the essence of traditional African-American cooking techniques. The simple, healthful, basic ingredients of lowcountry cuisine, like shrimp, oysters, crab, fresh produce, rice, and sweet potatoes, made it a bestseller.<ref>{{cite book|url= https://books.google.com/books?id=KX4u6rXRgiUC&q=Another+early+and+influential+soul+food+cookbook+is+Vertamae+Grosvenor%27s+Vibration+Cooking,+or+the+Travel+Notes+of+a+Geechee+Girl,+originally+published+in+1970,+focused+on+South+Carolina+Lowcountry/Geechee/Gullah+cooking.|title= Vibration Cooking: or, The Travel Notes of a Geechee Girl|isbn= 978-0-8203-3959-7|last1= Smart-Grosvenor|first1= Vertamae|date= 15 April 2011|publisher= University of Georgia Press}}</ref>

[[File:The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro.JPG|thumb|The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro]]

Usher boards and Women's Day committees of various religious congregations large and small, and even public service and social welfare organizations such as the [[National Council of Negro Women]] (NCNW) have produced cookbooks to fund their operations and charitable enterprises.<ref name="Witt1999b">{{cite book |last1=Witt |first1=Doris |title=Black Hunger: Food and the Politics of U.S. Identity |year=1999 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-535498-0 |page=219 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSuArSmUcn8C&pg=PA219 |archive-date=2023-07-30 |access-date=2023-08-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230730172633/https://books.google.com/books/?id=VSuArSmUcn8C&pg=PA219 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=C. Eves |first1=Rosalyn |title=A Recipe for Remembrance: Memory and Identity in African-American Women's Cookbooks |journal=Rhetoric Review |date=2005 |volume=24 |issue=3 |pages=280–297 |doi=10.1207/s15327981rr2403_3 |jstor=20176662 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20176662 |access-date=1 July 2024 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=5 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240705053355/https://www.jstor.org/stable/20176662 |url-status=live }}</ref> The NCNW produced its first cookbook, ''The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro'', in 1958, and revived the practice in 1993, producing a popular series of cookbooks featuring recipes by famous Black Americans, among them: ''The Black Family Reunion Cookbook'' (1991), ''Celebrating Our Mothers' Kitchens: Treasured Memories and Tested Recipes'' (1994), and ''Mother Africa's Table: A Chronicle of Celebration'' (1998). The NCNW also recently reissued ''The Historical Cookbook''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Perry |first1=Michiel |title=National Council of Negro Women: Cookbooks to add to your coffee table |url=https://www.blacksouthernbelle.com/national-council-of-negro-women-cookbooks-to-add-to-your-coffee-table/ |website=www.blacksouthernbelle.com |date=9 March 2024 |publisher=Black Southern Belle |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601141355/https://www.blacksouthernbelle.com/national-council-of-negro-women-cookbooks-to-add-to-your-coffee-table/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=African American Cookbooks |url=https://exhibitions.library.vanderbilt.edu/cookbooks/section/african-american-cookbooks/ |website=Vanderbilt Library and Exhibition |publisher=Vanderbilt University |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601142127/https://exhibitions.library.vanderbilt.edu/cookbooks/section/african-american-cookbooks/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The Historical Cookbook of the American Negro |url=https://exhibitions.library.vanderbilt.edu/cookbooks/item/the-historical-cookbook-of-the-american-negro/ |website=Vanderbilt Library and Exhibition |publisher=Vanderbilt University |access-date=2024-06-01 |archive-date=2024-06-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601142128/https://exhibitions.library.vanderbilt.edu/cookbooks/item/the-historical-cookbook-of-the-american-negro/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The Special Collections at the [[University of Alabama]] has the largest collection of over 450 African-American cookbooks. Kate Matheney, a librarian at the University of Alabama, studied the history of African-American cookbooks and found that several Black cookbooks were authored by white women. As they were the primary cooks in [[Plantation complexes in the Southern United States|plantation houses]], enslaved Africans in Alabama influenced the foodways of whites there. During the Jim Crow era, African American women worked in the homes of white families as domestics and prepared their meals. Some white women authored Black cookbooks using stereotypical images of black women as [[Mammy stereotype|Mammies]] on the cover of cookbooks to better market the recipes they learned from black cooks to audiences. African Americans authored their cookbooks using non-stereotypical images and added recipes they learned from their family.<ref name="Blalock2019"/>

In 2011, culinary historian [[Jessica B. Harris]] published a book titled, ''[[High on the Hog (book)|High on the Hog]]'' that describes the origins and development of African-American dishes and their roots in [[Sub-Saharan Africa]]. Enslaved and free African Americans incorporated indigenous foods from North America such as plants, fruits, and animals but [[Africanisms#food|Africanized]] the foods by preparing and flavoring their dishes similarly to West and Central Africans.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Harris |first1=Jessica |title=High on the Hog: A Culinary Journey from Africa to America |date=2011 |publisher=Bloomsbury |isbn=9781596913950 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SaszAQAAQBAJ}}</ref> Harris' book later became a docuseries in 2021 on [[Netflix]] called ''[[High on the Hog: How African American Cuisine Transformed America]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=High on the Hog: How African American Cuisine Transformed America |url=https://www.docnyc.net/high-on-the-hog/ |website=www.docnyc.net |publisher=DOCNYC |access-date=2 June 2024 |archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602134404/https://www.docnyc.net/high-on-the-hog/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:African American railroad porters and cook standing outside a train car with "Olympia" printed on it, 1910s (WASTATE 2708).jpeg|thumb|In the early to mid-20th century, the majority of porters, cooks, and chefs working for railroad and steamboat companies were African Americans. They prepared Southern and soul food dishes for passengers.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=The President's Kitchen Cabinet The Story of the African Americans Who Have Fed Our First Families, from the Washingtons to the Obamas |year=2017 |publisher=University of North Carolina Press |isbn=9781469632544 |pages=121–129, 131–135 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=spYXDgAAQBAJ&q=railroad%20cooks}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Brief History of Blacks Cooking in America |url=https://museumofuncutfunk.com/2013/10/26/brief-history-of-blacks-cooking-in-america/ |website=Museum of Uncut Funk |access-date=4 August 2024 |archive-date=4 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240804134331/https://museumofuncutfunk.com/2013/10/26/brief-history-of-blacks-cooking-in-america/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Resources for the history of Black railroaders |url=https://railphoto-art.org/black-railroaders/ |website=Center for Railroad Photography and Art |access-date=4 August 2024 |archive-date=4 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240804134331/https://railphoto-art.org/black-railroaders/ |url-status=live }}</ref>]]

In 2018 African American author and culinary historian [[Michael W. Twitty|Michael Twitty]] published ''[[The Cooking Gene|The Cooking Gene: A Journey Through African American Culinary History in the Old South]]'' about the history, development, and evolution of soul food in Black communities in the Southern United States.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Twitty |first1=Michael |title=The Cooking Gene: A Journey Through African American Culinary History in the Old South |date=2018 |publisher=Harper Collins |isbn=9780062876577 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K15PDwAAQBAJ |archive-date=2025-02-25 |access-date=2024-06-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250225125103/https://books.google.com/books?id=K15PDwAAQBAJ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Terry |first1=Ruth |title=How Black Culinary Historians Are Rewriting the History of American Food |url=https://www.yesmagazine.org/social-justice/2020/02/26/food-african-american-history |website=www.yesmagazine.org |publisher=Yes Magazine |access-date=16 June 2024 |archive-date=16 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240616145947/https://www.yesmagazine.org/social-justice/2020/02/26/food-african-american-history |url-status=live }}</ref>

Gullah Geechee chef [[Emily Meggett]] was born on [[Edisto Island|Edisto Island, South Carolina]] in 1922.
