Meggett learned how to farm and cook from her family and published a book about Gullah cuisine in 2022 titled, ''Gullah Geechee Home Cooking: Recipes from the Matriarch of Edisto Island''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Meggett |first1=Emily |title=Gullah Geechee Home Cooking: Recipes from the Matriarch of Edisto Island |date=2022 |publisher=ABRAMS |isbn=9781647006907 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v-o7EAAAQBAJ&q=Gullah+Geechee+Home+Cooking:+Recipes+from+the+Matriarch+of+Edisto+Island+in+2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Tsioulcas |first1=Anastasia |title=For Gullah Geechee chef Emily Meggett, cooking was about heart |url=https://www.npr.org/2022/08/15/1116289080/for-this-89-year-old-gullah-geechee-chef-cooking-is-about-heart |website=South Carolina Public Radio |date=24 April 2023 |publisher=NPR |access-date=4 June 2024 |archive-date=12 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712095355/https://www.npr.org/2022/08/15/1116289080/for-this-89-year-old-gullah-geechee-chef-cooking-is-about-heart |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2024, Lakisha Harris became the first Black woman in the United States to give a presentation on soul food at the [[American Culinary Federation]] (ACF) National Convention titled ''Culinary Freedom of the Soul''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Key |first1=Marcus |title=Muskegon woman to be first Black woman in U.S. to present soul food at national chef's convention |url=https://www.wzzm13.com/article/news/community/muskegon-woman-first-to-present-soul-food-at-national-convention/69-04e9dc94-b5b8-4b41-806a-5a48cd5f3b7d |access-date=26 May 2024 |agency=13abc on your side |date=2024}}</ref>

Gullah Geechee chef [[Benjamin Dennis IV]], born in [[Charleston, South Carolina]], teaches about Gullah and African-American cuisine's origins in [[West African cuisine]] and its influence on American foodways.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Barna |first1=Stephanie |title=Chef BJ Dennis delves into his people's Gullah Geechee past to inspire his future |url=https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2012/10/10/chef-bj-dennis-delves-into-his-peoples-gullah-geechee-past-to-inspire-his-future/ |access-date=4 June 2024 |agency=Charleston City Paper |date=2012 |archive-date=4 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604204842/https://charlestoncitypaper.com/2012/10/10/chef-bj-dennis-delves-into-his-peoples-gullah-geechee-past-to-inspire-his-future/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sullivan |first1=Marian |title=We're All Ears |url=https://charlestonmag.com/features/we_re_all_ears |website=Charleston City Magazine |date=17 May 2016 |access-date=4 June 2024 |archive-date=4 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604204842/https://charlestonmag.com/features/we_re_all_ears |url-status=live }}</ref>

Professional chef [[Mashama Bailey]] cooks a fusion of foods derived from the African diaspora with Old World and New World cuisine (of the Southern United States) at ''The Grey'' restaurant in [[Savannah, Georgia]]. Bailey learned how to cook soul food from her mother and attended the [[Institute of Culinary Education]]; she then traveled to Burgundy, France, where she trained under French chefs. Bailey blends Gullah Geechee cuisine with other cuisines of the [[African diaspora]] and continues to educate the public about African-American food culture.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marsh |first1=Ariana |title=Chef Mashama Bailey on Getting Her Seat at the Table |url=https://www.harpersbazaar.com/culture/features/a34774041/chef-mashama-bailey/ |website=Harpers Barzar |date=25 November 2020 |access-date=3 August 2024 |archive-date=3 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240803174322/https://www.harpersbazaar.com/culture/features/a34774041/chef-mashama-bailey/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Soul Food with Mashama |url=https://weta.org/watch/shows/somewhere-south/soul-food-mashama-qaung8 |website=WETA |access-date=3 August 2024 |archive-date=3 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240803174322/https://weta.org/watch/shows/somewhere-south/soul-food-mashama-qaung8 |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Ashleigh Shanti]] is an [[Affrilachia]]n chef who owns the restaurant ''Good Hot Fish'' in [[Asheville, North Carolina]]. She opened a restaurant with a focus on Black [[Appalachian cuisine]] and culture. She said "A big part of why I fell in love with the restaurant industry was watching the women in my family and the power they had serving simple, humble food. I thought it was incredible: how their food could transform someone's mood, making them happy, making them cry."<ref>{{cite web |title=How Family Matriarchs Led Chef Ashleigh Shanti to Open Her First Restaurant |url=https://www.bonappetit.com/sponsored/story/how-family-matriarchs-led-chef-ashleigh-shanti-to-open-her-first-restaurant |website=Bon Appetit |date=15 November 2022 |access-date=3 August 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=White |first1=Taryn |title=This Affrilachian Chef Just Opened Asheville, North Carolina's 'Hottest' New Restaurant |url=https://www.travelandleisure.com/ashleigh-shanti-restaurant-asheville-north-carolina-black-appalachian-cuisine-8536164 |website=Travel and Leisure |access-date=3 August 2024 |archive-date=3 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240803192148/https://www.travelandleisure.com/ashleigh-shanti-restaurant-asheville-north-carolina-black-appalachian-cuisine-8536164 |url-status=live }}</ref>

African American chef [[Carla Hall]], author of the cookbook ''Carla Hall's Soul Food: Everyday and Celebration'', is a television personality and the culinary ambassador to the [[National Museum of African American History and Culture]] Sweet Home Cafe in Washington, D.C. Hall has [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] ancestors from Nigeria, West Africa, and [[Bubi people|Bubi]] ancestors from [[Equatorial Guinea]] in Central Africa.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rickman |first1=Catherine |title=How Carla's Hall Yoruba Roots inspired her Soul Food Journey |url=https://www.tastingtable.com/1270490/carla-hall-yoruba-roots-inspired-soul-food-journey/#:~:text=The%20television%20personality%20and%20cookbook%20author%2C%20known%20as,Nigeria%20and%20her%20Bubi%20ancestors%20from%20Equatorial%20Guinea. |website=Tasting Table |date=27 April 2023 |access-date=6 July 2024 |archive-date=6 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240706145957/https://www.tastingtable.com/1270490/carla-hall-yoruba-roots-inspired-soul-food-journey/#:~:text=The%20television%20personality%20and%20cookbook%20author%2C%20known%20as,Nigeria%20and%20her%20Bubi%20ancestors%20from%20Equatorial%20Guinea. |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Koman |first1=Tess |last2=Arnold |first2=Allison |title=Everything You Need To Know About Carla Hall, The Former Co-Host Of 'The Chew' |url=https://www.delish.com/food-news/g21097928/who-is-carla-hall/ |website=www.delish.com |date=2 December 2022 |publisher=Delish |access-date=6 July 2024 |archive-date=6 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240706145955/https://www.delish.com/food-news/g21097928/who-is-carla-hall/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Influences==

===African influence===
[[File:Ham hock and black-eyed peas (cropped).jpg|thumb|[[Ham hock]] and [[black-eyed pea]]s]]

Scholars have found substantial African influence in soul food recipes, especially from the [[West Africa|West]] and [[Central Africa|Central]] regions of [[Africa]]. This influence can be seen in the [[Pungency|heat level]] of many soul food dishes, as well as many ingredients used to prepare them.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=The Past Is Not Dead|last=Hall|first=Robert L.|publisher=University Press of Mississippi|year=2012|isbn=9781617033056|editor-last=Chambers|editor-first=Douglas B.|location=Jackson, Mississippi|pages=292, 294, 297, 305|editor-last2=Watson|editor-first2=Kenneth}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Twitty |first1=Michael |title=The Unbearable Taste: Early African American Foodways |url=https://commonplace.online/article/unbearable-taste-early-african-american-foodways/#:~:text=American%20crops%20parallel%20to%20African,early%20African%20America%20were%20born. |website=Common Place Journal of Early American Life |publisher=Common Place |access-date=30 June 2024 |archive-date=30 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240630134233/https://commonplace.online/article/unbearable-taste-early-african-american-foodways/#:~:text=American%20crops%20parallel%20to%20African,early%20African%20America%20were%20born. |url-status=live }}</ref> Peppers used to add spice to food include [[Aframomum melegueta|malagueta pepper]], as well as variants native to the [[Western Hemisphere]] such as [[Cayenne pepper|red (cayenne) peppers]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Whit |first1=William C. |url=https://archive.org/details/africanamericanf0000unse/page/34 |title=African American foodways: explorations of history and culture |last2=Hall |first2=Robert L. |publisher=University of Illinois Press |year=2007 |isbn=9780252031854 |editor-last=Bower |editor-first=Anne L. |pages=[https://archive.org/details/africanamericanf0000unse/page/34 34, 48] |oclc=76961285 |url-access=registration}}</ref> Several foods essential to Southern cuisine and soul food were domesticated or consumed in the [[Savanna|African savannah]] and the tropical regions of [[West Africa|West]] and [[Central Africa]]. The foods brought from Africa to North America include [[Cucumis anguria|gherkin]], [[cantaloupe]], [[eggplant]], [[kola nut]]s, [[watermelon]], [[pigeon pea]]s, [[black-eyed pea]]s, [[okra]], [[sorghum]], and [[guinea pepper]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name="VOA Arts and Culture"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Savannah Morning News |first1=Naftal |title=Black influences have shaped American food for centuries |url=https://www.savannahnow.com/story/lifestyle/2021/02/22/africans-brought-different-seeds-and-plants-americas/4505785001/ |access-date=21 June 2024 |agency=Savannah Morning News |date=2021 |archive-date=27 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250427173946/https://www.savannahnow.com/story/lifestyle/2021/02/22/africans-brought-different-seeds-and-plants-americas/4505785001/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=McLaughlin |first1=John |title=A Guide to Planting an African-American/African Focused Yard in Miami-Dade County: An Overview of Landscape Design and Plants Grown in Traditional African-American Yards |url=https://sfyl.ifas.ufl.edu/media/sfylifasufledu/miami-dade/documents/landscapes-amp-gardening/Historical-background-African-American-garden.pdf |website=University of Florida / IFAS Extension |access-date=12 July 2024 |archive-date=29 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240629193326/https://sfyl.ifas.ufl.edu/media/sfylifasufledu/miami-dade/documents/landscapes-amp-gardening/Historical-background-African-American-garden.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Bucket of raw okra pods.jpg|thumb|Okra is used in soul food dishes|left]]

A species of rice, ''[[Oryza glaberrima]]'' was domesticated in Africa, and many people brought to the Americas preserved rice cooking techniques. Rice was a [[cash crop]] in the [[South Carolina Lowcountry]], and during the slave trade, Europeans selected coastal inhabitants of West Africa who had knowledge of [[rice cultivation]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Rice in the Lowcountry |url=https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/exhibits/show/africanpassageslowcountryadapt/sectionii_introduction/rice_lowcountry#:~:text=In%20the%20early%20eighteenth%20century,economy%20into%20the%20nineteenth%20century. |website=Lowcountry Digital History Initiative |publisher=College of Charleston |access-date=1 June 2024 |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601204655/https://ldhi.library.cofc.edu/exhibits/show/africanpassageslowcountryadapt/sectionii_introduction/rice_lowcountry#:~:text=In%20the%20early%20eighteenth%20century,economy%20into%20the%20nineteenth%20century. |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Black rice: the African origins of rice cultivation in the Americas|last=Carney|first=Judith Ann|isbn=9780674029217|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|oclc=657619002|date=2009-06-30}}</ref> Rice is a staple [[side dish]] in the [[Lowcountry]] region and in Louisiana. It is a main ingredient in dishes such as [[jambalaya]] and [[red beans and rice]], popular in [[Acadiana|Southern Louisiana]]. Recipes for rice and beans developed in West Africa were brought to the [[South Carolina Lowcountry]] by enslaved Africans and continue to be prepared by their descendants, the [[Gullah]] people. A Gullah dish of rice, black-eyed peas, onions, and bacon is [[Hoppin' John]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Whit |first1=William |title=Soul Food as Cultural Creation |journal=Journal for the Study of Food and Society |date=1999 |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=40 |doi=10.2752/152897999786690717 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.2752/152897999786690717 |access-date=20 May 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Food historian [[Jessica B. Harris]] traces this dish to a [[Senegal]]ese food called ''Chiebou niebe'', made with rice and beef. Enslaved Black Americans in the United States thus created new dishes with origins in West Africa but using North American ingredients.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jao |first1=Carren |title=A brief look at Black American history told through 10 food traditions |url=https://www.abqjournal.com/clickable/a-brief-look-at-black-american-history-told-through-10-food-traditions/collection_39c010e5-39b6-5ef5-903f-063a04684965.html#10 |website=www.abqjournal.com |publisher=Albuquerque Journal |access-date=3 June 2024 |archive-date=3 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240603202844/https://www.abqjournal.com/clickable/a-brief-look-at-black-american-history-told-through-10-food-traditions/collection_39c010e5-39b6-5ef5-903f-063a04684965.html#10 |url-status=live }}</ref> A Gullah New Year tradition is eating Hoppin' John to bring in good luck. Customarily eaten on January 1 throughout the Lowcountry region, it is often paired with [[cornbread]] and collard greens, which are also said to bring prosperity.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Smith Miles |first1=Suzannah |title=Hoppin' John |url=https://charlestonmag.com/features/hoppin_john |website=www.charlestonmag.com |date=22 December 2014 |publisher=Charleston Magazine |access-date=20 May 2024 |archive-date=20 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520200314/https://charlestonmag.com/features/hoppin_john |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Authentic Gullah Hoppin John.jpg|thumb|Authentic Gullah [[Hoppin' John]]]]

[[Charleston red rice]] is made with rice and tomato paste. This dish originated from [[jollof rice]] in West Africa, a dish made with a tomato product that gives the rice its red color.<ref>{{cite web |title=Discover the History of Charleston in Three Mouthwatering Meals |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/sponsored/discover-history-charleston-three-mouthwatering-meals-180976563/ |website=Smithsonian Magazine |publisher=Smithsonian Institution |access-date=25 May 2024 |archive-date=25 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240525195317/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/sponsored/discover-history-charleston-three-mouthwatering-meals-180976563/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia, enslaved Gullah Geechee people's main source of food was rice paired with meats and shellfish. These rice cooking techniques, influenced by rice dishes made in West Africa, are practiced today in Gullah communities.<ref>{{cite web |title=Origins of Soul Food |url=https://libguides.sunysccc.edu/soulfood |website=SUNY Schenectady |publisher=Begley Library |access-date=3 June 2024 |archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602182932/https://libguides.sunysccc.edu/soulfood |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Food History and Family Travel: Rice Culture and Black Heritage in Berkeley County, SC |url=https://www.blacksouthernbelle.com/food-history-family-travel-rice-culture-black-heritage-in-berkeley-county-sc/#:~:text=Rice%2C%20which%20is%20oftentimes%20considered,%2C%20flour%2C%20puddings%20and%20cakes. |website=www.blacksouthernbelle.com | date=23 March 2021 |publisher=Black Southern Belle |access-date=3 June 2024}}</ref>

There are many documented parallels between the [[foodways]] of West Africans and soul food recipes.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|title=Hog & Hominy: Soul Food from Africa to America|last=Opie|first=Frederick Douglass|isbn=9780231517973|location=New York|oclc=648458580|date=2008-10-08}}</ref> The consumption of [[sweet potato]]es in the United States echoes the consumption of [[Yam (vegetable)|yams]] in West Africa. The presence of cornbread on African-American tables is analogous to West African use of [[fufu]] to soak up sauces and stews.<ref name=":4" />

Harris starred in the 2021 docuseries ''[[High on the Hog: How African American Cuisine Transformed America]]'' and traveled to [[Benin]], West Africa, where she saw women making a leafy sauce called ''feuille'', prepared similarly to how African Americans cook collard greens.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Batey |first1=Nicole |title=Soul food, African culture embedded in American cuisine |url=https://afro.com/soul-food-african-culture-embedded-in-american-cuisine/ |access-date=1 June 2024 |agency=Afro the Black Media Authority |date=2021}}</ref>

West Africans also cooked meat over open pits and brought their methods of barbecuing and making barbecue sauce to the Americas. The [[Hausa language|Hausa]] word for barbecue is ''babbake''.<ref name="Twitty2015"/> [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Indigenous peoples]] in North America also barbecued their meats. African Americans use African and Native American techniques of barbecue.<ref name="Rao2021"/><ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sofritoforyoursoul.com/baebecue-is-more-american-than-you-think-it-is-a-native-american-culinary-art/|title=Barbecue is more American than you think... it is a Native American culinary art.|website=Sofrito for Your Soul|language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-26|archive-date=2019-06-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190626181029/http://www.sofritoforyoursoul.com/baebecue-is-more-american-than-you-think-it-is-a-native-american-culinary-art/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

It was not uncommon to see food served out of an empty [[gourd]]. Many techniques to change the overall flavor of staple food items such as nuts, seeds, and rice contributed to added dimensions of evolving flavors. These techniques included roasting, frying with [[palm oil]], baking in ashes, and steaming in leaves such as banana leaf.<ref name=":13">{{Cite document|title=History of "Soul Food"|last=Arrington|first=Kathye Edwina|date=3 February 2013|id={{ProQuest|1283537628}}|publisher=Press & Sun-Bulletin|location=[[Binghamton, New York]]}}</ref>

===Native American influence===
[[File:2021-08-19 19 01 31 A half loaf of corn bread in the Franklin Farm section of Oak Hill, Fairfax County, Virginia.jpg|thumb|right|Cornbread, a traditional Native American food, became a staple in African-American cooking]]

Southeastern [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] culture is an important element of [[Southern cuisine]]. From their cultures came one of the main staples of the Southern diet: corn (maize), either ground into meal or limed with an alkaline salt to make [[hominy]], in a Native American process known as [[nixtamalization]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Cornbread Gospels |author=Dragonwagon, Crescent |publisher=Workman Publishing |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-7611-1916-6}}</ref> Corn was used to make all kinds of dishes, from the familiar [[cornbread]] and [[grits]] to liquors such as [[moonshine]] and whiskey (which are still important to the Southern economy<ref>X, Malcolm, and Alex Haley. The Autobiography of Malcolm X. Grove Press, 6. 1966</ref>). Black Americans in [[Tuskegee, Alabama]] combined [[molasses]] and leftover cooked grease, a combination they called "''sap''", to pour over their cornbread and "hoe cakes".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dirks |first1=Robert |title=What Early Dietary Studies of African Americans Tell Us About Soul Foods |journal=ResearchGate |page=6 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/356596105 |access-date=20 May 2024}}</ref> An additional Native American influence in soul food is the use of [[maple syrup]]. Indigenous people used maple syrup to sweeten and add flavor to dishes; this influenced the foodways of African Americans as they used maple syrup to sweeten their dishes and poured syrup over pancakes and other breakfast foods.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Sunmin, etl. |title=Native American foods: History, culture, and influence on modern diets |journal=Journal of Ethnic Food |date=2016 |volume=3 |issue=3 |page=176 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/356596105 |access-date=25 July 2024}}</ref>

The foods of [[Black Seminoles]] in Florida and Oklahoma are influenced by [[Gullah]] rice and bean dishes and [[Seminole]] foodways. Black Seminoles cooked rice, "sometimes applying a sauce of okra or spinach leaves".<ref>{{cite web |last1=Opala |first1=Joseph |title=Black Seminoles—Gullahs Who Escaped From Slavery |url=https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/Black%20Seminoles%20.pdf |website=The Gullah: Rice, Slavery, and the Sierre Leone Connection |publisher=Yale University |access-date=26 August 2022 |archive-date=10 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221110050153/https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/Black%20Seminoles%20.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Harris |first1=Jessica |title=High on the Hog: A Culinary Journey from Africa to America |date=2011 |publisher=Bloomsbury |isbn=9781596913950 |page=59 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SaszAQAAQBAJ&q=black%20seminoles}}</ref> Historian Ray Von Robertson conducted oral interviews with sixteen Black Seminoles from 2006 and 2007 and found that Seminole cultural influences were incorporated into their daily lives in practices such as foodways and herbal medicine. Black Seminoles cooked and ate fry bread, ''sofkee'', and grape dumplings.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Robertson |first1=Ray Von |title=Estelusti Marginality: A Qualitative Examination of the Black Seminole |journal=The Journal of Pan African Studies |date=2008 |volume=2 |issue=4 |page=70 |url=https://www.jpanafrican.org/docs/vol2no4/2.4_Estelusti_Marginality.pdf |access-date=6 April 2024 |archive-date=6 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240406143211/https://www.jpanafrican.org/docs/vol2no4/2.4_Estelusti_Marginality.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[File:Bowl of Grits.png|thumb|[[Grits]] originated among [[Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands|Southeastern Native American tribes]] and have become a staple in soul food dishes.]]

Many fruits are available in this region: blackberries, [[muscadine]]s, raspberries, and many other wild berries were part of Southern Native Americans' diets as well.{{Blockquote|To a far greater degree than anyone realizes, several of the most important food dishes that the Native Americans of the southeastern U.S.A live on today is the "soul food" eaten by both Black and White Southerners. Hominy, for example, is still eaten: Sofkee lives on as grits; cornbread [is] used by Southern cooks; Indian fritters -- variously known as "hoe cake" or "Johnny cake"; Indian boiled cornbread is present in Southern cuisine as "corn meal dumplings" and "hush puppies"; Southerners cook their beans and field peas by boiling them, as did the Native tribes; and, like the Native Americans, Southerners cured their meats and smoked it over hickory coals...|sign=Charles Hudson|source=''The Southeastern Indians''<ref name=c_hudson>{{cite book |last=Hudson |first=Charles |title=The Southeastern Indians |year=1976 |publisher=The University of Tennessee Press |chapter=A Conquered People |pages=498–99 |isbn=978-0-87049-248-8}}</ref>}}African, European, and Native Americans of the American South supplemented their diets with meats derived from the hunting of native game. What meats people ate depended on seasonal availability and geographical region. Common game included [[opossum]]s, rabbits, and squirrels.<ref>{{Cite book|title="To love the wind and the rain": African Americans and environmental history|last=Glitner|first=Scott|publisher=University of Pittsburgh Press|year=2006|isbn=9780822972907|editor-last=Glave|editor-first=Dianne D.|location=Pittsburgh, PA|pages=21–36|oclc=878132911|editor-last2=Stoll|editor-first2=Mark}}</ref>

==Sauces and seasoning==
[[File:Crystalhotsauce.jpg|thumb|Hot sauce is used to add heat and flavor to food.]]

Since the mid-20th century, Black Americans have seasoned cooked meats and vegetables with [[Lawry's Seasoned Salt]]. Because Lawry's is economical and offers multiple herbs and spices in one product, Black Americans use it in most of their dishes except sweet dishes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hutcherson |first1=Aaron |title=The Seasoning That Inspires Salty Looks and Kanye Hooks |url=https://tastecooking.com/seasoning-inspires-salty-looks-kanye-hooks/ |website=www.tastecooking.com |date=16 August 2018 |access-date=20 May 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Collette |first1=Abby |title=Body and Soul Food |year=2021 |publisher=Penguin Publishing Group |isbn=9780593336182 |pages=314–315 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gD8jEAAAQBAJ&q=hot%20sauce}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Leckey |first1=Ryan |title=Soul Food Recipes |url=https://www.wnep.com/article/entertainment/television/leckey-live/soul-food-recipes/523-5c161186-b074-4707-88b9-acc8b36e70b2 |website=www.wnep.com |date=6 February 2013 |publisher=16WNEP |access-date=20 May 2024 |archive-date=6 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240606185543/https://www.wnep.com/article/entertainment/television/leckey-live/soul-food-recipes/523-5c161186-b074-4707-88b9-acc8b36e70b2 |url-status=live }}</ref> For extra flavor and spice, hot sauce is sprinkled over [[fried chicken]] and fish, collard greens, and other cooked foods. West Africans made variations of hot spicy sauces using hot [[African pepper|peppers]] indigenous to the region. After their enslavement and transportation to the southern United States, they continued to make their own versions of hot sauces using spices and peppers from North America. By the mid-20th century, Black Americans were turning to store-bought hot sauces to add flavor and spice to their food.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lumpkins |first1=Charles |title=Soul Food |url=https://oxfordaasc.com/display/10.1093/acref/9780195301731.001.0001/acref-9780195301731-e-46221 |website=Oxford African American Studies Center |publisher=Oxford University |access-date=20 May 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Slave trade: How African foods influenced modern American cuisine |url=https://www.un.org/africarenewal/web-features/slave-trade-how-african-foods-influenced-modern-american-cuisine |website=www.un.org |date=27 March 2015 |publisher=United Nations |access-date=20 May 2024 |archive-date=20 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230320201241/https://www.un.org/africarenewal/web-features/slave-trade-how-african-foods-influenced-modern-american-cuisine |url-status=live }}</ref> During slavery times, enslaved people had flavored their vegetables with bacon grease or other parts of the pig. This tradition continues today with [[The Black Family in Slavery and Freedom|Black families]] using [[Pig's trotter|pig feet]], bacon grease, or turkey necks to flavor collard and turnip greens.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thomas |first1=Clarence |title=Soul food roots: West Africa in Central Georgia kitchens |url=https://maconmagazine.com/soul-food-roots/ |website=Macon Magazine |date=23 February 2024 |access-date=26 May 2024}}</ref>

[[File:Oldbayplastic.JPG|thumb|Old Bay Seasoning]]

Culinary historian [[Michael W. Twitty|Michael Twitty]] thinks enslaved African Americans likely influenced the creation of [[Old Bay Seasoning]], saying, "It's not that African Americans necessarily invented it, but without us, the story is impossible." In his travels to West Africa, Twitty observed how West Africans always add peppers, salt, and a hot condiment to their seafood dishes. Twitty believes enslaved West Africans were probably the first to put "kitchen pepper" on shellfish. In colonial America, kitchen pepper was a common kitchen spice blend that often included nutmeg, cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, allspice, ginger, black pepper, and mace. He notes that "there's always a peppery, salty kind of thing that you eat crustaceans with. It's always with a hot condiment—it's never just plain." Twitty believes that hundreds of years of cooking shellfish with kitchen pepper developed into the crab spice blends common in the Chesapeake Bay area when Gustav Brunn came to Baltimore.

The founder of the Old Bay Seasoning company, Gustav Brunn, was a German Jewish immigrant who came to the United States in the 1930s with his family to flee [[Adolf Hitler]]'s ascent to power. After Brunn arrived in Baltimore, he created his own seafood seasoning blend influenced by local seasoning recipes and called it ''Delicious Brand Shrimp and Crab Seasoning'', but it was not popular with the locals. Brunn changed the name to Old Bay and sold a few pounds of Old Bay to a nearby seafood wholesaler. Word spread and over time it became a popular seasoning.<ref>{{cite web |last1=McNamara |first1=Sylvie |title=Why Old Bay Is Suddenly on Everything |url=https://washingtonian.com/2022/07/14/why-old-bay-is-suddenly-on-everything/ |website=Washingtonian |date=14 July 2022 |access-date=5 August 2024 |archive-date=5 August 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240805205922/https://www.washingtonian.com/2022/07/14/why-old-bay-is-suddenly-on-everything/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Mayes |first1=Rose |title=I Heart Soul Food 100 Southern Comfort Food Favorites |date=2020 |publisher=Sasquatch Books |isbn=9781632173102 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=asPNDwAAQBAJ&q=old%20bay%20seasoning}}</ref> Seafood dishes in soul food cuisine today will have Old Bay as the primary seasoning combined with other herbs and sauces to add robust flavor.

==Cultural relevance==

[[File:Jacksonville August 2017 38 (Sylvia Mae's Soul Food).jpg|thumb|Soul food restaurant in Texas]]

Soul food originated in the southern region of the US and is consumed by African-Americans across the nation. Traditional soul food cooking is seen as one of the ways enslaved Africans passed their traditions to their descendants once they were brought to the US. It is a cultural creation stemming from slavery and Native American and European influences.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" />

Soul food recipes are popular in the South due to the accessibility and affordability of the ingredients.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6" /> Scholars have said that while white Americans provided the material supplies for soul food dishes, the cooking techniques found in many of the dishes have been visibly influenced by the enslaved Africans themselves.<ref name=":3" />

The bountiful vegetables found in Africa were substituted in dishes down south with new leafy greens consisting of dandelion, turnip, and beet greens. Pork, more specifically hog, was introduced into several dishes in the form of cracklins from the skin, pigs' feet, chitterlings, and lard used to increase the fat intake into vegetable dishes. Spices such as thyme, and bay leaf blended with onion and garlic gave dishes their own characteristics.<ref name=":13" />

[[Red drink]]s are common at African American social functions.  Restaurants with a mostly black clientele typically serve at least one red drink. Red drinks are important in soul food culture because they represent social connections between friends and family, and a link with the [[African diaspora]].<ref name="Miller2013">{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Adrian |title=Soul Food |year=2013 |pages=223–230 |publisher=UNC Press Books |isbn=978-1-4696-0763-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Od8VAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA223 |archive-date=2024-06-09 |access-date=2024-06-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609195750/https://books.google.com/books?id=Od8VAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA223 |url-status=live }}</ref>  Newbell Puckett, a southern sociologist who documented African American folk beliefs in his 1926 study, ''Folk Beliefs of the Southern Negro'',<ref name="Morrisey20018">{{cite web |last1=Morrisey |first1=Larry |title=Niles Newbell Puckett {{!}} (1897–1967) Scholar |url=https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/niles-newbell-puckett/ |website=Mississippi Encyclopedia |access-date=9 June 2024 |date=April 14, 2018 |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609195753/https://mississippiencyclopedia.org/entries/niles-newbell-puckett/ |url-status=live }}</ref> said that there was cultural and historical continuity between African American culture and West African societies where red had been an important ritual and royal color for hundreds of years. There were two notable red drinks in West Africa, kola tea and [[hibiscus tea]], by the time the Atlantic slave trade began. Kola tea was made from the nuts of West African trees, especially ''[[Cola nitida]]''. Tea made from the dried red flowers of the hibiscus ([[Hibiscus sabdariffa]]), a plant related to okra, is used to make a tea called ''bissap'' or zobo, which is served cool. It is popular in Senegal, Gambia, Nigeria and other West African countries. ''Bissap'' was called sorrel tea or red sorrel in the Americas.<ref name="Miller2013"/>

Figures such as LeRoi Jones (Amiri Baraka), [[Elijah Muhammad]], and [[Dick Gregory]] played notable roles in shaping the conversation around soul food.<ref name="Witt1999c">{{cite book |last1=Witt |first1=Doris |title=Black Hunger: Food and the Politics of U.S. Identity |year=1999 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-535498-0 |page=14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSuArSmUcn8C&pg=PA80 |archive-date=2023-07-31 |access-date=2023-08-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230731152913/https://books.google.com/books/?id=VSuArSmUcn8C&pg=PA80 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":4" /> Muhammad and Gregory opposed soul food because they felt it was unhealthy and was slowly killing African-Americans.<ref name=":5" /> They saw soul food as a remnant of oppression and felt it should be left behind. Many African-Americans were offended by the Nation of Islam's rejection of pork as it is a staple ingredient used to flavor many dishes.<ref name=":4" />

[[Stokely Carmichael]] also spoke out against soul food, claiming that it was not true African food due to its colonial and European influence.<ref name=":4" /> Many voices in the Black Power Movement saw soul food as something African-Americans should take pride in and used it to distinguish African-Americans from white Americans.<ref name="Witt1999a"/> Proponents of soul food embraced the concept and used it as a counterclaim to the argument that African-Americans had no culture or cuisine.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" />

Soul food spread throughout the United States when African-Americans from the South moved to major cities across the country such as [[Chicago]] and New York City during the Great Migration. They brought with them the foods and traditions of the Southern United States, where they had been enslaved.<ref name="Wallach2018"/> Later, the magazine ''Ebony Jr!'' was important in transmitting the cultural relevance of soul food dishes to middle-class African-American children who typically ate a more standard American diet.<ref name="Henderson2007"/> Today Soul food is frequently found at religious rituals and social events such as funerals, fellowship, Thanksgiving, and Christmas in the black community.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

Soul food is culturally similar to [[Romani cuisine]] in Europe.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://sfbayview.com/2013/09/african-americans-and-the-gypsies-a-cultural-relationship-formed-through-hardships/ | title=African Americans and the Gypsies: A cultural relationship formed through hardships | date=27 September 2013 | access-date=19 June 2022 | archive-date=9 December 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221209082147/https://sfbayview.com/2013/09/african-americans-and-the-gypsies-a-cultural-relationship-formed-through-hardships/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Health concerns==
{{Further|Soul food health trends}}

Soul food prepared traditionally and consumed in large amounts can be detrimental to one's health. Opponents of eating soul food have been vocal about health concerns surrounding the culinary traditions since the name was coined in the mid-20th century.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/soul-food-cuisine | title=Soul food &#124; Description, History, & Ingredients &#124; Britannica | access-date=2023-02-23 | archive-date=2022-07-11 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220711215828/https://www.britannica.com/topic/soul-food-cuisine | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Ford |first1=Alexander |title=Food from the soul: A history of African American culture and nutrition |url=https://thedo.osteopathic.org/columns/food-from-the-soul-a-history-of-african-american-culture-and-nutrition/ |website=www.thedo.osteopathic.org |date=December 2022 |publisher=American Osteopathic Association |access-date=20 May 2024 |archive-date=20 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240520204126/https://thedo.osteopathic.org/columns/food-from-the-soul-a-history-of-african-american-culture-and-nutrition/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Soul food has been criticized for its high [[starch]], [[fat]], [[Sodium in biology|sodium]], [[cholesterol]], and [[Caloric concentration|caloric content]], as well as the inexpensive and often low-quality nature of the ingredients such as [[Salt pork|salted pork]] and [[cornmeal]]. In light of this, soul food has been implicated by some in the disproportionately high rates of high blood pressure ([[hypertension]]), [[type 2 diabetes]], clogged arteries ([[atherosclerosis]]), [[stroke]], and [[heart attack]] suffered by African-Americans.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Singh |first1=Maanvi S. |title=Southern Diet Blamed For High Rates Of Hypertension Among Black Americans |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2018/10/02/653798353/southern-diet-blamed-for-high-rates-of-hypertension-among-blacks?t=1659856511016 |website=NPR |access-date=7 August 2022 |language=en |date=2 October 2018 |archive-date=21 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230621144916/https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2018/10/02/653798353/southern-diet-blamed-for-high-rates-of-hypertension-among-blacks?t=1659856511016 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Belle |first1=Genesis |title=Can the African-American Diet be Made Healthier Without Giving up Culture — York College / CUNY |website=www.york.cuny.edu |date=Spring 2009 |volume=5 |issue=2 |url=https://www.york.cuny.edu/english/writing-program/the-york-scholar-1/volume-5.2-spring-2009/can-the-african-american-diet-be-made-healthier-without-giving-up-culture |access-date=7 August 2022 |archive-date=21 June 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230621144924/https://www.york.cuny.edu/english/writing-program/the-york-scholar-1/volume-5.2-spring-2009/can-the-african-american-diet-be-made-healthier-without-giving-up-culture |url-status=live }}</ref> Figures who led discussions surrounding the negative impacts of soul food include Dr. [[Alvenia Fulton]], [[Dick Gregory]], and [[Elijah Muhammad]].<ref name="Witt1999c"/><ref name=":4" />

On the other hand, critics and traditionalists have argued that attempts to make soul food healthier also make it less tasty, as well as less culturally/ethnically authentic.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2006/0206/p20s01-lifo.html|title=Backstory: Southern discomfort food|last=Jonsson|first=Patrick|date=February 6, 2006|work=[[The Christian Science Monitor]]|publisher=[[The First Church of Christ, Scientist|The Christian Science Publishing Society]]|access-date=2006-11-09|archive-date=2006-10-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061012111703/http://www.csmonitor.com/2006/0206/p20s01-lifo.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=F. Mitchell |first1=William |title=African American Food Culture |date=2009 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=9780313346217 |pages=98–99 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UufEEAAAQBAJ&q=diet%20and%20health}}</ref>

The nutritional value of most processed foods, and not just those implicated in a traditional perception of soul food, has degraded as the agricultural system in the United States became industrialized, fueled by federal subsidies.<ref>{{cite book|last=Belasco|first=Warren|title=Food: The Key Concepts|date=2008|publisher=Berg|isbn=978-1845206734}}</ref> This urges a consideration of how concepts of racial authenticity evolve alongside changes in the structures that make some foods more available and accessible than others.<ref>{{cite book|last=Julier|first=Alice|title=The Political Economy of Obesity: The Fat Pay All|date=2008|publisher=Routledge|location=Food and Culture: A Reader|isbn=978-0415977777|pages=482–499}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Guthman|first=Julie|title=Weighing In: Obesity, Food Justice, and the Limits of Capitalism|date=2011|publisher=University California Press|isbn=978-0520266254}}</ref>

An important aspect of the preparation of soul food was the reuse of cooking [[lard]]. Because many cooks could not afford to buy new [[shortening]] to replace what they used, they would pour the liquefied cooking grease into a container. After cooling completely, the grease re-solidified and could be used again the next time the cook required lard.<ref>[https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/eat-run/articles/2017-01-26/healthy-soul-food-ideas-and-recipes Healthy soul food ideas and recipes] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230223193449/https://health.usnews.com/health-news/blogs/eat-run/articles/2017-01-26/healthy-soul-food-ideas-and-recipes |date=2023-02-23 }} US News January 26, 2017</ref> With changing fashions and perceptions of healthy eating, some cooks may use preparation methods that differ from those of cooks who came before them: using liquid oil like [[vegetable oil]] or [[canola oil]] for frying and cooking, and using smoked turkey instead of pork, for example. Changes in hog farming techniques have also resulted in drastically leaner pork, in the late 20th and 21st centuries. Some cooks have even adapted recipes to include vegetarian alternatives to traditional ingredients, including [[tofu]] and [[soy]]-based analogues. Several Black chefs have opened [[Black veganism|vegan soul food]] restaurants to cook healthier foods rooted in African American culture.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Carter |first1=Christopher |title=Is Black Veganism the Future of Soul Food |url=https://www.zocalopublicsquare.org/2022/01/31/black-veganism-future-soul-food/ideas/essay/ |website=www.zocalopublicsquare.org |date=31 January 2022 |publisher=Zocalo Public Square |access-date=8 June 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crimarco |first1=Anthony, etl. |title="We're Not Meat Shamers. We're Plant Pushers.": How Owners of Local Vegan Soul Food Restaurants Promote Healthy Eating in the African American Community |journal=Journal of Black Studies |date=2020 |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=168–193 |doi=10.1177/0021934719895575 |jstor=26985178 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/26985178 |access-date=1 July 2024 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=1 July 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701193131/https://www.jstor.org/stable/26985178 |url-status=live }}</ref> Others, such as Jenne Claiborne, author of the ''Sweet Potato Soul Cookbook'', have started a [[YouTube]] channel and show people how to prepare healthier soul food.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Givens |first1=Dana |title=Meet 5 Black Women Paving the Way for Vegan Soul Food |url=https://www.essence.com/lifestyle/essence-eats/black-women-vegan-soul-food/ |website=Essence Magazine |date=23 October 2020 |access-date=26 May 2024}}</ref>

Several of the ingredients included in soul food recipes have pronounced health benefits. [[Collard greens|Collard]] and other greens are rich sources of several [[vitamin]]s (including [[vitamin A]], [[vitamin B|B<sub>6</sub>]], [[folic acid]] or vitamin B<sub>9</sub>, [[vitamin K]], and [[vitamin C|C]]), minerals ([[manganese]], [[iron]], and [[calcium]]), [[Dietary fiber|fiber]], and small amounts of [[omega-3 fatty acid]]s. They also contain a number of [[phytonutrient]]s, which are thought to play a role in the prevention of [[ovarian cancer|ovarian]] and [[breast cancer]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.whfoods.com/genpage.php?tname=foodspice&dbid=138 |title=Collard greens |publisher=WHFoods |date=2006-05-04 |access-date=2009-06-20 |archive-date=2009-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090211061041/http://www.whfoods.com/genpage.php?tname=foodspice&dbid=138 |url-status=live }}</ref>{{dubious|reason=non-medical source, and everyone knows veggies are good -- doesn't make a high-fat/high-sodium diet with veggies okay.|date=October 2023}}

The traditional preparation of soul food vegetables often consists of high temperatures or slow cooking methods, which can lead the water-soluble vitamins (e.g., Vitamin C and the B complex vitamins) to be destroyed or leached out into the water in which the greens are cooked. This water is often consumed and is known as [[pot liquor]].<ref name=":0" /> Because it contains micronutrients from the greens cooked in it, pot liquor contributes to the nutritional value of a meal when consumed.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Aubrey |first1=Allison |title=Pot Liquor: A Southern Tip To Save Nutritious Broth From Greens |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2013/08/06/209543044/pot-liquor-a-southern-tip-to-save-nutritious-broth-from-greens |website=NPR |access-date=3 January 2022 |language=en |date=7 August 2013}}</ref> [[Pea]]s and [[legume]]s are inexpensive sources of [[protein]], and they also contain important vitamins, minerals, and fiber.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/beans-and-pulses-nutrition/|title=Beans and pulses in your diet|date=27 April 2018|access-date=2 November 2021|archive-date=19 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220319073630/https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/eat-well/beans-and-pulses-nutrition/|url-status=live}}</ref>

'''Tahini''' ({{IPAc-en|t|ə|ˈ|h|iː|n|i|,_|t|ɑː|-}}; {{Langx|ar|[[wikt:طحينة|طحينة]]|translit=ṭaḥīna}}, or, in Iraq, {{Langx|ar|راشي|translit=rāshī|label=none}}) is a [[Middle Eastern]] [[condiment]] (a [[seed butter]]) made from ground [[sesame]] seeds.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tahini {{!}} Definition of Tahini by Oxford Dictionary on Lexico.com also meaning of Tahini|url=https://www.lexico.com/en/definition/tahini|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200315040002/https://www.lexico.com/en/definition/tahini|url-status=dead|archive-date=15 March 2020|access-date=2021-01-11|website=Lexico Dictionaries {{!}} English|language=en}}</ref> The most common variety comes from [[hulled]] seeds, but unhulled ones can also be used;<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last1=Blythman |first1=Joanna |last2=Sykes |first2=Rosie |last3=Sykes |first3=with recipe by Rosie |date=2013-03-23 |title=Why tahini is good for you |url=https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2013/mar/23/good-for-you-tahini |access-date=2024-04-10 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> the latter variety is slightly bitter, but more nutritious.<ref name=":0" /> The seeds are more commonly roasted than raw. Tahini can be served by itself (as a [[Dip (food)|dip]]), made into a [[salad dressing]], or used as a major ingredient in [[hummus]], [[baba ghanoush]], or [[halva]]. 

Tahini is used in the cuisines of the [[Middle East]] and [[Eastern Mediterranean]], the [[South Caucasus]], the [[Balkans]], [[South Asia]], [[Central Asia]], and amongst [[Cyprus|Cypriots]], [[Ashkenazi Jews]], as well as parts of [[Russia]] and [[North African cuisine|North Africa]]. Sesame paste, used in some East Asian cuisines, may differ only slightly from tahini.

== Etymology ==
''Tahini'' is of [[Arabic language|Arabic]] origin and comes from a colloquial [[Levantine Arabic]] pronunciation of {{transliteration|ar|Wehr|ṭaḥīna}} ({{lang|ar|طحينة}}),<ref>{{Cite American Heritage Dictionary|tahini|access-date=11 May 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Tahini definition and meaning {{!}} Collins English Dictionary|url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/us/dictionary/english/tahini|access-date=2021-01-11|website=www.collinsdictionary.com|date=13 February 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref> or more accurately {{transliteration|ar|Wehr|ṭaḥīniyya}} ({{lang|ar|طحينية}}), whence also English "tahina" and Hebrew ''ṭḥina'' {{lang|he|טחינה}}. It is derived from the [[Classical Arabic]] [[triliteral|root]] {{lang|ar|ط ح ن}} {{transliteration|ar|Ṭ-Ḥ-N}}, which as a verb {{lang|ar|طحن}} {{transliteration|ar|Wehr|ṭaḥana}} means "to grind",<ref name="Me recipes">{{citation|title = The Middle Eastern Kitchen: A Book of Essential Ingredients with Over 150 Authentic Recipes, p.146 | author=Ghillie Basan, Jonathan Basan|publisher=Hippocrene Books|year=2006}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Definition of TAHINI|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/tahini|access-date=2021-01-11|website=www.merriam-webster.com|language=en}}</ref> and also produces the word {{lang|ar|طحين}} {{transliteration|ar|Wehr|ṭaḥīn}}, "flour" in some [[varieties of Arabic|dialects]].  The word tahini had appeared in English by the late 1930s.<ref name="mariposa">Mariposa, ''Hollywood Glamour Cook Book'', 1940, p. 101.</ref><ref>''Treasury decisions under customs and other laws'', 1938, p. 1080 [https://books.google.com/books?id=SOwWAQAAIAAJ&q=tahini&dq=tahini snippet]</ref> In earlier English-language sources, it is referred to as "sesame butter" or "sesame seed butter".<ref name=hist_sesame>{{cite book | first1=William|last1=Shurtleff|author-link1=William Shurtleff|first2=Akiko|last2=Aoyagi|title=History of Sesame (100 CE to 2022)|location=Lafayette, California|publisher=Soyinfo Center|date=2022|isbn=978-1-948436-71-7|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=c4hfEAAAQBAJ|page=7}}</ref>

== History ==
The oldest mention of sesame is in a [[cuneiform]] document written 4,000 years ago that describes the custom of serving the gods sesame wine. Historian [[Herodotus]] writes about the cultivation of sesame 3,500 years ago in the region of the [[Tigris]] and [[Euphrates]] in [[Mesopotamia]] (modern day Iraq). It was mainly used as a source of [[oil]].<ref>{{cite web|last=Laniado |first=Limor |url=https://www.haaretz.com/culture/food-wine/be-merry-the-glory-of-tahini-1.361176 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110514030808/http://www.haaretz.com/culture/food-wine/be-merry-the-glory-of-tahini-1.361176 |url-status=dead |archive-date=14 May 2011 |title=The glory of tahini |publisher=Haaretz.com |date=12 May 2011 |access-date=18 January 2013}}</ref>

In the 10th-century Arabic cookbook ''[[Ibn_Sayyar_al-Warraq#Kitāb_al-Ṭabīkh|Kitab al-Tabikh]]'', a recipe for ground sesame is mentioned; recipes call for its use as a condiment or to be eaten with bread.<ref name="NawalNasrallah">{{cite book |last1=Nasrallah |first1=Nawal |title=Annals of the Caliphs' Kitchens: Ibn Sayyār al-Warrāq's Tenth-Century Baghdadi Cookbook |date=31 December 2007 |publisher=BRILL |isbn=978-90-474-2305-8 |pages=575,583,619 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sQCwCQAAQBAJ |access-date=20 September 2025 |language=en |author1-link=Nawal Nasrallah}}</ref>

Tahini is mentioned as an ingredient of ''[[hummus]] kasa'', a recipe transcribed in an anonymous 13th-century Arabic cookbook, ''Kitab Wasf al-Atima al-Mutada''.<ref name=Fordham>{{cite web|title=Middle Eats: What are Lebanon's chances of legally laying claim to hummus?|author=Alice Fordham|publisher=NOW Lebanon|date=10 October 2008|url=http://www.nowlebanon.com/NewsArticleDetails.aspx?ID=62188|access-date=25 November 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081212214428/http://nowlebanon.com/NewsArticleDetails.aspx?ID=62188|archive-date=12 December 2008}}</ref>

In his 14th-century work ''Kaftor va-Perach'' ([[Hebrew language|Hebrew]]: כפתור ופרח), [[Ishtori Haparchi]] wrote that the inhabitants of the Middle East in his time consumed tahini, made by grinding sesame seeds and mixing them with [[date honey]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amar |first=Zohar |date=1993 |title=Estori ha-Parchi and the Identification of the Flora of Eretz Israel |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23536280 |journal=Proceedings of the World Congress of Jewish Studies |language=he |volume=11 |pages=137 |jstor=23536280 |issn=0333-9068}}</ref>

Sesame paste is an ingredient in some [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]] and [[Japanese cuisine|Japanese]] dishes; [[Sichuan cuisine]] uses it in some recipes for [[dandan noodles]]. Sesame paste is also used in [[Indian cuisine]].<ref>Sanjeev Kapoor, ''Khazana of Indian Vegetarian Recipes'', p. 94</ref>

In [[North America]], sesame tahini, along with other raw [[nut butter]]s, was available by 1940 in [[health food store]]s.<ref name='mariposa'/>

== Preparation and storage ==
[[File:Tahini with roasted sesame.JPG|thumb|190px|Tahini made with roasted sesame, dubbed "red tahini"]]
Tahini is made from sesame seeds that are soaked in water and then crushed to separate the [[bran]] from the kernels. The crushed seeds are then soaked again in salt water with a high salt content that causes the bran to sink. The floating kernels are skimmed off the surface, toasted, and ground to produce an oily paste.<ref name="Davidson 2014">{{cite book|first=Anissa|last=Helou|editor-first1=Alan|editor-last1=Davidson|title=The Oxford Companion to Food|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bIIeBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA802|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|pages=802–803|date=2014|isbn=9780191040726|via=Google Books}}</ref> It can also be prepared with untoasted seeds and called "raw tahini".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Coulombe |first1=Geneviève |last2=Tamber |first2=Sandeep |title=Salmonella enterica Outbreaks Linked to the Consumption of Tahini and Tahini-Based Products |journal=Microorganisms |date=19 November 2022 |volume=10 |issue=11 |pages=2299 |doi=10.3390/microorganisms10112299 |pmid=36422369 |pmc=9694856 |doi-access=free |issn=2076-2607}}</ref>

Because of tahini's high oil content, some manufacturers recommend refrigeration to prevent spoilage. Others do not recommend refrigeration, as it makes the product more viscous and more difficult to serve.<ref name="Ochef">{{cite web|url=http://www.ochef.com/1285.htm |title=Refrigerated or Not, How Long Does Tahini Last? |publisher=Ochef |access-date=18 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130120025426/http://www.ochef.com:80/1285.htm|archive-date=20 January 2013}}{{Self published inline|date=January 2019}}</ref>

The color of the produced tahini is affected by the kind of sesame used, untoasted sesame produces a bright-colored tahini; toasted or unshelled sesame produces tahini with a darker color,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Dimopoulos |first1=Johanna |title=Building Blocks: Greek Whole Grain Tahini, and the Artisans Behind It |url=https://culinarybackstreets.com/cities-category/athens/2021/building-blocks-37/ |website=Culinary Backstreets |access-date=24 July 2025 |language=en |date=26 March 2021}}</ref> [[black sesame]] produces a tahini with a deep black color (dubbed "black tahini").<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shap |first1=Elana |title=It's about tradition, not trend for one Arab tahini maker |url=https://www.israel21c.org/its-about-tradition-not-trend-for-one-arab-tahini-maker/ |website=Israel21c |access-date=11 May 2025 |date=28 December 2022}}</ref><ref name="elhaddad"/>

== Nutrition ==
Tahini is 53% [[fat]], 22% [[carbohydrate]]s, 17% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]], and 3% water (table). In a reference amount of {{cvt|100|g}}, it supplies 592 [[calorie]]s, and is a rich source of [[thiamine]] (133% of the [[Daily Value]], DV), several [[mineral (nutrient)|dietary minerals]] (25-63% DV), [[niacin]], and [[folate]] (25-35% DV, table). Tahini is a moderate source (10-19% DV) of [[calcium in biology|calcium]] and [[potassium in biology|potassium]] (table).

== Culinary uses ==
Tahini-based sauces are common in Middle Eastern restaurants as a side dish or as a garnish, usually including [[lemon juice]], salt, and [[garlic]], and thinned with water. Hummus is made of cooked, mashed [[chickpeas]] typically blended with tahini, lemon juice and salt. Tahini sauce is also a popular topping for meat and vegetables in [[Middle Eastern cuisine]]. A sweet spread, ''ḥalawa ṭaḥīniyya'' ("sweet tahini"), is a type of halva sweet. It sometimes has mashed or sliced [[pistachio]] pieces sprinkled inside or on top.

In many parts of the Middle East, it is spread on bread and eaten as a quick snack or breakfast. Alternatively, bread can be dipped into tahini sweetened by a syrup such as [[grape syrup]], [[Carob#Syrup_and_drinks|carob syrup]], or [[date_honey|date syrup]]; the sweetener may vary by region.<ref name="rkassis">{{cite book |last1=Kassis |first1=Reem |title=The Palestinian Table |date=23 October 2017 |publisher=Phaidon Press |isbn=978-0-7148-7496-8 |page=108 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pmm2tAEACAAJ |language=en}}</ref>

=== For sweets ===
Tahini is also used in [[sweet dishes]] such as [[cake]]s, [[cookies]], [[halva]], and [[ice cream]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Davidson">{{cite book |last=Davidson |first=Alan |author-link=Alan Davidson (food writer) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bIIeBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA378 |title=The Oxford Companion to Food |publisher=Oxford University press |year=1999 |isbn=0-19-211579-0 |location=Oxford |pages=378}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Akis Petretzikis LTD |title=Tahini ice cream |url=https://akispetretzikis.com/en/recipe/4938/pagwto-tachini |access-date=2024-04-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Salamandra |title=Make a blissful cake of chocolate and tahini |url=https://www.israel21c.org/21see/make-a-blissful-cake-of-chocolate-and-tahini/ |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=ISRAEL21c |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-12-07 |title=Dark Cocoa Tahini Cookies (Gluten-Free) |url=https://www.celiac.com/celiac-disease/dark-cocoa-tahini-cookies-gluten-free-r3948/ |access-date=2024-04-10 |website=Celiac.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== By region ===
{{more citations needed section|date=January 2019}}
==== Armenia ====
In [[Armenia]], tahini can be used as a sauce to put on ''[[lahmajoun]]''.

==== China ====
[[File:Black sesame paste.jpg|thumb|Black sesame paste, sometimes called "black tahini" (not to be confused with [[Qizha]], also called black tahini<ref name="viceBlackTahini" />), is popular in Chinese cuisine]]
In [[Chinese cuisine]], sesame paste (zhīmájiàng) is used as a condiment in many dishes. Chinese sesame paste differs from the Middle Eastern tahini in that the sesame is roasted; the paste is much darker, and has far less astringency. Often, white sesame paste is used in salty dishes, while black sesame paste is used in desserts (not to be confused with [[black sesame soup]], which is made in a different manner from sesame paste{{clarification needed|reason=image shown in that article is the same as here|date=July 2026}}). Sesame paste is a primary condiment in the [[hot dry noodles]] of [[Hubei cuisine]] and ma jiang mian (sesame paste noodles) of [[Northeastern Chinese cuisine]] and [[Taiwanese cuisine]]. Sesame paste is also used as a bread or [[mantou]] [[Spread (food)|spread]], and may be paired with or baked into [[Bing (bread)|bing (Chinese flatbread)]]. Sesame paste is used as a seasoning, condiment and dip in cold dishes (such as ''[[liangfen]]'') and [[hot pot]].

==== Cyprus ====
In [[Cyprus]], tahini, locally pronounced as ''tashi'', is used as a dip for bread and sometimes in ''pitta [[souvlaki]]'' rather than ''tzatziki'', which is customary in Greece; it is also used to make "tahinopitta" ([[Tahini roll|tahini pie]]).<ref>{{cite book |title=Food and Celebration, from Fasting to Feasting: Proceedings of the 13th Conference of the International Commission for Ethnological Food Research, Ljubljana, Preddvor, and Piran, Slovenia, June 5–11, 2000 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AHGHEAAAQBAJ |editor-last=Lysaght |editor-first=Patricia |chapter=Fasting in Cyprus |last1=Egoumenidou |first1=Euphrosyne |last2=Michaelides |first2=Demetrios |date=2002 |publisher=Založba ZRC |location=Ljubljana |isbn=9789616358545 |page=[https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=AHGHEAAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PA60 60] |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref>

==== Egypt ====
In [[Egypt]], tehina is a fundamental component of the country's [[Egyptian cuisine|cuisine]], serving as an ingredient, a condiment, and a dipping sauce. Derived from toasted, hulled sesame seeds ground into a creamy paste, tehina boasts a rich, nutty flavor with a slightly bitter undertone.<ref name=cheznermine>{{cite web |last1=Mansour |first1=Nermine |title=Egyptian tehina sauce|url=https://cheznermine.com/2023/12/02/egyptian-tehina-sauce-%D8%B5%D9%88%D8%B5-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D8%AD%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A9-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B7%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%82%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B5%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9/ |website=Chez Nermine |date=2 December 2023 |access-date=March 15, 2025}}</ref>

In Egyptian culinary traditions, tehina is often made by blending it with lemon juice, garlic, and water, resulting in a smooth, ivory-colored condiment. This sauce is commonly seasoned with salt and cumin to enhance its flavor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Tahini sauce |url=https://toriavey.com/tahini-sauce/ |website=Tori Avey |date=20 January 2010 |access-date=March 15, 2025}}</ref> The consistency can be adjusted by varying the amount of water, making it suitable as a dip, dressing, or accompaniment to various dishes.<ref>{{cite web |title=How To Make Egyptian Tahini Sauce |url=https://www.healthylifetrainer.com/tahini-dressing-recipe/ |website=Healthy Life Trainer |date=26 April 2023 |access-date=March 15, 2025}}</ref>

Tehina sauce holds a prominent place in [[Egyptian cuisine]], frequently accompanying dishes such as [[falafel|ta'miya]], [[ful medames]] and grilled meats like [[Koftet el hati|kofta]]. Its creamy texture and tangy profile complement the robust flavors of most foods, making it a staple on Egyptian dining tables.<ref name=cheznermine/>

==== Greece ====
In [[Greece]], tahini is used as a spread on bread either alone or topped with honey or jam. Jars of tahini ready-mixed with honey or cocoa are available in the breakfast food aisles of Greek supermarkets.

==== Iran ====
In [[Iran]], tahini is called ''ardeh'' in [[Persian language|Persian]]. It is used to make {{Interlanguage link|halvardeh|fa|حلوا ارده|italic=1}}, a kind of [[halva]] made of tahini, [[sugar]], [[Egg white|egg whites]], and other ingredients. It is also eaten during breakfast, usually with an accompanying sweet substance, such as [[grape syrup]], [[date syrup]], [[honey]], or [[Fruit preserves|jam]]. Ardeh and halvardeh are among the souvenirs of the Iranian cities of [[Yazd, Iran|Yazd]] and [[Ardakan, Iran|Ardakan]].

==== Iraq ====
In [[Iraq]], tahini is known as ''rashi'', and is mixed with [[Phoenix dactylifera|date]] syrup ([[Rub (syrup)|rub]]) to make a sweet dessert usually eaten with bread.

==== Israel ====
In [[Israel]], tahini (''ṭḥina'') is a staple foodstuff. It is served as a dip with flat bread or [[pita]], a topping for many foods such as [[falafel]], [[sabich]], [[Jerusalem mixed grill]] and [[shawarma]], and as an ingredient in various spreads. It is also used as a sauce for meat and fish, and in sweet desserts like halva,<ref>Rogov, Daniel, [https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/Food/Halvahparfait.html Halvah Parfait]</ref> [[halva ice cream]] and [[tahini cookie]]s. It is also served baked in the oven with ''[[kufta]]'' made of lamb or beef with spices and herbs, or with a whole fish in the coastal areas and the [[Sea of Galilee]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==== Levant ====
In the [[Levant]], tahini is a staple food and is used in various spreads and culinary preparations. It is the main ingredient of the [[Tarator (sauce)|Ṭaraṭor (sauce)]] which is used with falafel and shawarma. It is also used as a sauce for meat and fish. It is an ingredient in a seafood dish called ''[[siyadiyeh|ṣiyadiyeh]]''. 

==== Palestine ====
In the [[Gaza Strip]], a rust-colored variety known as "red tahina" is served in addition to ordinary tahina. It is achieved by a different and lengthier process of roasting the sesame seeds, and has a more intense taste. Red tahina is used in ''[[sumaghiyyeh|sumagiyya]]'' (lamb with chard and sumac) and salads native to the [[Fellah|falaḥeen]] from the surrounding villages, as well as southern Gaza.<ref name="elhaddad">
{{cite book
|last1=el-Haddad
|first1=Laila
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hrSIjgEACAAJ
|title=The Gaza Kitchen: A Palestinian Culinary Journey
|date=February 2016
|publisher=Garnet Publishing, Limited
|isbn=9781859644621
|language=en
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Gold |first1=Rozanne |title=The Search for Red Tahina |url=https://www.rozannegold.com/blog-new/2021/7/7/the-search-for-red-tahina |website=Rozanne Gold |access-date=11 May 2025 |date=7 July 2021}} By [[Rozanne Gold]]</ref>

In the [[West Bank]] city of [[Nablus]], tahina is mixed with ''[[qizha|qizḥa]]'' paste to make "black tahina", used in baking.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Berger |first=Miriam |title=Is the world ready for this Palestinian dish? |url=http://www.bbc.com/travel/story/20190327-is-the-world-ready-for-this-palestinian-dish |access-date=2019-03-28 |website=www.bbc.com |date=28 March 2019 |language=en}}</ref> It is distinct from the "black tahini" made from black sesame seeds.<ref name="viceBlackTahini">{{cite news |last1=Pyenson |first1=Luke |title=Black Tahini Is the Dark Magic of Palestine |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/black-tahini-is-the-dark-magic-of-palestine/ |access-date=24 July 2025 |work=VICE |date=17 September 2014}}</ref>

It is also commonly sweetened with [[grape syrup]] and eaten with [[pita]] bread.<ref name="rkassis"/>

==== Turkey ====
In [[Turkey]], tahini is mixed with [[pekmez]] to make ''tahin-pekmez'', which is often served as a [[breakfast]] item or after meals as a sweet dip for breads.
