======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Taiwanese cuisine
======================================================================

{{Short description|Culinary traditions of Taiwan}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=September 2020}}
[[File:Taiwanese khong bah png, Tofu, Milkfish Skin Soup.jpg|thumb|Taiwanese [[khòng-bah-pn̄g]], tofu and milkfish skin soup]]
'''Taiwanese cuisine''' ({{lang-zh|t={{linktext|臺灣|料理}}|p=Táiwān liàolǐ|poj=Tâi-oân liāu-lí}} or {{lang-zh|t=臺灣菜|p=Táiwāncài|poj=Tâi-oân-chhài|first=t|labels=no}}) is a popular style of food with several variations, including [[Chinese cuisine|Chinese]] and that of [[Taiwanese indigenous peoples]], with the earliest cuisines known of being the indigenous ones. With over a hundred years of historical development, southern [[Fujian cuisine]] has had the most profound impact on mainstream Taiwanese cuisine but it has also been influenced by [[Hakka cuisine]], the cuisines of the ''[[waishengren]]'' (people of other provinces), and [[Japanese cuisine]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chang |first1=Erchen |date=12 May 2023 |title=A taste of Taiwan, from comforting noodles to spicy broths |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/taste-taiwan-comforting-noodles-spicy-broths |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230512093331/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/taste-taiwan-comforting-noodles-spicy-broths |archive-date=12 May 2023 |access-date=18 May 2023 |website=[[National Geographic]]}}</ref>

Taiwan's cuisine is tied to its history of colonization and modern politics makes the description of Taiwanese cuisine difficult. As Taiwan developed economically, [[fine dining]] became increasingly popular. Taiwanese cuisine has significant regional variations.

[[Night markets in Taiwan]] form a significant part of the food culture. Vegetarian and vegan food are very common. Taiwanese cuisine is popular around the world with some items like [[bubble tea]] and [[Taiwanese fried chicken]] becoming global phenomena.

==History==
[[File:At a Fruit and Vegetable Market in Taihoku 1938-1942.jpg|thumb|At a fruit and vegetable market in Taihoku Prefecture (now Taipei) 1938–1942.]]
According to Katy Hui-wen Hung, "Taiwanese food history is as murky as Taiwanese politics". This is because Taiwanese cuisine is intricately tied to patterns of migration and colonization. Local and international Taiwanese cuisine, including its history, is a politically contentious topic.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wahn |first1=I-Liang |title=Food, Politics and Solidarity Economies in Taiwan |url=https://taiwaninsight.org/2022/02/08/food-politics-and-solidarity-economies-in-taiwan/ |website=Taiwan Insight |date=8 February 2022 |publisher=University of Nottingham Taiwan Studies Programme |access-date=14 May 2023}}</ref><ref name="Eater 2019">{{cite web |last1=Nguyen-Okwu |first1=Leslie |date=6 March 2019 |title=16 Dishes That Define Taiwanese Food |url=https://www.eater.com/2019/3/6/18241036/what-is-taiwanese-food-traditional-cuisine |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413203539/https://www.eater.com/2019/3/6/18241036/what-is-taiwanese-food-traditional-cuisine |archive-date=13 April 2020 |access-date=27 April 2020 |website=Eater}}</ref> Taiwan's complex and diverse identity makes Taiwanese cuisine difficult to define.<ref name="Japan Times 2022" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=Rao |first1=Tejal |date=16 August 2022 |title=In a Tense Political Moment, Taiwanese Cuisine Tells Its Own Story |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/08/16/dining/taiwanese-cuisine.html |access-date=13 August 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Tense political relations between Taiwan and China also complicate the history.<ref name="NYT August 2023" />

The history of Taiwanese cuisine began with the cuisine of the aboriginal peoples of the islands of Taiwan. In the 16th century Hokkien and Hakka communities immigrated to Taiwan and brought their cuisines with them. Due to this part of its heritage Taiwanese cuisine is often considered as a part of regional Han cuisine. Early European influences came from the Dutch, Spanish, and Portuguese.<ref name="Not that simple">{{cite web |last1=Chen |first1=Lina |date=19 March 2017 |title=Origins of Taiwanese Fusion Cuisine: It's Not That Simple |url=https://international.thenewslens.com/article/63903 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[The News Lens]]}}</ref>

Due to the period of [[Taiwan under Japanese rule|Japanese rule]], Taiwanese cuisine was also strongly influenced by Japanese ''[[washoku]]'' and ''[[yōshoku]]''.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}} During Japanese rule Japanese dishes and foodways such as bento,<ref name= "Night Market Treats" /> sashimi, rice balls, and miso soup were introduced to Taiwanese cuisine.<ref name= "Not that simple" />

After WWII, the [[Kuomintang]] retreat to Taiwan brought along many Han cuisines outside the province of [[Fujian]] or Southeast China. After that, the dishes from [[China]] especially [[Cantonese cuisine|Guangdong]], [[Teochew cuisine|Chaoshan]], [[Shanghai cuisine|Shanghai]], [[Sichuan cuisine|Sichuan]] and [[Beijing cuisine|Beijing]] could be easily found in [[Taiwan]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Chen |first=Yujen |title=Taiwan's Cuisines |date=2026-06-11 |work=Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Food Studies |editor-last=Goldstein |editor-first=Darra |url=https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/61795/chapter/565400482 |access-date=2026-08-15 |edition=1 |publisher=Oxford University PressNew York, NY |language=en |doi=10.1093/9780197852538.003.0229 |isbn=978-0-19-785253-8|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

According to Taiwanese chef [[Fu Pei-mei]], authentic Chinese culinary traditions were properly preserved in Taiwan. This claim to authenticity, common among Fu's generation, was in part due to the [[Kuomintang]]'s Chinese nationalist political messaging which extended well beyond cuisine.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |title=Culinary nationalism in Asia |date=2019 |isbn=978-1-350-07869-7 |editor-last=King |editor-first=Michelle Tien |editor-link=Michelle T. King |location=London, UK |pages=56–72 |oclc=1100471127}}</ref> The authenticity of regional Han cuisine in Taiwan has been challenged.<ref name="NYT August 2023">{{cite news |last1=Yuan |first1=Li |date=8 August 2023 |title=What Cuisine Means to Taiwan's Identity and Its Clash With China |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/08/08/business/taiwan-cuisine.html |access-date=13 August 2023 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Some sources trace the origin of [[instant noodles]] to Taiwan's jisi noodles, in particular a variation deep-fried in pork fat to be later boiled in water before serving introduced by the Qingji Ice Dessert Parlor in 1951. Following the commercialization of instant noodles Taiwanese companies including [[Uni-President]]. In 1973 Wei Lih Food Industrial introduced the first packaged instant noodle meant to be consumed "dry" (without soup or with soup on the side).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tseng |first1=Esther |title=Tradition and Innovation: The Protein Power of Instant Noodles |url=https://international.thenewslens.com/article/186813 |access-date=9 February 2024 |website=[[The News Lens]]|date=6 February 2024 }}</ref>

The [[Tatung Company|Tatung]] electric steamer was introduced in the 1960s and became a staple of Taiwanese home and restaurant kitchens.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wei |first1=Clarissa |date=2 October 2022 |title=Forget the Instant Pot, Taiwanese steamer Tatung makes everything from fish to rice to cake – and at last it's easier to buy in the US |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/food-drink/article/3194217/forget-instant-pot-taiwanese-steamer-tatung |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> The widespread adoption of the [[food court]] during the 20th century formalized more traditional hawkers and vendors. Food courts also became an important part of the malls and shopping centers which proliferated across Taiwan.<ref name= "Night Market Treats" />

In 2002, the accession of Taiwan to the [[World Trade Organization]] forced Taiwanese farmers to compete with global markets. Many responded by shifting from staple crops to high end and niche produce primarily for local consumption. [[Agrotourism]] was also more widely adopted, with visitors to farms often being served and/or taught how to prepare dishes with the products from the farms.<ref name="Plenty to Chew On">{{cite web |date=13 July 2023 |title=Plenty to Chew on at the Taiwan Culinary Exhibition |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2023/07/plenty-to-chew-on-at-the-taiwan-culinary-exhibition/ |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

In the early 21st century, ideas about sustainability and local food became more prominent in Taiwanese culinary and agricultural circles.<ref>{{cite web |last1=OUNG |first1=ANGELICA |date=31 January 2023 |title=Green Dining Gains Recognition in Taiwan |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2023/01/green-dining-gains-recognition-in-taiwan/ |access-date=5 February 2023 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref> An increased emphasis has been placed on understanding the history of food as well as incorporating indigenous foodways into mainstream Taiwanese cuisine.<ref name="NYT August 2023" />

=== Ingredients and culture ===
{{Further|Agriculture in Taiwan|Maritime industries of Taiwan}}
[[File:Taiwan in HDR (4243621343).jpg|thumb|[[Paddy field]] in [[Hualien County]]]]
[[File:Vegetable Farming Park, Nangan, Matsu, Taiwan.JPG|thumb|[[Shanlong Vegetable Park|Vegetable farmland]] in [[Matsu Islands|Lienchiang County]]]]
[[File:Jiangjyun Village.JPG|thumb|Fishing port in [[Penghu County]]]]
Common ingredients of Taiwanese cuisine are [[pork]], [[seafood]], [[Chicken (food)|chicken]], [[rice]], and [[soy]].<ref name="goossaert"/> Traditionally, rice formed the basis of most Taiwanese diets. Before the Japanese colonial period, most rice grown in Taiwan was long-grained [[indica rice]]. The Japanese introduced short-grained [[japonica rice]] which quickly changed both the farming and eating patterns of the Taiwanese. Due to Japanese influence, the Taiwanese generally prefer rice that is plump, aromatic, slightly firm, and sweet. Differences between the Taiwanese and Japanese rice preferences are demonstrated by differences in their cuisine with Taiwan's more flavorful and aggressive cooking methods calling for highly aromatic rice while the Japanese prefer a more subtle and pure taste and smell.<ref name="Taiwan Panorama Rice 2020">{{cite web |last1=Su |first1=Lynn |title=A Rice Renaissance |url=https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=3dc62a1a-3462-4498-b9e6-24b2be98221b&CatId=9 |access-date=16 December 2020 |website=Taiwan Panorama}}</ref> During the Japanese Colonial period, Taiwanese cuisine was divided. High-end restaurants, or wine houses, served Chinese cuisine such as [[Peking duck]], shark fin with [[bird's nest soup]], and braised turtle to the colonial elite. In the meantime, those without wealth or connections primarily ate rice, [[porridge]], [[pickled vegetables]], and [[sweet potato leaves]]. [[Cooking oil]] was considered a luxury and was only used for special occasions.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lin |first1=Sean |date=30 October 2014 |title=History behind Taiwanese cuisine revealed |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2014/10/30/2003603264 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603055252/https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2014/10/30/2003603264 |archive-date=3 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |work=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

Taiwan's cuisine has also been influenced by its geographic location. Living on a crowded island, the Taiwanese had to look aside from the farmlands for sources of protein. As a result, seafood figures prominently in their cuisine. This seafood encompasses many different things, from large fish such as [[Tuna as food|tuna]] and [[grouper]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chang |first1=Meg |date=31 July 2009 |title=Groupers help boost nation's aquaculture industry |url=https://taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=6,23,45,6,6&post=8625 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200607213312/https://taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=6,23,45,6,6&post=8625 |archive-date=7 June 2020 |access-date=7 June 2020 |website=[[Taiwan Today]]}}</ref> to [[Sardine (food)|sardines]] and even smaller fish such as [[Anchovy (food)|anchovies]]. [[Crustacean]]s, [[Squid (food)|squid]], and [[cuttlefish]] are also eaten.{{citation needed|date=August 2023}} [[Milkfish]] is the most popular fish in Taiwanese cuisine; it is valued for its versatility as well as its tender meat and economical price.<ref name="CNN 2015" />

[[Beef]] is less common than other proteins, and some Taiwanese (particularly the elderly generation) still refrain from eating it.<ref name="goossaert">{{cite book |last=Goossaert |first=Vincent |title=The Religious Question in Modern China |author2=David A. Palmer |publisher=[[University of Chicago Press]] |year=2011 |isbn=9780226304168 |pages=281–283}}</ref> This stems from traditional reluctance toward slaughtering precious [[cattle]] needed for [[agriculture]], and an emotional attachment and feeling of gratitude and thanks to the animals traditionally used for very hard labor.<ref name="goossaert"/> However, due to influences from the influx of Chinese in the 1900s, the Taiwanese version of [[Taiwanese beef noodle soup|beef noodle soup]] is now one of the most popular dishes in Taiwan. American [[food aid]] in the decades following WWII which primarily consisted of wheat, beef, and processed meats like [[Spam (food)|Spam]] permanently changed the Taiwanese diet with wheat-based noodles, breads, and dumplings taking a more central role in the cuisine.<ref name="Eater 2019" /> Rice consumption in Taiwan reached a height of 80-90 kilograms per person per year in the 1960s and 1970s before falling as consumers shifted consumption to wheat-based foods. However, the Taiwanese still consume a large quantity of rice, particularly brown rice and exotic varieties like black, purple, and red rice. Recently rice consumption in Taiwan has enjoyed a renaissance with both growers and consumers devoting the level of care and attention to the rice that is given to high-value crops like tea.<ref name="Taiwan Panorama Rice 2020" />

Dumplings were a minor part of Taiwanese cuisine until the expansion in wheat consumption following WWII. Dumplings and dumpling like foods (such as [[xiaolongbao]] which is actually a small steamed bun because its wrapper contains yeast) are very popular in modern Taiwanese cuisine with most combining Chinese and Taiwanese influences. In Taiwan dumplings are often paired with [[hot and sour soup]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gardner |first1=Dinah |date=11 January 2023 |title=Decoding Dumplings in Taiwan |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2023/01/decoding-dumplings-in-taiwan/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

Because of the island's sub-tropical location, Taiwan has an abundant supply of various fruit, such as [[papaya]]s, [[carambola|starfruit]], [[melon]]s, and [[citrus]] fruit. A wide variety of tropical fruits, imported and native, are also enjoyed in Taiwan. Other agricultural products in general are rice, [[Maize|corn]], [[tea]], pork, poultry, beef, fish, and other fruits and vegetables. Fresh ingredients in Taiwan are readily available from markets.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Taiwan Country Profile |url=https://www.foodexport.org/export-insights/market-and-country-profiles/taiwan-country-profile |access-date=2021-07-21 |website=Food Export Association of the Midwest USA and Food Export USA–Northeast}}</ref>

In many of their dishes, the Taiwanese have shown their creativity in their selection of spices. Typical spice mixes in Taiwanese cuisine are [[five-spice powder]] and hujiaoyan (literally pepper salt; a mixture of white pepper, salt, MSG, and sugar).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lee |first1=Daphne K. |date=4 May 2022 |title=In New York, Taiwanese Chefs Are Attempting To Define Their Cuisine |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/new-york-taiwanese-chefs-define-cuisine-food/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]]}}</ref> A local variety of [[basil]] ("nine-pagoda") is used "lavishly in many dishes" after being heated.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tchea |first1=Michelle |date=27 October 2021 |title=Taiwanese basil is more than a garnish — it's the main event |url=https://www.sbs.com.au/food/article/2021/10/27/taiwanese-basil-more-garnish-its-main-event |access-date=27 October 2021 |website=[[Special Broadcasting Service|SBS]]}}</ref> Widespread use of [[sugar]] is part of the legacy of Taiwan's commercial sugar industry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chang |first1=Erchen |date=12 May 2023 |title=A taste of Taiwan, from comforting noodles to spicy broths |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/taste-taiwan-comforting-noodles-spicy-broths |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230512093331/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/travel/article/taste-taiwan-comforting-noodles-spicy-broths |archive-date=12 May 2023 |access-date=12 May 2023 |website=[[National Geographic]]}}</ref><ref name="bbc 2023-09-22">{{cite web |last1=Wei |first1=Clarissa |title=Sweet and sour pineapple prawns |url=https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20230922-sweet-and-sour-pineapple-prawns |website=[[BBC Travel]] |access-date=23 September 2023 |language=en |date=22 September 2023}}</ref> Taiwanese food, however, is not highly reliant on spices.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Yu |first=Mallory |last2=Chang |first2=Ailsa |last3=Jarenwattananon |first3=Patrick |last4=Mehta |first4=Jonaki |date=February 22, 2024 |title=Feast your eyes on Taiwan's distinct food (and understand a history of colonization) |url=https://www.npr.org/2024/02/22/1229886464/taiwan-food-china-colonization-history-cookbook |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260211184919/https://www.npr.org/2024/02/22/1229886464/taiwan-food-china-colonization-history-cookbook |archive-date=2026-02-11 |access-date=2026-10-18 |work=NPR |language=en}}</ref>

Taiwanese [[black vinegar]] has more in common with [[Worcestershire sauce]] than other black vinegars and is considered an outlier among black vinegars. Its base is sticky rice which is then aged with other ingredients in clay pots. It is used as a condiment and seasoning. Kong Yen is the largest producer of Taiwanese black vinegar. According to ''[[Bon Appetit]]'', compared to Chinese black vinegars it is "simpler, fruitier, and cleaner."<ref name="Bon Appetit 2021">{{cite web |last1=Wei |first1=Clarissa |date=29 May 2021 |title=Black Vinegar Doesn't Just Season a Dish–It Transforms It |url=https://www.bonappetit.com/story/black-vinegar |access-date=30 May 2021 |website=Bon Appétit}}</ref> Taiwanese soy paste is a soy sauce based paste thickened with rice flour and sugar.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wei |first1=Clarissa |date=25 January 2023 |title=Taiwanese Soy Paste Is the Sweet, Glossy Base of My Favorite Sauces |url=https://www.bonappetit.com/story/what-is-taiwanese-soy-paste |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Bon Appétit}}</ref> Taiwanese [[mayonnaise]] is made with both egg whites and egg yolks and is sweetened.<ref>{{cite web |title=How Did Taiwan Become an Eaters' Paradise? |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4969815 |access-date=9 February 2024 |website=[[Taiwan News]]|date=12 August 2023 }}</ref>

An important part of Taiwanese cuisine is ''[[xiaochi]]'' (小吃),<ref name="GIO">{{cite web |last=Lin |first=Ming-teh |year=2006 |url=http://www.gio.gov.tw/taiwan-website/5-gp/culture/food/ |title=Popular Food Culture in Taiwan |publisher=[[Government Information Office]] |access-date=15 December 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120620025602/http://www.gio.gov.tw/taiwan-website/5-gp/culture/food/ |archive-date=20 June 2012 }}</ref> substantial snacks along the lines of [[Spanish cuisine|Spanish]] [[tapas]] or [[Levantine cuisine|Levantine]] [[meze]]. The Taiwanese ''xiaochi'' has gained much reputation internationally. Many travelers go to Taiwan just for xiǎochī. The most common place to enjoy xiǎochī in Taiwan is in a [[Night markets in Taiwan|night market]]. Each night market also has its famous xiǎochī.<ref name="Eater 2019" /> Moreover, the Taiwanese xiǎochī has entered more "refined" eating environments. Nowadays, Taiwanese xiǎochī can be found in luxury and high-end restaurants. These restaurants use higher quality ingredients and creative presentations, reinventing dishes whilst keeping the robust flavors. The prices usually jump by twice the price or even higher in the restaurants. The Taiwanese government supports the Taiwanese xiǎochī and has held national xiǎochī events in Taiwan regularly.{{Citation needed|date=December 2020}}

Grilling is an important part of Taiwanese cuisine with many Taiwanese grilling at home and street side grills being a ubiquitous feature of night markets.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tsai |first1=Luke |date=26 July 2023 |title=Why Taiwanese People Love Outdoor Grilling |url=https://www.kqed.org/arts/13932035/taiwanese-barbecue-grilling-good-to-eat-dumplings-emeryville |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=KQED}}</ref> ''[[Rechao]]'' ({{lang-zh|t=熱炒|s=热炒|first=t,s|l=hot stir-frying}}) is a style of Taiwanese cuisine that uses a [[wok]] to [[stir frying|stir-fry]] food. ''Rechao'' establishments create settings for numerous Taiwanese to connect with each other as they dine and converse.<ref name="Horton2019-02-12">{{cite news |last=Horton |first=Chris |date=2019-02-12 |title=Taiwanese cuisine's delicious secret set to emerge: Cheap and cheerful rechao restaurants are a cultural institution |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Taiwanese-cuisine-s-delicious-secret-set-to-emerge |newspaper=[[The Nikkei]] |accessdate=2024-09-23 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923085141/https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Taiwanese-cuisine-s-delicious-secret-set-to-emerge |archivedate=2024-09-23 }}</ref><ref name="Hsieh2020-09-05">{{cite magazine |last=Hsieh |first=Terence |date=2020-09-05 |title=Midnight in Taipei |url=https://www.theworldofchinese.com/2020/09/midnight-in-taipei/ |magazine=[[The World of Chinese]] |accessdate=2024-09-23 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923085211/https://www.theworldofchinese.com/2020/09/midnight-in-taipei/ |archivedate=2024-09-23 }}</ref><ref name="Wei2023-05-02">{{cite magazine |last=Wei |first=Clarissa |author-link=Clarissa Wei |date=2023-05-02 |title=Move Over, Night Markets—Why Rechao Restaurants Are the Place to Be in Taiwan. Across Taiwan, rechao restaurants offer diners noisy, communal, no-frills, and positively joyful eating experiences. |url=https://www.afar.com/magazine/what-is-taiwanese-rechao-and-its-cultural-significance |magazine=[[Afar (magazine)|Afar]] |pages=[https://issuu.com/afarmag/docs/afar_spring_2023_hospitality_issue 96–104] |accessdate=2024-09-23 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20240923085202/https://www.afar.com/magazine/what-is-taiwanese-rechao-and-its-cultural-significance |archivedate=2024-09-23 }}</ref>

Roadside banquet chefs are ubiquitous in Taiwan; these small (often single-person) catering firms provide on-location cooking for wedding banquets and other celebrations often held on the roadside. During the COVID-19 pandemic these chefs saw a significant downturn in business due to the lack of people hosting large traditional functions, especially those around the [[Lunar New Year]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Jen |first1=Victoria |title=Taiwan local street banquet chefs hit hard by dampened Chinese New Year festivities amid COVID-19 |url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/asia/taiwan-local-street-banquet-chefs-hit-hard-by-dampened-chinese-14145882 |access-date=17 February 2021 |website=[[Channel News Asia]] |archive-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210209101934/https://www.channelnewsasia.com/news/asia/taiwan-local-street-banquet-chefs-hit-hard-by-dampened-chinese-14145882 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The banquet industry returned after the pandemic but have faced criticism for a lack of innovation and the repetition of traditional dishes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Scanlan |first1=Sean |date=4 January 2023 |title=Netizens complain of boring Taiwanese banquet dishes |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4770545 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref>

===Vegetarianism and veganism===
[[Vegetarian]] restaurants are commonplace in Taiwan with a wide variety of dishes, mainly due to the influence of [[Buddhism]] and other syncretistic religions like [[I-Kuan Tao]].<ref name="goossaert"/> These vegetarian restaurants vary in style from all-you-can-eat to pay-by-the-weight and the regular order-from-a-menu. Vegetarian restaurants and foods are often marked with a left-facing [[swastika]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Somekh |first1=Simone |date=22 February 2018 |title=Hungry for Kosher Food in Taiwan? Look for the Swastikas. |url=https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/news/articles/hungry-for-kosher-food-in-taiwan-look-for-the-swastikas |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704215244/https://www.tabletmag.com/sections/news/articles/hungry-for-kosher-food-in-taiwan-look-for-the-swastikas |archive-date=4 July 2020 |access-date=4 July 2020 |website=Tablet Magazine}}</ref>

In the 21st century, Taiwan has seen a rise in non-religious vegetarians, especially among the young. There has also been a rise in [[veganism]] with concerns about animal welfare, personal health, environmental sustainability, and climate change driving both trends.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tseng |first1=Esther |title=Taiwan's Vegetarian Awakening |url=https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=12921bb2-071c-4fe5-913f-f51eb4f9384d&CatId=7 |access-date=29 January 2021 |website=Taiwan Panorama}}</ref> Taiwan's traditional vegetarian products companies have also expanded into the booming [[fake meat]] market. The traditional culinary use of fake meat in Taiwan has given Taiwanese companies an edge and Taiwan is now a market leader in the fake meat sector. Taiwanese companies do a significant amount of export business, particularly in the European, North American, and Southeast Asian markets. Hung Yang Foods, one of the largest producers of fake meat products, does 80% of their business overseas with their products being stocked in 90% of Australian supermarkets.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Xie |first1=Tina |title=Meeting New Demand for Vegetarian Foods |url=https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=d9bf478e-587e-4821-afb0-ccc9d916b38f&CatId=7 |access-date=29 January 2021 |website=Taiwan Panorama}}</ref>

In 2010 the [[Ministry of Education (Taiwan)]] began encouraging educational institutions to go entirely vegetarian one day a week. By 2018 vegetarianism and veganism were widespread with 12-16% of Taiwan's population reporting that they did not eat meat.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Crook |first1=Steven |last2=Hung |first2=Katy Hui-wen |title=A Culinary History of Taipei: Beyond Pork and Ponlai |date=8 October 2018 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-5381-0138-4 |page=50 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8RBqDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA50 |access-date=18 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref> In 2023, there were approximately 6,000 vegetarian restaurants in Taiwan.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 May 2023 |title=Taiwan's meatless success a vegetarian paradise |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4883403 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref>

There is a type of outdoor [[barbecue]] called {{interlanguage link|khòng-iô|zh|焢窯}}. To barbecue in this manner, one first builds a hollow pyramid up with dirt clods. Next, charcoal or wood is burnt inside until the temperature inside the pyramid is very high (the dirt clods should be glowing red). The ingredients to be cooked, such as [[taro]], [[yam (vegetable)|yam]], or [[Chicken (food)|chicken]], are placed in cans, and the cans are placed inside the pyramid. Finally, the pyramid is toppled over the food until cooked.

Many non-dessert dishes are usually considered snacks, not entrees; that is, they have a similar status to [[Cantonese cuisine|Cantonese]] [[dim sum]] or [[Spanish cuisine|Spanish]] [[tapas]]. Such dishes are usually only slightly salted, with many vegetables accompanying the main meat or seafood item.

== Desserts ==
{{Main|List of Taiwanese desserts and snacks}}
[[File:Bing guan cau mei.jpg|thumb|A plate of ''[[tshuah-ping]]'' with strawberries and condensed milk]]
* [[Aiyu jelly]] – a gelatinous dessert made from the seeds of a [[creeping fig]], ''[[Ficus pumila var. awkeotsang]]''. Served on ice.<ref name="Eater 2019" /><ref name="CNN 2015" />
* {{ill|ō͘-á-peng|zh|芋仔冰}} ({{lang-zh|c=芋仔冰|poj=ō͘-á-peng|labels=no}}) – an ice cream made of [[taro]] root paste.
* [[Tshuah-ping]] (also known as ''Baobing'') – a Taiwanese [[shaved ice]] dessert very common in China, Taiwan, Malaysia, and Vietnam.<ref name="Eater 2019" />
* [[Xue-bing]] (雪花冰) - also called "xue hua bing," translated to "snow ice," "snowflake ice," or "shaved snow." This is different from baobing/tshuah-ping in that the base mixture for the ice is creamy (milk is generally added, but it can be dairy or plant based), the ice itself often has a flavor dissolved in (milk, taro, chocolate, coffee, etc.), the texture of the shaved snow is very fine, and it melts near-instantaneously, upon contact. The ice for this is typically cylindrical, and the shaved snow comes out of the machine in ruffled ribbons. Some additional common toppings include but are not limited to: [[sweetened condensed milk]], [[mangoes]], sweetened red beans, sweetened [[mung beans]], [[Tapioca balls|boba]] pearls, or [[taro]].
* [[Bubble tea]], aka boba milk tea; also known as pearl milk tea - chewy [[tapioca balls]] added to [[milk tea]].<ref name="CNN 2015">{{cite web |last1=Hiufu Wong |first1=Maggie |date=24 July 2015 |title=40 of the best Taiwanese foods and drinks |url=https://www.cnn.com/travel/article/40-taiwan-food/index.html |access-date=29 September 2020 |website=[[CNN]]}}</ref>
* Traditional [[cake]]s are not always of the same composition depending on the flavor. There is the [[moon cake]] which has a thick filling usually made from [[Nelumbo nucifera|lotus]] seed paste or sweetened red bean paste and surrounded by a relatively thin (2–3&nbsp;mm) crust and may contain yolks from salted duck eggs. It is traditionally eaten during the festival for lunar worship and moon watching. Mooncakes are offered between friends or on family gatherings while celebrating the festival. The [[Mid-Autumn Festival]] is one of the four most important [[Chinese festival]]s.

:There are other cakes that can mix salty ingredients with sweet ones to create a balance while enjoying these delicacies with [[Taiwanese tea|tea]]. The crust could be shiny from applying a layer of egg yolk before putting in the oven, or not in that case it is often whiter and the crust has more layers.
* [[Grass jelly]] ({{lang-zh|c=仙草|poj=sian-chháu}}) – (''[[Mesona]] procumbens'') Served hot or cold.
* Moachi ({{lang-zh|c=麻糍|poj=môa-chî|labels=no}}), a soft rice cake like Japanese [[daifuku]] [[mochi]]. Flavors of the fillings can vary, ranging from all kinds of beans to nuts.<ref name="CNN 2015" />
* [[Pineapple cake]] ({{lang-zh|c=王梨酥|poj=ông-lâi-so͘}})- a square short crust pie filled with pineapple filling. One of Taiwan's best known dessert pastries and souvenir of choice.<ref name="Eater 2019" />
* [[Chhau-a-koe]] – Cakes made with a dough from glutinous rice flour and combine with a ground cooked paste of ''[[Gnaphalium affine]]'' or ''[[Mugwort]]'' to give it a unique flavor and green color. The dough is commonly filled with ground meat or sweet bean pastes.
* [[Douhua|Douhua (豆花)]] - Soft tofu served with syrup and toppings such as [[peanut]]s, [[adzuki bean]]s, [[tapioca]], and [[mung bean]]s. Served hot or cold.
* [[Chocolate]] - Taiwan's cocoa production is centered in Pingtung in Southern Taiwan. As of 2020 approximately 200-300 acres was under cultivation in Pingtung supporting around 30 chocolate making companies.<ref name="Taipei Times 2020">{{cite web |last1=Cheung |first1=Han |date=15 September 2020 |title=Tree to bar to gold |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2020/09/15/2003743432 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200917101009/https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2020/09/15/2003743432 |archive-date=17 September 2020 |access-date=25 September 2020 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref><ref name="Taiwan Panorama Chocolate">{{cite web |last1=Su |first1=Lynn |title=A Sweet Vision: Taiwanese Chocolate's Road to the World |url=https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=de76440b-c3e1-4fe1-b9f6-967b0d5b7e34&CatId=10 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031922/https://www.taiwan-panorama.com/en/Articles/Details?Guid=de76440b-c3e1-4fe1-b9f6-967b0d5b7e34&CatId=10 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=10 December 2019 |website=Taiwan Panorama}}</ref> Taiwan is one of the few mature chocolate making countries to also be a cocoa producer.<ref name="Taipei Times 2020" />

== Night market dishes ==
Taiwan's best-known snacks are present in the [[Night markets in Taiwan|night markets]], where street vendors sell a variety of different foods, from finger foods, drinks, sweets, to sit-down dishes. In these markets, one can also find fried and steamed meat-filled buns, [[oyster omelette|oyster-filled omelets]], fruit ices, and much more. Aside from snacks, appetizers, entrees, and desserts, night markets also have vendors selling clothes and accessories, and offer all kinds of entertainment and products.<ref name="Guardian 2014" /> Street vendors used to be common across Taiwan but due to increasing regulations and health safety concerns are now primarily found at night markets and food courts. Taiwanese food courts incorporate ideas from traditional night markets as well as importing ideas from the United States and Japan. Food courts have become ubiquitous across Taiwan. Many night market dishes can now be found outside night markets.<ref name="Night Market Treats">{{cite web |last1=Quartly |first1=Jules |date=22 January 2017 |title=From Night Market Treats to Food Court Fine Dining |url=https://international.thenewslens.com/article/59900 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[The News Lens]]}}</ref>

In 2014, ''[[The Guardian]]'' called Taiwan's night markets the "best street food markets in the world".<ref name="Guardian 2014" >{{cite web |last1=Gillan |first1=Audrey |title=Taiwan, home to the best street food markets in the world |url=https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2014/may/17/taiwan-taipei-street-food-markets |work=The Guardian |date=17 May 2014 |access-date=27 April 2020 |archive-date=16 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200516133639/https://www.theguardian.com/travel/2014/may/17/taiwan-taipei-street-food-markets |url-status=live }}</ref> Some, such as [[Shilin Night Market]], have become as popular with tourists as they are with locals, leading to complaints that they have lost a measure of their authentic flavor though commercialization.<ref name= "Night Market Treats" />
