== Food of the Taiwanese Aborigines ==
{{More citations needed section|date=November 2022}}
Taiwan's food and food culture is very much diversified and largely influenced by the exodus of Han people. However, one part of the Taiwanese food culture that remains integral is that of the Taiwanese indigenous people. Though indigenous populations only make up approximately 1.5% of Taiwan's overall population,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Trejaut |first1=Jean A |last2=Kivisild |first2=Toomas |last3=Loo |first3=Jun Hun |last4=Lee |first4=Chien Liang |last5=He |first5=Chun Lin |last6=Hsu |first6=Chia Jung |last7=Li |first7=Zheng Yuan |last8=Lin |first8=Marie |title=Traces of Archaic Mitochondrial Lineages Persist in Austronesian-Speaking Formosan Populations |journal=PLOS Biology |date=July 5, 2005 |volume=3 |issue=8 |pages=e247 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.0030247 |doi-access=free |pmid=15984912 |pmc=1166350 }}</ref> it is notable that their foods eaten and ways of preparation are distinguishable from the more typical Chinese-influenced cuisine.

The aborigines' diet very much depends on nature. With profuse vegetation and wild animals, the aborigines were natural hunter-gatherers. Essentially, much of what Aborigines ate depended on their environment – that is, whether they lived in coastal or mountainous areas.<ref>{{Cite web |last=國際化,雙語編排,文化整合,全球華人的雜誌 |first=台灣光華雜誌 Taiwan Panorama {{!}} |title=Indigenous Food: The Authentic Flavors of Taiwan |url=http://www.taiwan-panorama.com/Articles/Details?Guid=02de86ad-67ed-4067-886f-3a8901ce984b&langId=3&CatId=7 |access-date=2024-03-05 |website=台灣光華雜誌 Taiwan Panorama {{!}} 國際化,雙語編排,文化整合,全球華人的雜誌 |language=zh-Hant-TW}}</ref> Tribes like Amis, Atayal, Saisiyat and Bunun hunt what they can, and gather what they cultivate. On the other hand, tribes like the Yamis and the Thao have fish as a predominant source of food. Most foods consisted of millet, taro, sweet potato, wild greens and game like boar and rat. This is in contrast to the main foods eaten by the Han, which consisted of rice and chicken.

Game meats for those living in the mountainous areas include deer, and flying squirrel intestines, a delicacy as regarded by the Bunun people. Another is 'stinky' meat – that is, 'maggoty game' that has begun to rot, which is then barbecued, fried, seasoned with garlic and ginger then served with spicy sauce.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Aboriginal Cuisine Comes to Town |url=https://taiwanreview.nat.gov.tw/print.php?unit=12&post=22202&unitname=Society-Taiwan-Review&postname=Aboriginal-Cuisine-Comes-to-Town |access-date=2024-03-05 |website=Taiwan Today}}</ref>

The Amis, apart from meat, had much greens to eat, largely due to the assumption that anything a cow ate, was also edible by humans. The Bununs, who are primarily hunters of wild animals, would dine on stone-grilled pork, boar, deer, and hog roast. The Yami tribe, located off Taitung coast, fed on many types of fish, including the prized 'flying fish' (or Alibangbang). A speciality includes rice, mixed with river fish and wild vegetables, served in large bamboo trunks.

Apart from being a staple-food, millet was always produced as wine. Not just for drinking, millet wine played an important role in being used as offerings during festivals, births and weddings. Millet wines are all made in the homes of the Aborigines. Sticky rice is put into a wooden steamer after being soaked in water. Once cooled, the rice is put into a pot of water, then pulled out and combined with rice yeast. After four or five days of being placed in a large jar, the rice is placed in a sieve or rice bag, whilst the alcoholic liquid drips out and is stored away.

Also important to the Indigenous Taiwanese people's cuisine are the sweet potato and taro, favored for their perennial nature and low maintenance. The cultivation of root vegetables rather than typical seedling plants was notably prominent, with archaeological evidence suggesting as early as fourth millennium BC, from the Dapenkeng site, in Guanyin Mountain, New Taipei City.

Given the versatility of both vegetables, they were usually boiled or steamed, and eaten by itself or as ingredients in soups and stews. Without the need for advanced agricultural technology, taro and sweet potatoes were a prime preference for farming. Canadian missionary George MacKay said of 19th century Taiwan: 'the bulb of the sweet potato is planted in March. In about six weeks the vines are cut into pieces eight inches long, which are planted in drills, and from these vine-cuttings the bulbs grow and are ripe about the end of June. A second crop is planted in a similar way in July and is ripe in November.' <ref>{{Cite book |last1=Mackay |first1=George Leslie |url=http://archive.org/details/fromfarformosais00mackrich |title=From far Formosa : the island, its people and missions |last2=MacDonald |first2=James A. (James Alexander) |date=1896 |publisher=Edinburgh : Oliphant Anderson and Ferrier |others=University of California Libraries |pages=67}}</ref> The influence of sweet potatoes and taro has been vast. They are still widely present in modern-day Taiwan, be it on the streets, night markets, or in successful food chains like '[[Meet Fresh]]' (or 鮮芋仙).

Due to the absence of contemporary culinary utensils such as the refrigerator, gas stovetops and ovens, the Indigenous resorted to other means to prepare their food. Upon bringing back hunted game meat, the Aborigines would preserve the meat with either millet wine or salt. Another cooking technique involved the heating up of stones by fire, which are then placed inside a vessel with other certain meats and seafood, which are cooked from the heat of the stones. Foods were mostly prepared by steaming, boiling or roasting, in order to infuse flavors together, yet preserve the original flavors. This again is contrasted with the Han, who adopted skills like stir-frying and stewing.<ref>Chen, Y. J. (2010, June 15). Embodying nation in food consumption : changing boundaries of "Taiwanese cuisine" (1895-2008). Retrieved from <nowiki>https://hdl.handle.net/1887/15690</nowiki></ref> Meat was also put on a bamboo spit and cooked over the fire.

Taiwanese indigenous cuisine incorporates certain flavors that are distinct from Han Chinese-influenced cuisine. Mountain peppercorns (''shan hujiao'' in Chinese or ''magao,'' derived from the Atayal term ''maqaw)'' are one of these distinctive ingredients.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Crook |first1=Steven |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8RBqDwAAQBAJ&q=taiwan+indigenous+aboriginals+game+meat+stinky+meat+ |title=A Culinary History of Taipei: Beyond Pork and Ponlai |last2=Hung |first2=Katy Hui-wen |date=2018-10-08 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield |isbn=978-1-5381-0138-4 |pages=20–21 |language=en}}</ref> Other indigenous ingredients include Tana, herbal [[Aralia]], large-leaved nanmu, and indigenous cinnamon.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chen |first=Sabine |date=26 February 2019 |title=5 Indigenous Ingredients From Taiwan That Will Wow Your Tastebuds |url=https://guide.michelin.com/en/article/dining-in/5-taiwan-aboriginal-ingredients |website=[[Michelin Guide]] |translator-last1=Leung |translator-first1=Vincent}}</ref>

A cookbook published in 2000 by the CIP and [[National Kaohsiung University of Hospitality and Tourism]], listed some foods of the main Taiwanese Aboriginal tribes, showing the Aborigines' adherence and passion for natural foods.
* Amis Nation: [[Alivongvong]] (meat and [[sticky rice]] [[dumpling]] packed in leaves) (阿里鳳鳳); Stir-fried wild vegetables
* Atayal Nation: Grilled meat on stone (石板烤肉); Langying (steamed sticky rice cake) (朗應)
* Bunun Nation: Bunun [[millet]] cake (布農粿); Millet rice (小米飯)
* Paiwan Nation: [[Cinavu]] (millet and pork meat-ball) (小米吉拿富); Jinbole (Sorghum and pork dumpling packed in a banana leaf) (金伯樂)
* Puyuma Nation: Yinafei mountain cake (以那馡山地粿); Fried wild rat with basil (九層野鼠)
* Rukai Nation: Cinavu (taro and meat dumpling) (吉拿富); Grilled boar
* Saisiyat Nation: Grilled [[boar]] with papaya (木瓜拌山豬肉); Assorted wild flowers (野花拼盤); Cassava and spareribs soup (樹薯排骨湯)
* Tsou Nation: Bamboo cooked rice (竹筒飯); Banana cake (香蕉糕)
* Yami Nation: Boiled [[taro]] and crab (芋泥加蟹肉); Grilled fish Steamed dried fish (蒸魚乾)

===Modern Aboriginal cuisine===
It seems that an interest in Taiwanese indigenous cuisine gained traction in the media in the mid-1990s, developing alongside increasing governmental action to protect and recognize Taiwanese indigenous peoples. There are restaurants around Taipei that keep the spirit of Indigenous cuisine alive. Whilst chefs in such restaurants often tweak traditional recipes to suit contemporary tastebuds, emphasis of natural foods is still extant. The annual Indigenous Peoples Healthy Cuisine and Innovative Beverage Competition, partly sponsored by the Council of Indigenous Peoples and the Tourism Bureau provides prize money to contestants who creatively use traditional indigenous ingredients in healthy ways. Other similar competitions are held by local governments (such as Kaohsiung City). In Tainan, indigenous people may sell their food at the Cha Ha Mu Aboriginal Park. Such trends are all to promote the wonderful taste of Aboriginal Taiwanese cuisine.<ref name=":0" /> The cultural value of indigenous dishes and ingredients has become more widespread among non-indigenous people, but there are many implications with this growth in recent years. Cultivating or foraging for traditional ingredients is often limited on the small plots of land that are legally owned by indigenous people. Some urban Pangcah/Amis people have resorted to foraging without permission on others' land.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sugimoto |first=Tomonori |date=2018 |title="Someone Else's Land is Our Garden!": Risky Labor in Taipei's Indigenous Food Boom |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/26499172 |journal=Gastronomica |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=46–58 |doi=10.1525/gfc.2018.18.2.46 |jstor=26499172 |issn=1529-3262|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

During the martial law period indigenous culture was repressed by the government, despite this indigenous cuisine became a part of Taiwan's national identity.<ref name="NYT August 2023" />

[[Siraw]] is an Amis dish of [[pickled]] pork.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheung |first1=Han |date=21 October 2022 |title=Eating local in indigenous Taitung |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2022/10/21/2003787444 |access-date=18 November 2022 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

The importance of wild greens to aboriginal cuisine is being increasingly appreciated. Wild greens refers to both wild plants found in the forest and to those same plants cultivated in domestic gardens.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheung |first1=Han |date=30 April 2022 |title=Taiwan's 'godmother of wild greens' |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2022/04/30/2003777454 |access-date=5 May 2022 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref> Rinari, in rural Pingtung County, is an aboriginal restaurant of national significance whose twenty seats are notoriously hard to secure. Rinari primarily serves Rukai cuisine.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tham |first1=Davina |date=20 April 2019 |title=Restaurants: Modern Aboriginal cuisine |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2019/04/20/2003713719 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

==Beverages==
The Taiwanese drink less alcohol per capita than neighboring South Koreans and Japanese. This is believed to be because approximately half of Taiwan's population does not possess the necessary gene to successfully metabolize alcohol. During the Japanese colonial period the production of [[alcoholic beverages]] was industrialized and in 1922, production of alcohol was monopolized by the colonial authorities. Modern Taiwanese drinking culture and beverage production is still influenced by the Japanese colonial period.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Crook |first1=Steven |date=23 April 2021 |title=Highways & Byways: Taiwan's boozy past and present |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2021/04/23/2003756192 |access-date=6 May 2021 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

===Beer===
{{Main|Beer in Taiwan}}
Beer is a popular beverage in Taiwan. Taiwan both imports and produces a wide variety of beers from mass market lagers to niche craft ales. Some of the well-developed brands include Long Chuan (龍泉), Le Blé d'Or (金色三麥), Jolly Brewery+Restaurant (卓莉手工醸啤酒泰食餐廳), North Taiwan Brewing (北台灣麥酒) and Taihu Brewing (臺虎精釀).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chou |first1=Cybil Huichen |date=11 May 2019 |title=How Taiwanese craft beers are finding fans in Asia and the West |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/news-trends/article/3009707/how-taiwanese-craft-beers-are-finding-fans-asia-and |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190918002431/https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/news-trends/article/3009707/how-taiwanese-craft-beers-are-finding-fans-asia-and |archive-date=18 September 2019 |access-date=28 July 2020 |work=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref>

===Coffee===
The first coffee plants on Taiwan were imported by the British to Tainan in 1884 with the first significant small scale cultivation taking place in New Taipei City's [[Sanxia District]]. Tainan remains the heart of Taiwanese coffee culture.<ref name="Coffee Culture">{{cite web |author=Staff Writer |date=17 February 2021 |title=FEATURE: Growers along Tainan's 'Coffee Road' want to put local brew on national map |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2021/02/17/2003752399 |access-date=17 February 2021 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

During the Japanese colonial period between 1895 and 1945, [[coffee plantation]]s were set up in Taiwan. Coffee, like other colonial introductions, was regarded as a sign of modernity. It was often made using a siphon, and tended to be strong and bitter.<ref name="abc 2024-10-26">{{cite news |last1=Issak |first1=Ilham |title=Famous for bubble tea, Taiwan is now brewing a path to coffee fame |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-10-26/taiwan-coffee-capital-of-east-asia/104510622 |access-date=4 January 2025 |work=[[ABC News (Australia)]] |date=26 October 2024 |language=en-AU}}</ref> Production reached a peak in 1941 following the introduction of [[arabica coffee]] plants by the Japanese colonial authorities.<ref name="Coffee Culture"/>

More recently, [[Starbucks]]' outlets in Taiwan have introduced local drinkers to [[espresso]]-based milk beverages, which are often milder than the brews traditionally served there.<ref name="abc 2024-10-26"/> Domestic production is still small, but of high quality; imported beans account for the vast majority of coffee sold in Taiwan. In 2016, domestic production was 900 tons while 30,000 tons was imported.<ref>{{cite web |title=Coffee culture booms in Taiwan |url=https://www.efe.com/efe/english/life/coffee-culture-booms-in-taiwan/50000263-3137444 |access-date=30 November 2020 |website=[[Agencia EFE]]}}</ref> That year, a Taiwanese, Berg Wu, won the [[World Barista Championship]]; the victory helped bring to attention Taiwan's substantial involvement in [[coffee culture]].<ref name="abc 2024-10-26"/>

By 2020, there were more than 15,000 [[coffeehouse|coffee shop]]s in Taiwan, including Starbucks, Taiwanese coffee shop chains, [[convenience stores]], and independent outlets.<ref>{{cite web |author=News Desk |title=Coffee culture on the rise in Taiwan |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/life/2020/07/28/coffee-culture-on-the-rise-in-taiwan.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729125048/https://www.thejakartapost.com/life/2020/07/28/coffee-culture-on-the-rise-in-taiwan.html |archive-date=29 July 2020 |access-date=4 January 2025 |work=[[The Jakarta Post]]}}</ref> During that year, average coffee consumption surpassed average tea consumption for the first time.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Yuan-ting |first1=Yang |last2=Chung |first2=Jake |date=31 August 2021 |title=Coffee consumption exceeds that of tea for the first time |url=https://taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2021/08/31/2003763532 |access-date=31 August 2021 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref> By 2024, a significant percentage of specialty coffee shops were roasting their own beans, and tourists had started visiting Taiwan specifically to go "cafe hopping". Taiwan had become the third-largest coffee consumer per capita in Asia, and the average Taiwanese person was drinking 177 cups of coffee per year.<ref name="abc 2024-10-26"/>

===Kaoliang liquor===
{{Main|Kaoliang liquor}}
[[File:kaoliang.jpg|thumb|100px|Kinmen 58% Kaoliang]]
[[Kinmen Kaoliang Liquor]] is one of the most popular brands of [[kaoliang liquor]] in Taiwan. As its name indicates, it is produced on the island of Kinmen. The mainstays of the range are the standard 58 percent and 38 percent alcohol bottlings. Kinmen's kaoliang production traces its roots back to the Chinese Civil War when Chinese nationalist general [[Hu Lien]] encouraged Kinmenese farmers to grow sorghum to produce hard liquor as importing alcohol from Taiwan caused financial strain. Kaoliang liquor has become an integral part of Kinmen's economy and plays a significant role in the culture of Kinmen.<ref>{{Cite web |last=China (Taiwan) |first=Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Republic of |date=2011-03-18 |title=Kaoliang serves Kinmen a tasty future |url=https://taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=&post=17771 |access-date=2020-06-12 |website=[[Taiwan Today]] |language=en}}</ref>

Yusan Kaoliang Chiew ({{lang-zh | t=玉山高粱酒 | p=Yùshān Gāoliáng Jiǔ}}) is produced by the [[Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation]]. It is named after the highest mountain in Taiwan, [[Yushan (mountain)|Yushan]]. One of the most notable products in the range is an "X.O." kaoliang aged for five years in tanks before bottling.<ref>{{cite web |title=嘉義酒廠目前主力產品 |url=https://event.ttl.com.tw/cy/about/01main.aspx?cateid=99}}</ref>

Matsu Tunnel 88 Kaoliang Liquor ({{lang-zh | t=馬祖八八坑道高粱酒 | p=Bā Bā Kēngdào Gāoliáng Jiǔ}}) is produced by the [[Matsu Distillery]] in [[Nangan, Lienchiang|Nangan Township]], [[Matsu Islands|Lienchiang County]]. The name is derived from the name of an abandoned military tunnel called [[Tunnel 88]] which the distillery took over as storage space for their kaoliang and aged rice wine. All of the distillery's aged kaoliangs are stored in the tunnel for at least five years.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.tunnel88.com.tw/index.php|title=八八坑道, 高粱酒,八八坑道高粱酒, 88石敢當, 石敢當高粱酒, 88紅酒-世華企業官網, 未成年請勿飲酒, 酒後不開車, 安全有保障|website=www.tunnel88.com.tw}}</ref>

===Rum===
Commercial rum production was introduced into Taiwan along with commercial sugar production during the Japanese colonial period.<ref>{{cite web |last1=du Toit |first1=Nick |date=29 July 2011 |title=Yo-ho-ho and a bottle of Koxinga Gold rum |url=https://taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=2&post=1927 |access-date=8 June 2021 |website=[[Taiwan Today]]}}</ref> Rum production continued under the ROC however it was neglected by [[Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation]] which held the national liquor monopoly. The industry diversified after democratization and the de-monopolization of the Taiwanese alcoholic beverage industry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Koutsakis |first1=George |date=6 June 2021 |title=Will Japanese whisky be eclipsed by Taiwan? The island's gin and rum also show promise – with one distillery promising spirits 'good enough for God' |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/leisure/article/3136191/will-japanese-whisky-be-eclipsed-taiwan-islands-gin-and-rum |access-date=8 June 2021 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref>

===Tea===
{{Main|Taiwanese tea|Taiwanese tea culture}}
Taiwanese tea is widely regarded as high-quality, with the region possessing a distinct tea culture.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Crook |first1=Steven |date=9 July 2020 |title=Exploring the World of Taiwanese Tea |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2020/07/exploring-taiwanese-tea/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200715012254/https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2020/07/exploring-taiwanese-tea/ |archive-date=15 July 2020 |access-date=28 July 2020 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

===Whisky===
{{Main|Taiwanese whisky}}
Taiwan has a young whisky industry buoyed by a large domestic market for whisky, namely single malt scotch. Taiwan is the only whisky market which drinks more single malt whisky than blended whisky.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Koutsakis |first1=George |date=6 October 2019 |title=Can Taiwan's premium gin producers take on the world – and Taiwanese drinkers who prefer foreign liquor? |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/leisure/article/3031413/can-taiwans-premium-gin-producers-take-world-and-taiwanese |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191123172731/https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/leisure/article/3031413/can-taiwans-premium-gin-producers-take-world-and-taiwanese |archive-date=23 November 2019 |access-date=28 July 2020 |work=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref>

===Wine===
{{Main|Taiwanese wine}}
Independent [[winemaking]] was illegal in Taiwan for a long time due to the monopoly granted to the [[Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation]].<ref name="Beverage Daily">{{cite web |last1=Whithead |first1=Richard |date=5 May 2020 |title=Tropical terroir made to produce award-winning wines |url=https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2020/05/05/Tropical-terroir-Taiwan-grows-its-quality-wine-scene |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200509222316/https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2020/05/05/Tropical-terroir-Taiwan-grows-its-quality-wine-scene |archive-date=9 May 2020 |access-date=5 May 2020 |website=Beverage Daily}}</ref> Independent winemakers became legal in 2002 and in 2014, a Taiwanese wine won its first gold medal at an international competition.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cheung |first1=Han |date=21 March 2020 |title=Vina Formosa comes of age |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2020/03/21/2003733092 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200323233104/https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/feat/archives/2020/03/21/2003733092 |archive-date=23 March 2020 |access-date=23 March 2020 |website=[[Taipei Times]] |publisher=}}</ref> In 2019, a red wine from Taichung was awarded a gold medal at the 25th Vinalies Internationales in France.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hui-ning |first1=Hu |date=10 March 2019 |title=Taichung red wine wins gold medal in France |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2019/03/10/2003711212 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190902234916/http://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2019/03/10/2003711212 |archive-date=2 September 2019 |access-date=30 April 2020 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref> Two of the most acclaimed wineries are Domaine Shu Sheng and Weightstone Vineyard Estate & Winery.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Huichen Chou |first1=Cybil |date=14 September 2019 |title=Why Hong Kong connoisseurs – and Michelin-star chefs – are taking note of Taiwan's wines |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/luxury/article/3026900/why-hong-kong-connoisseurs-and-michelin-star-chefs-are |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200707214519/https://www.scmp.com/magazines/style/luxury/article/3026900/why-hong-kong-connoisseurs-and-michelin-star-chefs-are |archive-date=7 July 2020 |access-date=30 April 2020 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> Although it was once largely lost, Taiwan's indigenous winemaking culture is staging a comeback.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wang |first1=Ann |title=Taiwan's award-winning winemaker aims to revive fading tradition |url=https://www.thejakartapost.com/life/2020/08/07/taiwans-award-winning-winemaker-aims-to-revive-fading-tradition.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200810074838/https://www.thejakartapost.com/life/2020/08/07/taiwans-award-winning-winemaker-aims-to-revive-fading-tradition.html |archive-date=10 August 2020 |access-date=8 August 2020 |website=[[The Jakarta Post]] |agency=[[Reuters]]}}</ref>

===Sake===
[[Sake]] consumption started during the Japanese colonial period. The first sake was made in Taiwan in 1914, the largest contemporary domestic brand is Yuchun produced by the Taiwan Tobacco and Liquor Corporation. A number of smaller producers also exist with an emphasis placed on unique products made with local rice. Taiwan also imports large amounts of sake from Japan. Its proximity and the volume of the trade allows merchants in Taiwan to stock fresh and limited production sake which is not widely available elsewhere outside Japan.<ref>{{cite web |last1=CHOU |first1=CYBIL |title=Taiwan sake boom starts to challenge Japanese traditions |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Taiwan-sake-boom-starts-to-challenge-Japanese-traditions |access-date=14 March 2022 |website=[[Nikkei Asia]]}}</ref>

==Fine dining==
{{Further|List of Michelin starred restaurants in Taiwan}}
Fine dining in Taiwan is often of a mixed identity. For example, wedding banquets in Taiwan typically feature Japanese [[sashimi]] as the first course with traditional Taiwanese and Chinese dishes following.<ref name="News Lens 2020">{{cite web |last1=Haggerty |first1=Nicholas |date=25 September 2020 |title=Beyond the Michelin Guide: What Is Real Taiwanese Gourmet? |url=https://international.thenewslens.com/article/141102 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031923/https://international.thenewslens.com/article/141102 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=26 September 2020 |website=[[The News Lens]]}}</ref> In the 21st century, indigenous ingredients, dishes, and techniques have made their way into high end restaurants.<ref>{{cite web |last1=KRICH |first1=JOHN |title=Taiwan chefs go back to island's roots |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Taiwan-chefs-go-back-to-island-s-roots |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Nikkei Asia]]}}</ref>

In 2018, [[La Liste]] listed 10 restaurants in Taiwan among the world's 1,000 best.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Yang |first1=Sophia |date=15 December 2018 |title=10 Taiwan restaurants listed among world's top 1000 by La Liste |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/3597630 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref>

The [[Michelin Guide]] began reviewing restaurants in Taipei in 2018 and Taichung in 2020. The 2020 Michelin awarded stars to 30 restaurants in Taiwan, four in Taichung and 26 in Taipei. With three stars, the Cantonese restaurant Le Palais is the country's highest rated restaurant. The 2020 list also bestowed the [[Bib Gourmand]] on 54 restaurants in Taipei<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sontag |first1=Elazar |date=25 August 2020 |title=Michelin Announces 2020 Stars for Taiwan |url=https://www.eater.com/2020/8/25/21401133/michelin-announces-2020-stars-for-taiwan |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031935/https://www.eater.com/2020/8/25/21401133/michelin-announces-2020-stars-for-taiwan |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=25 September 2020 |website=Eater}}</ref> and 21 in Taichung.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hsin-Yin |first1=Lee |title=Michelin Guide releases Bib Gourmand list for Taipei, Taichung |url=https://focustaiwan.tw/society/202008110013 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031936/https://focustaiwan.tw/society/202008110013 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=25 September 2020 |website=[[Focus Taiwan]] |date=11 August 2020 |publisher=}}</ref> The expansion of the Michelin Guide to Taiwan increased international recognition for Taiwanese restaurants.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Teo |first1=Mavis |date=15 February 2023 |title=6 of the best fine-dining restaurants in Taiwan's capital, Taipei, for Taiwanese, Japanese, Cantonese and Huaiyang cuisine |url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/food-drink/article/3210133/6-best-fine-dining-restaurants-taiwans-capital-taipei-taiwanese-japanese-cantonese-and-huaiyang |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> In 2023, the Michelin Guide was expanded to Tainan and Kaohsiung.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shan |first1=Shelley |date=24 August 2023 |title=Michelin reveals Taiwan's Bib Gourmand eateries |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/front/archives/2023/08/24/2003805198 |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

There are significant differences between the fine dining scenes in Taipei and Taichung. In Taichung, an emphasis is placed on ceremony with large tables and private rooms common, a premium is also placed on parking with restaurants having more than 100 parking spaces. This is due in part to Taichung's strong small and medium enterprises as well as a multitude of informal recreational and fraternal organizations. In Taipei, fine dining restaurants and tables are generally smaller with most customers being couples or small groups, in general, service is less formal than in Taichung. In Taipei, there is more international influence in the fine dining scene while Taichung retains a strong affinity with traditional dishes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wu |first1=Sunny |date=15 January 2021 |title=Michelin Guide Taiwan – Taipei vs. Taichung |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2021/01/michelin-guide-taiwan-taipei-vs-taichung/ |access-date=15 January 2021 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref> In the 2010s, fine dining restaurants which more closely followed international trends proliferated in Taichung. [[Lanshu Chen]] was particularly important in gaining Taichung international recognition.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Teo |first1=Mavis |date=7 March 2023 |title=Where to eat and drink in Taichung, Taiwan's up-and-coming fine-dining hub – from Michelin-star yakiniku to a French bistro by former Asia's Best Female Chef winner |url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/food-drink/article/3212556/where-eat-and-drink-taichung-taiwans-and-coming-fine-dining-hub-michelin-star-yakiniku-french-bistro |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref>

==Foreign cuisine in Taiwan==

===Fusion===
[[Fusion cuisine]] is very popular in Taiwan. Many Taiwanese dishes are a result of cultural fusion, such as the Taiwanese version of [[pastel de nata]] which are a legacy of Portuguese colonialism in neighboring Macao.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chen |first1=Lina |date=19 March 2017 |title=Origins of Taiwanese Fusion Cuisine: It's Not That Simple |url=https://international.thenewslens.com/article/63903 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603055253/https://international.thenewslens.com/article/63903 |archive-date=3 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |website=[[The News Lens]]}}</ref>

===Italian===
[[Italian cuisine]] has been popular in Taiwan for a long time, but the country had few authentic Italian restaurants and even fewer Italian chefs until the late 1990s and early 2000s. Due to the [[2008 financial crisis]], many Italians emigrated from Italy to healthier economies. This led to a rapid increase in both the number of Italian restaurants and the number of Italian expats in Taiwan. While most restaurants follow the traditional Italian course style, the meal proportions are influenced by [[Italian-American cuisine]]. Taiwanese diners have become increasingly passionate and discerning about Italian cuisine.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fulco |first1=Matthew |date=12 January 2018 |title=Discovering a Little Italy in Taipei |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2018/01/discovering-little-italy-taipei/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200618141728/https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2018/01/discovering-little-italy-taipei/ |archive-date=18 June 2020 |access-date=1 May 2020 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref> Michael de Prenda was one of the innovators of Italian cuisine in Taiwan, starting multiple restaurants, a market, and a farm.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chou |first1=Min |title=An Italian Entrepreneur Realizing 'His Meaning of Life' in Taiwan |url=https://english.cw.com.tw/article/article.action?id=1834 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031943/https://english.cw.com.tw/article/article.action?id=1834 |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=1 May 2020 |website=Commonwealth}}</ref>

==== Pizza ====
Pizza is one of the most popular foods in Taiwan. The first pizza restaurant opened in the 1970s and the industry grew rapidly in the 2000s driven by an increasing demand for quality Italian and American style pizza from an affluent younger generation which had spent time abroad and brought back a taste for it.<ref name="Taiwan Topics Pizza"/>

Chain pizza restaurants like [[Pizza Hut]] and [[Domino's Pizza]] are known for running promotional pizzas with outrageous toppings like spicy hotpot, cilantro and century egg with pig's blood, beef and kiwi, glutinous rice, ramen, and stinky tofu in an attempt to get national and international publicity. Pizza Hut entered the Taiwanese market in 1986 and Domino's followed in the late 1980s. In 2022, each company had more than 150 stores in Taiwan.<ref name="Taiwan Topics Pizza">{{cite web |last1=Quartly |first1=Jules |date=17 January 2022 |title=A Golden Era for Pizza in Taiwan |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2022/01/a-golden-era-for-pizza-in-taiwan/ |access-date=5 May 2022 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref><ref name="ao 2024-12-10">{{cite web |last1=Wei |first1=Clarissa |title=Pizza Hut Taiwan Knows It's Making Italians Angry |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/pizza-hut-taiwan-weird-toppings |website=[[Atlas Obscura]] |access-date=7 January 2025 |language=en |date=10 December 2024}}</ref>

===Indian===
Historically overseas Chinese from India would travel to Taiwan to learn cooking. Indian restaurants existed in Taiwan, but overall the cuisine was slow to catch on.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ferry |first1=Timothy |date=19 January 2018 |title=Indian Cuisine Heats Up in Taipei |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2018/01/indian-cuisine-heats-taipei/ |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

Indian food became popular in Taiwan in the 2000s. The number of Indian restaurants has grown along with the growth of the Indian and larger South Asian community in Taiwan, however, most customers in Indian restaurants are local with Indian food also being found in university cafeterias and other institutional settings.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Banka |first1=Neha |date=18 December 2021 |title=In Taipei, Indian food makes for good business |url=https://indianexpress.com/article/world/taipei-taiwan-indian-food-business-7679175/ |access-date=19 December 2021 |website=Indian Express}}</ref>

===Russian===
Along with the fleeing KMT came [[White émigré|White Russian]] refugees who had sought shelter from the Russian Revolution in China. George Elsner founded the first Russian restaurant, The Café Astoria, in Taiwan in 1949. The [[Cafe Astoria|Café Astoria]] was a center of Russian expat life in Taiwan during its early years. [[Chiang Ching-kuo]] and his Russian wife, [[Faina Vakhreva]], often brought their children with them to eat there. Elsner died [[stateless person|stateless]] in Taiwan.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Strong |first1=Matthew |date=20 June 2020 |title=Taiwan's Café Astoria inherits spirit of Russia |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/3950995 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200622170750/https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/3950995 |archive-date=22 June 2020 |access-date=20 June 2020 |work=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref>

===Nordic===
[[New Nordic Cuisine|Nordic haute cuisine]] is popular in Taiwan's major cities, with restaurants offering both authentic Nordic cuisine and Nordic cuisine adapted to local ingredients and tastes.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Alamin |first1=Jasmine |title=How this young Singaporean chef is making culinary waves in Taiwan |url=https://cnaluxury.channelnewsasia.com/remarkableliving/singaporean-chef-in-taiwan-12219354 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191231132249/https://cnaluxury.channelnewsasia.com/remarkableliving/singaporean-chef-in-taiwan-12219354 |archive-date=31 December 2019 |access-date=27 April 2020 |website=Channel NewsAsia}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sgarbi |first1=Giulia |title=Asia's Highest Climber Mume brings Taiwanese produce into the global spotlight |url=https://www.theworlds50best.com/stories/News/asias-highest-climber-mume-brings-taiwanese-produce-into-global-spotlight.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031952/https://www.theworlds50best.com/stories/News/asias-highest-climber-mume-brings-taiwanese-produce-into-global-spotlight.html |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=27 April 2020 |website=The World's 50 Best}}</ref>

===Hong Kong===
The increase in immigration from [[Hong Kong]] following the [[2019–20 Hong Kong protests|pro-democracy protests]] brought an increased focus on [[Hong Kong cuisine]], along with a fusion between Hong Kong and Taiwan cuisines. Taiwan is considered a safe haven for [[Hongkongers]], with many opening shops and restaurants to serve food they were unable to find in Taiwan, or which they did not feel was up to Hong Kong standards.<ref>{{cite web |last1=GLAUERT |first1=RIK |title=Hong Kong protesters revolutionize Taiwan restaurant scene |url=https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Hong-Kong-protesters-revolutionize-Taiwan-restaurant-scene2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603035158/https://asia.nikkei.com/Life-Arts/Life/Hong-Kong-protesters-revolutionize-Taiwan-restaurant-scene2 |archive-date=3 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |website=[[Nikkei Asia]]}}</ref>

===Japanese===
Taiwan, in particularly Taipei, is regarded as having some of the best Japanese food outside of Japan. This is due to the legacy of Japanese colonialism as well as ongoing cultural and commercial exchange.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fulco |first1=Matthew |date=21 January 2021 |title=Experiencing Taipei's Authentic Japanese Cuisine |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2021/01/taipei-authentic-japanese-cuisine/ |access-date=24 January 2021 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

====Ramen====
Ramen restaurants in Taiwan often create unique ramen dishes including [[durian]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thomas |first1=Jono |date=16 June 2023 |title=Durian ramen to go on sale in south Taiwan |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4920892 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref> whole [[giant isopod]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Everington |first1=Keoni |date=23 May 2023 |title=Taipei eatery features giant isopod ramen |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4899689 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Mok |first1=Charmaine |date=24 May 2023 |title='Dream ingredient': alien-like isopod ramen dish made with a 14-legged deep-sea creature goes viral in Taiwan |url=https://www.scmp.com/lifestyle/food-drink/article/3221636/dream-ingredient-alien-ramen-dish-made-14-legged-deep-sea-creature-goes-viral-taiwan |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref> [[crocodile]] leg,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marcus |first1=Lilit |last2=Chang |first2=Wayne |date=30 June 2023 |title=Crocodile ramen is Taiwan's latest food fad |url=https://www.cnn.com/travel/crocodile-ramen-taiwan-intl-hnk/index.html |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[CNN]]}}</ref> and whole [[frog]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Thomson |first1=Jono |date=13 June 2023 |title=Whole, 'uncut, unpeeled' frog ramen on the menu in central Taiwan |url=https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4917855 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Taiwan News]]}}</ref>

===Burmese===
Burmese and Chinese Burmese restaurants are primarily located in the Little Burma section of Taipei. Chinese Burmese immigration to Taiwan began in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite web |last1=BARON |first1=JAMES |date=18 January 2023 |title=Little Burma: Where Great Food Meets Fascinating History |url=https://topics.amcham.com.tw/2023/01/little-burma-where-great-food-meets-fascinating-history/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Taiwan Business Topics}}</ref>

===Chinese===
In the decades since the KMT's retreat, these regional dishes have evolved and become part of Taiwanese cuisine.<ref name="Japan Times 2022">{{cite web |last1=Rao |first1=Tejal |date=21 August 2022 |title=In a tense political moment, Taiwanese cuisine tells its own story |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/life/2022/08/21/food/taiwanese-cuisine-politics/ |access-date=21 August 2022 |website=[[Japan Times]]}}</ref>

According to Taiwanese chef [[Fu Pei-mei]], authentic Chinese culinary traditions were properly preserved in Taiwan. This claim to authenticity, common among Fu's generation, was in part due to the Kuomintang's Chinese nationalist political messaging which extended well beyond cuisine.<ref name=":6"/> The authenticity of regional Chinese cuisine in Taiwan has been challenged.<ref name="NYT August 2023"/>

===Singaporean===
Taiwan has a significant Singaporean community. In 2020, the Taichung-based [[JL Studio]] from Singaporean chef [[Jimmy Lim Tyan Yaw]] was awarded a second Michelin star, becoming the highest rated Singaporean restaurant in the world.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tee |first1=Karen |date=7 August 2023 |title=Restaurant with most Michelin stars for Singaporean food... is in Taiwan. Welcome to JL Studio |url=https://www.scmp.com/magazines/post-magazine/food-drink/article/3230194/worlds-only-2-michelin-star-restaurant-serving-singaporean-cuisine-taiwan |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=[[South China Morning Post]]}}</ref>

==Taiwanese cuisine abroad==
[[File:Chinese-style geng with meat, fish cakes, and squid.jpg|thumb|right|A pork [[geng (dish)|keⁿ]], a thick soup with [[tofu]] and [[surimi]]-coated pork]]
Taiwanese cuisine has a global presence.<ref name="Taiwan Today 2011">{{cite web |date=4 March 2011 |title=Taiwanese cuisine reflects nation's historical odyssey |url=https://taiwantoday.tw/news.php?unit=18%2C23%2C45%2C18&post=24443 |access-date=27 April 2020 |website=[[Taiwan Today]]}}</ref> Taiwanese chefs have been extremely successful abroad cooking both Taiwanese and international cuisine. Well known chefs include [[André Chiang]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Koutsakis |first1=George |title=What Makes A Great Chef? Andre Chiang on Cuisine, Growth, And Taiwan's Culinary Beauty |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/georgekoutsakis/2019/03/21/what-makes-a-great-chef-andre-chiang-on-cuisine-growth-and-taiwans-culinary-beauty/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322141528/https://www.forbes.com/sites/georgekoutsakis/2019/03/21/what-makes-a-great-chef-andre-chiang-on-cuisine-growth-and-taiwans-culinary-beauty/ |archive-date=22 March 2019 |access-date=27 April 2020 |work=[[Forbes (magazine)|Forbes]]}}</ref>

===Culinary diplomacy===
Along with its semiconductor industry, Taiwan's cuisine is one of its most prominent aspects internationally.<ref name="NYT August 2023" /> Taiwan has used [[culinary diplomacy]] to bolster its tourism sector and to conduct diplomacy in countries with which it has [[Foreign relations of Taiwan|limited official ties]].<ref name="Chapple-Sokol">{{Cite journal |last1=Chapple-Sokol |first1=Sam |year=2013 |title=Culinary Diplomacy: Breaking Bread to Win Hearts and Minds |url=http://booksandjournals.brillonline.com/content/10.1163/1871191x-12341244 |journal=[[The Hague Journal of Diplomacy]] |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=161–183 |doi=10.1163/1871191x-12341244|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2010, [[Ministry of Economic Affairs (Taiwan)|Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs]] launched a £20-million culinary diplomacy campaign called "All in Good Taste: Savor the Flavors of Taiwan".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-07-02 |title=Eight Great Gastrodiplomacy Nations |url=https://uscpublicdiplomacy.org/story/eight-great-gastrodiplomacy-nations |website=[[USC Center on Public Diplomacy]]}}</ref> It promoted Taiwanese venues internationally, sponsored chefs, hosted food festivals and competitions, and emphasized elements such as [[bubble tea]], [[oyster omelette]], and Taiwan's [[Night markets in Taiwan|night markets]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Booth |first1=Robert |title=Taiwan launches 'gastro-diplomacy' drive |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2010/aug/08/taiwan-launches-gasto-diplomacy-drive |website=[[The Guardian]] |date=8 August 2010 |access-date=1 April 2020}}</ref> Since 2010, the ministry has sent chefs abroad to promote Taiwanese cuisine.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tzu-hsuan |first1=Liu |date=21 April 2023 |title=Chefs selected for global six-month cultural tour |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2023/04/21/2003798354 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Taipei Times]]}}</ref>

==== Banquets ====
[[State banquet]]s have formed an important part of Taiwanese diplomacy since the era of one-party rule by the KMT. [[General Tso's chicken]] was invented by the KMT's head chef [[Peng Chang-kuei]] in the 1950s to feed visiting American military dignitaries.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Tsoi |first1=Grace |last2=Chang |first2=Joy |title=General Tso's chicken to bento bowls: A food guide to Taiwan politics |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-67874131 |access-date=9 February 2024 |website=[[BBC News]]|date=6 January 2024 }}</ref>

The banquets are meant to present a message to guests and as such dishes and styles have varied over the years under different administrations. There has been an increasing emphasis on serving Taiwanese ingredients cooked in a distinctly Taiwanese style.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tzu-hsuan |first1=Liu |title=Taiwanese cuisine wows at state banquets |url=https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2024/02/09/2003813313 |access-date=9 February 2024 |website=[[Taipei Times]]|date=9 February 2024 }}</ref>

===United States===
Taiwanese immigrant restaurateurs were largely responsible for the shift of [[American Chinese food]] from Cantonese-focused cuisine to diverse cuisine featuring dishes from many regions in China. The immigration of Taiwanese chefs to the United States began in the 1950s. At the time, cooks in Taiwan were trained in traditional Chinese regional cooking as this fit the chosen identity of the KMT. Taiwanese restaurateurs changed the food landscape of many American cities, including [[New York City]], and pioneered innovations such as picture menus and food delivery. Many of the immigrants to the United States during this period had been born in China and fled to Taiwan with the retreating KMT, particularly former residents of the Dachen Islands who had been evacuated in 1955.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Pio Kuo |first1=Chunghao |title=Taiwaneze immigrand spark a golden age fore Chinese food |url=https://www.nyfoodstory.com/articles/taiwanese-immigrants-spark-a-golden-age-for-chinese-food/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921005953/https://www.nyfoodstory.com/articles/taiwanese-immigrants-spark-a-golden-age-for-chinese-food/ |archive-date=21 September 2020 |access-date=29 April 2020 |website=NY Food Story}}</ref>

Traditionally, Taiwanese food has been hard to differentiate from Chinese and Japanese food abroad, since many Taiwanese chefs cooked simplified or westernized versions of traditional Taiwanese, Japanese, or Chinese dishes. In 2018, there was a rapid growth in the number of authentic Taiwanese restaurants in New York City<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wu |first1=Stephenie |date=5 November 2018 |title=Taiwanese food is finally having a moment in New York City's crowded restaurant scene |url=https://www.mic.com/articles/192243/taiwanese-food-is-finally-having-a-moment-in-new-york-citys-crowded-restaurant-scene |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200926031951/https://www.mic.com/articles/192243/taiwanese-food-is-finally-having-a-moment-in-new-york-citys-crowded-restaurant-scene |archive-date=26 September 2020 |access-date=27 April 2020 |website=Mic}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Gross |first1=Matt |date=25 July 2018 |title=New York City's Taiwanese-Food Boom (It's About Time) |url=https://www.tastecooking.com/new-york-citys-taiwanese-food-boom-its-about-damn-time/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603052430/https://www.tastecooking.com/new-york-citys-taiwanese-food-boom-its-about-damn-time/ |archive-date=3 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |website=Taste Cooking}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Sietsema |first1=Robert |date=22 June 2017 |title=14 Exceptional Taiwanese Restaurants in NYC |url=https://ny.eater.com/maps/best-taiwanese-food-nyc-brooklyn-queens-manhattan |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=Eater New York}}</ref> and across the country, which coincided with an increased interest in regional Chinese food and in Taiwan itself.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Moskin |first1=Julia |date=11 June 2019 |title=A New Generation of Chefs Reframes Taiwanese Cuisine in America |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/11/dining/taiwanese-food.html |url-access=limited |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200601134923/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/11/dining/taiwanese-food.html |archive-date=1 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> Some object to the [[Political status of Taiwan|politically fraught]] inclusion of Taiwanese cuisine under the banner of regional Chinese food and point out that it is inaccurate.<ref name="KQED 2021">{{cite web |last1=Tsai |first1=Luke |date=19 May 2021 |title=The Bay Area's Taiwanese Food Scene Comes Into Its Own |url=https://www.kqed.org/arts/13897272/bay-area-taiwanese-food-scene-nostalgia |access-date=22 May 2021 |website=KQED}}</ref>

Taiwanese American cuisine is emerging as a full cuisine in its own right. Myers + Chang in Boston was one of the first restaurants to explicitly describe their food as such. In 2018, James Beard Award-winning chef [[Stephanie Izard]] opened a Taiwanese snack/dessert shop in [[Chicago]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Erway |first1=Cathy |title=How Today's Taiwanese-American Chefs Rewrote the Rules and Made a New Cuisine |url=https://www.foodandwine.com/lifestyle/taiwanese-american-chefs-food |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200603053328/https://www.foodandwine.com/lifestyle/taiwanese-american-chefs-food |archive-date=3 June 2020 |access-date=3 June 2020 |website=Food and Wine}}</ref> Taiwanese cuisine has a significant presence in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]].<ref name= "KQED 2021" /> Most Taiwanese restaurants in the Bay Area are located in the suburbs.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tsai |first1=Luke |date=11 May 2023 |title=Taiwanese Food Is Taking Over Union Square — For One Day, Anyway |url=https://www.kqed.org/arts/13929007/taiwanese-american-culture-festival-union-square-sf |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=KQED}}</ref> Increasing interest in authentic Taiwanese food is coming from ex-pats and second generation Taiwanese Americans.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Addison |first1=Bill |date=3 March 2016 |title=Tradition and Innovation in America's Taiwanese Cooking |url=https://www.eater.com/2016/3/3/11156510/tradition-and-innovation-americas-taiwanese-cooking |access-date=24 August 2023 |website=Eater}}</ref>

A Taiwanese American cookbook, ''First Generation'', was published by Frankie Gaw in 2022.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Choe |first1=Caroline |date=6 December 2022 |title=Frankie Gaw explores Taiwanese American identity through recipes like Cinnamon Toast Crunch mochi |url=https://www.today.com/food/first-generation-frankie-gaw-explores-taiwanese-american-identity-through-food-t274187 |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Today}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Varriano |first1=Jackie |date=26 October 2022 |title=This Seattleite's debut cookbook explores what Taiwanese American food looks like |url=https://www.seattletimes.com/life/food-drink/what-does-taiwanese-american-food-look-like-this-seattle-cook-explores-with-his-debut-cookbook/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=[[Seattle Times]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Ngo |first1=Hope |date=16 October 2022 |title=New Cookbook First Generation Is A Love Story To Taiwanese-American Cuisine |url=https://www.tastingtable.com/1056004/new-cookbook-first-generation-is-a-love-story-to-taiwanese-american-cuisine/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Tasting Table}}</ref> In 2023, [[Cathy Erway]] published ''Win Son Presents: A Taiwanese American Cookbook''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Rega |first1=Konstantin |date=29 July 2023 |title=Embracing Taiwanese Cuisine |url=https://virginialiving.com/food/trigg-brown-cookbook/ |access-date=13 August 2023 |website=Virginia Living}}</ref>

[[Kato (restaurant)|Kato]] by Chef Jon Yao is a Michelin-starred restaurant serving Taiwanese food in Los Angeles.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chaplin |first1=Cathy |date=2023-07-06 |others=Photography by Wonho Frank Lee |title=Kato Already Has One Michelin Star. Chef Jon Yao Wants More — But Only on His Terms. |url=https://la.eater.com/2023/7/6/23784764/kato-restaurant-los-angeles-jon-yao-fine-dining-taiwanese-chinese-interview-michelin-ambition |access-date=9 February 2024 |website=Eater Los Angeles}}</ref>

==Culinary education==
Historically, culinary education was informal with apprentices learning from a master for many years before they practice the craft on their own. The first college level course in cooking was implemented in 1986 at Danshui Technical College.<ref name="Taiwan Today 2011" />

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Wine and food pairing
======================================================================

{{Short description|Process of pairing food dishes with wine to enhance the dining experience}}
[[Image:Vin Jaune.jpg|right|thumb|A pairing of ''[[vin jaune]]'' with [[walnut]]s and [[Comté cheese]]]]
'''Wine and food pairing''' is the process of pairing [[Human food|food]] dishes with [[wine]] to enhance the dining experience. In many cultures, wine has had a long history of being a [[Staple food|staple]] at the dinner table and in some ways both the [[winemaking]] and [[culinary]] traditions of a region have evolved together over the years. Rather than following a set of rules, local cuisines were paired simply with local wines. The modern "[[art]]" of food pairings is a relatively recent phenomenon, fostering an industry of books and media with guidelines for pairings of particular foods and wine. In the [[restaurant]] industry, [[sommelier]]s are often present to make food pairing recommendations for the guest. The main concept behind pairings is that certain elements (such as texture and flavor) in both food and wine interact with each other, and thus finding the right combination of these elements can make the entire dining experience more enjoyable. However, [[Taste (sociology)|taste]] and enjoyment are [[subjectivity|subjective]] and what may be a "textbook perfect" pairing for one taster could be less enjoyable to another.<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88">K. MacNeil ''The Wine Bible'' pg 83–88 Workman Publishing 2001 {{ISBN|1-56305-434-5}}</ref>

While there are many books, magazines and websites with detailed guidelines on how to pair food and wine, most food and wine experts believe that the most basic element of food and wine pairing is understanding the balance between the "weight" of the food and the weight (or [[body (wine)|body]]) of the wine. Heavy, robust wines like [[Cabernet Sauvignon]] can overwhelm a light, delicate dish like a [[quiche]], while light-bodied wines like [[Pinot Grigio]] would be similarly overwhelmed by a hearty [[stew]]. Beyond weight, flavors and textures can either be contrasted or complemented. From there a food and wine pairing can also take into consideration the [[sugar (wine)|sugar]], [[acid (wine)|acid]], [[alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] and [[tannin (wine)|tannin]]s of the wine and how they can be accentuated or minimized when paired with certain types of food.<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235">M. Oldman ''"Oldman's Guide to Outsmarting Wine"'' pg 219–235 Penguin Books 2004 {{ISBN|0-14-200492-8}}</ref>

==History==
[[Image:Carracci - Der Bohnenesser.jpeg|left|thumb|For most of history, wine has been a regular accompaniment to meals. Often the culinary and winemaking traditions of a region would evolve together, creating a natural pairing between the local wine and the local cuisine.]]
Wine has had a long history of being served as an accompaniment to food. The early [[history of wine]] has its origins as another dietary staple and a beverage that was often more sanitary than the local [[drinking water]] supply. There is little evidence that much serious thought was given to pairing particular dishes to particular wines with most likely whatever wine was available being used. However, as culinary traditions in a region developed, so too did local winemaking tradition.<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88"/>

Many pairings that are considered "classics" today emerged from the centuries-old relationship between a region's cuisine and their wines. In Europe, [[lamb and mutton|lamb]] was a staple meat of the diet for many areas that today are leading [[wine region]]s. The red wines of regions such as [[Bordeaux (wine)|Bordeaux]], [[Greece (wine)|Greece]], [[Rioja (wine)|Rioja]], [[Ribera del Duero]], [[Rhone (wine)|Rhone]] and [[Provence (wine)|Provence]] are considered classic pairings with the lamb dishes found in the local cuisines of those regions. In [[Italy (wine)|Italy]], the intimate connection between food and wine is deeply embedded in the culture and is exemplified by the country's wine. Historically, Italians rarely dined without wine and a region's wine was crafted to be "food friendly", often with bright acidity. While some Italian wines may seem [[Tannin|tannic]], lean or tart by themselves they often exhibit a different profile when paired with boldly flavored Italian foods.<ref name="MacNeil pg 255 & 318">K. MacNeil ''The Wine Bible'' pg 255 & 318 Workman Publishing 2001 {{ISBN|1-56305-434-5}}</ref>

There have been some historical [[anecdote]]s that have related to food and wine pairing before modern times. One anecdote often attributed to British wine merchants is ''"Buy on an [[apple]] and sell on [[cheese]]"'' meaning that if a wine tastes good when paired with a raw, uncooked apple it must be truly good and pairing any wine with cheese would make it more palatable to the average consumer and easier to sell. The principles behind this anecdote lies in the food pairing properties of both fruit and cheeses. Fruits that are high in sugar and acidity (such as the [[malic acid]] in green apples) can make wines taste metallic and thin bodied. In contrast, hard cheeses such as [[Cheddar cheese|cheddar]] can soften the tannins in wines and make them taste fuller and fruitier.<ref name="Oxford pg 277-278">J. Robinson (ed) ''"The Oxford Companion to Wine"'' Third Edition pg 277–278 Oxford University Press 2006 {{ISBN|0-19-860990-6}}</ref>

Another historical anecdote, still repeated today, is ''"White wine with fish; Red wine with meat"''. The root of this [[adage]] rests on the principle of matching the body (weight) of the wine with the weight of the food. Meat was generally heavier and "red" in color so it was assumed that a red wine (which was usually heavier than white wine) paired better. Similarly fish was generally light and "white" in color so it was often paired with white wine. This adage has become outdated somewhat due to the variety of wine styles prevalent in modern winemaking where there are now many "heavy" white wines such as "[[New World (wine)|New World]]" [[oak (wine)|oaky]] [[Chardonnay]] that can have more body than lighter reds such as [[Pinot noir]] or Italian [[Merlot]]s.<ref name="MacNeil pg 107">K. MacNeil ''The Wine Bible'' pg 107 Workman Publishing 2001 {{ISBN|1-56305-434-5}}</ref>

Another older idea was "to pair strong cheeses with strong wines," for example, [[Asiago cheese|asiago]], a sharply flavored cheese, with [[Zinfandel]], a dark red wine with fruit tones.<ref name="Say Cheese">Engleman, Peter, "Say Cheese!", ''New York Lawyer'', January 2001, p. 14.</ref>

===Modern history===
In recent years, the popularity and interest in food and wine pairings have increased and taken on new connotations. Industries have sprung up with print publications and media dedicated to expounding on the principles and ideals of pairing the perfect wine with the perfect dish. In the restaurant industry, there is often a dedicated individual or staff of sommeliers who are trained to recommend wine pairings with the restaurant's fare. The origins of this recent phenomenon can be traced to the [[United States]] in the 1980s when the wine industry began to advertise wine-drinking as a component of dining rather than as just an alcoholic beverage meant for consumption and intoxication. Winemakers started to emphasize the kind of food dishes that their wines would go well with, some even printing pairing suggestions on back [[wine label]]s. Food magazines began to suggest particular wines with recipes and restaurants would offer multi-course dinners matched with a specific wine for each course.<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88"/>

Today there are multiple sources for detailed guidelines and tips on food and wine pairing. But many wine drinkers select wine pairings based on instinct, the mood of the meal or simply a desire to drink a particular wine at the moment they desire to eat a particular meal.<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88"/> The subjective nature of taste makes it possible to drink any kind of wine with any kind of food and have an enjoyable experience. Wine expert [[Mark Oldman]] has noted "Food and wine pairing can be like sex and pizza: even when it's bad, it can still be pretty good" and gives the example of [[wedding cake]] with a [[dry (wine)|dry]] [[sparkling wine]]. A dry wine with a sweet food is, according to Oldman, "the equivalent of [[Chalkboard scraping|nails on a chalkboard]]" and is not a "good pairing" according to most guidelines but the atmosphere of the occasion and the subjective nature of taste can trump any rule or guideline.<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/> Today, many wine experts and advocates in the realm of food and wine pairing try to focus on the more objective physical aspects of food that have an effect on the palate, altering (or enhancing) the perception of various aspects of the wine.<ref name="Oxford pg 277-278"/>

==Matching weight==
In food and wine pairings, the most basic element considered is "weight"-the balance between the weight of the food (a heavy, red sauce pasta versus a more delicate salad) and the weight or "body" of the wine (a heavy Cabernet Sauvignon versus a more delicate Pinot grigio). In [[wine tasting]], body is determined primarily by the [[alcohol level]] of the wine and can be influenced by the perceptions of tannins (from the grape skins or [[oak (wine)|oak]]) and extract (the dissolved solids in the wine derived from winemaking processes like extended [[maceration (wine)|maceration]] and [[sur lie]] aging). An oaked Chardonnay from a warm wine region, such as [[Australia (wine)|Australia]] is typically "heavier" in body than a stainless steel fermented Chardonnay from a cooler wine region such as [[Chablis (wine)|Chablis]]. Pairing heavy wines with light dishes or vice versa, can result in one partner overwhelming the other.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27">E. Goldstein ''"Perfect Pairings"'' pg 14–27 University of California Press 2006 {{ISBN|978-0-520-24377-4}}</ref> The "weight" of a food can also be described in terms of the intensity of its flavors – such as delicate and more subtle flavors versus dishes that have more robust and hearty flavors.<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88"/> A key to pairing upon this principle is to identify the dominant flavor of the dish. Sauces can be the dominant flavor instead of the meat or main component. While poached fish is usually light bodied and better served with a light white, if the fish is served with a heavy cream sauce it could be better balanced with a fuller bodied white wine or light red.<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/>

Weight is also especially important when considering the wine style to pair with one of the most classic wine pairing dishes: cheese. Cheeses come in a wide range of flavors and textures, and it is important to consider the qualities of each in order to choose the right wine to pair. Soft, rindless cheeses that have not been aged usually sport a delicate texture and mild, tangy flavor, which go best with dry or even off-dry white wines, along with light-bodied red wines and rosés. For example, fresh [[mozzarella]] or [[burrata]] can pair well with Italian Pinot Grigio, while a fresh goat cheese pair nicely with Riesling from the Finger Lakes or Germany. Creamy cheeses with a bloomy rind, like Camembert or Brie, are compatible with a traditional method sparkling wine, like Champagne or Cava. The acidity of these wines cuts the richness of the cheese, while the yeasty autolytic aromas and medium body complement the creaminess of the latter. Semi-soft cheeses like Gruyere are best with full-bodied white wines with some oak age, like a Meursault or Viognier. And finally, hard cheeses with some age on them, like a nutty Parmesan or Cheddar tend to go with equally nuanced and nutty Sherry or a full-bodied and complex red wine, like a Bordeaux or Barolo.<ref name="Cheese and Wine Pairing Guide">{{cite web |last1=Millesima USA |first1=Millesima USA |title=Cheese and Wine Pairing Guide |url=https://www.millesima-usa.com/wine-and-cheese-pairing.html |website=Millesima USA |access-date=26 April 2022}}</ref>

===Weights of wine===
[[Image:GruenerVeltlinerWeissenkirchen.jpg|right|thumb|[[Gruner Veltliner]] is often made as a light-bodied wine.]]
Below is a rough guideline of the various weights of wines. Winemaker and regional style as well as [[oak (wine)|oak treatment]] can cause a wine to be lighter or heavier in body. For example, Pinot noir can vary from being light to more medium bodied. Another example is the influence of regional climates. Warmer climate wine regions tend to produce wines with higher alcohol levels and thus more fuller bodied wines so that a [[Sauvignon blanc]] from [[California (wine)|California]] may have a heavier weight than a Sauvignon blanc from the [[Loire (wine)|Loire]].<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/>

;Lighter whites: Pinot gris, [[Pinot blanc]], [[Riesling]], Sauvignon blanc, Chablis, [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]] and sparkling wines, [[Gruner Veltliner]], [[Vinho Verde]], [[Muscadet]]
;Medium to heavy whites: Oaked Sauvignon blanc, [[Alsatian wine]]s, [[Albarino]], White Bordeaux ([[Semillon]]), White Burgundy, Rhone whites ([[Viognier]], [[Roussanne]], [[Marsanne]]), [[Tămâioasă Românească]] and New World Chardonnay
;Lighter reds: [[Beaujolais]], [[Dolcetto]], some Pinot noir
;Medium reds: [[Chianti]], [[Barbera]], [[Burgundy wine|Burgundy]], [[Chinon (wine)|Chinon]], Rioja, [[Cabernet franc]], [[Merlot]], [[Malbec]], [[Zinfandel]], some Pinot noir
;Heavier reds: [[Syrah]], [[Brunello di Montalcino]], [[Cabernet Sauvignon]], [[Port (wine)|Port]], [[Barbaresco]] and [[Barolo]]

===Focus of the pairing===
While a perfect balance where both food and wine are equally enhanced is theoretically possible, typically a pairing has a more enhancing influence on one or the other. [[Master Sommelier]] Evan Goldstein notes that food and wine pairing is like two people having a conversation: ''"One must listen while the other speaks or the result is a muddle".'' This means either the food or the wine is the dominant focus of the pairing, with the other serving as a complement to enhance the enjoyment of the first. Regarding weight and intensity, if the focus of the pairing is the wine then a more ideal balance would be a food that is slightly lighter in weight to where it does not compete for attention with the wine but not too light to where it is completely overwhelmed. If the focus of the pairing is to highlight a dish then the same thought would apply in pairing a wine.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/>

==Complement and contrast==
[[Image:Champagne.jpg|right|thumb|The racy acidity of [[sparkling wine]] and the rich texture of [[foie gras]] is an example of a ''contrasting'' pairing.]]
After considering weight, pairing the flavors and texture can be dealt with using one of two main strategies — complement or contrast.

The first strategy tries to bring wine together with dishes that complement each other such as an earthy, Burgundian Pinot noir with an earthy, mushroom dish.

The second strategy operates under the truism that "opposites attract" and brings together food and wine that have contrasting traits such as a crisp, acidic Sauvignon blanc and a fish with a creamy lemon sauce. The crisp acidity of the wine serves as a contrast that can cut through the creaminess of the sauce and give a different, refreshing sensation for the palate as opposed to what a complementary pairing, such as a creamy, buttery Chardonnay, would bring. For most of history, the "complementary strategy" was the prevailing thought on food and wine pairing. In the 1980s, as more people started to discover and experiment with pairings, the idea of using contrast started to gain more favor. It follows the same idea that the "salty/sweet" pairing does in cooking (such as salty peanut butter with sweet jelly).<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/>

The same food may be complemented {{em|or}} contrasted: a hard, nutty cheese such as [[Hirtenkase]] should have "a nutty, slightly sweet wine with it,"<ref name="SF Gate">A reviewer at the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' wrote, "I want a nutty, slightly sweet wine with [[Hirtenkase|it]], such as an oloroso [[sherry]] or a [[Madeira wine|Madeira]]." Janet Fletcher, "Cheese Course: Hirtenkäse fans party when the cows come home," ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'', February [https://web.archive.org/web/20080220081236/http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2008/02/15/WIMQUSGJ7.DTL SF Gate website]. Accessed March 17, 2009.</ref> {{em|or}} a full bodied red wine.{{Unreliable source?|date=December 2010}}<ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=December 2010}}[http://www.igourmet.com/St/recipe_view.asp?ID=15694 iGourmet website]. Accessed March 17, 2009.</ref>

==Physical properties of wine==
While it is often said that "taste is subjective", there are quantifiable taste characteristics (like [[Bitter (taste)|bitter]], [[sweet]], [[Saltiness|salty]] or [[sour]]) that can be perceived and measured as low, moderate or high — such as measuring the sweetness of honey or the saltiness of oysters. Flavors, such as butterscotch, char and strawberry, are more personal and can not be quantifiable. Flavors are either perceived to be present or not. The perception of flavors is linked to our sense of smell, while tastes come from the sensory glands of the [[taste bud]]s. Though individual sensitivity to the different taste "senses" can vary, wine experts often recommend pairings based on these more objective measurements rather than the more subjective concept of "flavors". In wine there are three basic tastes-bitter, sweet and sour. These three tastes can each be identified with a primary component of the wine-tannins (bitter), [[residual sugar]] (sweet) and acidity (sour). A fourth component, alcohol, is identified in wine tasting with a perception of "heat" or hotness in the back of the mouth and is the primary factor influencing the body of the wine. The residual heat of the alcohol can be considered in food pairing with some ingredients minimizing the heat of the wine while some accentuating it.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/>

===Acidity===
[[Image:Beaujolais salad.jpg|left|thumb|The acidity of salad dressing and tomatoes can cancel some of the tartness in a Beaujolais wine, allowing the fruit to be more noticeable.]]
Acidity is a dominant player in any food and wine pairing due to the pronounced and complex ways that it can heighten the perception of flavors. In wine tasting, acidity is perceived by a mouth watering response by the [[salivary gland]]s. This mouth watering can also serve to stimulate the appetite. In wine there are three main acids that have their own associated flavors – malic (green apples), [[lactic acid|lactic]] (milky) and [[tartaric acid|tartaric]] (bitter). In dishes that are fatty, oily, rich or salty, acidity in wine can "cut" (or standout and contrast) through the heaviness and be a refreshing change of pace on the palate. In cooking, acidity is often used in similar fashions such as a lemon wedges with a briny seafood dish such as oysters. The acidity of the lemon juices can make the oysters seem less briny. A wine that is less tart than the dish it is served with may taste thin and weak. A wine that comes across as "too tart" on its own may seem softer when paired with an acidic and tart dish. The complementing "tartness" of the food and wine cancels each other out and allows the other components (fruit of the wine, other flavors of the food) to be more noticeable.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/>

===Sweetness===
The sweetness of wines is determined by the amount of [[residual sugar]] left in the wine after the [[fermentation (wine)|fermentation]] process. Wines can be bone dry (with the sugars fully fermented into alcohol), off-dry (with a hint of sweetness), semi-dry (medium-sweet) and dessert level sweetness (such as the high sugar content in [[Sauternes (wine)|Sauternes]] and [[Tokaji|Tokay]]s). Sweet wines often need to be sweeter than the dish they are served with. Vintage brut [[champagne]] paired with sweet, [[wedding cake]] can make the wine taste tart and weak while the cake may have off flavors. In food pairings, sweetness balances spice and heat. It can serve as a contrast to the heat and alleviate some of the burning sensation caused by [[Jalapeño|peppers]] and [[spices]], e.g. in [[Thai cuisine|Thai]] or [[Sichuan cuisine]].<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/> It can accentuate the mild sweetness in some foods and can also contrast with salt such as the European custom of pairing salty [[Stilton cheese]] with a sweet [[Port wine|Port]].<ref name="MacNeil pg 83-88"/> Sweetness in a wine can balance tartness in food, especially if the food has some sweetness (such as dishes with [[sweet and sour sauce]]s).<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/>

===Bitterness===
[[Image:Wine & cheese reception 0120 - MicroTAS 2007.jpg|right|thumb|The [[protein]]s and [[fat]]s in [[cheese]] can soften the perception of [[tannin (wine)|tannin]]s in wine, making a wine seem less bitter and more fruity.]]
The astringency<ref>{{cite journal| doi=10.1016/j.aca.2003.10.017 | volume=513 | title=Taste and mouth-feel properties of different types of tannin-like polyphenolic compounds and anthocyanins in wine | year=2004 | journal=Analytica Chimica Acta | pages=57–65 | last1 = Vidal | first1 = Stéphane | last2 = Francis | first2 = Leigh | last3 = Noble | first3 = Ann | last4 = Kwiatkowski | first4 = Mariola | last5 = Cheynier | first5 = Véronique | last6 = Waters | first6 = Elizabeth| issue=1 | bibcode=2004AcAC..513...57V }}</ref> associated with wine is usually derived from a wine's tannins. Tannins add a gritty texture and chalky, astringent taste. It can enhance the perception of "body" or weight in the wine. Tannins are normally derived from the skins, seeds, and stems of the grapes themselves (leached out during the maceration process) or from contact with oak during barrel aging. Tannins react with [[proteins]]. When paired with dishes that are high in proteins and fats (such as red meat and hard cheeses), the tannins bind to the proteins and come across as softer. In the absence of protein from the food, such as some [[vegetarian]] dishes, the tannins react with the proteins on the tongue and sides of the mouth – accentuating the astringency and having a drying effect on the palate. Various cooking methods, such as [[grilling]] and [[blackening (cooking)|blackening]] can add a bitter "char" component to the dish that allows it to play well with a tannic wine, while [[fish oils]] can make tannic wines taste metallic or off.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/> Astringent tannic wines like Barolo and Cabernet Sauvignon can overwhelm a lot of foods but can be softened by fatty foods with a lot of proteins such as hard cheeses or meats. The dry tannins also serve as a cleansing agent on the palate by binding to the grease and oils left over in the mouth. Spicy and sweet foods can accentuate the dry, bitterness of tannins and make the wine seem to have off flavors.<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/>

===Alcohol===
Alcohol is the primary factor in dictating a wine's weight and body. Typically the higher the alcohol level, the more weight the wine has. An increase in alcohol content increases the perception of density and texture. In food and wine pairing, salt and spicy heat accentuates the alcohol and the perception of "heat" or hotness in the mouth.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/> Conversely, the alcohol can also magnify the heat of spicy food, making a highly alcoholic wine paired with a spicy dish generate significant heat for the taster.<ref name="Oldman pg 219-235"/>

==Other pairing principles==
Beyond the basic guidelines listed above, food pairings can dive even further into matching several layers of texture and flavors. The term "bridge ingredients" refers to ingredients and flavors that have certain affinities in wine pairing (such as slow-cooked onions with creamy wines, etc.). It can also refer to using particular herbs and spices perceived in the wine (such as [[rosemary]] in some Cabernet Sauvignon) and adding them to the dish as an ingredient. Their presence in a dish may increase the likelihood that the certain wines would pair well.<ref name="Goldstein pg 14-27"/>

The above principles can be used for pairing wines with Asian cuisine. Pair for the flavor of the dish – whatever the 'main ingredient' may be – it is not the meat, seafood, or vegetables that stand out as the predominant flavor. Rather the true flavor of the dish is determined by the cooking method (for example, the toasty flavors of a stir fry), the sauce (from curries to sweet-and-sour), the use of seasonings (such as ginger and coriander leaves to mask fishy tastes), or the blending of ingredients to form new flavors (as in [[sukiyaki]] or satay). Indeed, it may result from a combination of any of these elements. Also, note that in the case of an Asian meal, several dishes are served at the same time and are shared by everyone present. The wine chosen for such a meal has to be versatile.<ref>{{cite book | author=Guy, P |author2=Soon, E |title=Wine With Asian Food |page=1 |publisher=Tide-Mark Press| year=2008 |isbn=978-1-59490-114-0}}</ref>
